title: Do Synthetic Personas Predict Real Audience Response? A Sim-to-Real Study Where a No-Persona Baseline Beats Persona-Based Copy Simulation
summary: Marketers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as "synthetic personas" to predict how an audience will react to a piece of copy before it ships, encouraged by evidence that profile-conditioned LLMs mimic human samples. But is that prediction actually valid against real behaviour - and does the persona machinery help? We present a sim-to-real validity study using the Upworthy Research Archive - thousands of headline A/B tests on shared real traffic, with measured click-through - as held-out ground truth. We compare a ten-persona panel, grounded in the real audience's demographics, against a no-persona zero-shot baseline that simply asks the model how likely a typical reader is to click. Two findings stand out. First, ground-truth reliability is the binding constraint: most A/B tests have no statistically distinguishable winner, so validity can only be measured on the reliable subset (n = 399). Second, and counter to the persona-simulation premise, persona conditioning degrades predictive validity: the no-persona baseline ranks variants markedly better (Kendall τ = 0.361, a medium effect; top-1 accuracy 49.2%) than the persona panel (τ = 0.084; top-1 34.6%), with non-overlapping confidence intervals. Asking the model directly taps an accurate population-level prior; forcing it to role-play specific personas injects bias and noise. The result replicates across three independent Upworthy splits, holds in direction on a different-domain news dataset, and is robust to seed, prompt phrasing, and model choice - across three Gemini tiers and a different model family (OpenAI gpt-4.1, significant paired gap). The takeaway: for predicting aggregate engagement, a plain LLM ranker beats persona simulation - synthetic personas are not merely a weak predictor, they are worse than not using them. All numbers regenerate from a public, artifact-first replication package.

AI.tldr: Using thousands of Upworthy headline A/B tests as real-world ground truth, the authors show that a no-persona zero-shot LLM baseline predicts aggregate click-through far better than a ten-persona panel grounded in audience demographics (τ = 0.361 vs. 0.084; top-1 49.2% vs. 34.6%), indicating that persona conditioning degrades sim-to-real predictive validity.
AI.motivation: Marketers increasingly rely on LLMs as "synthetic personas" to forecast audience reactions to copy, encouraged by evidence that profile-conditioned LLMs mimic human samples. The paper questions whether this prediction is actually valid against real behaviour and whether the persona machinery adds value.
AI.method: A sim-to-real validity study using the Upworthy Research Archive — thousands of headline A/B tests on shared real traffic with measured click-through — as held-out ground truth. The authors compare a ten-persona panel grounded in the real audience's demographics against a no-persona zero-shot baseline that simply asks the model how likely a typical reader is to click. Validity is assessed only on the statistically reliable subset (n = 399), since most A/B tests lack a distinguishable winner. Robustness checks cover three independent Upworthy splits, a different-domain news dataset, seed, prompt phrasing, model choice (three Gemini tiers and OpenAI gpt-4.1), and a public artifact-first replication package.
AI.result: Ground-truth reliability is the binding constraint: most A/B tests have no statistically distinguishable winner, so validity can only be measured on the reliable subset (n = 399). Counter to the persona-simulation premise, persona conditioning degrades predictive validity: the no-persona baseline ranks variants markedly better (Kendall τ = 0.361, a medium effect; top-1 accuracy 49.2%) than the persona panel (τ = 0.084; top-1 34.6%), with non-overlapping confidence intervals. The result replicates across three independent Upworthy splits, holds in direction on a different-domain news dataset, and is robust to seed, prompt phrasing, and model choice, including a significant paired gap for OpenAI gpt-4.1.
AI.conclusion: For predicting aggregate engagement, a plain LLM ranker beats persona simulation: synthetic personas are not merely a weak predictor, they are worse than not using them. Asking the model directly taps an accurate population-level prior, whereas forcing it to role-play specific personas injects bias and noise.

title: Do Existing Preconditioners Improve Biomedical Tabular Foundation Learning? An Empirical Study on TabPFN Optimization
summary: Tabular foundation models have recently shown strong potential for structured biomedical data analysis. Among them, TabPFN has emerged as an effective approach for low-data tabular classification tasks. However, the impact of optimization and preconditioning strategies on biomedical fine-tuning remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present a comprehensive empirical investigation of five AdamW-based preconditioning strategies for fine-tuning TabPFN v2.5 on 59 biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease, breast cancer, schizophrenia, significant memory concern (SMC), KEEL biomedical datasets, and UCI biomedical benchmarks. The evaluation considers predictive performance, computational efficiency, and statistical significance analysis. Experimental results demonstrate that the original AdamW optimizer consistently achieves the best overall performance and statistical ranking, while existing curvature-aware preconditioners fail to provide reliable improvements across diverse biomedical learning scenarios. The findings suggest that generic preconditioning approaches may not adequately capture the optimization characteristics of biomedical tabular learning, motivating the development of biomedical-aware preconditioners specifically tailored for healthcare-oriented tabular foundation models.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically benchmarks five AdamW-based preconditioning strategies for fine-tuning TabPFN v2.5 across 59 biomedical datasets, finding that vanilla AdamW yields the best overall performance and that curvature-aware preconditioners do not reliably improve results.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN are promising for structured biomedical data, yet the influence of optimization and preconditioning strategies on biomedical fine-tuning is largely unexplored, leaving practitioners without clear guidance on optimizer choice.
AI.method: A comprehensive empirical study comparing five AdamW-based preconditioning strategies for fine-tuning TabPFN v2.5 on 59 biomedical datasets covering Alzheimer's disease, breast cancer, schizophrenia, significant memory concern (SMC), KEEL biomedical datasets, and UCI biomedical benchmarks. Evaluation spans predictive performance, computational efficiency, and statistical significance analysis.
AI.result: The original AdamW optimizer consistently achieves the best overall performance and statistical ranking, whereas existing curvature-aware preconditioners fail to deliver reliable improvements across diverse biomedical learning scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Generic preconditioning approaches do not adequately capture the optimization characteristics of biomedical tabular learning, motivating the development of biomedical-aware preconditioners specifically tailored for healthcare-oriented tabular foundation models.

title: 4DGS-JEPA: Temporally Compositional Joint-Embedding Prediction for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting
summary: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting provides an explicit representation of evolving 3D scenes, but existing approaches are primarily optimized for reconstruction, future-state generation, or rendering rather than for learning reusable predictive dynamics. We propose 4DGS-JEPA, a Gaussian-native joint-embedding predictive architecture for causal multi-horizon prediction over dynamic Gaussian scenes. The model uses a hierarchical scene-, motion-group-, and Gaussian-level representation together with a horizon-conditioned transition operator that supports both direct prediction and recursive rollout. Its central principle is temporal composition: different chronological transition paths reaching the same future endpoint should produce compatible predictive states. Endpoint and multi-horizon path supervision anchor these predictions to future target embeddings, while a selective geometry decoder and geometry-level composition ground the learned dynamics in consistent group motion and Gaussian geometry without requiring complete future appearance reconstruction. We further introduce a hybrid correspondence mechanism that combines persistent canonical identity with residual optimal-transport matching under reordering and topology change. We characterize zero-loss path agreement and finite-error rollout accumulation theoretically. Three controlled experiments provide mechanism-level evidence that temporal composition reduces latent path dependence while retaining predictive accuracy, geometry-level composition improves consistency of decoded motion, and hybrid correspondence preserves reliable identity while remaining robust when correspondence becomes ambiguous. Together, 4DGS-JEPA provides a predictive, temporally compositional formulation of dynamic Gaussian worlds.

AI.tldr: 4DGS-JEPA is a Gaussian-native joint-embedding predictive architecture that learns reusable, causally composition-consistent multi-horizon dynamics over dynamic Gaussian scenes, using hierarchical scene/motion-group/Gaussian representation, horizon-conditioned transitions, and hybrid canonical/optimal-transport correspondence.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods are optimized for reconstruction, future-state generation, or rendering, not for learning reusable predictive dynamics. The paper aims to learn a predictive dynamics representation rather than reproduce appearance.
AI.method: The model combines: (1) a hierarchical scene-, motion-group-, and Gaussian-level representation; (2) a horizon-conditioned transition operator supporting direct prediction and recursive rollout; (3) temporal composition, where different chronological transition paths to the same future endpoint yield compatible predictive states; (4) endpoint and multi-horizon path supervision against future target embeddings; (5) a selective geometry decoder plus geometry-level composition for consistent group motion and Gaussian geometry without full future appearance reconstruction; (6) a hybrid correspondence mechanism mixing persistent canonical identity with residual optimal-transport matching under reordering and topology change. Theoretical characterization covers zero-loss path agreement and finite-error rollout accumulation.
AI.result: Theory characterizes zero-loss path agreement and finite-error rollout accumulation. Three controlled experiments provide mechanism-level evidence: temporal composition reduces latent path dependence while retaining predictive accuracy; geometry-level composition improves consistency of decoded motion; and hybrid correspondence preserves reliable identity while staying robust when correspondence becomes ambiguous.
AI.conclusion: 4DGS-JEPA offers a predictive, temporally compositional formulation of dynamic Gaussian worlds, enabling reusable multi-horizon dynamics learning rather than appearance-centric reconstruction.

title: An Accurate and Interpretable Hyper Graph Neural Network for GBM Survival Prediction
summary: Survival prediction for glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) demands models that are both accurate and interpretable, yet existing approaches treat these objectives as com- peting, where performant models sacrifice transparency, while interpretable models accept degraded predictive power. We argue that this trade-off is not inherent. Graph neural net- works offer a structural foundation for extracting interpretable, explainable representations without compromising discriminative ability. Furthermore, current methods typically rely on a single imaging modality, underutilizing the complementary information available across multi-modal MRI and clinical metadata. We propose a multi-modal framework that inte- grates three components to address both objectives simultaneously: (1) a sheaf hypergraph neural network that captures higher-order relationships among tissue patches through direc- tional, asymmetric message passing; (2) a concept bottleneck layer that compresses learned representations into clinically grounded concepts, enforcing ante-hoc interpretability; and (3) an extension sufficiency test (EST) regularizer that penalizes unfaithful explanations during training, ensuring that model explanations genuinely reflect the internal decision process. Clinical and genomic features are incorporated through gated fusion, preserving the dominant prognostic signal of molecular markers while retaining concept-level traceabil- ity. Evaluated on 593 patients from the UPenn-GBM dataset under 5-fold cross-validation, our framework achieves a concordance index of 0.643 with the lowest fold-level variance among all compared models (std = 0.015). To our knowledge, this is the first work to unify sheaf hypergraph convolution, concept bottleneck supervision, and EST regularization for interpretable survival prediction from brain MRI

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-modal, interpretable framework for GBM survival prediction that unifies a sheaf hypergraph neural network, a concept bottleneck layer, and an extension sufficiency test regularizer, achieving a C-index of 0.643 with the lowest fold-level variance.
AI.motivation: Existing survival prediction models for glioblastoma multiforme treat accuracy and interpretability as competing objectives—performant models sacrifice transparency while interpretable models lose predictive power. Additionally, current methods typically rely on a single imaging modality, underutilizing complementary information from multi-modal MRI and clinical metadata.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-modal framework with three components: (1) a sheaf hypergraph neural network capturing higher-order tissue-patch relationships via directional, asymmetric message passing; (2) a concept bottleneck layer compressing learned representations into clinically grounded concepts for ante-hoc interpretability; and (3) an extension sufficiency test (EST) regularizer penalizing unfaithful explanations during training. Clinical and genomic features are incorporated via gated fusion, preserving the dominant prognostic signal of molecular markers while retaining concept-level traceability.
AI.result: Evaluated on 593 patients from the UPenn-GBM dataset under 5-fold cross-validation, the framework achieves a concordance index of 0.643 with the lowest fold-level variance among all compared models (std = 0.015).
AI.conclusion: The work argues that the accuracy-interpretability trade-off is not inherent. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first work to unify sheaf hypergraph convolution, concept bottleneck supervision, and EST regularization for interpretable survival prediction from brain MRI.

title: Towards Adaptive Interaction Strategies for Human Companion Robot via Deep Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted by IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics: Systems
summary: In the field of Human-Robot Interaction (HRI), achieving flexibility in human-accompanying within real-world environments holds great potential for various applications but also poses significant challenges. Traditional methods typically restrict robots to fixed positions relative to humans, such as tracking from behind, in front, or side-by-side, which limits robot adaptability in dynamic workspaces. This study introduces a novel human-companioning strategy that uses Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to enable mobile robots to dynamically adjust their tracking positions according to varying conditions. An interaction space is defined to capture the relationship between the human and the robot while considering the environment, which serves as the basis for state spaces in DRL to assist the robot in adapting to environmental changes. A human-robot companion controller is developed by integrating Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control with Control Barrier Functions (CBF), ensuring that the robot accurately follows the target's movement in both position and orientation while avoiding obstacles and enhancing social acceptance and safety. The proposed approach is evaluated in real-world scenarios, both indoors and outdoors, and compared with other studies. The results show that the proposed method improves the success rate and tracking accuracy by at least 24% and 47%, respectively, while enhancing human comfort. Experiments demonstrate the robot's ability to flexibly accompany a person walking at speeds of up to 1.7 m/s, dynamically adjusting its strategy without being confined to a fixed position. Additionally, the robot respects the human's intimate space to ensure safety, comfort, and effective obstacle avoidance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a DRL-based human-companioning strategy that lets mobile robots dynamically adjust tracking positions, using an interaction space for the state representation and an MPPI+CBF controller, achieving at least 24% higher success rate and 47% better tracking accuracy than prior work.
AI.motivation: Traditional human-accompanying robots are restricted to fixed relative positions (behind, in front, side-by-side), which limits adaptability in dynamic, real-world workspaces. Flexible companionship is highly promising but challenging.
AI.method: A DRL-based companioning strategy that dynamically adjusts tracking position. An interaction space captures the human-robot relationship considering the environment and forms the state space for DRL. A companion controller integrates Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control with Control Barrier Functions (CBF) to follow the target in position and orientation while avoiding obstacles and ensuring social acceptance and safety.
AI.result: Evaluated in real indoor and outdoor scenarios. Success rate and tracking accuracy improved by at least 24% and 47% respectively versus other studies, with enhanced human comfort. The robot flexibly accompanies a person walking at up to 1.7 m/s, dynamically adjusting strategy without fixed positioning, and respects the human's intimate space for safety, comfort, and effective obstacle avoidance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DRL-based interaction-space strategy with MPPI+CBF control enables flexible, socially aware human-companioning in real-world environments, outperforming fixed-position baselines in success rate, tracking accuracy, and comfort.

title: Ovis-Embedding: Pushing the Frontiers of Universal Omni-Modal Embeddings
summary: In this report, we introduce \textbf{Ovis-Embedding}, a state-of-the-art omni-modal embedding family built on native integration of text, image, video, and audio. Instead of assembling separate modality towers, Ovis-Embedding uses a shared multimodal backbone to encode different modalities in a common representation space. Specifically, we make \textbf{three key advances}: (1) \textbf{native omni-modal initialization}: we adopt a pretrained Qwen-omni model as the embedding backbone and adapt it through contrastive training with low-rank initialization; (2) \textbf{data-centric omni-modal training}: we construct a broad, high-quality corpus spanning text, images, video, audio, and interleaved multimodal data. To improve data efficiency, we introduce homogeneous-source sampling to form task-consistent batches with informative in-batch negatives; and (3) \textbf{embedding-specific training and inference optimization}: we use focal loss to emphasize hard examples and similarity-based Embedding Distillation to transfer fine-grained similarity structure from complementary experts. At inference time, low-rank feature decomposition enables compact embeddings with flexible dimensionality and minimal performance loss. Empirical evaluations show that the \textbf{Ovis-Embedding} family achieves state-of-the-art performance on \textbf{MMEB-v3}, \textbf{MMEB-v2}, \textbf{MVEB}, \textbf{MAEB}, and \textbf{RTEB}, demonstrating its effectiveness across text, image, video, and audio modalities. These results highlight the potential of unified omni-modal training to overcome modality fragmentation and advance universal embedding models for any-to-any retrieval.

AI.tldr: Ovis-Embedding is a state-of-the-art omni-modal embedding family that uses a single shared multimodal backbone (initialized from a pretrained Qwen-omni model) to encode text, image, video, and audio into a common representation space, achieving SOTA results on MMEB-v3, MMEB-v2, MVEB, MAEB, and RTEB.
AI.motivation: Conventional embedding systems assemble separate modality towers, which leads to modality fragmentation and prevents unified any-to-any retrieval. The paper aims to overcome this fragmentation by natively integrating all modalities within one shared backbone and a common representation space.
AI.method: The approach rests on three advances: (1) native omni-modal initialization, adopting a pretrained Qwen-omni model as backbone and adapting it via contrastive training with low-rank initialization; (2) data-centric omni-modal training, constructing a broad high-quality corpus over text, images, video, audio, and interleaved data, with homogeneous-source sampling to form task-consistent batches containing informative in-batch negatives; (3) embedding-specific training and inference optimization, using focal loss to emphasize hard examples and similarity-based Embedding Distillation to transfer fine-grained similarity structure from complementary experts, plus low-rank feature decomposition at inference for compact, flexible-dimensionality embeddings with minimal loss.
AI.result: Ovis-Embedding achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v3, MMEB-v2, MVEB, MAEB, and RTEB, demonstrating effectiveness across text, image, video, and audio modalities.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the potential of unified omni-modal training to overcome modality fragmentation and advance universal embedding models for any-to-any retrieval.

title: Cosserat Modeling of Trimmed Helicoid Soft Arms with a Separated-Section Constitutive Law
summary: Cosserat rod models for soft robots usually construct sectional stiffness by summing material properties over a common cross-section. This assumption becomes inaccurate for trimmed helicoid arms, where load-bearing helix domains are separated and connected only through sparse fused crossings. This paper formulates a separated-section constitutive law that evaluates each helix domain in its local frame and pulls its constitutive response back to the backbone, yielding an effective backbone stiffness. Sparse-fusion mechanics captures the additional compliance caused by relative motion between neighboring domains and determines channel-wise reduction profiles $η_c(s/L)$ for bending, torsion, and extension. The resulting effective sectional stiffness is strongly anisotropic: bending and extension are reduced by about one order of magnitude, whereas torsion remains close to the effective backbone stiffness. The resulting sectional law is embedded in a geometrically exact dynamic Cosserat model with GVS discretization and routed-tendon actuation. Across 103 measured configurations, the three datasets give pooled normalized position errors of \SI{7.7}{\percent}, \SI{6.7}{\percent}, and \SI{7.8}{\percent}, while each full-arm solve requires approximately \SI{0.3}{s} on one CPU core (Intel Xeon, Cascade Lake, \SI{2.8}{GHz}), enabling rapid model-based planning, state and load estimation, and morphology--control co-design for architected soft robots.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a separated-section constitutive law for trimmed helicoid soft robot arms, capturing anisotropic compliance from sparse helix fusions, and embeds it in a geometrically exact dynamic Cosserat model reaching ~7% position errors at ~0.3 s per solve.
AI.motivation: Conventional Cosserat rod models build sectional stiffness by summing material properties over a common cross-section. This is inaccurate for trimmed helicoid arms, where load-bearing helix domains are separated and connected only through sparse fused crossings, so the true compliance and anisotropy are misrepresented.
AI.method: A separated-section constitutive law evaluates each helix domain in its local frame and pulls its constitutive response back to the backbone to obtain an effective backbone stiffness. Sparse-fusion mechanics models extra compliance from relative motion between neighboring domains and yields channel-wise reduction profiles η_c(s/L) for bending, torsion, and extension. The resulting sectional law is embedded in a geometrically exact dynamic Cosserat model with GVS discretization and routed-tendon actuation.
AI.result: The effective sectional stiffness is strongly anisotropic: bending and extension are reduced by roughly one order of magnitude, while torsion stays close to the effective backbone stiffness. Across 103 measured configurations, three datasets give pooled normalized position errors of 7.7%, 6.7%, and 7.8%, with each full-arm solve taking about 0.3 s on one CPU core (Intel Xeon, Cascade Lake, 2.8 GHz).
AI.conclusion: The proposed constitutive formulation yields an accurate, strongly anisotropic sectional law for architected soft arms and enables rapid model-based planning, state and load estimation, and morphology–control co-design for trimmed helicoid soft robots.

title: X-Planner: Event-Structured Task Planning for Embodied Intelligence
summary: Task planning bridges high-level instructions and executable behavior in long-horizon manipulation, yet modern Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems often leave this intermediate structure implicit. Existing chain-of-thought (CoT) planners also tend to rely on coarse task-level annotations or serialize long reasoning traces token by token. We present X-Planner, a planning front-end that addresses both the supervision and representation of embodied reasoning. Our planning data combine Ego, UMI, and teleoperation under a hierarchy granularity with source-dependent annotation depth. Takeover-time annotations and human-designed failures supervise ongoing error recognition. On the model side, a shared VLM backbone exposes two event-structured plan forms: a discrete interface that emits interpretable event states and a latent interface that relays continuous CoT states across staggered Transformer depths through Staircase Decoding. A frozen latent-to-text reconstruction objective provides a semantic anchor for the latent representation. Offline two-step planning evaluation places X-Planner second among four evaluated models on both BERTScore-F1 and a judge-based Overall score. In real-robot experiments, respectively, outperforming the evaluated baselines. These results characterize planning-text quality and downstream execution.

AI.tldr: X-Planner is a planning front-end for embodied long-horizon manipulation that unifies supervision (Ego/UMI/teleoperation data with graded annotation depth, takeover-time and failure annotations) and representation (a shared VLM backbone with a discrete event-state interface and a latent, event-structured interface via Staircase Decoding anchored by a frozen latent-to-text reconstruction loss). It ranks second among four models on offline two-step planning (BERTScore-F1 and judge Overall) and outperforms baselines in real-robot experiments.
AI.motivation: Task planning links high-level instructions to executable behavior in long-horizon manipulation, but modern VLA systems leave this intermediate structure implicit. Existing CoT planners rely on coarse task-level annotations and serialize long reasoning traces token by token, limiting both supervision quality and the representation of embodied reasoning.
AI.method: A planning front-end with two components: (1) Planning data combining Ego, UMI, and teleoperation under a hierarchy granularity with source-dependent annotation depth, where takeover-time annotations and human-designed failures supervise ongoing error recognition. (2) A shared VLM backbone exposing two event-structured plan forms: a discrete interface emitting interpretable event states, and a latent interface relaying continuous CoT states across staggered Transformer depths via Staircase Decoding, with a frozen latent-to-text reconstruction objective as a semantic anchor.
AI.result: Offline two-step planning evaluation ranks X-Planner second among four evaluated models on both BERTScore-F1 and a judge-based Overall score. In real-robot experiments it outperforms the evaluated baselines. Results characterize planning-text quality and downstream execution.
AI.conclusion: X-Planner addresses both supervision and representation of embodied reasoning, yielding competitive planning-text quality and improved downstream execution, suggesting event-structured, dual-interface planning is an effective front-end for long-horizon manipulation.

title: Beyond the Flat Seafloor: A Closed-Form Two-View Constraint to Aid Sidescan Sonar Reconstruction
comment: Copyright 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media. This work was accepted for publication in the Proceedings of IEEE OCEANS 2026 Monterey
summary: Sidescan sonar is a common sensor for both manned and autonomous marine exploration and mapping, yet very few methods build upon or exploit the geometric projection model of the sensor. As sidescan sonar is limited to a 1D range measurement, many approximations are frequently used, including the long-standing assumption of a flat seafloor. Rather than make similar approximations, this paper focuses on a multi-view geometry based approach and formalizes a two-view geometric constraint and proves that a shared feature is constrained to a locus within the intersection of a sphere and a plane. In addition, we characterize what governs the size of the ambiguity locus through Monte Carlo simulation that is grounded in real aperture and mounting geometry for both a surface vessel and an underwater vehicle. We translate additional simulations of relative trajectories for both vehicle platforms into concrete survey-planning guidance. Our results show that locus length is strongly governed by elevation misalignment, and peaks at a moderate oblique crossing angle of approximately 20 degrees, with minimal locus lengths obtained at near parallel and anti-parallel passes.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes a two-view geometric constraint for sidescan sonar, proving that shared features lie on a locus at the intersection of a sphere and a plane, and characterizes the ambiguity locus to derive survey-planning guidance.
AI.motivation: Sidescan sonar is widely used in marine exploration and mapping, but few methods exploit its geometric projection model. Because sidescan sonar provides only 1D range measurements, common approximations—such as assuming a flat seafloor—limit accuracy. The authors aim to avoid such approximations by developing a rigorous multi-view geometry framework.
AI.method: The authors adopt a multi-view geometry based approach and formalize a two-view geometric constraint for sidescan sonar. They prove that a shared feature is constrained to a locus within the intersection of a sphere and a plane. Monte Carlo simulation, grounded in real aperture and mounting geometry for both a surface vessel and an underwater vehicle, is used to characterize the size of the ambiguity locus. Additional simulations of relative trajectories for both platforms are translated into concrete survey-planning guidance.
AI.result: The locus length is strongly governed by elevation misalignment. It peaks at a moderate oblique crossing angle of approximately 20 degrees, while minimal locus lengths are obtained at near parallel and anti-parallel passes.
AI.conclusion: The two-view geometric constraint provides a principled foundation for sidescan sonar feature localization without flat-seafloor assumptions. Survey planning should prioritize trajectory geometries that minimize elevation misalignment, favoring near parallel or anti-parallel passes and avoiding moderate oblique crossing angles around 20 degrees.

title: Learning to Plan in Human-Robot Collaboration: Multimodal Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Interaction
summary: Robot assistants for older adults and people with disabilities need to perform collaborative tasks with users effectively. The core component of these systems is an interaction manager whose job is to observe and assess the task and infer the state of the human and their intent for the robot to choose the best course of action. Due to the sparseness of the data in this domain, the policy for such multimodal systems is often crafted by hand; as the complexity of interactions grows, this process is not scalable. This paper proposes a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to automatically generate the multimodal policy of the robot. Our system focuses on a realistic scenario where a robot assists a user in locating objects within a home environment, managing multimodal signals, including language and physical actions, to select the best action. In contrast to traditional dialog systems, our agent is trained with a simulator that uses human data and can deal with multiple modalities. We use a simple high-level reward function that needs no fine-tuning and enforce some preconditions to speed up the training process. A human study evaluating the system in a real-world setting demonstrates promising results, indicating high usability and effective task completion. This RL-based approach offers a scalable and interpretable alternative for designing interaction managers in multimodal human-robot collaborations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reinforcement learning approach to automatically generate a multimodal policy for a robot interaction manager, replacing hand-crafted policies. Tested in a home object-finding task with language and physical actions, the RL-trained system achieved promising usability and task completion in a real-world human study.
AI.motivation: Robot assistants for older adults and people with disabilities need effective collaboration. The interaction manager—observing and assessing the task and inferring the human's state and intent—is central, but sparse data in this domain means its policy is often hand-crafted. As interaction complexity grows, manual design does not scale.
AI.method: An RL approach to automatically generate the robot's multimodal policy. The system targets a realistic scenario where a robot helps a user locate objects at home, managing multimodal signals including language and physical actions. Unlike traditional dialog systems, the agent is trained with a simulator built on human data that handles multiple modalities. A simple high-level reward function requiring no fine-tuning is used, with preconditions enforced to speed up training.
AI.result: A human study evaluating the system in a real-world setting shows promising results, indicating high usability and effective task completion.
AI.conclusion: The RL-based approach offers a scalable and interpretable alternative for designing interaction managers in multimodal human-robot collaboration.

title: The AI Neuroscientist: An Interactive Agentic Interface for Neuroimaging Analysis
summary: Analyzing neuroimaging data requires specialized coding and statistical expertise, which limits accessibility for researchers without computational backgrounds. We present the AI Neuroscientist, a language agent for interactive data exploration. The system integrates a large language model (LLM) with a neuroimaging toolset to perform quality control, modeling, and visualization. This allows researchers to query data quality and specify analysis parameters directly in natural language, providing a transparent and interactive alternative to conventional scripted pipelines for small-scale data exploration. We demonstrate these capabilities using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data, and evaluate the agent on a custom fNIRS benchmarking suite against general-purpose LLM agents with code sandboxes. Future extensions will generalize the architecture to additional modalities, including functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, and expand the benchmarking suite to additional fNIRS tasks.

AI.tldr: The AI Neuroscientist is an LLM-based language agent integrated with a neuroimaging toolset that performs quality control, modeling, and visualization via natural-language queries, demonstrated on fNIRS data and benchmarked against general-purpose code-sandbox agents.
AI.motivation: Neuroimaging analysis demands specialized coding and statistical expertise, restricting accessibility for researchers lacking computational backgrounds. Existing scripted pipelines offer limited transparency and interactivity for small-scale data exploration.
AI.method: The system couples a large language model with a neuroimaging toolset, enabling researchers to query data quality and specify analysis parameters in natural language for quality control, modeling, and visualization. Capabilities are demonstrated on functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data and evaluated on a custom fNIRS benchmarking suite against general-purpose LLM agents equipped with code sandboxes.
AI.result: The agent supports interactive, transparent data exploration via natural language as an alternative to conventional scripted pipelines for small-scale analysis. Evaluation on the custom fNIRS benchmark compares its performance with general-purpose LLM code-sandbox agents.
AI.conclusion: The AI Neuroscientist lowers barriers to neuroimaging analysis through natural-language interaction. Future work will generalize the architecture to additional modalities, such as fMRI, and expand the benchmarking suite to more fNIRS tasks.

title: JAMB: Joint Action-Motion Diffusion for Bimanual Manipulation
summary: Coordinated bimanual manipulation is challenging because the motion of either arm can alter the shared 3D scene and thereby affect the other arm. Yet most diffusion policies generate actions without explicitly modeling these future geometric consequences, while predictive variants typically use future state only as auxiliary supervision or fixed conditioning. We address this limitation by proposing JAMB, a diffusion policy that jointly denoises bimanual actions and future 3D point tracks. By allowing action and track hypotheses to evolve together within a shared Transformer, each can inform and refine the other throughout denoising. We further ground multimodal representations in a shared spatiotemporal coordinate system to facilitate geometry-aware interaction during joint denoising. We evaluate JAMB on diverse bimanual manipulation tasks in RoboTwin 2.0 and on a real-world robot, comparing it with action-only policies and alternative future-prediction approaches spanning different state representations and learning objectives. Across 16 simulation tasks, JAMB achieves an average success rate of 83.4%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 23.9 percentage points. On three real-world tasks, it outperforms the action-only and auxiliary geometry prediction methods by 50.0 and 21.2 percentage points, respectively. Beyond these performance gains, JAMB shows stronger generalization to cluttered scenes and out-of-distribution backgrounds than the evaluated baselines. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of our joint action-motion modeling framework for coordinated bimanual manipulation. Our project website is available at https://jam-bimanual.github.io/

AI.tldr: JAMB is a diffusion policy that jointly denoises bimanual actions and future 3D point tracks in a shared Transformer, enabling mutual refinement during denoising, and achieves large gains in simulated and real-world coordinated bimanual manipulation.
AI.motivation: Coordinated bimanual manipulation is hard because each arm's motion changes the shared 3D scene and affects the other arm. Most diffusion policies generate actions without explicitly modeling future geometric consequences, while predictive variants treat future state only as auxiliary supervision or fixed conditioning, limiting geometric reasoning.
AI.method: JAMB jointly denoises bimanual actions and future 3D point tracks within a shared Transformer, letting action and track hypotheses co-evolve and refine each other throughout denoising. Multimodal representations are grounded in a shared spatiotemporal coordinate system to support geometry-aware interaction during joint denoising.
AI.result: Evaluated on 16 RoboTwin 2.0 simulation tasks and three real-world tasks against action-only policies and alternative future-prediction approaches. JAMB reaches 83.4% average success in simulation, surpassing the strongest baseline by 23.9 points; on real-world tasks it exceeds action-only and auxiliary geometry prediction methods by 50.0 and 21.2 points respectively. It also generalizes better to cluttered scenes and out-of-distribution backgrounds.
AI.conclusion: Joint action-motion modeling where actions and future 3D point tracks are denoised together is effective for coordinated bimanual manipulation, delivering substantial performance and generalization improvements over action-only and auxiliary-prediction baselines.

title: MedGate-Fusion: Integrating First-Encounter Semantic Narratives and Physiological Biomarkers for Prospective Stroke Risk Stratification
comment: 7 pages,2 tables, 2 figures. Submitted to EMBC 2026
summary: Prospective stroke risk stratification in primary care is challenging because early risk signals are distributed across routine biomarkers and unstructured clinical narratives. We propose MedGate-Fusion, a multi-modal gated architecture that integrates transformer-based embeddings of first-encounter narratives with ten routinely recorded risk markers. We used electronic medical record data from the Canadian Primary Care Sentinel Surveillance Network (CPCSSN). Starting from 808,921 encounter-level observations, we constructed a first-encounter cohort and retained 102,736 unique patient records with non-empty narratives and sufficient data to evaluate a five-year stroke outcome. To reduce explicit target leakage from diagnostic mentions in notes, we applied dictionary-based redaction of stroke-related terms prior to semantic encoding.

AI.tldr: MedGate-Fusion is a multi-modal gated architecture that fuses transformer-based narrative embeddings with ten routine risk markers to stratify 5-year stroke risk in primary care. Using CPCSSN electronic medical records, the authors built a first-encounter cohort of 102,736 unique patients (from 808,921 encounter-level observations) with non-empty, stroke-term-redacted narratives and applied dictionary-based redaction to mitigate explicit target leakage.
AI.motivation: Prospective stroke risk stratification in primary care is difficult because early risk signals are dispersed across routine biomarkers and unstructured clinical narratives, which conventional single-source models cannot jointly capture.
AI.method: A multi-modal gated architecture (MedGate-Fusion) combining transformer-based embeddings of first-encounter clinical narratives with ten routinely recorded risk markers. Data came from the Canadian Primary Care Sentinel Surveillance Network (CPCSSN): an initial 808,921 encounter-level observations were reduced to a first-encounter cohort of 102,736 unique patient records with non-empty narratives and sufficient data for a five-year stroke outcome. Dictionary-based redaction of stroke-related terms was applied before semantic encoding to reduce explicit target leakage.
AI.result: Not reported in the provided abstract (the text describes cohort construction and leakage control only; no performance metrics or evaluation results are stated).
AI.conclusion: The abstract presents the study design and data preprocessing pipeline for multi-modal, narrative-informed stroke risk stratification, with explicit leakage mitigation. Empirical findings and comparative performance are to be reported in the full paper.

title: GINIO: A Geometric SO(3)-Equivariant Interface for Neural Inertial Odometry
comment: Accepted at the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026). 26 pages, 14 figures
summary: Neural inertial odometry increasingly uses networks as learned measurements inside filtering pipelines. Such measurements should transform consistently under arbitrary IMU mounting conventions: their mean must transform as a vector, and their covariance must transform congruently as a second-order tensor. We present GINIO, a geometric SO(3)-equivariant interface for neural inertial odometry under arbitrary rotations of the IMU measurement frame. Given calibrated IMU windows, our framework predicts a motion measurement and uncertainty obeying these tensorial laws. To support efficient sensor-frame learning, we introduce Last-Frame Alignment (LFA), a deterministic preprocessing step that is provably equivalent to world-frame training for SO(3)-equivariant predictors. The connected estimator tracks sensor-local states such as IMU bias, separating nuisance estimation from the geometric law enforced by the learned measurement. We instantiate the same interface in filter-connected NIO, AirIO-style recurrent aerial prediction, EqNIO-style full-SO(3) canonicalization, and ResNet-style temporal backbones. On TLIO, GINIO achieves 2.018 m ID/SO(3) ATE while EqNIO degrades to 76.389 m, using 11.6x fewer FLOPs. On NanoBench, our AirIO-style instantiation improves ATE from 5.579 m to 1.430 m without external attitude input, and our ResNet-style instantiation reaches 0.581 m ATE versus 0.645 m for ResNet1D. On Fetch, GINIO empirically reduces unseen physical-remount ATE from 8.15 m to 0.50 m without retraining, demonstrating robustness beyond the exact coordinate-frame guarantee. For uncertainty, spectral covariance reduces covariance-equivariance error by over three orders of magnitude compared with a diagonal head.

AI.tldr: GINIO introduces an SO(3)-equivariant interface for neural inertial odometry that predicts motion measurements and uncertainties obeying tensorial transformation laws under arbitrary IMU mounting rotations. Using Last-Frame Alignment for efficient sensor-frame training, it provides consistent mean and covariance behavior and significantly improves ATE and remount robustness across TLIO, NanoBench, and Fetch benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Neural inertial odometry increasingly places learned measurements inside filtering pipelines. Such measurements must transform consistently under arbitrary IMU mounting conventions: the predicted mean should transform as a vector and the covariance as a second-order tensor. Existing learned measurements often violate these geometric requirements, limiting robustness, uncertainty consistency, and generalization to unknown sensor-frame rotations or remounts.
AI.method: The paper proposes GINIO, a geometric SO(3)-equivariant interface for neural inertial odometry under arbitrary rotations of the IMU measurement frame. Given calibrated IMU windows, it predicts a motion measurement and uncertainty satisfying tensorial transformation laws. It introduces Last-Frame Alignment (LFA), a deterministic preprocessing step provably equivalent to world-frame training for SO(3)-equivariant predictors, enabling efficient sensor-frame learning. A connected estimator tracks sensor-local states such as IMU bias, separating nuisance estimation from the enforced geometric law. The interface is instantiated in filter-connected NIO, AirIO-style recurrent aerial prediction, EqNIO-style full-SO(3) canonicalization, and ResNet-style temporal backbones. Spectral covariance is used for uncertainty.
AI.result: On TLIO, GINIO achieves 2.018 m ID/SO(3) ATE, while EqNIO degrades to 76.389 m, with 11.6x fewer FLOPs. On NanoBench, the AirIO-style instantiation improves ATE from 5.579 m to 1.430 m without external attitude input, and the ResNet-style instantiation reaches 0.581 m ATE versus 0.645 m for ResNet1D. On Fetch, GINIO empirically reduces unseen physical-remount ATE from 8.15 m to 0.50 m without retraining. For uncertainty, spectral covariance reduces covariance-equivariance error by more than three orders of magnitude compared with a diagonal head.
AI.conclusion: GINIO enforces correct SO(3)-equivariant transformation of learned motion measurements and uncertainties in neural inertial odometry, enabling consistent filtering behavior under arbitrary IMU frame rotations. It improves accuracy, computational efficiency, uncertainty calibration, and robustness to unseen physical remounts across multiple benchmarks and backbone instantiations, demonstrating robustness beyond the exact coordinate-frame guarantee.

title: When LLM Agents Fail to Read the Room: ReAdapt for Relational Social Reasoning
summary: A social agent's most basic decisions (should I react to this post? who should I reach out to?) are not purely content problems. The right action often hinges on the latent relationship between people -- tie strength, reciprocity, mutual connections -- rather than on which content is most salient. Standard LLM agent loops do not explicitly represent how new relational evidence should revise the agent's current social hypothesis, leaving them prone to surface-obvious choices when relational and content cues diverge. We formalize this failure mode with a relationship-reasoning benchmark: 500 synthetic social worlds with friendships, follows, reaction histories, and feeds, yielding 1,000 queries over two tasks, reaction selection and warm introduction (finding the best bridge to a target person). By construction, the surface-obvious candidate differs from the relationship-grounded oracle in about 53% of queries, forming an overturn subset where the agent must use relational evidence to revise an initially plausible choice. We propose ReAdapt (Relationship-Adaptive Agent with Policy-driven sTate), which augments the ReAct loop with an explicit structured social state z = (G, B, R, N, D) capturing goal, belief, relationship, norm, and disclosure. After each tool observation, ReAdapt runs a typed Adapt step that updates this state and emits a policy operation (continue, switch, abandon, or clarify) before choosing the next action. With Gemini-3-Flash on a stratified subset of n = 150 queries per task, ReAdapt improves warm-introduction accuracy from 37% to 51% (+14 points) and reaction-selection accuracy from 69% to 77% (+8 points). Oracle regret drops from 0.260 to 0.152 and from 0.095 to 0.053, respectively. Holding the model, tools, and environments fixed, these results suggest that explicit relational-state adaptation helps LLM agents turn retrieved social evidence into revised decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a relationship-reasoning benchmark of 500 synthetic social worlds (1,000 queries across reaction selection and warm introduction) where the surface-obvious candidate differs from the relationship-grounded oracle ~53% of the time, and proposes ReAdapt, a ReAct-style agent with an explicit structured social state and a typed Adapt step, improving warm-introduction accuracy by +14 points and reaction-selection accuracy by +8 points over a baseline.
AI.motivation: Social agents' basic decisions are not purely content problems; the correct action often depends on latent relational structure (tie strength, reciprocity, mutual connections) rather than content salience. Standard LLM agent loops lack an explicit mechanism for revising a social hypothesis with new relational evidence, so they default to surface-obvious choices when relational and content cues conflict.
AI.method: The authors formalize the failure mode with a relationship-reasoning benchmark: 500 synthetic social worlds containing friendships, follows, reaction histories, and feeds, producing 1,000 queries over two tasks—reaction selection and warm introduction (identifying the best bridge to a target person). They then propose ReAdapt (Relationship-Adaptive Agent with Policy-driven sTate), which augments the ReAct loop with an explicit structured social state z = (G, B, R, N, D) for goal, belief, relationship, norm, and disclosure. After each tool observation, a typed Adapt step updates this state and emits a policy operation (continue, switch, abandon, or clarify) before the next action is chosen.
AI.result: With Gemini-3-Flash on a stratified subset of n = 150 queries per task, ReAdapt raises warm-introduction accuracy from 37% to 51% (+14 points) and reaction-selection accuracy from 69% to 77% (+8 points). Oracle regret decreases from 0.260 to 0.152 and from 0.095 to 0.053, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Holding the model, tools, and environments fixed, explicit relational-state adaptation helps LLM agents convert retrieved social evidence into revised decisions, indicating that representing and updating social hypothesis state is an effective approach to relationship-aware agent behavior.

title: Learning from Humans for Proactive Assistance in Human-Robot Collaborative Transport
summary: We focus on human-robot collaborative transport, a challenging task of broad relevance spanning logistics, manufacturing, and the home, in which a user and a robot work together to relocate a large or heavy object. To act as an effective partner, the robot should reduce the user's effort by contributing to efficient relocation of the object while remaining physically responsive to them. Prior work often addresses these capabilities separately, producing robots that may move the object efficiently but resist user input, or accommodate the user but depend on continuous guidance. Our key insight is that obstacle-constrained collaborative transport requires integrating predictions of human collaborative behavior with compliant robot control. To this end, we introduce PROACT, a framework for human-robot collaborative transport that incorporates anticipation into compliant whole-body control through a learned model of human collaborative behavior. Trained on a large-scale, real-world dataset of dyadic human transport demonstrations, our transformer architecture distills collaborative behavior into predictions of future object motion. Across 108 real-world trials with a 9-DoF mobile manipulator, PROACT reduces mean interaction work by 59.2\% and 20.4\%, and mean completion time by 12.9\% and 6.9\%, relative to compliance-only and MPC baselines, respectively. Footage from our experiments can be found at https://youtu.be/qAGvQfVPjbk.

AI.tldr: PROACT integrates anticipatory prediction of human collaborative behavior with compliant whole-body control to improve human-robot collaborative transport.
AI.motivation: Human-robot collaborative transport is broadly relevant (logistics, manufacturing, home) but challenging. A good robot partner should reduce user effort by efficiently relocating objects while remaining physically responsive. Prior work treats these capabilities separately, yielding robots that either move objects efficiently but resist user input, or accommodate users but require continuous guidance.
AI.method: The key insight is that obstacle-constrained collaborative transport requires combining predictions of human collaborative behavior with compliant robot control. PROACT incorporates anticipation into compliant whole-body control via a learned model of human collaborative behavior. A transformer architecture, trained on a large-scale real-world dataset of dyadic human transport demonstrations, distills collaborative behavior into predictions of future object motion.
AI.result: Across 108 real-world trials with a 9-DoF mobile manipulator, PROACT reduces mean interaction work by 59.2% and 20.4%, and mean completion time by 12.9% and 6.9%, relative to compliance-only and MPC baselines, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Combining learned anticipatory human-behavior predictions with compliant whole-body control enables more efficient and responsive human-robot collaborative transport, outperforming compliance-only and MPC baselines in real-world trials.

title: Attention as a Routing Graph: Live Circuit Extraction from a Single Forward Pass
summary:
Finding circuits in language models usually means running many careful interventions. We try something simpler: treat attention as a routing map from one forward pass, keep a small set of routes that point toward the answer, and ask whether those routes actually matter.
  They often do. On induction and IOI (tasks where the "right" circuit is already known), ablating our extracted edges hurts the model much more than ablating a random set of the same size. We evaluate n=100 prompts per cell on GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium, and Pythia-410M, with paired gap tests and bootstrap confidence intervals. The extract step costs one forward; a head-by-head patch sweep costs about two orders of magnitude more.
  We are not claiming a complete circuit atlas. We are claiming a cheap sketch that carries real causal signal on known tasks, with clear failure modes when it does not. Code and evaluation artifacts are at https://github.com/Aquinf03/live-circuit-routing.

AI.tldr: A single forward pass's attention map can be used to extract a small set of routes toward the answer; ablating these edges causes substantially greater model degradation than ablating random edges of equal size on induction and IOI tasks across GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium, and Pythia-410M, at ~100x lower cost than head-by-head patch sweeps.
AI.motivation: Finding circuits in language models typically requires many careful interventions, which is computationally expensive. The authors seek a simpler, cheaper alternative: whether attention from one forward pass can serve as a routing map whose selected routes carry real causal signal.
AI.method: Treat attention as a routing map from a single forward pass, keep a small set of routes pointing toward the answer, and test whether those routes matter causally. Evaluate via ablation of extracted edges versus random edges of matched size, using n=100 prompts per cell on GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium, and Pythia-410M, with paired gap tests and bootstrap confidence intervals. Compare cost against head-by-head patch sweeps.
AI.result: On induction and IOI (tasks with known ground-truth circuits), ablating extracted edges hurts the model much more than ablating a random set of the same size, with paired gap tests and bootstrap confidence intervals supporting the effect. Extraction costs one forward pass versus ~two orders of magnitude more for a head-by-head patch sweep.
AI.conclusion: The approach does not claim a complete circuit atlas; rather it offers a cheap sketch that carries real causal signal on known tasks and exhibits clear failure modes when it does not. Code and evaluation artifacts are released.

title: HOTICE: Whole-Body Humanoid Object Transportation in Cluttered Environments
summary: Object transportation is a fundamental capability for humanoid robots operating in real-world, human-centric environments, yet existing methods struggle when clutter constrains free space around both the robot and its carried payload. We present HOTICE, a whole-body humanoid learning framework for transporting objects through such cluttered environments. First, we introduce Humanoid-Object Decoupled Potential Fields, which jointly encode collision-avoidance guidance for the robot and the carried object, enabling coordinated, obstacle-aware motion for both. Second, to address the large action space inherent to whole-body loco-manipulation, we design a dual-agent reinforcement learning architecture that decouples upper- and lower-body control while preserving whole-body coordination via shared state observations and rewards. To train a policy that generalizes across diverse cluttered scenes, we further employ a specialist-to-generalist distillation strategy, in which privileged teacher policies are distilled into a single deployable student policy. We evaluate HOTICE in MuJoCo simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid, demonstrating effective and robust object transportation across cluttered scenarios for objects of varying shapes. Our results show that HOTICE reliably coordinates whole-body motion and object-aware collision avoidance, generalizing effectively to previously unseen cluttered environments while achieving strong performance in sim2real deployment.

AI.tldr: HOTICE is a whole-body humanoid learning framework that transports objects through cluttered environments using decoupled potential fields, a dual-agent RL architecture, and specialist-to-generalist distillation, validated in MuJoCo and on a Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Object transportation is fundamental for humanoid robots in human-centric settings, but existing methods fail when clutter restricts free space around both the robot and its payload. This calls for coordinated, obstacle-aware whole-body motion that accounts for the carried object as well.
AI.method: The framework has three components: (1) Humanoid-Object Decoupled Potential Fields that jointly encode collision-avoidance guidance for robot and payload; (2) a dual-agent reinforcement learning architecture decoupling upper- and lower-body control while maintaining whole-body coordination through shared state observations and rewards, addressing the large loco-manipulation action space; (3) a specialist-to-generalist distillation strategy distilling privileged teacher policies into a single deployable student policy for generalization across cluttered scenes.
AI.result: Evaluated in MuJoCo and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid, HOTICE achieves effective and robust transportation of variously shaped objects across cluttered scenarios, reliably coordinating whole-body motion and object-aware collision avoidance, generalizing to unseen cluttered environments, and showing strong sim2real performance.
AI.conclusion: HOTICE demonstrates that combining decoupled potential fields with dual-agent RL and teacher-student distillation enables reliable, generalizable whole-body object transportation in clutter, with successful real-robot deployment.

title: Learned Enterprise Data Comprehension: Compression and Routing for Data Agents
summary: Structured-data agents in enterprise settings must reason over complex data environments whose relevant evidence is distributed across schemas, relationships, policies, and recurring business roles. Modern agentic systems often address this burden through reusable markdown-style memory or skill files that preserve previously discovered information for later queries, reducing the need to rediscover the same structure repeatedly. This is useful, but it obscures a natural division of labor: agents are well suited to semantic reasoning, while learned systems are well suited to predicting and organizing recurring structure. We introduce latent equivalence learning to bridge this gap. The framework separates persistent task-relevant identities from their dataset-relative realizations. In our realization, supporting and opposing evidence shape support-realized Gaussian prototypes that learn how those identities are expressed in a particular data environment, while soft-membership profiles retain distinctions lost under a hard assignment. A separate learned query-prototype system represents recurring evidential requirements and maps them through a learned compatibility function into the same persistent identity structure. This identity-factorized, query-conditioned routing materializes the relevant dataset-specific evidence for downstream reasoning, allowing the agent to operate over an already organized evidential state rather than reconstructing cross-schema structure at every query. On the Data Agent Benchmark, spanning 54 queries across 12 heterogeneous datasets, our full implementation achieves 94.67% dataset-macro stratified Pass@1 over five complete trials and 258/270 successful raw query attempts, compared with 55.51% for the benchmark's Claude Opus 4.6 reference agent, ranking first among 40 leaderboard entries at submission.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces latent equivalence learning, a framework that factorizes persistent task-relevant identities from their dataset-relative realizations, enabling structured-data agents to route query-conditioned evidence into an organized state rather than reconstructing structure per query, achieving 94.67% Pass@1 on the Data Agent Benchmark.
AI.motivation: Enterprise structured-data agents must reason over evidence scattered across schemas, relationships, policies, and recurring business roles. Current reusable memory or skill files (markdown-style) reduce rediscovery but blur a natural division of labor: agents excel at semantic reasoning while learned systems excel at predicting and organizing recurring structure.
AI.method: Latent equivalence learning separates persistent task-relevant identities from dataset-relative realizations. Support and opposing evidence shape support-realized Gaussian prototypes that learn how identities manifest in a given environment, while soft-membership profiles preserve distinctions lost under hard assignment. A separate learned query-prototype system represents recurring evidential requirements and maps them via a learned compatibility function into the same persistent identity structure, yielding identity-factorized, query-conditioned routing.
AI.result: On the Data Agent Benchmark (54 queries, 12 heterogeneous datasets), the full implementation achieves 94.67% dataset-macro stratified Pass@1 over five trials and 258/270 successful raw query attempts, versus 55.51% for the Claude Opus 4.6 reference agent, ranking first among 40 leaderboard entries.
AI.conclusion: Identity-factorized, query-conditioned routing materializes dataset-specific evidence for downstream reasoning, letting agents operate over an already organized evidential state and substantially outperforming strong reference agents on heterogeneous structured-data tasks.

title: Capability-Aware Arbitration for Semantic Intent-Based Shared Control
summary: Shared control often allocates robot authority based on confidence in inferred human intent, assuming reliable autonomous execution. When this assumption fails, high intent confidence can cause over-helping. We present a capability-aware shared-control framework in which a vision-language model (VLM) infers human intent and provides semantic-intent confidence, while a vision-language-action (VLA) policy generates autonomous actions. VLA capability confidence is estimated online from the dispersion and local instability of stochastic action trajectories. We design a nonlinear arbitration policy that combines Bayesian-filtered semantic-intent confidence with VLA capability confidence through a sigmoid mapping to adapt robot authority. Our evaluation combined VLM/VLA confidence assessment with a study involving 12 participants performing pick-and-place and bidirectional stacking under in-distribution and out-of-distribution conditions. The proposed method achieved the highest task success rate (92%), compared with manual teleoperation (83%), intent-only arbitration (44%), and fixed equal-weight blending (10%). It also achieved higher control friendliness and lower authority-weighted disagreement than both shared-control baselines. These results demonstrate the benefit of incorporating VLA capability into authority allocation to mitigate over-helping and improve shared-control performance.

AI.tldr: A capability-aware shared-control framework combines VLM semantic-intent confidence with online-estimated VLA capability confidence via a nonlinear (sigmoid-based) arbitration policy to allocate robot authority, mitigating over-helping and achieving 92% task success.
AI.motivation: Conventional shared control allocates robot authority based on confidence in inferred human intent while assuming the autonomous system executes reliably. When this assumption fails, high intent confidence leads to over-helping, degrading shared-control performance.
AI.method: A VLM infers human intent and outputs semantic-intent confidence; a VLA policy generates autonomous actions, with its capability confidence estimated online from the dispersion and local instability of stochastic action trajectories. A nonlinear arbitration policy fuses Bayesian-filtered semantic-intent confidence with VLA capability confidence through a sigmoid mapping to adapt robot authority.
AI.result: Evaluation combined VLM/VLA confidence assessment with a 12-participant study on pick-and-place and bidirectional stacking across in- and out-of-distribution conditions. The method reached 92% task success versus manual teleoperation (83%), intent-only arbitration (44%), and fixed equal-weight blending (10%), with higher control friendliness and lower authority-weighted disagreement than both shared-control baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating VLA capability into authority allocation mitigates over-helping and improves shared-control performance.

title: Making Agents More Consistent: Skills Should Form Habits for Repeat Tasks
summary:
On repeated work, agents are inconsistent. We ran 42 tasks three times each and found that, depending on the model, 38% to 74% returned answers that did not agree. Consistency is what a buyer, an auditor, or a regulator requires, and agents do not have it. They are wasteful too: 95.3% to 97.2% of what an agent generates goes to re-deriving a plan the system already knows.
  We propose skill habit formation. An agent mines its own execution history for candidate skills, deterministic variants that compete against the incumbent rather than replacing it. A candidate declares the region of input space it claims, so the common case runs as a script and the rest falls through to reasoning. Four gates of ascending cost admit candidates; the central one tests a candidate's execution trace against a retained reference, within a tolerance measured from that reference's own run-to-run variability.
  On text-to-SQL, three of four reasoning arms reproduced their own output on 11 to 13 of 42 repeated questions and the fourth on 26 of 42, while a habit-formed variant reproduced on all 456 dispatches we repeated and was non-inferior to every arm it replaced (p<0.0001). It also used 14% to 56% fewer tokens, turning net positive after 7 to 53 reuses.
  We measured what this costs in accuracy. The guard admitted work it should have deferred on 2.6% of natural paraphrases and 26% of inputs near its boundary, and 11 of 13 such failures were invisible to the trace-conformance gate at any threshold. Deterministic errors repeat exactly: a bad habit is as reliable as a good one, and that is the price of the property that makes the system auditable. Separating routing from parameter extraction raised end-to-end accuracy from 0.888 to 0.952 at 43% of the cost.

AI.tldr: Agents are unreliable (38–74% inconsistent across repeated runs) and wasteful (95.3–97.2% of generated tokens re-derive known plans). The paper proposes "skill habit formation": an agent mines its execution history for deterministic candidate skills that compete with the incumbent rather than replace it, each declaring its claimed input-space region so common cases run as scripts and edge cases fall through to reasoning. On text-to-SQL, the habit-formed variant reproduced all 456 repeated dispatches (vs. 11–26 of 42 for reasoning arms), was non-inferior to every replaced arm (p<0.0001), and used 14–56% fewer tokens, turning net positive after 7–53 reuses.
AI.motivation: Consistency is required by buyers, auditors, and regulators, yet agents lack it: across 42 tasks run three times each, 38–74% of runs disagreed by model. Agents are also wasteful, spending 95.3–97.2% of their generated output re-deriving plans the system already knows. The paper targets determinism, auditability, and token efficiency without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: Skill habit formation: the agent mines its own execution history for candidate deterministic skills that compete against the incumbent rather than replacing it. Each candidate declares the input-space region it claims, so the common case executes as a script while the rest falls through to reasoning. Four gates of ascending cost admit candidates; the central gate tests a candidate's execution trace against a retained reference, using a tolerance calibrated from that reference's own run-to-run variability. Routing is separated from parameter extraction.
AI.result: On text-to-SQL, three of four reasoning arms reproduced their own output on 11–13 of 42 repeated questions and the fourth on 26 of 42, while the habit-formed variant reproduced all 456 repeated dispatches and was non-inferior to every arm it replaced (p<0.0001). It used 14–56% fewer tokens, turning net positive after 7–53 reuses. Accuracy cost: the guard admitted work it should have deferred on 2.6% of natural paraphrases and 26% of boundary-near inputs, and 11 of 13 such failures were invisible to the trace-conformance gate at any threshold. Separating routing from parameter extraction raised end-to-end accuracy from 0.888 to 0.952 at 43% of the cost.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic errors repeat exactly: a bad habit is as reliable as a good one, which is the price of the auditability property. Habit formation yields reproducible, auditable, token-efficient agent behavior non-inferior to replaced reasoning arms, with residual failures concentrated near input-space boundaries and largely undetectable by trace conformance. Decoupling routing from parameter extraction further improves accuracy at reduced cost.

title: Angular momentum analysis on Karate roundhouse kicks: a longitudinal case study
summary: Human gait in reality extends beyond straight-line walking, with some situations even requiring drastic back-and-forth rotations. A smooth and stable execution may seem intuitive, but the underlying mechanics remains unknown. The Karate roundhouse kick may be an extreme case of exhibiting dynamic back-and-forth rotations, but investigating the angular momentum (AM) management can potentially inform stability analysis in dynamic human motions and smoother gait in robots and exoskeletons. This paper introduces two new AM-based measures and analyzes AM-related variables to study the target-less retractable back-leg Karate roundhouse kick. The purpose is to understand the underlying AM management, analyze the differences between stable and unstable kicks, and investigate how these variables and measures change over time with improvement. A one-year longitudinal study was conducted with the first author as a Karate student, and a Karate instructor was also recruited for one session as an expert, whose data is used for comparison. Results show that unstable kicks have higher peak total AM before Strike and smaller braking peak after Strike. The proposed AM-based measures are able to identify the cause of some unstable kicks, though no clear distinction could be made between stable and unstable kicks since kicks can be unstable for different reasons. Nonetheless, the proposed measures can be applied as performance measures to analyze other types of dynamic motions. To incorporate them as stability criteria, however, it is recommended to also consider their coordination with time, kinematics, and center of pressure.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two new angular-momentum (AM)-based measures and analyzes AM-related variables in the target-less retractable back-leg Karate roundhouse kick, using a one-year longitudinal study plus an expert comparison, to understand AM management in dynamic back-and-forth rotational motions.
AI.motivation: Real human gait involves not only straight-line walking but also drastic back-and-forth rotations, whose underlying mechanics remain unknown. The Karate roundhouse kick serves as an extreme case to study angular momentum management, with potential implications for stability analysis of dynamic human motion and smoother gait in robots and exoskeletons.
AI.method: Two new AM-based measures are proposed, and AM-related variables are analyzed for the target-less retractable back-leg Karate roundhouse kick. A one-year longitudinal study was conducted with the first author as a Karate student, with one session from a Karate instructor as an expert for comparison.
AI.result: Unstable kicks exhibit higher peak total AM before Strike and a smaller braking peak after Strike. The proposed AM-based measures can identify the cause of some unstable kicks, but no clear distinction could be made between stable and unstable kicks, since kicks can be unstable for different reasons.
AI.conclusion: The proposed measures can serve as performance measures for analyzing other dynamic motions. However, to use them as stability criteria, their coordination with time, kinematics, and center of pressure should also be considered.

title: Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as course-specific tutors, but their usefulness depends on grounding in vetted instructional materials that are often revised mid-semester. Our prior work built a multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system over an authentic machine learning course corpus (Foundations of Machine Learning) and found that retrieval improved contextual grounding, but that fixed retrieval strategies were suboptimal. That motivates a different question: whether how a corpus is structured at ingest time matters more than how much is retrieved at query time. We present a controlled head-to-head comparison of two knowledge representations over an identical classroom corpus: (A) vector RAG, replicating the best-performing configuration from our prior study, and (B) an LLM-compiled wiki (Karpathy framework), in which the corpus is synthesized at ingest into linked concept pages with explicit cross-references and citations back to source materials. We evaluate 59 questions spanning single-fact recall, cross-unit concept linking, synthesis and explanation, and currency after a syllabus revision, scored by an LLM judge against a human-authored rubric. Both representations answered single-fact questions about equally well (9.33 vs. 9.96 of 10), but diverged sharply on questions requiring links across course units. The compiled wiki remained accurate and grounded (9.93; 100% grounded in cited sources), while retrieval scored lower and was markedly less grounded (8.14; 64%). The wiki's citations let students and instructors trace any claim back to the lecture that introduced it, adding a layer of dynamic retrieval that machine learning courses require. While further testing is needed, instructors using AI to support learning in ML courses should consider wiki-based structure for its potential to support foundational elements of best practice.

AI.tldr: A controlled comparison of vector RAG versus an LLM-compiled wiki over the same ML course corpus shows both handle single-fact questions equally, but the compiled wiki substantially outperforms retrieval on cross-unit linking and grounding.
AI.motivation: LLMs are being used as course-specific tutors, but their value depends on grounding in vetted instructional materials that are frequently revised mid-semester.
