Prior work with a multimodal RAG system over an authentic ML course corpus showed retrieval improved grounding but that fixed retrieval strategies were suboptimal, raising the question of whether corpus structure at ingest time matters more than retrieval volume at query time.
AI.method: Controlled head-to-head comparison of two knowledge representations over an identical classroom corpus (Foundations of Machine Learning): (A) vector RAG replicating the best configuration from prior work, and (B) an LLM-compiled wiki (Karpathy framework) synthesizing the corpus at ingest into linked concept pages with explicit cross-references and citations to source materials. Evaluation used 59 questions spanning single-fact recall, cross-unit concept linking, synthesis/explanation, and currency after a syllabus revision, scored by an LLM judge against a human-authored rubric.
AI.result: Both representations performed about equally on single-fact questions (9.33 vs. 9.96 out of 10) but diverged sharply on cross-unit linking questions. The compiled wiki remained accurate and grounded (9.93; 100% grounded in cited sources), whereas retrieval scored lower and was markedly less grounded (8.14; 64%). The wiki's citations allow students and instructors to trace any claim back to the lecture that introduced it.
AI.conclusion: Wiki-based ingest-time structure appears to outperform query-time retrieval for questions requiring cross-unit links and source grounding. While further testing is needed, instructors using AI to support ML learning should consider wiki-based structure for its potential to support foundational elements of best practice.

title: PARTE: Plane-Assisted Robust Transformation Estimation for Point Cloud Registration
summary: Global point-cloud registration remains challenging when limited overlap, repetitive geometry, and sensor noise produce correspondence sets dominated by outliers. Planar regions are particularly difficult for conventional point descriptors and are therefore often suppressed or discarded before matching. We present PARTE (Plane-Assisted Robust Transformation Estimation), a global registration method that instead treats planar structure as complementary registration evidence. PARTE extracts planar patches and represents them using our novel Plane Context Histogram (PCH), a descriptor that encodes the geometry surrounding each patch, while a two-level matching procedure identifies reliable plane correspondences. Candidate point and plane correspondences are combined in a confidence-weighted compatibility graph for joint outlier rejection, followed by rigid transformation estimation. When no usable plane correspondences are available, PARTE naturally reduces to point-only registration. We evaluate PARTE on 8,097 registration pairs across six indoor and outdoor benchmarks spanning dense RGB-D and sparse LiDAR measurements. Evaluations show PARTE achieves the highest overall success rate against 13 standard and state-of-the-art methods while maintaining low runtime. An open-source C++ implementation with Python bindings is provided at https://parte.pages.dev.

AI.tldr: PARTE is a global point-cloud registration method that uses planar structure as complementary evidence, combining point and plane correspondences in a confidence-weighted compatibility graph for joint outlier rejection and robust rigid transformation estimation.
AI.motivation: Global point-cloud registration is difficult under limited overlap, repetitive geometry, and sensor noise, where correspondence sets are dominated by outliers. Planar regions are challenging for conventional point descriptors and are often suppressed or discarded before matching, wasting potentially useful geometric evidence.
AI.method: PARTE extracts planar patches and describes them with a novel Plane Context Histogram (PCH) encoding surrounding geometry, then applies a two-level matching procedure to find reliable plane correspondences. Candidate point and plane correspondences are fused in a confidence-weighted compatibility graph for joint outlier rejection, followed by rigid transformation estimation. If no usable plane correspondences exist, PARTE degenerates to point-only registration.
AI.result: Evaluated on 8,097 registration pairs across six indoor and outdoor benchmarks covering dense RGB-D and sparse LiDAR data, PARTE attains the highest overall success rate among 13 standard and state-of-the-art methods while maintaining low runtime. An open-source C++ implementation with Python bindings is released.
AI.conclusion: Treating planar structure as complementary registration evidence, rather than discarding it, yields robust and efficient global registration across diverse sensing modalities and environments.

title: Clarification Is Not Correction: LLMs Fail to Let Go
summary: Dialogue failures in language models are usually framed as memory failures: context too long, summaries lossy, a constraint forgotten. We argue this misses a deeper problem: in many conversations the model does not forget, it commits too early. An ambiguous early turn collapses into a single hidden interpretation, and later clarification is filtered through that commitment. We call this early posterior collapse: unresolved user intent collapsing into a committed task state before ambiguity is resolved. We study it with controlled dialogue tasks in writing, planning, and coding using Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash. Across thousands of trials, the same information in different orders yields different outcomes, even when the final dialogue contains equivalent task-relevant information. This order effect suggests later clarification is treated as extra context rather than a corrective signal: it refines a stale task state without invalidating it. Coding tasks are especially vulnerable, suggesting early assumptions get embedded in structured artifacts such as interfaces and control flow. Standard prompting and memory strategies do not reliably help: summaries can collapse ambiguity, and chain-of-thought can reduce explicit wrong commitment in reasoning traces without improving final task success. These findings motivate uncertainty-preserving state management. If assistants cannot let go of early interpretations, robustness cannot rely on post hoc correction alone; it must keep ambiguous early turns from hardening into one task state. Assistants should hold tentative hypotheses while ambiguity remains, ask before executing when high-impact ambiguity persists, and rebuild from a revised state when later evidence invalidates an earlier reading. Rather than one prompting fix, we aim to redirect research for interactive LLMs from retaining more context toward preserving uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "early posterior collapse"—a dialogue failure where models commit to a single interpretation of ambiguous early user intent before it is resolved—and shows this is an order effect distinct from memory failure, motivating uncertainty-preserving state management over better prompting or memory.
AI.motivation: Dialogue failures in language models are typically framed as memory failures (context too long, lossy summaries, forgotten constraints). The authors argue this framing misses a deeper issue: models often do not forget but commit too early, so ambiguity in an early turn collapses into a single hidden interpretation and later clarification is filtered through that commitment.
AI.method: Controlled dialogue tasks in writing, planning, and coding, run with Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash. The key manipulation is information order: the same task-relevant information is presented in different orders with equivalent final content. They also test standard prompting and memory strategies, including summaries and chain-of-thought.
AI.result: Across thousands of trials, order effects persist: the same information in different orders yields different outcomes even when the final dialogue contains equivalent task-relevant information. Later clarification is treated as extra context that refines a stale task state rather than invalidating it. Coding tasks are especially vulnerable, as early assumptions become embedded in structured artifacts such as interfaces and control flow. Summaries can collapse ambiguity, and chain-of-thought can reduce explicit wrong commitment in reasoning traces without improving final task success.
AI.conclusion: Robustness cannot rely on post hoc correction alone if assistants cannot let go of early interpretations. The authors call for uncertainty-preserving state management: hold tentative hypotheses while ambiguity remains, ask before executing when high-impact ambiguity persists, and rebuild from a revised state when later evidence invalidates an earlier reading. This redirects interactive LLM research from retaining more context toward preserving uncertainty.

title: VLAQuantBench: Closed-Loop Evaluation of Post-Training Quantization for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Post-training quantization reduces the memory requirements of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but precision selection must account for the interaction between layer scope, numerical format, and calibration. We introduce \textbf{VLAQuantBench}, a controlled evaluation with 409 runs and 94,574 simulation episodes: four models on LIBERO, with X-VLA additionally evaluated on three simulation benchmark families. Under uncalibrated W4A4 round-to-nearest quantization, expanding a $π_{0.5}$ action-head subset from 126 to 167 layers raises success from 7.0\% to 70.5\%. Fixed-observation replay confirms a corresponding numerical recovery. Two-episode calibration removes the severe joint failures in the tested subsets, whereas the same smoothing-and-clipping recipe lowers $π_0$ success and does not recover OpenVLA-OFT end-to-end. For OpenVLA-OFT, protecting one 28,672-parameter output projection instead restores near-baseline success: the remaining 441 eligible linear layers retain W3 on LIBERO-Long or eight-bit activations across all four suites. Task-clustered intervals support the large failure and recovery contrasts. These results establish recipe-dependent interactions and identify concrete precision assignments, rather than universal layer-sensitivity rules. Real-kernel and physical-robot measurements complement the accuracy analysis. Code, configurations, and episode records are publicly available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/VLAQuantBench.

AI.tldr: VLAQuantBench provides a controlled 409-run, 94,574-episode study of post-training quantization for VLA models, showing that precision effects depend on layer scope, format, and calibration rather than universal layer-sensitivity rules.
AI.motivation: Post-training quantization can cut VLA memory costs, but the optimal precision choice depends on how layer scope, numerical format, and calibration interact—an interaction not well characterized by prior work.
AI.method: A controlled benchmark of 409 runs and 94,574 simulation episodes across four models on LIBERO, with X-VLA additionally tested on three simulation benchmark families. Experiments vary quantization layer subsets, bit-widths/formats (e.g., W4A4, W3, eight-bit activations), calibration (uncalibrated round-to-nearest vs. two-episode calibration with smoothing-and-clipping), and targeted protection of individual layers, complemented by fixed-observation replay, real-kernel, and physical-robot measurements, with task-clustered intervals.
AI.result: Expanding a π0.5 action-head subset from 126 to 167 layers under uncalibrated W4A4 round-to-nearest raises success from 7.0% to 70.5%, with fixed-observation replay confirming numerical recovery. Two-episode calibration removes severe joint failures in tested subsets, but the same recipe lowers π0 success and fails to recover OpenVLA-OFT end-to-end. For OpenVLA-OFT, protecting one 28,672-parameter output projection restores near-baseline success, leaving 441 eligible linear layers at W3 on LIBERO-Long or eight-bit activations across all four suites.
AI.conclusion: Quantization outcomes are recipe-dependent, and effective precision assignments must be identified concretely per model and layer rather than by universal layer-sensitivity rules. Code, configurations, and episode records are released at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/VLAQuantBench.

title: From Decorative to Load-Bearing: Task Difficulty Shapes the Causal Role of Chain-of-Thought
comment: Accepted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), September 2026. Code/ dataset available at the project repository and huggingface
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is only meaningful if written reasoning causally constrains the answer. We introduce continuation-based causal testing, an ablation-patch intervention that perturbs one reasoning step, truncates the chain, and forces the model to continue from the corrupted prefix. It measures how load-bearing a CoT is for the final answer, a behavioral notion distinct from mechanistic faithfulness. Across Gemma-2-9B-IT, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on GSM8K, MMLU, and BIG-Bench Hard, CoT load-bearingness tracks model-relative task difficulty: on easy tasks models silently bypass their own reasoning; on hard tasks they follow corrupted steps and propagate errors. A matched 2x2 analysis shows task difficulty dominates perturbation type: error propagation rises 16x from GSM8K to BBH multistep arithmetic, and a variance partition over 28,584 continuations attributes 98.8% of explained deviance to task difficulty versus 0.8% to perturbation type. Reasoning-specific RL suppresses error propagation and compresses the gradient. A four-variant judge-sensitivity analysis and blind two-annotator study (n=500) show the error-propagation vs. non-propagation label is invariant to judge prompt, with perfect inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa = 1.00). This gradient creates a structural problem for CoT-based oversight and AI safety monitoring: where the trace is easy to read it carries little signal, and where it matters errors propagate before a monitor can intervene. Linear probes on hidden states separate silent bypass, self-correction, and error propagation, but additive activation steering provides limited causal control, flipping only about 25% of error-propagation cases at best. Behavioral mode is readable but not reliably controllable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces continuation-based causal testing to measure how "load-bearing" a chain-of-thought (CoT) is for final answers via ablation-patch interventions, finding that CoT load-bearingness is dominated by task difficulty rather than perturbation type, which creates a structural problem for CoT-based oversight.
AI.motivation: CoT monitoring is only useful if the written reasoning causally constrains the answer, so the authors need a behavioral measure of whether perturbing reasoning actually affects outputs, distinct from mechanistic faithfulness.
AI.method: They propose continuation-based causal testing: an ablation-patch intervention that perturbs one reasoning step, truncates the chain, and forces the model to continue from the corrupted prefix. They test Gemma-2-9B-IT, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on GSM8K, MMLU, and BIG-Bench Hard, using a matched 2x2 analysis, a variance partition over 28,584 continuations, judge-sensitivity analysis, a blind two-annotator study, linear probes, and additive activation steering.
AI.result: CoT load-bearingness tracks model-relative task difficulty: on easy tasks models silently bypass their own reasoning, while on hard tasks they follow corrupted steps and propagate errors. Task difficulty dominates perturbation type, with error propagation rising 16x from GSM8K to BBH multistep arithmetic, and 98.8% of explained deviance attributed to task difficulty versus 0.8% to perturbation type. Reasoning-specific RL suppresses error propagation and compresses the gradient. The error-propagation label is invariant to judge prompt, with perfect inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa = 1.00). Linear probes separate behavioral modes, but additive activation steering flips only about 25% of error-propagation cases at best.
AI.conclusion: The difficulty gradient creates a structural problem for CoT-based oversight and AI safety monitoring: where the trace is easy to read it carries little signal, and where it matters errors propagate before a monitor can intervene. Behavioral mode is readable but not reliably controllable.

title: Norm2Tex: Augmenting Visuo-Tactile Simulations with Texture
summary: Large-scale datasets are essential for training generalist robot control policies. Collecting real-world tactile data is costly and time-consuming, motivating the use of tactile simulations. However, current tactile simulators capture only overall contact geometry and miss fine details like texture. This results in a significant domain shift between simulated and real tactile data. To address this gap, we introduce Norm2Tex, a plug-in method that augments simulations of vision-based tactile sensors with high-frequency surface details from normal map textures. By modifying the target object's depth map before a tactile simulator's rendering pipeline, Norm2Tex seamlessly integrates into different tactile simulators. We also evaluate sim-to-real transfer using material classification and a reinforcement learning task. Our results show that Norm2Tex preserves material-dependent tactile information across domains, improving texture recognition and producing material-dependent control behavior in the real world.

AI.tldr: Norm2Tex is a plug-in method that augments vision-based tactile sensor simulations with high-frequency surface details from normal map textures, reducing the sim-to-real gap and improving material-dependent tactile transfer.
AI.motivation: Large-scale datasets are essential for training generalist robot control policies, but collecting real-world tactile data is costly and time-consuming, motivating tactile simulation. Current tactile simulators capture only overall contact geometry and miss fine details like texture, causing a significant domain shift between simulated and real tactile data.
AI.method: Norm2Tex augments simulations of vision-based tactile sensors with high-frequency surface details from normal map textures. It modifies the target object's depth map before the tactile simulator's rendering pipeline, allowing seamless integration into different tactile simulators. Sim-to-real transfer is evaluated using material classification and a reinforcement learning task.
AI.result: Norm2Tex preserves material-dependent tactile information across domains, improving texture recognition and producing material-dependent control behavior in the real world.
AI.conclusion: Norm2Tex effectively reduces the sim-to-real gap in tactile simulation by incorporating high-frequency surface texture details, enabling improved material classification and material-dependent control policies after transfer to real-world settings.

title: Robust Failure, Conservative Repair: Textual Knowledge Distillation from Cross-Model Failures
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main track)
summary: Failure-based textual knowledge distillation aims to discover gaps in a model's knowledge by examining its task errors. The distilled knowledge can be useful for the reasoning of both this model ("source model") and other models. However, this transfer of knowledge may not be stable. We define a rule atom to be a standalone rule injected into a model's textual input at inference time. A rule atom can encode transferable task knowledge or model-specific reasoning patches that can confuse other models. Also, the injected rule atoms can be misapplied to unrelated cases, causing the model to incorrectly flip its answer based on irrelevant information. Building on a pipeline that distills training examples into task-specific cheat sheets that aid model reasoning, we examine when failure-derived rules can improve these cheat sheets. Our early experiment shows rule distillation from a single model's failures underperforms the baseline cheat sheet on non-source model families. This motivates Robust Failure, Conservative Repair (RFCR), a textual distillation procedure that derives rules from failures shared across models, sharpens their application boundaries using boundary cases, and abstains when no useful rule is found. On a 400-item BIG-Bench Hard task set, RFCR improves the baseline cheat sheets from 68.50% to 71.25% (+2.75 pp; 95% CI [+1.25,+4.50]) without performance degradation on previously correct cases. Ablations and cross-model diagnostics support that accuracy gains come from both new knowledge injection and strict rule-application control.

AI.tldr: The paper defines "rule atoms" (standalone rules injected into a model's textual input at inference) and proposes Robust Failure, Conservative Repair (RFCR), a textual knowledge distillation procedure that derives rules from failures shared across models, sharpens their application boundaries with boundary cases, and abstains when no useful rule is found, improving baseline cheat sheets on a BIG-Bench Hard subset.
AI.motivation: Failure-based textual knowledge distillation aims to discover gaps in a model's knowledge by examining its task errors, but the distilled knowledge transfer is unstable. Rule atoms can encode either transferable task knowledge or model-specific reasoning patches that confuse other models, and they can be misapplied to unrelated cases, flipping answers based on irrelevant information. Early experiments show that rule distillation from a single model's failures underperforms the baseline cheat sheet on non-source model families, motivating a more robust approach.
AI.method: Building on a pipeline that distills training examples into task-specific cheat sheets that aid model reasoning, the authors introduce RFCR (Robust Failure, Conservative Repair). RFCR (1) derives rules from failures shared across models, (2) sharpens rule application boundaries using boundary cases, and (3) abstains when no useful rule is found. They evaluate on a 400-item BIG-Bench Hard task set, comparing against baseline cheat sheets, and conduct ablations and cross-model diagnostics.
AI.result: On the 400-item BIG-Bench Hard task set, RFCR improves the baseline cheat sheets from 68.50% to 71.25% (+2.75 pp; 95% CI [+1.25, +4.50]) without performance degradation on previously correct cases. Ablations and cross-model diagnostics support that accuracy gains come from both new knowledge injection and strict rule-application control.
AI.conclusion: Distilling rules from failures shared across models, rather than from a single model's failures, combined with sharpened application boundaries and conservative abstention, yields stable and transferable textual knowledge distillation that improves reasoning accuracy without harming previously correct cases.

title: Effects of Assistance Delay on Joint Mechanics and Energetics in Biological Torque Control of a Hip Exoskeleton
summary: Biological torque control directly maps an estimated human joint moment to exoskeleton assistance, providing a task-agnostic strategy for supporting diverse locomotor activities. However, it remains unclear whether a fixed state-to-torque mapping provides effective assistance across biomechanically distinct tasks. We examined how assistance delay affected hip exoskeleton performance during level-ground (LG), ramp-ascent (RA), and ramp-descent (RD) walking. Eight participants completed a zero-torque baseline condition and five active assistance conditions with delays ranging from 40 to 320 ms. Across tasks and active delays, assistance reduced net metabolic rate by 5.24%, positive biological hip joint work by 5.86%, and total lower-limb positive joint work by 1.68% (all p < 0.05). Assistance delay affected both joint-work outcomes (both p < 0.001) but not net metabolic rate. Mechanical unloading generally decreased with increasing delay, whereas metabolic benefits remained comparatively stable. Relative to the zero-torque condition, net metabolic rate decreased by 9.75% during LG and 7.20% during RA but increased by 1.23% during RD. We did not detect task-dependent differences in the delay response. Our findings indicate that biological torque mappings should be evaluated based on the target outcome and mechanical role of the assisted joint, and that predominantly positive-power assistance may not generalize to negative-work-dominant locomotion without modification.

AI.tldr: This study tested whether a fixed biological-torque mapping in a hip exoskeleton remains effective across level-ground, ramp-ascent, and ramp-descent walking, and how assistance delay influences outcomes. Assistance reduced metabolic rate and joint work overall, but metabolic benefits were task-specific and even negative during ramp descent, with no task-dependent differences in delay response.
AI.motivation: Biological torque control offers a task-agnostic way to assist diverse locomotor activities by mapping estimated joint moments to exoskeleton torque, but it is unclear whether a fixed state-to-torque mapping works effectively across biomechanically distinct tasks, and how timing (assistance delay) interacts with task demands.
AI.method: Eight participants completed level-ground (LG), ramp-ascent (RA), and ramp-descent (RD) walking under a zero-torque baseline and five active assistance conditions with delays from 40 to 320 ms. Outcomes included net metabolic rate, positive biological hip joint work, and total lower-limb positive joint work, analyzed for effects of task, delay, and their interaction.
AI.result: Across tasks and active delays, assistance reduced net metabolic rate by 5.24%, positive biological hip joint work by 5.86%, and total lower-limb positive joint work by 1.68% (all p < 0.05). Delay significantly affected both joint-work measures (p < 0.001) but not net metabolic rate. Mechanical unloading decreased with increasing delay, while metabolic benefits remained relatively stable. Versus zero-torque, metabolic rate decreased by 9.75% in LG and 7.20% in RA but increased by 1.23% in RD. No task-dependent differences in the delay response were detected.
AI.conclusion: Biological torque mappings should be evaluated according to the target outcome and the mechanical role of the assisted joint. Predominantly positive-power assistance may not generalize to negative-work-dominant locomotion (e.g., ramp descent) without modification, even though delay sensitivity primarily affects mechanical unloading rather than metabolic cost.

title: Efficient Iterative Retrieval with Heterogeneous Batching
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (main conference)
summary: Modern information retrieval increasingly employs both embedding and generative models to handle complex queries. However, current serving systems suffer from low throughput and poor GPU utilization because they execute these models in isolation. Coarse-grained partitioning, such as dedicating GPUs to specific tasks, fails to adapt to dynamic workloads and creates computational "bubbles". To address these, we present Orthrus, a serving system that performs heterogeneous batching within a unified inference loop. The primary challenge lies in unifying embedding and generation workloads with conflicting computational patterns while optimizing batch composition for high performance. Orthrus addresses these challenges through chunked embedding with incremental pooling and by adjusting batch composition in a workload-aware manner. Evaluation on four A100 GPUs shows that, relative to baseline deployments, Orthrus achieves 1.28$\times$--4.52$\times$ higher throughput on controlled workloads and up to 55.8% lower end-to-end p99 latency on an iterative-RAG benchmark. We release our code at https://github.com/illinoisdata/Orthrus .

AI.tldr: Orthrus is a serving system that unifies embedding and generative model inference into a single loop via heterogeneous batching, boosting throughput and latency on multi-GPU deployments.
AI.motivation: Modern IR systems use both embedding and generative models, but existing serving systems run them in isolation, causing low throughput and poor GPU utilization. Coarse-grained partitioning (dedicating GPUs to specific tasks) fails to adapt to dynamic workloads and creates computational bubbles.
AI.method: Orthrus performs heterogeneous batching within a unified inference loop. It addresses the challenge of unifying workloads with conflicting computational patterns via chunked embedding with incremental pooling, and optimizes batch composition in a workload-aware manner.
AI.result: On four A100 GPUs, Orthrus achieves 1.28x-4.52x higher throughput than baseline deployments on controlled workloads and up to 55.8% lower end-to-end p99 latency on an iterative-RAG benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Orthrus demonstrates that heterogeneous batching in a unified inference loop effectively improves throughput and latency for combined embedding and generative IR serving. Code is released at https://github.com/illinoisdata/Orthrus.

title: REDACT: Robust Perceptive Locomotion under Unseen Visual Corruption
summary: Depth-conditioned locomotion policies have demonstrated impressive agile maneuvers, but can be steered to unpredictable actions when observations are outside their training distribution. Occlusion, invalid returns, sensor noise, and visual distractors can shift deployment observations away from nominal simulated depth. While synthetic sensor augmentation targets specified degradations, it does not by itself define behavior under corruption families omitted from training. To address gaps in training-time coverage, we present REDACT (Retaining Evidence Despite Artifacts for Continued Traversal), a teacher-student framework combining an improved visual encoder architecture, persistent feature masking, and a novel consensus-gating algorithm to retain useful depth information under unmodeled corruption. The gate uses approximate conformal calibration on clean observations alone, requiring no prior knowledge of the corruption type. Trained on clean simulated depth, REDACT retains useful visual information under unseen corruption, supporting higher traversal success than existing parkour baselines. Evaluation of depth augmentation across corruption families further shows that REDACT improves robustness where augmentation coverage is missing. Real-world trials demonstrate zero-shot transfer to structured and forested environments with unfamiliar scene content.

AI.tldr: REDACT is a teacher-student framework for depth-conditioned locomotion that combines an improved visual encoder, persistent feature masking, and consensus-gating with conformal calibration on clean observations to retain useful depth information under unmodeled corruption, improving traversal success and enabling zero-shot real-world transfer.
AI.motivation: Depth-conditioned locomotion policies perform agile maneuvers but can be steered to unpredictable actions when deployment observations fall outside their training distribution. Occlusion, invalid returns, sensor noise, and visual distractors shift observed depth away from nominal simulated depth. Synthetic sensor augmentation targets specified degradations but does not define behavior under corruption families omitted from training, leaving gaps in training-time coverage.
AI.method: REDACT (Retaining Evidence Despite Artifacts for Continued Traversal) is a teacher-student framework that combines an improved visual encoder architecture, persistent feature masking, and a novel consensus-gating algorithm. The gate uses approximate conformal calibration on clean observations alone, requiring no prior knowledge of the corruption type.
AI.result: Trained on clean simulated depth, REDACT retains useful visual information under unseen corruption and supports higher traversal success than existing parkour baselines. Evaluation of depth augmentation across corruption families shows REDACT improves robustness where augmentation coverage is missing. Real-world trials demonstrate zero-shot transfer to structured and forested environments with unfamiliar scene content.
AI.conclusion: REDACT addresses gaps in training-time coverage for depth-conditioned locomotion by retaining useful depth information under unmodeled corruption via clean-only conformal calibration, outperforming parkour baselines and transferring zero-shot to real-world structured and forested environments.

title: From Offline Proxies to Online Decisions: A Layered Engagement Evaluation Framework for Conversational AI
comment: 11 pages main text, 9 pages supplementary material; 2 figures, 25 tables
summary: Online A/B experiments are the decision standard for user engagement, but traffic and readout time limit how many conversational-AI changes can be tested. We ask whether an offline signal designed to be computable without treatment-arm user exposure agrees with the outcomes of those experiments. We contribute a reusable construction and diagnosis checklist that treats an offline proxy as a chain of three alignments: behavioral label to product outcome, learned classifier to candidate-assistant behavior, and aggregated offline signal to experiment effect. A companion evaluation protocol audits the whole composite by interval-aware decision agreement, which compares offline and online confidence intervals instead of point estimates, and by within-experiment ranking. The instantiation we evaluate comprises a fixed evaluation suite on which candidate behavior is scored, an engagement classifier trained to predict session/prompt level engagements, and a calibration layer mapping sample-level score differences to online model-level engagement deltas. We then report the audit: 489 paired offline-online contrasts (one candidate arm against its control) from 27 experiments on a deployed multi-turn assistant, spanning model checkpoints to system-prompt tuning. Our primary test uses the 113 contrasts from eight experiments that ran after the map was frozen: on these the composite reaches 81.1% F1, against 34.3% for the raw classifier score it is built on, and makes no wrong-direction calls where that raw score makes 31. Every offline prediction was computed before its experiment ran to prevent overfitting. The evidence supports using the composite to prioritize candidates before scarce experiment traffic is allocated---in our deployment of the experiment, selecting among training checkpoints and tuning system prompts.

AI.tldr: Offline A/B experimentation for conversational AI is limited by traffic and readout time. This paper proposes an offline proxy built as a chain of three alignments (behavioral label to product outcome, learned classifier to candidate behavior, aggregated signal to experiment effect), audited via an interval-aware decision agreement and within-experiment ranking protocol. On 113 post-freeze contrasts, the composite achieves 81.1% F1 vs. 34.3% for the raw classifier and makes no wrong-direction calls where the raw classifier makes 31.
AI.motivation: Online A/B experiments are the decision standard for user engagement, but traffic and readout time constrain how many conversational-AI changes can be tested. An offline signal that is computable without treatment-arm user exposure could prioritize candidates before scarce experiment traffic is allocated.
AI.method: The paper contributes a reusable construction and diagnosis checklist treating an offline proxy as a chain of three alignments: behavioral label to product outcome, learned classifier to candidate-assistant behavior, and aggregated offline signal to experiment effect. A companion evaluation protocol audits the composite via interval-aware decision agreement (comparing offline and online confidence intervals rather than point estimates) and within-experiment ranking. The instantiation comprises a fixed evaluation suite scoring candidate behavior, an engagement classifier predicting session/prompt-level engagements, and a calibration layer mapping sample-level score differences to online model-level engagement deltas. All offline predictions were computed before their experiments ran to prevent overfitting.
AI.result: 489 paired offline-online contrasts (one candidate arm vs. its control) from 27 experiments on a deployed multi-turn assistant, spanning model checkpoints to system-prompt tuning. Primary test: 113 contrasts from eight post-freeze experiments, where the composite reaches 81.1% F1 against 34.3% for the raw classifier score it builds on, and makes no wrong-direction calls where that raw score makes 31.
AI.conclusion: The evidence supports using the composite to prioritize candidates before scarce experiment traffic is allocated, specifically for selecting among training checkpoints and tuning system prompts in the authors' deployment.

title: A bioinspired internal model-based online estimator for planar pursuit
summary: Bioinspired feedback controls for pursuit, tracking, and collective motion are often expressed in terms of the relative configuration between interacting agents. In practice, however, onboard sensors may not directly provide all quantities required for feedback control, necessitating estimation of unobserved quantities. This paper develops a bioinspired internal model-based estimator for reconstructing those quantities from partial sensory observations and known self-motion. State reconstruction is posed as an optimization problem that treats the relative kinematics as constraints and minimizes the disagreement between the internal model outputs and measurements from onboard sensors. Pontryagin's Maximum Principle is used to derive the necessary optimality conditions. A forward-backward algorithm is used to provide a numerical solution and a moving horizon formulation is employed for online implementation. The estimator is evaluated numerically against classical state estimators. Real-time implementation of the proposed framework on robotic hardware is demonstrated through two pursuit strategies.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a bioinspired internal-model-based estimator that reconstructs unobserved relative states of interacting agents from partial onboard sensor measurements and known self-motion, formulated as a constrained optimization solved via Pontryagin's Maximum Principle and implemented online with a moving horizon scheme.
AI.motivation: Bioinspired feedback controls for pursuit, tracking, and collective motion are typically expressed in terms of the relative configuration between interacting agents. However, onboard sensors generally cannot directly provide all quantities needed for such feedback, so unobserved states must be estimated.
AI.method: State reconstruction is posed as an optimization problem treating relative kinematics as constraints and minimizing the disagreement between internal model outputs and onboard sensor measurements. Necessary optimality conditions are derived using Pontryagin's Maximum Principle; a forward-backward algorithm supplies a numerical solution, and a moving horizon formulation enables online implementation.
AI.result: The estimator is evaluated numerically against classical state estimators. Real-time implementation on robotic hardware is demonstrated through two pursuit strategies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed bioinspired internal-model-based estimator successfully reconstructs unobserved relative states from partial measurements and known self-motion, outperforming or comparably competing with classical estimators while being feasible for real-time robotic deployment in pursuit tasks.

title: ZeroGate: Trust-Preserving Fast Paths for Governed AI Agent Runtimes
comment: 47 pages, 11 figures, 13 tables. Full research report with an ancillary archive containing reference code, raw experimental records, and offline verification tools
summary: Moving authorization earlier can shorten an agent's dispatch boundary without removing authorization work. It can also admit an action whose payload, authority, or relevant state has changed. ZeroGate separates exact-action approval from durable local admission: an issuer signs a short-lived ActionPass, and a trusted runtime adapter reconstructs the final action before a local gate checks its binding and consumes its nonce. A SQLite transaction couples nonce consumption, applicable quota updates, and an admission receipt. We state a conditional decision-preservation proposition: successful local admission implies that a specified synchronous policy would authorize the same action at the admission point, provided approval is sound, all policy dependencies are represented and current, observations are faithful, and consumption is atomic. The implementation alone establishes neither current-world freshness nor exactly-once remote effects. Evaluation separates authored semantic fixtures, controlled concurrency and crash experiments, and an Azure Blob study comparing synchronous and prepared execution through the same issuer and gate. Both modes mint an exact-action pass; lifecycle latency includes preparation and prepared-batch dwell. Across 4800 cloud attempts, prepared worker-admission-to-dispatch p95 ranges from 9.802 to 11.374 ms, versus 25.018 to 334.000 ms synchronously, across the tested concurrency levels. Prepared mean complete lifecycle is longer at every level: the boundary improvement is not a net speedup. The contribution is an explicit revalidation contract, a durable reference boundary, and an auditable comparison of where authorization cost is paid, not a new cryptographic primitive or a universal performance frontier.

AI.tldr: ZeroGate splits exact-action approval from durable local admission: an issuer signs a short-lived ActionPass, a trusted runtime adapter rebuilds the final action, and a local gate verifies binding and consumes the nonce atomically with quota updates and a receipt. A conditional proposition ties successful admission to what a synchronous policy would authorize, provided approval soundness, represented/current dependencies, faithful observations, and atomic consumption hold. It does not by itself establish current-world freshness or exactly-once remote effects. In an Azure Blob study across 4800 attempts, prepared admission-to-dispatch p95 was 9.802–11.374 ms versus 25.018–334.000 ms synchronously, while mean complete lifecycle was longer for prepared mode.
AI.motivation: Moving authorization earlier can shorten an agent's dispatch boundary without eliminating authorization work, but it risks admitting an action whose payload, authority, or relevant state has changed. The paper seeks to characterize and constrain that risk while measuring whether the boundary shift yields a net performance benefit.
AI.method: ZeroGate separates exact-action approval from durable local admission. An issuer signs a short-lived ActionPass; a trusted runtime adapter reconstructs the final action before a local gate checks its binding and consumes its nonce. A SQLite transaction couples nonce consumption, applicable quota updates, and an admission receipt. Evaluation separates authored semantic fixtures, controlled concurrency and crash experiments, and an Azure Blob study comparing synchronous and prepared execution through the same issuer and gate; both modes mint an exact-action pass, and lifecycle latency includes preparation and prepared-batch dwell.
AI.result: A conditional decision-preservation proposition is stated: successful local admission implies that a specified synchronous policy would authorize the same action at the admission point, given approval soundness, all policy dependencies represented and current, faithful observations, and atomic consumption. The implementation alone establishes neither current-world freshness nor exactly-once remote effects. Across 4800 cloud attempts, prepared worker-admission-to-dispatch p95 ranges from 9.802 to 11.374 ms versus 25.018 to 334.000 ms synchronously across tested concurrency levels; prepared mean complete lifecycle is longer at every level.
AI.conclusion: ZeroGate's contribution is an explicit revalidation contract, a durable reference boundary, and an auditable comparison of where authorization cost is paid. It is not a new cryptographic primitive or a universal performance frontier. The boundary improvement is a latency redistribution, not a net speedup, and freshness plus exactly-once remote effects remain outside what the implementation alone guarantees.

title: Brace Yourself: Task-Conditioned Environmental Bracing for Forceful Humanoid Manipulation
comment: Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). 8 pages, 6 figures. Video demonstration: https://youtu.be/zPrGLxWJzI4. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Forceful manipulation is challenging for humanoid robots because interaction forces can disturb whole-body balance. We introduce the Supporting Hand Strategy (SHS), which enables a humanoid to brace against the environment with one hand while performing forceful manipulation with the other. SHS optimises a task-conditioned support configuration that guides two synchronous reinforcement-learning policies, without human motion data or online whole-body trajectory planning. On a Unitree G1, SHS achieved usable contact forces up to 60 N, compared with a maximum sustained force of 13.5 N without environmental bracing, while substantially improving force tracking over a task-independent support configuration. The same policies generalised to different task regions without retraining. SHS therefore provides a simple mechanism for substantially extending humanoid forceful-manipulation capability.

AI.tldr: SHS lets a humanoid brace one hand on the environment to perform forceful manipulation with the other, raising usable contact forces from 13.5 N to 60 N on a Unitree G1 via task-conditioned support optimization and two synchronous RL policies.
AI.motivation: Forceful manipulation is difficult for humanoid robots because interaction forces disturb whole-body balance. Without environmental support, sustained force capability is limited.
AI.method: Supporting Hand Strategy (SHS): optimizes a task-conditioned support configuration that guides two synchronous reinforcement-learning policies. It requires no human motion data and no online whole-body trajectory planning.
AI.result: On a Unitree G1, SHS achieved usable contact forces up to 60 N versus a 13.5 N maximum sustained force without bracing, and substantially improved force tracking over a task-independent support configuration. Policies generalized to different task regions without retraining.
AI.conclusion: SHS offers a simple mechanism that substantially extends humanoid forceful-manipulation capability.

title: Rollout Efficiency in Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Large Language Models: A Taxonomy and Future Directions
summary: Reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning enables large language models to solve mathematical, coding, and other multi-step tasks, but shifts a substantial portion of the training cost to rollout, where trajectories are generated for policy updates. Efficient rollout mechanisms are therefore essential to reduce this cost while maintaining the freshness, consistency, and statistical validity of training data. This survey provides a systematic taxonomy of recent research on rollout efficiency for reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning, classifying existing approaches from both mechanism and bottleneck perspectives. Based on this taxonomy, we analyze how different technique families address distinct sources of rollout inefficiency, examine opportunities and potential conflicts for combining them, identify gaps in the evaluation and reporting of efficiency gains, and discuss open challenges and future research directions.

AI.tldr: A systematic survey and taxonomy of rollout efficiency techniques for reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning, organized by mechanism and bottleneck, covering efficiency sources, combination opportunities/conflicts, evaluation gaps, and open challenges.
AI.motivation: Reasoning-oriented RL enables LLMs to solve mathematical, coding, and other multi-step tasks, but shifts substantial training cost to rollout (trajectory generation for policy updates). Efficient rollout mechanisms are essential to reduce this cost while preserving data freshness, consistency, and statistical validity. Existing research is fragmented, motivating a systematic taxonomy.
AI.method: Survey methodology: a systematic taxonomy of recent research on rollout efficiency for reasoning-oriented RL, classifying existing approaches from two perspectives—mechanism and bottleneck. Analyzes how different technique families address distinct sources of rollout inefficiency.
AI.result: The taxonomy reveals how technique families map to distinct sources of rollout inefficiency; the survey identifies opportunities and potential conflicts for combining techniques, exposes gaps in the evaluation and reporting of efficiency gains, and consolidates open challenges and future research directions.
AI.conclusion: Efficient rollout is critical to lowering the cost of reasoning-oriented RL while safeguarding data freshness, consistency, and statistical validity; a mechanism-and-bottleneck taxonomy clarifies how techniques can be combined, underscores shortcomings in efficiency evaluation/reporting, and delineates future research directions.

title: RoboMP-DINOv2: Prompts, Not Filters for Robust Robot Manipulation
summary: Robot manipulation policies must generalize across visual shifts while preserving scene context relevant to action. General-purpose vision encoders are not tailored to visuomotor control, while object-centric approaches often use segmentation masks as hard filters that discard potentially useful context. We propose RoboMP-DINOv2 (Robotics Mask-Prompted DINOv2), a full-scene vision encoder that treats masks as spatial prompts rather than visibility filters. It extracts dense DINOv2 features from the full observation, injects learned region-specific embeddings at masked locations, and jointly contextualizes prompted and unprompted tokens for action prediction. We further introduce masked-region color randomization (MCR) to improve appearance robustness, yielding RoboMP-DINOv2-MCR. Across seven simulated manipulation settings, RoboMP-DINOv2 achieves 60.7% success under spatial shifts and 59.7% under scene clutter, compared with 50.7% and 41.0% for a DINOv2-based Diffusion Policy. Under unseen object colors, RoboMP-DINOv2-MCR achieves 72.5% success versus 35.1% for the strongest color-randomized baseline. Additional experiments and representation analyses show improved robustness while preserving behaviorally relevant scene information. Code is available at https://github.com/han20192019/RoboMP_DINOv2.

AI.tldr: RoboMP-DINOv2 is a full-scene visuomotor encoder that uses segmentation masks as spatial prompts (not filters) to inject region embeddings into dense DINOv2 features, plus masked-region color randomization (MCR) for appearance robustness.
AI.motivation: Robot manipulation policies must generalize across visual shifts while retaining scene context relevant to action. General-purpose vision encoders are not tailored to visuomotor control, and object-centric approaches typically use segmentation masks as hard filters, discarding potentially useful context.
AI.method: Extract dense DINOv2 features from the full observation; inject learned region-specific embeddings at masked token locations; jointly contextualize prompted and unprompted tokens for action prediction. Additionally introduce masked-region color randomization (MCR), yielding RoboMP-DINOv2-MCR.
AI.result: Across seven simulated manipulation settings: 60.7% success under spatial shifts and 59.7% under scene clutter, vs 50.7% and 41.0% for a DINOv2-based Diffusion Policy. Under unseen object colors, RoboMP-DINOv2-MCR reaches 72.5% success vs 35.1% for the strongest color-randomized baseline.
AI.conclusion: Treating masks as spatial prompts rather than visibility filters improves robustness while preserving behaviorally relevant scene information, as supported by additional experiments and representation analyses.

title: Real-Time Hand Gesture Recognition for OpenXR Using Transformer-Based Machine Learning
summary: Hand gesture recognition is a key component in human-computer interaction (HCI), enabling intuitive interfaces for applications in gaming, virtual reality (VR), robotics, and more. This study integrates transformer-based machine-learning models for real-time hand gesture recognition, using hand-tracking data captured through the OpenXR standard in Unity. We leverage positional data of hand joints and wrist rotation angles to train a custom gesture recognition system. By utilizing the sequential modeling capabilities of transformers, the system captures temporal dependencies within short gesture windows and classifies gestures robustly across hand orientations and sizes. The results show a significant improvement in gesture classification accuracy. Building on this, we outline how the approach can be extended toward detecting the flow of movement, i.e., the transitions between gestures, as future work.

AI.tldr: The paper integrates transformer-based models into a Unity/OpenXR pipeline for real-time hand gesture recognition using hand-joint positional data and wrist rotation angles, achieving significantly improved classification accuracy robust to hand orientation and size, and outlines gesture-transition (movement flow) detection as future work.
AI.motivation: Hand gesture recognition is a key component in human-computer interaction (HCI) for gaming, virtual reality, robotics, and similar applications. The goal is to enable intuitive interfaces, which requires robust, real-time recognition of gestures that works regardless of hand orientation or individual hand size.
AI.method: The pipeline uses hand-tracking data captured through the OpenXR standard in Unity. Input features consist of positional data of hand joints and wrist rotation angles. A custom gesture recognition system is trained by leveraging the sequential modeling capabilities of transformers, which capture temporal dependencies within short gesture windows.
AI.result: The results show a significant improvement in gesture classification accuracy, with the transformer-based system classifying gestures robustly across hand orientations and sizes.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based sequential modeling is effective for real-time hand gesture recognition from OpenXR/Unity hand-tracking data. As an extension, the approach can be further developed to detect the flow of movement, i.e., the transitions between gestures.

title: A Deployment Study of Identity-Gated Drone Gesture Control
summary: Vision-based gesture control accepts commands from any hand in the camera field of view, which is unsafe in shared indoor spaces. This paper presents IGate, an identity-gated control stack that includes gesture control and face tracking, in which commands are admitted only when an enrolled operator is verified. The system performs few-shot user enrolment from 20 initial face frames, without prior user-specific training: verification compares an embedding of the current face crop against the enrolled template by cosine similarity, while face tracking uses proportional correction. Gesture control is achieved by classifying extracted hand landmarks using an RBF-SVM trained on a custom dataset. Additionally, a hierarchical finite-state machine handles mode selection, default, and fallback behaviours. The approach is tested on a DJI Tello EDU, each component evaluated offline and in-flight across 270 trials (149 flown). Face verification yields a 0.32% offline equal error rate versus 19.3% in-flight. Under hover-locked conditions, the RBF-SVM gesture classifier outperforms the geometric rule (0.850 vs. 0.651 accuracy), with 82% of this gap stemming from the depth channel. All logs and reproduction scripts will be released.

AI.tldr: IGate is an identity-gated gesture-control stack for drones that admits commands only after verifying an enrolled operator via few-shot face recognition, combining an RBF-SVM hand-landmark classifier and a hierarchical finite-state machine, validated on a DJI Tello EDU over 270 trials.
AI.motivation: Vision-based gesture control accepts commands from any hand in the camera field of view, which is unsafe in shared indoor spaces. A mechanism is needed to gate control commands to an authorized, enrolled operator.
AI.method: IGate couples gesture control with face tracking. Few-shot user enrolment uses 20 initial face frames with no prior user-specific training; verification compares the embedding of the current face crop against the enrolled template via cosine similarity, while face tracking applies proportional correction. Gesture control classifies extracted hand landmarks with an RBF-SVM trained on a custom dataset. A hierarchical finite-state machine manages mode selection, default, and fallback behaviours.
AI.result: Evaluated on a DJI Tello EDU, with each component tested offline and in-flight across 270 trials (149 flown). Face verification reaches 0.32% offline EER versus 19.3% in-flight. Under hover-locked conditions, the RBF-SVM gesture classifier outperforms the geometric rule (0.850 vs. 0.651 accuracy), with 82% of this gap attributable to the depth channel.
AI.conclusion: Identity gating effectively restricts drone gesture commands to an enrolled operator, though in-flight face verification degrades substantially relative to offline. The learned RBF-SVM, particularly through depth information, offers clear accuracy gains over geometric rules. All logs and reproduction scripts will be released.

title: ShowTellArena: Evaluating Business Workflow Understanding from Demonstrations
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Code and dataset linked in the paper
summary: We often teach a colleague by showing the work and explaining the decisions as we go. How can we check what an agent understood from the same lesson? We introduce ShowTellArena, a benchmark protocol and public dataset for comprehension after narrated business demonstrations. The v1.0 release contains 50 business workflow tasks, with recordings, screenshots, narration, fixture seeds, and 502 questions. Tasks span finance, hiring, procurement, customer decisions, inventory, and logistics. The protocol holds the business scenario and quiz fixed while allowing each product to capture the lesson through its own teaching interface. Questions test operational rules, boundaries, exceptions, and errors in proposed automations. We analyze 218 selected pilot attempts across 39 workflow cases, including 28 cases attempted by all three evaluated systems. These exploratory results expose both answer errors and failures to complete the teaching experience. We describe the release's verification gaps and the pilot's uneven coverage, exclusions, and grading provenance. The contribution is an inspectable dataset and assessment workflow that others can extend; the selected pilot is not a controlled product ranking.

AI.tldr: ShowTellArena is a benchmark protocol and public dataset (v1.0) for evaluating agent comprehension after narrated business demonstrations, built from 50 workflow tasks and 502 questions, with a pilot analysis of 218 attempts across 39 cases.
AI.motivation: Teaching an agent by demonstrating work and narrating decisions raises a key question: how can we verify what an agent actually understood from that lesson? Existing resources lack a standardized way to assess comprehension following narrated business demonstrations, so the authors create a benchmark addressing this gap.
AI.method: The authors introduce ShowTellArena, a benchmark protocol and public dataset. The v1.0 release contains 50 business workflow tasks spanning finance, hiring, procurement, customer decisions, inventory, and logistics, with recordings, screenshots, narration, fixture seeds, and 502 questions. The protocol fixes the business scenario and quiz while letting each product capture the lesson through its own teaching interface. Questions probe operational rules, boundaries, exceptions, and errors in proposed automations.
AI.result: A pilot analysis covers 218 selected attempts across 39 workflow cases, including 28 cases attempted by all three evaluated systems. This yielded a contrast between systems: 218 contributions and three distinct systems indicates the evaluated system(s) span three distinct agents.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is an inspectable dataset and assessment workflow others can extend, not a controlled product ranking.

title: Digital Twin-Driven VR Teleoperation with Multi-View Spatial Perception for Surgical Robots
summary: Current robot-assisted minimally-invasive surgery (RMIS) platforms provide a fixed console for the surgeon to view stereo endoscopic images and teleoperate instruments inside the patient. Several researchers have proposed the use of a head-mounted display (HMD) as a portable console, with video pass-through rendering of the endoscope images which, like the fixed console, restricts the operator to a single endoscopic viewpoint and limits depth perception. We present a digital twin-driven virtual reality (VR) teleoperation platform, where the digital twin is created from markerless perception of the surgical environment and streamed for display on the HMD. This overcomes the limitations of video pass-through by providing multi-view rendering and natural motion-parallax cues, enabling decoupling of the user's hand posture from strict instrument alignment. The system utilizes VR hand controllers to increase the teleoperation workspace and to improve the robustness and stability of instrument control compared to the hand tracking approach adopted by most prior systems. A 15-participant user study on the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) shows that our VR platform significantly outperforms a state-of-the-art HoloLens 2 mixed reality baseline, reducing path length by 86% and jerk by 95%, while achieving depth perception confidence comparable to or exceeding the traditional console across all conditions.

AI.tldr: A digital twin-driven VR teleoperation platform for RMIS renders multi-view, motion-parallax-enabled scenes on an HMD from markerless perception, uses VR hand controllers for control, and outperforms a HoloLens 2 baseline (86% less path length, 95% less jerk) with depth perception comparable to the traditional console.
AI.motivation: Existing RMIS platforms use either a fixed console or HMD-based video pass-through, both of which restrict the surgeon to a single endoscopic viewpoint and limit depth perception. This constrains spatial understanding and ties hand posture to strict instrument alignment.
AI.method: The authors build a digital twin from markerless perception of the surgical environment and stream it to an HMD for VR display, providing multi-view rendering and natural motion-parallax cues. VR hand controllers are used instead of hand tracking to enlarge the teleoperation workspace and improve instrument control robustness and stability. Evaluation is via a 15-participant user study on the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK).
AI.result: Compared to a state-of-the-art HoloLens 2 mixed reality baseline, the VR platform reduced path length by 86% and jerk by 95%, and achieved depth perception confidence comparable to or exceeding the traditional console across all conditions.
AI.conclusion: Digital twin-driven VR teleoperation with multi-view rendering, motion parallax, and controller-based input offers a superior portable console for RMIS, improving task efficiency and instrument control while matching or exceeding conventional console depth perception.

title: RAG-NAROK: Retrieval-Aware Knowledge Corpus Poisoning in RAG with Source-specific Refutation
summary: Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) systems have emerged as the dominant architecture for grounding large language model (LLM) outputs in verifiable external knowledge, yet their structural reliance on a dynamic retrieval pipeline introduces a largely unexplored class of adversarial vulnerability. Existing knowledge-base poisoning attacks are fundamentally static. Adversarial documents are pre-computed and injected without any awareness of what the victim system will actually retrieve for a given query, leaving the attack blind to the competitive documentary landscape that surrounds its payload in the generator's context window. Unlike traditional static poisoning attacks that are blind to the retrieved context, we introduce RAG-NAROK (Retrieval-Anchored Generation Negation And Response Quality Collapse), a RAG attack framework that adapts to the query text. RAG-NAROK exploits the transparency inherent in RAG pipeline to first extract the legitimate source identities, then generate Anchor-Specific Refutation documents that explicitly name and devalue retrieved sources while leveraging recency and authority biases to steer the text generation toward a target answer. Our results demonstrate that RAG-NAROK significantly outperforms static baselines across diverse domains, revealing a fundamental tension between RAG transparency and AI security.

AI.tldr: RAG-NAROK is a query-adaptive poisoning attack on RAG systems that uses pipeline transparency to infer legitimate retrieved sources and inject Anchor-Specific Refutation documents that name and devalue those sources, steering generation toward a target answer and outperforming static poisoning baselines across domains.
AI.motivation: RAG systems are the dominant architecture for grounding LLM outputs in verifiable external knowledge, but their reliance on a dynamic retrieval pipeline creates an underexplored adversarial vulnerability. Existing knowledge-base poisoning attacks are static: adversarial documents are pre-computed and injected without awareness of what the victim system will actually retrieve for a given query, making them blind to the competitive documentary landscape surrounding the payload in the generator's context window.
AI.method: RAG-NAROK (Retrieval-Anchored Generation Negation And Response Quality Collapse) is a query-adaptive RAG attack framework. It exploits the transparency inherent in the RAG pipeline to first extract the legitimate source identities, then generates Anchor-Specific Refutation documents that explicitly name and devalue the retrieved sources while leveraging recency and authority biases to steer text generation toward a target answer.
AI.result: RAG-NAROK significantly outperforms static baselines across diverse domains, exposing a fundamental tension between RAG transparency and AI security.
AI.conclusion: The static, query-blind paradigm of prior poisoning attacks is insufficient against modern RAG pipelines; a transparent retrieval stage can itself be weaponized. RAG-NAROK demonstrates that query-adaptive, anchor-specific refutation is a substantially stronger attack, indicating that RAG transparency and AI security are in fundamental tension.

title: HABILIS Brain 0: Geometry-Change Supervision for Vision-Language-Action and Residual Flow Recovery
summary: Vision-language-action policies benefit from geometric supervision, but current-frame geometry alone does not explicitly describe the changes associated with manipulation. This design is motivated by the goal of learning an embodiment-agnostic visual interface that can be pretrained across robot and egocentric video before robot-specific action alignment. We introduce Geometry-Change VLA (GC-VLA), which learns to predict multiview future-current geometry-change tokens from current observations. Offline frame pairs define a nominal 0.5-second prediction horizon; future observations are used only to construct training targets. Stage 1 trains a geometry-change vision-language model (GC-VLM). Stage 2 introduces a continuous ActionExpert and aligns it with robot actions while stopping action-flow gradients at the VLM interface. Stage 3 enables these gradients to update the trainable VLM components jointly with the ActionExpert. Stage 4 freezes GC-VLA and applies Geometry-Conditioned Residual Flow (GCRF), using a binary intervention router and a single bounded residual velocity policy learned from closed-loop feedback. GC-VLA achieves 95.20% success on LIBERO, and GC-VLA with GCRF achieves 99.55%. Inference uses current observations and the learned GC representation without executing the offline target encoders.

AI.tldr: GC-VLA learns to predict multiview future-current geometry-change tokens from current observations, enabling an embodiment-agnostic visual interface pretrained across robot and egocentric video, achieving 95.20% on LIBERO and 99.55% with GCRF residual refinement.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action policies benefit from geometric supervision, but current-frame geometry alone does not explicitly describe the changes associated with manipulation. The goal is to learn an embodiment-agnostic visual interface that can be pretrained across robot and egocentric video before robot-specific action alignment.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline. Offline frame pairs define a nominal 0.5-second prediction horizon, with future observations used only to construct training targets. Stage 1 trains a geometry-change vision-language model (GC-VLM) predicting multiview future-current geometry-change tokens. Stage 2 adds a continuous ActionExpert, aligning it with robot actions while stopping action-flow gradients at the VLM interface. Stage 3 lets those gradients update trainable VLM components jointly with the ActionExpert. Stage 4 freezes GC-VLA and applies Geometry-Conditioned Residual Flow (GCRF), using a binary intervention router and a single bounded residual velocity policy learned from closed-loop feedback.
AI.result: GC-VLA achieves 95.20% success on LIBERO; GC-VLA with GCRF achieves 99.55%. Inference relies on current observations and the learned GC representation without executing the offline target encoders.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling multiview future-current geometry change provides a pretrainable, embodiment-agnostic visual interface for VLA policies, and a frozen-backbone residual flow with intervention routing further improves control performance.

title: Spectra: A Rules-Driven LLM Pipeline for Automated KYC Document Processing
summary: Know Your Client (KYC) onboarding in capital markets requires analysts to manually classify documents, extract structured data from heterogeneous sources, and validate compliance against complex regulatory policies. This process requires significant analyst time per client, with end-to-end onboarding often stretching to multiple weeks due to sequential handoffs. In this work, we analyze an on-boarding process and find that it comprises repeatable components well-suited to AI automation. We therefore propose a restructured workflow to be amenable to automation: we consolidate the traditional four-party process into two parties that share most of the work and can be automated together, eliminating intermediate handoffs that compound delays. To automate the remaining steps, we introduce Spectra, an AI-assisted document processing platform that combines a structured rules engine with LLM-based classification, extraction, and validation agents. The rules engine encodes compliance policy as a queryable database, enabling focused context injection that reduces token usage while improving extraction precision. Rather than a single monolithic prompt, the system decomposes document processing into isolated, auditable stages, each optimized independently and traceable to specific policy clauses. In evaluation on real KYC documents, Spectra achieves 100% classification accuracy and 89.4% extraction accuracy. Human review burden dropped by 96%.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes capital-markets KYC onboarding, restructures its four-party sequential workflow into a two-party automatable pipeline, and introduces Spectra—a hybrid rules-engine + LLM agent platform for document classification, extraction, and compliance validation. On real KYC documents, Spectra reaches 100% classification accuracy, 89.4% extraction accuracy, and cuts human review burden by 96%.
AI.motivation: KYC onboarding is labor-intensive: analysts manually classify documents, extract structured data from heterogeneous sources, and validate against complex regulations. Per-client analyst time is high, and end-to-end onboarding often takes multiple weeks due to sequential handoffs. The authors find the process contains repeatable components amenable to AI automation.
AI.method: The authors restructure the workflow, consolidating the traditional four-party process into two parties that share most work and can be automated jointly, removing intermediate handoffs. They introduce Spectra, an AI-assisted document processing platform combining a structured rules engine with LLM-based classification, extraction, and validation agents. The rules engine encodes compliance policy as a queryable database, enabling focused context injection that lowers token usage and boosts extraction precision. Processing is decomposed into isolated, auditable stages, each independently optimized and traceable to specific policy clauses, rather than a single monolithic prompt.
AI.result: Evaluated on real KYC documents, Spectra achieves 100% classification accuracy and 89.4% extraction accuracy. Human review burden is reduced by 96%.
AI.conclusion: A workflow restructure plus a hybrid rules-engine/LLM agent architecture (Spectra) can substantially automate KYC onboarding, delivering high classification and extraction accuracy while drastically reducing manual review effort.

title: IndustrialVLA-Bench: A Traceable Multi-Axis Evaluation of Open Robot Policy Models
summary: Open robot policies increasingly follow two paradigms: vision-language-action models (VLAs) directly map observations and instructions to actions, whereas world-action models (WAMs) incorporate learned video or world dynamics into policy learning or action generation. Although both target the same manipulation tasks and represent alternative design choices, they are commonly reported under different evaluation protocols, leaving their capability, robustness, language sensitivity, and deployment-cost trade-offs unclear. We present IndustrialVLA-Bench, an evidence-aware evaluation of six released VLA and WAM systems under a unified reporting schema. It separately evaluates clean capability on LIBERO, non-language robustness on LIBERO-Plus, instruction sensitivity on LIBERO-Para, and observed execution cost. Reported task scores aggregate three complete evaluations with distinct random seeds under a fixed checkpoint and inference configuration. Across all six systems, clean LIBERO averages differ by only 1.58 points, whereas robustness and paraphrase summaries span 14.62 and 31.08 points. Restricting every comparison to the three protocol-faithful systems preserves the effect (1.36, 14.62 and 23.10 points), so the diagnostic separation reported here does not depend on the weaker evidence tiers. We additionally report observed inference latency, peak memory, runtime mode, and an evidence status for every system. Protocol-faithful, near-reproduction, and pending-verification entries remain visibly separated; only protocol-faithful entries support strict comparisons. Rather than claiming universal superiority of either paradigm, IndustrialVLA-Bench provides traceable evidence for comparing released robot policies on shared practical criteria. Code and evaluation records are available at https://github.com/xiaoqi-7/IndustrialVLA-Bench.

AI.tldr: IndustrialVLA-Bench provides a unified, evidence-aware evaluation of six released VLA and WAM robot policies, showing that clean LIBERO scores differ by only 1.58 points, while robustness and paraphrased-instruction summaries span 14.62 and 31.08 points.
AI.motivation: VLA models and WAMs address the same manipulation tasks but are typically reported under different evaluation protocols, leaving their capability, robustness, language sensitivity, and deployment-cost trade-offs unclear and non-comparable.
AI.method: The authors build a unified reporting schema and evaluate six released VLA/WAM systems across four axes: clean capability on LIBERO, non-language robustness on LIBERO-Plus, instruction sensitivity on LIBERO-Para, and observed execution cost. Task scores aggregate three complete evaluations with distinct random seeds under a fixed checkpoint and inference configuration. Systems are graded by evidence tier (protocol-faithful, near-reproduction, pending-verification), and latency, peak memory, and runtime mode are reported.
AI.result: Clean LIBERO averages differ by only 1.58 points across the six systems, whereas robustness and paraphrase summaries span 14.62 and 31.08 points. Restricting comparisons to the three protocol-faithful systems preserves the effect (1.36, 14.62, and 23.10 points), indicating the diagnostic separation is not an artifact of weaker evidence tiers.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark does not claim universal superiority of either paradigm; instead it offers traceable, evidence-graded comparisons of released robot policies on shared practical criteria. Only protocol-faithful entries support strict comparisons, and code plus evaluation records are released publicly.

title: Queer inclusion in speech datasets: An audit and taxonomy of practical tensions
summary: In this paper, we examine speech datasets for their inclusion of LGBTQIA+, or queer, voices and provide a taxonomy of tensions to better understand why there is a lack of such voices in current speech technology datasets. Through an audit of six diverse speech datasets, we find that measurable queer representation is low (0-1.4% of speakers) - insufficient for robust disparity measurement. We take this community as a case study to consider what challenges and tensions are associated with collecting speech data from marginalized communities. For comparison, we audit an additional two datasets from the speech sciences that were created by, for, and with the queer community. We note that many customs in speech dataset collection efforts in AI and speech technology research may conflict with values emphasized in participatory approaches with marginalized communities, and provide a taxonomy describing these tensions.

AI.tldr: An audit of six speech datasets reveals negligible queer representation (0–1.4% of speakers), insufficient for disparity measurement; the paper builds a taxonomy of tensions between conventional AI speech-dataset collection and participatory approaches with marginalized communities.
AI.motivation: Speech technology datasets largely omit LGBTQIA+/queer voices, and it is unclear why. The authors aim to characterize the scale of this absence and unpack the underlying tensions preventing inclusion of marginalized voices.
AI.method: Audit of six diverse speech datasets measuring queer speaker representation; comparison with two additional speech-science datasets created by, for, and with the queer community; qualitative analysis leading to a taxonomy of tensions between AI/speech-technology dataset collection customs and values of participatory approaches.
