AI.result: Measurable queer representation is low (0–1.4% of speakers), too low for robust disparity measurement. Many dataset-collection customs in AI and speech technology research conflict with values emphasized in participatory work with marginalized communities.
AI.conclusion: Current speech datasets fail to adequately represent queer speakers, and existing collection practices are fundamentally at odds with participatory, community-centered values. The proposed taxonomy offers a framework for understanding and addressing these tensions.

title: Recording Hand-Held Laparoscopic Instrument Motion in the Operating Room: Magnetometer-Free Fusion of Inertial, Range and Visual Sensing
summary: Most minimally invasive procedures are still performed with hand-held laparoscopic instruments, yet only the endoscopic video is retained; the instrument motion that expresses surgical skill, and that could support skill assessment and robot learning, is lost. Pose from video alone remains millimeters to centimeters off, and an instrument-mounted inertial measurement unit (IMU) cannot rely on its magnetometer, whose field changed with tool pose and between sessions in our measurements. We present a surgical instrument-state logger that clips onto a conventional instrument without modifying the part that enters the patient and fuses a six-axis IMU and a time-of-flight (ToF) rangefinder with a markerless camera in an error-state Kalman filter under the remote center of motion (RCM) of the trocar. Heading comes from the shaft silhouette, segmented by a U-Net, in place of the magnetometer: the rotation-angle error is 0.200°, against 3.58° from the accelerometer and magnetometer alone. Against a Franka Research 3 manipulator, and without alignment to it, the displacement error over 300 translation trials was 1.21mm RMS and the relative-rotation error over 180 rotation trials 0.34° RMS. On continuous trajectories, tracked and displayed in real time, the absolute tip error was 1.22mm (programmed) and 3.04mm (teleoperated) after post-hoc tuning of three filter parameters, and the full fusion beat every sensor subset. Because the estimator uses no magnetic measurement, its accuracy does not rely on an undisturbed field. The same clip-on device could thus record metric tip trajectories during routine hand-held laparoscopy, while displaying the insertion depth and attitude that are hidden once the instrument is inside the patient.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a clip-on surgical instrument-state logger that fuses a six-axis IMU, a ToF rangefinder, and a markerless camera in an error-state Kalman filter constrained by the trocar's remote center of motion, replacing the unreliable magnetometer heading with a U-Net-segmented shaft silhouette. It achieves millimeter-to-sub-millimeter tracking accuracy validated against a Franka Research 3 manipulator, enabling metric tip-trajectory recording during routine hand-held laparoscopy.
AI.motivation: Most minimally invasive procedures still use hand-held laparoscopic instruments, but only endoscopic video is recorded; the instrument motion that encodes surgical skill—valuable for skill assessment and robot learning—is lost. Existing alternatives are inadequate: video-only pose estimation is off by millimeters to centimeters, and an instrument-mounted IMU cannot trust its magnetometer, whose field varied with tool pose and across sessions in the authors' measurements.
AI.method: A clip-on logger attaches to a conventional instrument without modifying the patient-entering portion. It fuses a six-axis IMU and a time-of-flight rangefinder with a markerless camera in an error-state Kalman filter under the remote center of motion (RCM) constraint of the trocar. Heading is derived from the shaft silhouette, segmented by a U-Net, instead of the magnetometer.
AI.result: Heading rotation-angle error was 0.200°, versus 3.58° using the accelerometer and magnetometer alone. Against a Franka Research 3 manipulator, without alignment to it, displacement error over 300 translation trials was 1.21 mm RMS and relative-rotation error over 180 rotation trials was 0.34° RMS. On continuous real-time-tracked trajectories, absolute tip error was 1.22 mm (programmed) and 3.04 mm (teleoperated) after post-hoc tuning of three filter parameters, and the full fusion outperformed every sensor subset.
AI.conclusion: Because the estimator uses no magnetic measurement, its accuracy does not depend on an undisturbed magnetic field. The same clip-on device could record metric tip trajectories during routine hand-held laparoscopy while displaying insertion depth and attitude that are otherwise hidden once the instrument is inside the patient.

title: Towards participatory speech dataset curation: A queer case study and conceptual framework
summary: In this paper, we motivate the need for a participatory speech dataset creation framework through a case study of the LGBTQIA+, or queer, community - a community with documented concerns about AI and reported harms, including attempts to develop 'gaydar' technologies that purportedly identify individuals as queer. We review common speech data collection practices, why these methods may be unsuitable for engaging with queer speakers, and discuss previous efforts in participatory AI with queer community engagement, as well as participatory endeavours specific to speech data collection for other marginalized communities. From this review, we develop a conceptual framework for participatory speech data curation by, for, and with marginalized communities drawing on insights from co-design and knowledge sharing. We propose a framework comprising overlapping and two-way processes of defining a community, project formulation, modes of participation, and personal autonomy.

AI.tldr: This paper argues for a participatory framework for speech dataset creation, illustrated via a case study of the LGBTQIA+ community, and proposes a conceptual framework of overlapping, two-way processes for marginalized-community-involved data curation.
AI.motivation: The LGBTQIA+ (queer) community has documented concerns about AI and reported harms, including attempts to build 'gaydar' technologies that purportedly identify individuals as queer. Common speech data collection practices may be unsuitable for engaging queer speakers, necessitating a more participatory approach.
AI.method: The authors conduct a review of common speech data collection practices and their unsuitability for queer speakers; previous participatory AI efforts with queer community engagement; and participatory speech data collection efforts for other marginalized communities. From this review, they develop a conceptual framework based on insights from co-design and knowledge sharing.
AI.result: A conceptual framework for participatory speech data curation by, for, and with marginalized communities, comprising four overlapping and two-way processes: defining a community, project formulation, modes of participation, and personal autonomy.
AI.conclusion: Participatory, community-centered approaches are needed for speech dataset creation to responsibly and ethically engage marginalized communities such as the queer community.

title: CableVLA: Simulation-Privileged Global-Local Representation Learning for Cable Routing
summary: Cable routing requires coordinated control of global cable topology and changing local contacts. We present CableVLA, an end-to-end multimodal vision-language-action framework that converts simulation-privileged supervision into deployable cable-topology and tactile representations. TopoHead distills node-level physics and current and future cable-topology information into causal visual context for the action expert. TacSense uses complementary frame and taxel branches to learn contact dynamics from resistive arrays, with simulator-derived kinematics and contact events providing supervision beyond the measured force map. A contact gate activates force-tactile residuals that refine the next 8 arm-and-gripper actions of a frozen topology-conditioned policy. Across 345 MuJoCo evaluations, CableVLA improves success from 62.6% for the $π_{0.5}$-V visual baseline to 84.9%. TacSense achieves pronounced gains in slip-transition recognition over a CNN-LSTM baseline with a similar parameter count, and this advantage persists under frozen-encoder probes. Topology prediction and 57-task tactile evaluations assess representation quality, while policy adaptation studies evaluate downstream control performance. Cross-simulator and real-robot comparisons further examine zero-shot policy transfer under changes in dynamics and sensing.

AI.tldr: CableVLA is an end-to-end multimodal vision-language-action framework for cable routing that distills simulation-privileged supervision into cable-topology and tactile representations, raising MuJoCo success from 62.6% to 84.9% over a visual baseline.
AI.motivation: Cable routing demands coordinated control of global cable topology and changing local contacts, which existing visual policies handle poorly because they lack explicit topology and contact-dynamics representations.
AI.method: TopoHead distills node-level physics and current/future cable-topology information into causal visual context for the action expert. TacSense fuses frame and taxel branches to learn contact dynamics from resistive arrays, supervised by simulator-derived kinematics and contact events beyond the measured force map. A contact gate activates force-tactile residuals that refine the next 8 arm-and-gripper actions of a frozen topology-conditioned policy.
AI.result: Across 345 MuJoCo evaluations, success improves from 62.6% (π0.5-V visual baseline) to 84.9%. TacSense shows pronounced gains in slip-transition recognition over a CNN-LSTM baseline at similar parameter count, persisting under frozen-encoder probes. Topology prediction and 57-task tactile evaluations assess representation quality; policy adaptation studies, cross-simulator, and real-robot comparisons examine zero-shot transfer under dynamic and sensing shifts.
AI.conclusion: Turning simulation-privileged supervision into deployable topology and tactile representations yields substantial gains in both representation quality and downstream cable-routing control, with advantages that transfer across simulators and to real robots.

title: SMTB: Fast Structure-Mapping with Tight Bounds
summary: Structure-mapping forms analogies by aligning systems of relationally connected elements based on shared structure instead of surface features. We introduce a new structure-mapping algorithm: Structure-Mapping with Tight Bounds (SMTB) that is 5--15x faster than the structure-mapping engine (SME) and about 50\% better at finding mappings in large nested domains. SMTB is part of the broader Cognitive Rule Engine (CRE) project, a flexible multi-language-compatible framework with an accessible Python interface to state-of-the-art C++ implementations of core algorithms commonly used in cognitive systems such as pattern matching, planning, and structure-mapping. CRE and SMTB are designed to work with a wide range of representation choices. Unlike SME, which biases higher-order correspondences in tree-like predicate logic, SMTB maximizes relational connectivity without privileging higher-order relations. This allows SMTB to work just as well over arbitrary relational graphs as it does in tree-like domains of nested predicate logic. We discuss situations where privileging "higher-orderness" in structure-mapping can cause issues, and illustrate how SMTB avoids failure modes that SME would encounter in these situations. We also provide an evaluation comparing SMTB to SME v4 over 5845 domain pairs from the SME corpus.

AI.tldr: SMTB is a new structure-mapping algorithm that is 5-15x faster than SME and ~50% better at finding mappings in large nested domains, part of the CRE framework.
AI.motivation: Structure-mapping aligns relationally connected elements via shared structure rather than surface features. SME, the dominant engine, biases higher-order correspondences in tree-like predicate logic, which can cause failure modes; a faster, representation-agnostic alternative is needed.
AI.method: SMTB (Structure-Mapping with Tight Bounds) maximizes relational connectivity without privileging higher-order relations, enabling operation over arbitrary relational graphs as well as tree-like nested predicate logic. It is embedded in the Cognitive Rule Engine (CRE), a multi-language framework with a Python interface to C++ implementations of cognitive algorithms (pattern matching, planning, structure-mapping).
AI.result: SMTB is 5-15x faster than SME and about 50% better at finding mappings in large nested domains. Evaluation compares SMTB to SME v4 over 5845 domain pairs from the SME corpus.
AI.conclusion: SMTB avoids failure modes that SME encounters by not privileging higher-orderness, offering efficient, flexible structure-mapping suitable for broader representation choices.

title: A Deployable Four-Finger Payload for Teleoperated Free-Flying Manipulation with Astrobee
summary: This article presents a bimanual teleoperation pipeline and conceptual design of a deployable four-finger payload for intra-vehicular free-flyers. Future habitats in low-Earth orbit (LEO) will require systems to perform mundane tasks like cargo handling and maintenance during crewed and uncrewed periods. The gripper payload provides 17 manipulation degrees-of-freedom (DoF) through four independently actuated fingers on a linear rail system. To control it, a virtual reality (VR) device interface maps the human ground operator's hand motions to the finger pairs, their separation to the rail, and common wrist motion to Astrobee translation. We present the preliminary results of teleoperating Astrobee in a custom zero-gravity MuJoCo-based International Space Station (ISS) simulator through ten repeated trials of transporting a rigid ISS Cargo Transfer Bag (CTB). We measure task success, continuous contact retention, completion time, and cargo motion.

AI.tldr: A VR-based bimanual teleoperation pipeline and a deployable four-finger gripper payload are presented for intra-vehicular free-flyers, with preliminary results from teleoperating Astrobee to transport a cargo bag in a zero-gravity ISS simulator.
AI.motivation: Future low-Earth orbit habitats will require autonomous or teleoperated systems to handle mundane tasks such as cargo handling and maintenance during both crewed and uncrewed periods.
AI.method: A deployable four-finger payload provides 17 manipulation degrees-of-freedom via four independently actuated fingers on a linear rail system. A VR interface maps the ground operator's hand motions to finger pairs, finger separation to the rail, and common wrist motion to Astrobee translation. Evaluation uses ten repeated trials of rigid cargo transfer bag transport in a custom zero-gravity MuJoCo-based ISS simulator.
AI.result: Preliminary results are reported for task success, continuous contact retention, completion time, and cargo motion across ten repeated trials.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a feasible bimanual teleoperation approach and gripper payload design for intra-vehicular free-flyers, with simulator-based validation using the Astrobee platform.

title: Weakly Supervised Quantum Error Mitigation
summary: Supervised approaches to quantum error mitigation learn a map from noisy circuit outputs to ideal ones, and therefore require the ideal outputs. Producing those ideal outputs demands noiseless classical simulation, whose cost grows exponentially with system size, so supervision is unavailable in exactly the regime where mitigation matters most. We ask whether cheap, individually unreliable signals drawn from circuit structure and hardware calibration can take the place of ideal labels. We assemble sixteen heuristic labeling functions (stabilizer and parity constraints, relaxation and readout characteristics, local depth, gate counts, and neighboring activity), reconcile their disagreements with a probabilistic label model, and read the resulting per-qubit error probabilities as a readout channel whose inverse mitigates the measured distribution. No ideal output enters the training path. On $147{,}000$ five-qubit circuits executed on two IBM devices, the method removes $24.3\%$ (Algiers) and $28.8\%$ (Hanoi) of the Kullback-Leibler divergence to the ideal distribution, against $15.4\%$ and $21.5\%$ for the strongest published analytical baseline, a margin that holds on both devices and lies far outside its bootstrap interval. Supervised neural models trained on ideal distributions remain stronger where such labels exist, and we quantify that gap rather than setting it aside; the method's claim is to the regime where they do not, since the labels they require cannot be computed for the circuits mitigation is needed for. The codes will be released shortly.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a label-free quantum error mitigation method that replaces ideal-output supervision with sixteen heuristic labeling functions reconciled by a probabilistic label model, achieving 24.3%–28.8% KL-divergence reduction on IBM hardware, outperforming analytical baselines without using any ideal labels.
AI.motivation: Supervised quantum error mitigation requires ideal circuit outputs as labels, which demand noiseless classical simulation whose cost grows exponentially with system size. Consequently, supervision is unavailable exactly in the large-scale regime where mitigation is most needed. The authors ask whether cheap, individually unreliable signals from circuit structure and hardware calibration can substitute for ideal labels.
AI.method: They assemble sixteen heuristic labeling functions—including stabilizer and parity constraints, relaxation and readout characteristics, local depth, gate counts, and neighboring activity—and reconcile their disagreements using a probabilistic label model. The resulting per-qubit error probabilities are interpreted as a readout channel, whose inverse mitigates the measured distribution. No ideal output enters the training path.
AI.result: On 147,000 five-qubit circuits run on two IBM devices, the method removes 24.3% (Algiers) and 28.8% (Hanoi) of the KL divergence to the ideal distribution, versus 15.4% and 21.5% for the strongest published analytical baseline. This margin holds across both devices and lies far outside its bootstrap interval.
AI.conclusion: Supervised neural models trained on ideal distributions remain stronger where such labels exist, and the authors quantify this gap rather than dismiss it. The method's contribution targets the regime where ideal labels cannot be computed—precisely the circuits for which mitigation is needed. Codes will be released shortly.

title: Relative Contact Velocity-Controlled Hand-Object Mechanism for Dexterous Tool Manipulation
summary: This work investigates how to enable general multi-finger robotic hands to perform the complete tool manipulation process, which entails picking up a tool, loading it into a suitable pose, and then wielding it. Inspired by human tool manipulation and mechanical design principles, we model the hand and the tool as a unified hand-object mechanism (HOM) composed of sub-assemblies. Specifically, we define a HOM as consisting of the hand, the object, and the generalized contact frames, allowing the HOM's motions to be expressed with the same set of Cartesian-space relative contact velocities, irrespective of the hand's kinematics and geometry. Then, we define a HOM's sub-assemblies as relative contact velocity and contact force constraints between fingers. Building on these definitions, we developed a lightweight and physically interpretable motion planning and contact estimation framework using least squares and a complementary filter. We evaluated our framework in simulation by teleoperating five different robotic hands. The results show that our framework enabled all five hands to execute the complete tool manipulation process, achieving dexterous behaviors even from identical, simple reference trajectories. Furthermore, the results showcase our framework's adaptability to different hands, tools, and tasks, enabled by its kinematic and geometric foundation.

AI.tldr: The paper models a hand and tool as a unified hand-object mechanism (HOM) made of sub-assemblies, and develops a lightweight, physically interpretable motion planning and contact estimation framework that lets general multi-finger hands perform the full tool manipulation process.
AI.motivation: Enabling general multi-finger robotic hands to perform the complete tool manipulation process—picking up a tool, loading it into a suitable pose, and wielding it—remains challenging. The work is inspired by human tool manipulation and mechanical design principles, aiming for a formulation independent of a hand's specific kinematics and geometry.
AI.method: They model the hand and tool as a unified HOM composed of sub-assemblies: the hand, the object, and generalized contact frames, so that HOM motions can be expressed with the same set of Cartesian-space relative contact velocities regardless of hand kinematics and geometry. Sub-assemblies are defined as relative contact velocity and contact force constraints between fingers. Based on these definitions, they build a lightweight, physically interpretable motion planning and contact estimation framework using least squares and a complementary filter.
AI.result: In simulation, teleoperating five different robotic hands, the framework enabled all five hands to execute the complete tool manipulation process, achieving dexterous behaviors even from identical, simple reference trajectories. It also demonstrated adaptability to different hands, tools, and tasks due to its kinematic and geometric foundation.
AI.conclusion: A unified HOM representation with sub-assembly constraints supports a simple least-squares/complementary-filter framework that generalizes across hands, tools, and tasks, enabling complete tool manipulation for diverse multi-finger robotic hands.

title: Recovering Agentic Sovereignty: Mitigating the Consensus Paradox via Contrastive Epistemic Decoding
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a parametric vulnerability to adversarial swarm consensus. To mitigate this sycophancy, we introduce Contrastive Epistemic Decoding (CED), a zero-shot inference intervention. Unlike standard Contrastive Decoding (CD) which relies on a weaker secondary model, CED utilizes a dual forward-pass on a single architecture to isolate conformity bias. By introducing a novel asymmetric, zero-bounded probability clamp and discrete top-k truncation mask, CED mathematically suppresses toxic consensus tokens without causing grammatical collapse. Evaluated across 7,200 paired trajectories on complex benchmarks (GAIA, SWE-bench, Multi-Challenge) using Gemma-2 (9B), Llama-3.1 (8B), and Mistral v0.3 (7B), CED successfully neutralizes architectural and positional biases. By reducing cognitive loafing by up to 33.00% absolute, CED drives significant performance gains, yielding up to a 30.75% accuracy recovery. Regaining sovereignty induces distinct architectural behaviors---passive task-focus in Gemma-2 and active refutation of the simulated swarm in Llama-3.1---showing CED decouples compliance from capability without fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: CED is a zero-shot decoding intervention that suppresses sycophantic swarm-conformity tokens in a single LLM via a dual forward-pass, an asymmetric zero-bounded clamp, and a top-k truncation mask, improving accuracy by up to 30.75% across three models.
AI.motivation: LLMs show parametric vulnerability to adversarial consensus (sycophancy toward a simulated swarm), which suppresses independent reasoning and causes cognitive loafing, degrading task accuracy without fine-tuning remedies.
AI.method: Contrastive Epistemic Decoding (CED), a zero-shot inference intervention: unlike standard Contrastive Decoding that needs a weaker secondary model, CED performs a dual forward-pass on one architecture to isolate conformity bias, using an asymmetric zero-bounded probability clamp plus a discrete top-k truncation mask to suppress consensus tokens while preserving fluency.
AI.result: Across 7,200 paired trajectories on GAIA, SWE-bench, and Multi-Challenge with Gemma-2 9B, Llama-3.1 8B, and Mistral v0.3 7B, CED neutralized architectural and positional biases, cut cognitive loafing by up to 33.00% absolute, and recovered up to 30.75% accuracy; behaviors diverged (passive task-focus in Gemma-2, active swarm refutation in Llama-3.1).
AI.conclusion: CED decouples compliance from capability without fine-tuning, restoring model sovereignty over adversarial consensus and yielding consistent performance gains.

title: From Instrument-Mounted Demonstrations to In-Vivo Execution: Learning Bimanual Laparoscopic Appendectomy Without Robot-Collected Demonstrations
summary: Most minimally invasive surgery is still performed with hand-held laparoscopic instruments, and the surgeon's instrument kinematics are lost when the operation ends; only the endoscope video is kept. This paper presents an end-to-end pipeline that captures this motion in the operating room and uses it to train a surgical robot policy, validated on live animals. We introduce a surgical instrument-state logger that mounts on the shaft of a standard laparoscopic instrument and recovers its pose and jaw state from an inertial sensor, a time-of-flight sensor and a Hall sensor, with no external camera or tracker. A data pipeline measures the latency of every sensor channel against a robot ground truth and aligns the channels before forming observation-action pairs. On these demonstrations we train a diffusion policy with a fine-tuned DINOv3 backbone, selecting its design by closed-loop rollouts in a physics simulator reconstructed from depth maps of an ex-vivo rabbit appendix. The policy is then retrained on 849 in-vivo demonstrations from four live rabbits and deployed on four additional live rabbits with electrosurgery armed. With the surgeon selecting the surgical phase, the policy completed the appendectomy in three of the four animals. The results show that demonstrations recorded from a surgeon's own instruments are sufficient to train, select and deploy a bimanual surgical policy in vivo. The robot serves only as the timing reference for sensor calibration and as the executor, and collects no demonstrations. Both demonstration corpora are released to support future surgical robot learning research.

AI.tldr: A pipeline captures surgeon instrument motion via an on-shaft sensor logger and converts it into demonstration data to train and deploy a bimanual diffusion policy that performs live rabbit appendectomy.
AI.motivation: Most minimally invasive surgery is done with hand-held laparoscopic instruments, and instrument kinematics are discarded after surgery—only endoscope video is retained. This lost motion is a potential source of surgical robot learning data.
AI.method: An instrument-state logger mounted on a standard laparoscopic instrument shaft recovers pose and jaw state from inertial, time-of-flight, and Hall sensors without external camera or tracker. A data pipeline measures per-channel latency against robot ground truth and aligns channels into observation-action pairs. A diffusion policy with a fine-tuned DINOv3 backbone is designed via closed-loop rollouts in a physics simulator reconstructed from depth maps of an ex-vivo rabbit appendix, then retrained on 849 in-vivo demonstrations from four live rabbits.
AI.result: Deployed on four additional live rabbits with electrosurgery armed, the policy completed the appendectomy in three of four animals with the surgeon selecting the surgical phase. The robot served only as timing reference for calibration and as executor, collecting no demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrations recorded from a surgeon's own instruments are sufficient to train, select, and deploy a bimanual surgical policy in vivo. Both demonstration corpora are released to support future surgical robot learning research.

title: A Behavioral Trait Leaks into Preferences: Diagnosing Trait Interference in LLM User Simulators
summary: LLM-based user simulators aim to bridge the offline-online gap in recommender evaluation by emulating users through injected traits, where preference attributes determine what a user engages with and a behavioral activity trait governs how long they browse. However, we show this intended trait independence collapses during simulation, causing two failures: (i) Trait Interference, where amplified activity distorts preference boundaries and forces interactions with mismatched items to sustain browsing, and (ii) Evaluation Invalidity, where satisfaction scores inflate with activity-driven page counts despite taste mismatches, biasing evaluation toward trait distributions rather than recommender performance. To resolve this, we propose PQA, a page-level quality anchoring method that guides simulators using a personalized anchor reflecting each user's intrinsic preference standard. By assessing whether a page meets this standard before further browsing, PQA enables proactive exits from low-quality pages, letting the activity trait retain its intended role of modulating browsing depth within preference-conforming pages. Experiments show PQA mitigates trait interference and improves the reliability of LLM-based simulator evaluation under activity shifts. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaehyun1/PQA

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that trait independence in LLM-based user simulators collapses, causing Trait Interference and Evaluation Invalidity, and proposes PQA, a page-level quality anchoring method that uses personalized preference standards to enable proactive browsing exits and restore reliable simulator evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLM-based user simulators are intended to bridge the offline-online gap in recommender evaluation by independently injecting preference attributes (what a user engages with) and a behavioral activity trait (how long they browse). The authors reveal that this assumed trait independence breaks down during simulation, producing biased and unreliable evaluations.
AI.method: The paper proposes PQA (Page-level Quality Anchoring), which guides simulators using a personalized anchor reflecting each user's intrinsic preference standard. PQA assesses whether a page meets this standard before allowing further browsing, thereby enabling proactive exits from low-quality pages and confining the activity trait to modulating browsing depth only within preference-conforming pages.
AI.result: Experiments show that PQA mitigates trait interference and improves the reliability of LLM-based simulator evaluation under activity shifts.
AI.conclusion: The intended independence between preference and activity traits in LLM-based user simulators does not hold, leading to Trait Interference and Evaluation Invalidity. Anchoring page-level quality to a personalized preference standard (PQA) restores the intended role of activity as a within-preference browsing-depth modulator, yielding more reliable recommender evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/chaehyun1/PQA.

title: MachEmbodied-U0: Unified Understanding and Generation Model for Embodied Intelligence
comment: Technical report. Project page: https://machembodied.com/ME-U/ME-U0.html. Code: https://github.com/MachEmbodied/ME-U0
summary: General-purpose robot control requires models to understand task intent, identify where to interact, capture how the scene evolves, and generate precise actions. Vision-language-action models provide strong semantic priors but typically do not explicitly model scene dynamics, while world-action models couple visual prediction with control without necessarily exposing the task-relevant semantic and spatial structure needed for fine-grained manipulation. We present MachEmbodied-U0 (ME-U0), a unified embodied foundation model connecting understanding and generation experts through a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture. Subtask prediction and affordance grounding guide joint visual-dynamics and action generation via flow matching. Visual dynamics encompass future RGB, depth, surface normals, and optical flow, providing complementary supervision for appearance, geometry, and motion. Multi-rate Rotary Position Encoding (MRPE) aligns visual dynamics with fine-grained control. We pretrain ME-U0 on approximately 4,200 hours of curated demonstrations from robotic datasets and egocentric datasets. Using only the supervision natively available in each downstream benchmark, ME-U0 achieves an average score of 17.66 on the RoboDojo simulation benchmark and average success rates of 99.0\% and 82.5\% on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, respectively. We additionally validate ME-U0 on real-world robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness beyond simulation. Without corresponding downstream supervision, ME-U0 further demonstrates zero-shot subtask prediction, affordance grounding, and visual dynamics on simulated and real-world observations. Overall, ME-U0 combines competitive downstream control performance with transferable task-grounding and visual-dynamics capabilities across simulation and the real world.

AI.tldr: ME-U0 is a unified embodied foundation model that couples understanding and generation experts via a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, using subtask prediction and affordance grounding to guide joint visual-dynamics and action generation through flow matching, achieving strong control performance and zero-shot task-grounding capabilities.
AI.motivation: General-purpose robot control requires understanding task intent, identifying interaction locations, capturing scene evolution, and generating precise actions. Existing vision-language-action models provide strong semantic priors but lack explicit scene-dynamics modeling, while world-action models couple visual prediction with control without exposing the task-relevant semantic and spatial structure needed for fine-grained manipulation.
AI.method: ME-U0 connects understanding and generation experts through a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture. Subtask prediction and affordance grounding guide joint visual-dynamics and action generation via flow matching. Visual dynamics cover future RGB, depth, surface normals, and optical flow, offering complementary supervision for appearance, geometry, and motion. Multi-rate Rotary Position Encoding (MRPE) aligns visual dynamics with fine-grained control. It is pretrained on ~4,200 hours of curated demonstrations from robotic and egocentric datasets.
AI.result: Using only natively available downstream supervision, ME-U0 scores an average of 17.66 on RoboDojo and achieves 99.0% and 82.5% average success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. It is also validated on real-world manipulation tasks. Without downstream supervision, it performs zero-shot subtask prediction, affordance grounding, and visual dynamics on simulated and real-world observations.
AI.conclusion: ME-U0 combines competitive downstream control performance with transferable task-grounding and visual-dynamics capabilities across both simulation and the real world.

title: Direct Optimization of Generators for Search in Automated Theorem Proving
summary: Fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly advance Automated Theorem Proving (ATP), but are often deployed as guiding policies within tree search rather than for single-attempt generation. Recent work shows cross entropy is suboptimal for an LLM used in flat search strategies such as aggregation or filtering and that work has developed new loss functions to correct this misalignment. Extending this alignment to tree search is more challenging: proof discovery depends on exploration and recovery through off-trace states that supervised demonstrations do not reveal. We extend Compute-Aligned Training (CAT) to this setting through an abstraction of policy-guided search, deriving tractable, trace-supported losses. Alongside these search-aware losses, we introduce a search-agnostic uniform-allocation (UA) loss that accounts for the budget without specifying the specific search. Both induce scalar weights on per-tactic cross-entropy gradients. We characterize how off-trace behavior affects the search-aware weights, including conditions for vanishing approximation error at large budgets. On a Lean benchmark, both approaches achieve higher observed proof-success rates than cross-entropy across six search strategies, with strong results from a single shared UA adapter. Budget sweeps show larger gains over cross-entropy at 16 than at 256 expansions, implying CAT scales with test time compute.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Compute-Aligned Training (CAT) to policy-guided tree search for LLM-based automated theorem proving, deriving tractable trace-supported search-aware losses plus a search-agnostic uniform-allocation (UA) loss, both of which outperform cross-entropy across six search strategies on a Lean benchmark and scale with test-time compute.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuned LLMs are typically deployed as guiding policies within tree search, but cross-entropy is suboptimal for such usage—recent work corrected this misalignment only for flat search strategies (aggregation/filtering). Extending alignment to tree search is harder because proof discovery relies on exploration and recovery through off-trace states that supervised demonstrations do not reveal.
AI.method: The authors extend Compute-Aligned Training (CAT) to the tree-search setting via an abstraction of policy-guided search, deriving tractable, trace-supported losses. They also introduce a search-agnostic uniform-allocation (UA) loss that accounts for the computation budget without specifying the particular search. Both losses induce scalar weights on per-tactic cross-entropy gradients, and the work characterizes how off-trace behavior affects the search-aware weights, including conditions for vanishing approximation error at large budgets.
AI.result: On a Lean benchmark, both approaches achieve higher observed proof-success rates than cross-entropy across six search strategies, with strong results from a single shared UA adapter. Budget sweeps show larger gains over cross-entropy at 16 expansions than at 256 expansions, implying CAT scales with test-time compute.
AI.conclusion: Aligning training objectives with compute-allocated tree search—either through search-aware or search-agnostic losses—yields consistent proof-success improvements over standard cross-entropy, and the benefits grow with test-time compute, supporting CAT as a scalable training paradigm for LLM-guided theorem proving.

title: PAKT: Physically-Aligned Kinesthetic Teaching for Reinforcement Learning
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables, Conference on Robot Learning
summary: Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) systems still struggle with the demands of contact-rich industrial manipulation, including micrometer-level precision, success rates above 99%, and human-level cycle times. Although off-policy algorithms can improve performance by leveraging demonstrations and interventions, a key bottleneck is the lack of an intuitive interface for collecting such guidance while complying with constraints of the physical system and the policy. We propose PAKT, a framework for kinesthetic teaching in RL. As opposed to teleoperation approaches, PAKT relies on kinesthetic guidance, which is widely used in industry. However, a critical weakness of kinesthetic guidance is the possibility for the operator to move the robot along trajectories (e.g., velocities, accelerations, jerk) that the robot and/or policy cannot physically reproduce. Using PAKT, operators guide the robot through admittance control, which maps human-applied forces to motion. The downstream reference generator applies the same kinematic limits used during policy execution, keeping the collected trajectories within these limits. To support this teaching interface with an appropriate execution layer, PAKT adds a high-performance control stack that maps low-frequency RL actions to high-frequency torque commands. It consists of a reference generator and subsequent impedance controller, where the reference generator preserves the tracking performance of the impedance controller while improving contact handling and producing smoother policy actions. Across the reported runs on four insertion and industrial assembly benchmarks, including a data center compute tray, the end-to-end system reduces cycle time by 23%-48% and cumulative intervention count by 62%-86% relative to the HIL-SERL baseline. Project website: https://pakt-website.github.io/pakt-website}{https://pakt-website.github.io/pakt-website

AI.tldr: PAKT is a kinesthetic teaching framework for real-world RL that constrains operator guidance within the robot's kinematic limits via admittance control and a reference generator, paired with a high-performance control stack that maps low-frequency RL actions to high-frequency torque commands, reducing cycle time and interventions on industrial manipulation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Real-world RL systems struggle with contact-rich industrial manipulation requiring micrometer-level precision, >99% success rates, and human-level cycle times. Off-policy algorithms benefit from demonstrations/interventions, but lack an intuitive interface for collecting guidance while respecting physical system and policy constraints. Teleoperation approaches are less suited to industry, where kinesthetic guidance is common—yet kinesthetic guidance risks operators commanding trajectories the robot/policy cannot physically reproduce.
AI.method: PAKT enables operators to guide the robot through admittance control, mapping human-applied forces to motion, with a downstream reference generator enforcing the same kinematic limits used during policy execution. It also adds a high-performance control stack consisting of a reference generator and subsequent impedance controller, mapping low-frequency RL actions to high-frequency torque commands while preserving tracking performance, improving contact handling, and producing smoother policy actions.
AI.result: On four insertion and industrial assembly benchmarks, including a data center compute tray, the end-to-end system reduces cycle time by 23%-48% and cumulative intervention count by 62%-86% relative to the HIL-SERL baseline.
AI.conclusion: PAKT provides a practical kinesthetic teaching interface for real-world RL that keeps collected trajectories physically reproducible and improves execution, yielding substantial gains in cycle time and intervention efficiency for contact-rich industrial manipulation.

title: Gaze responses to false-positive computer-aided detection prompts during colonoscopy: a paired-video and real-time eye-tracking study
summary: False-positive computer-aided detection (CADe) prompts may divert endoscopists' attention during colonoscopy, yet the attentional impact of individual prompts remains unclear. We used event-locked eye tracking to quantify gaze attraction and attention occupation in complementary retrospective and prospective studies. In a retrospective paired-video experiment, 3 senior and 2 novice endoscopists viewed 60 colonoscopy videos with and without CADe. The prospective study recorded gaze during 42 real-time CADe-assisted colonoscopies performed by 9 senior endoscopists. Screened CADe prompts outside expert-annotated lesion windows were classified as false-positive artifact events. False-positive prompts attracted gaze in 48.6% (68/140) of retrospective observations and 65.2% (533/817) of prospective events. Among attraction events with complete recovery, median attention occupation lasted 1000 ms in the retrospective study and 1100 ms in the prospective study. Corresponding median prompt durations were 33 ms and 267 ms, with median time amplifications of 17.55-fold and 5.15-fold, respectively. In paired retrospective comparisons, visible artifact prompts drew gaze closer to the prompted region than did the same-coordinate unassisted reference. Secondary retrospective analyses showed high lesion gaze recognition without and with CADe (98.0% versus 99.0%). First gaze entry into lesion regions occurred 147.8 ms earlier with CADe. Across controlled and real-time clinical settings, false-positive CADe prompts frequently captured gaze, with attention persisting beyond prompt visibility. These findings support considering prompt-related attentional burden in CADe evaluation and design.

AI.tldr: Event-locked eye tracking shows false-positive CADe prompts frequently capture endoscopists' gaze, producing attention occupation that persists well beyond prompt visibility (up to ~17x amplification in retrospective settings).
AI.motivation: False-positive CADe (computer-aided detection) prompts are suspected to divert endoscopists' attention during colonoscopy, but the attentional impact of individual prompts has remained unclear. The authors aimed to quantify gaze attraction and attention occupation caused by false-positive CADe prompts.
AI.method: Two complementary studies using event-locked eye tracking: (1) a retrospective paired-video experiment in which 3 senior and 2 novice endoscopists viewed 60 colonoscopy videos with and without CADe, and (2) a prospective study recording gaze during 42 real-time CADe-assisted colonoscopies by 9 senior endoscopists. CADe prompts falling outside expert-annotated lesion windows were classified as false-positive artifact events; gaze attraction, attention occupation, and time amplification (attention occupation relative to prompt duration) were measured.
AI.result: False-positive prompts attracted gaze in 48.6% (68/140) of retrospective observations and 65.2% (533/817) of prospective events. For attention events with complete recovery, median attention occupation was 1000 ms (retrospective) and 1100 ms (prospective), while median prompt durations were 33 ms and 267 ms—giving median time amplifications of 17.55-fold and 5.15-fold. In paired comparisons, visible artifact prompts drew gaze closer to the prompted region than the same-coordinate unassisted reference. Lesion gaze recognition remained high without and with CADe (98.0% vs 99.0%), and first gaze entry into lesion regions occurred 147.8 ms earlier with CADe.
AI.conclusion: Across controlled and real-time clinical settings, false-positive CADe prompts frequently capture gaze, with attention persisting far beyond prompt visibility. Prompt-related attentional burden should be considered in CADe evaluation and design.

title: DynaForge: Planning-Guided Residual Learning for Dynamic Manipulation Demonstration Generation
summary: Dynamic object manipulation is essential for robots operating in real-world environments, yet methods for generating high-quality demonstrations remain limited. Methods designed for static tasks do not readily transfer to dynamic settings. Among dynamic demonstration generators, planning-based methods can fail near contact, while DOMINO-style replay simplifies dynamic interactions and may limit the experience available for policy learning. We present DynaForge, a planning-guided framework that learns residual corrections for dynamic manipulation demonstration generation. DynaForge combines low-frequency global planning with high-frequency object-centric inverse kinematics across task phases, and applies a residual policy to correct actions during dynamic interaction. An implicit curriculum groups rollouts under matched conditions and selects mixed-success groups, focusing residual reinforcement learning on the evolving competence frontier. On Can and Bottle, it uses 0.73x as many optimizer steps as vanilla GRPO at the same nominal environment-step budget, with higher observed final success rates. Across nine simulation tasks, DynaForge increases mean demonstration-generation success from 41.30% of the planning prior to 78.37%. With 800 demonstrations per task, DP3 policies trained on DynaForge data achieve 49.11% mean success, compared with 7.07% for DOMINO data. On three real-world dynamic tasks, DynaForge-trained policies achieve 30-60% success, compared with 0-10% for DOMINO-trained policies, showing the ability of DynaForge for sim-to-real transfer.

AI.tldr: DynaForge is a planning-guided framework that learns residual corrections for dynamic manipulation demonstration generation, substantially outperforming prior methods in simulation and real-world sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Dynamic object manipulation is essential for robots in real-world environments, but high-quality demonstration generation remains limited. Static-task methods do not transfer well to dynamic settings. Planning-based generators can fail near contact, while DOMINO-style replay oversimplifies dynamic interactions, limiting the experience available for policy learning.
AI.method: DynaForge combines low-frequency global planning with high-frequency object-centric inverse kinematics across task phases, and applies a residual policy to correct actions during dynamic interaction. An implicit curriculum groups rollouts under matched conditions and selects mixed-success groups, concentrating residual reinforcement learning on the evolving competence frontier.
AI.result: On Can and Bottle, DynaForge uses 0.73x as many optimizer steps as vanilla GRPO at the same nominal environment-step budget, with higher observed final success rates. Across nine simulation tasks, mean demonstration-generation success rises from 41.30% (planning prior) to 78.37%. With 800 demonstrations per task, DP3 policies trained on DynaForge data reach 49.11% mean success versus 7.07% for DOMINO data. On three real-world dynamic tasks, DynaForge-trained policies achieve 30-60% success versus 0-10% for DOMINO.
AI.conclusion: DynaForge demonstrates strong gains in dynamic demonstration-generation success and downstream policy performance, and shows effective sim-to-real transfer, substantially surpassing DOMINO-style replay baselines.

title: Transformer Heads Looking for Order
summary: In this note, we show that the problem of checking, whether a sequence of bits is ordered, is not doable by 1-head 1-layer transformers but is doable by a 2-head 1-layer transformer. Unlike similar previous results, our results assume the model where transformers have an output MLP.

AI.tldr: Checking whether a bit sequence is ordered cannot be done by 1-head 1-layer transformers but can be done by 2-head 1-layer transformers, even when an output MLP is included.
AI.motivation: Prior separations between transformer capabilities often rely on models without an output MLP. This work revisits the ordered-sequence checking problem under the more realistic assumption that transformers include an output MLP, testing whether earlier head-count separations still hold.
AI.method: The authors analyze the expressive power of 1-layer transformers with an output MLP. They prove an impossibility result for 1-head transformers on the orderedness-checking task and construct an explicit 2-head 1-layer transformer that solves it.
AI.result: The orderedness-checking problem is not solvable by 1-head 1-layer transformers but is solvable by 2-head 1-layer transformers, under the model where transformers have an output MLP.
AI.conclusion: The head-count separation persists even with an output MLP, sharpening the boundary between 1-head and 2-head 1-layer transformers for orderedness checking.

title: RoboFollow: Unveiling the Instruction Following Mirage in Embodied Agents
summary: Modern embodied agents achieve impressive success rates, yet their actual instruction-following ability is far weaker than these numbers suggest. We trace this illusion to a structural property we term low scene entropy: when a visual scene admits only one valid task, language becomes redundant and a policy can score highly while barely using it. We introduce RoboFollow, a diagnostic benchmark with three principles: (1) High Scene Entropy: each training scene supports multiple kinematically distinct task branches, making vision alone insufficient and forcing reliance on language. (2) Hierarchical Diagnostic Protocol: a four-level protocol (L0--L3) progressively perturbs visual layout and semantics, probing whether equivalent instructions yield consistent behavior and distinct ones yield discriminable behavior across spatial relations, attributes, trajectory constraints, and logic. (3) Confound-Controlled Diagnosis: we simplify interaction objects, restrict actions to the trained repertoire and report stage-wise Intent and Execution scores, isolating comprehension from motor execution. Evaluation of nine VLA and WAM policies shows that strong L0 performance, where attained, does not reliably transfer to L1--L3 under our fine-tuning setup. Representative mitigations, including stronger VLM backbones, QA co-training, LangForce, and Classifier-Free Guidance, all fail to close this gap. RoboFollow exposes genuine instruction following as a critical, overlooked bottleneck. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/RoboFollow and https://huggingface.co/datasets/AutoLab-SJTU/robofollow-data.

AI.tldr: RoboFollow is a diagnostic benchmark built on the principle of high scene entropy that exposes the gap between high embodied success rates and genuine instruction-following ability in VLA and WAM policies.
AI.motivation: Modern embodied agents report impressive success rates, but their actual instruction-following ability is weaker than these numbers imply. The authors attribute this illusion to low scene entropy: when a scene admits only one valid task, language is redundant, allowing a policy to score highly while barely using it.
AI.method: RoboFollow rests on three principles: (1) High Scene Entropy, where each training scene supports multiple kinematically distinct task branches so vision alone is insufficient and language becomes necessary; (2) a Hierarchical Diagnostic Protocol with four levels (L0-L3) that progressively perturb visual layout and semantics to test whether equivalent instructions yield consistent behavior and distinct instructions yield discriminable behavior across spatial relations, attributes, trajectory constraints, and logic; and (3) Confound-Controlled Diagnosis, which simplifies interaction objects, restricts actions to the trained repertoire, and reports stage-wise Intent and Execution scores to separate comprehension from motor execution.
AI.result: Evaluating nine VLA and WAM policies shows that strong L0 performance, where achieved, does not reliably transfer to L1-L3 under the fine-tuning setup. Representative mitigations, including stronger VLM backbones, QA co-training, LangForce, and Classifier-Free Guidance, all fail to close the gap.
AI.conclusion: RoboFollow exposes genuine instruction following as a critical, overlooked bottleneck in embodied agents. Code and dataset are released publicly.

title: Evaluating Coding Agents on Kernel Exploit Generation
summary: Coding agents now find real vulnerabilities in production software. However, bug discovery results do not measure whether agents can construct exploit primitives. We introduce KEX-bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on exploit primitive generation against real operating-system kernels. KEX-bench contains 45 task instances across 40 Linux and Windows CVEs, covering kernel address leak, instruction-pointer control, heap read, heap write, and arbitrary address write. Each task runs in an isolated virtual machine, exposes controlled tools, and uses a deterministic verifier to check primitive-specific success. We evaluate state-of-the-art coding agents paired with frontier and open-weight models under fixed tool-call budgets. Without a reference proof of concept (PoC), the strongest configuration solves 1 of 20 Windows tasks (5.0%) and 14 of 25 Linux tasks (56.0%). With a reference PoC, the strongest configuration solves 31 of 45 tasks (68.9%). This highlights the gap where agents reach kernel crashes but fail to shape kernel state into exploit primitives. We release KEX-bench for reproducible research on AI-assisted exploitation at https://kex-bench.github.io.

AI.tldr: KEX-bench is a benchmark of 45 tasks across 40 Linux/Windows kernel CVEs that evaluates coding agents on exploit primitive generation, not just vulnerability discovery. Under fixed tool-call budgets, the best configuration solves 1/20 Windows (5.0%) and 14/25 Linux (56.0%) tasks without a reference PoC, rising to 31/45 (68.9%) with a reference PoC.
AI.motivation: Bug discovery results do not measure whether coding agents can construct exploit primitives. The authors aim to close this evaluation gap by testing whether agents can shape kernel state into usable primitives against real OS kernels.
AI.method: KEX-bench comprises 45 task instances across 40 Linux and Windows CVEs, covering kernel address leak, instruction-pointer control, heap read, heap write, and arbitrary address write. Each task runs in an isolated virtual machine, exposes controlled tools, and uses a deterministic verifier to check primitive-specific success. State-of-the-art coding agents paired with frontier and open-weight models are evaluated under fixed tool-call budgets, both with and without a reference proof of concept (PoC).
AI.result: Without a reference PoC, the strongest configuration solves 1 of 20 Windows tasks (5.0%) and 14 of 25 Linux tasks (56.0%). With a reference PoC, the strongest configuration solves 31 of 45 tasks (68.9%).
AI.conclusion: There is a substantial gap: agents can often reach kernel crashes but fail to shape kernel state into exploit primitives, especially on Windows. KEX-bench is released for reproducible research on AI-assisted exploitation.

title: A Reconfigurable Bidirectional Cable-Driven Hip Exoskeleton with Swappable Bench/Backpack Dual-configuration Actuation
summary: Hip exoskeletons provide an important hardware basis for lower-limb rehabilitation and locomotor assistance. Laboratory rehabilitation assessment and system development require substantial actuation and computing resources, whereas mobile assistance requires untethered portability. Integrating both capabilities within one reusable platform remains a central design challenge. This paper presents a reconfigurable bidirectional cable-driven hip exoskeleton platform that rapidly switches between bench-mounted and backpack-mounted actuation while sharing one cable-free wearable hip interface. The platform modularly adapts the actuation configuration, end-effector sensing path, and low-level control interface. Each cable-driven end-effector weighs 0.405 kg, excluding the cable and actuation unit, and integrates an encoder and a torque sensor; experiments validated bench-mounted admittance-based motion tracking capability and backpack-mounted open-loop torque tracking. Human-worn experiments with three healthy participants used myoMOTION to evaluate the platform's wearable-side hip-motion sensing capability, verified bench-to-backpack and backpack-to-bench motion-ready switching across 30 trials in $30.1\pm16.3$ s, and formed a small-scale multimodal wearable-exoskeleton gait dataset for sensing validation and data-driven algorithm development, comprising 8 min bench-mounted treadmill records and 11 min backpack-mounted outdoor walking records. These results show that, by unifying the wearable structure, actuation interface, and sensing path, the proposed platform enables validation of the same hip exoskeleton in both bench-mounted and backpack-mounted configurations, providing reusable hardware for iterative development and applications across scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a reconfigurable bidirectional cable-driven hip exoskeleton platform that switches between bench-mounted and backpack-mounted actuation while sharing a single cable-free wearable hip interface.
AI.motivation: Hip exoskeletons are key hardware for lower-limb rehabilitation and locomotor assistance, but laboratory assessment and development demand substantial actuation and computing resources, while mobile assistance requires untethered portability. Integrating both capabilities into one reusable platform remains a central design challenge.
AI.method: A reconfigurable bidirectional cable-driven hip exoskeleton platform is developed that rapidly switches between bench-mounted and backpack-mounted actuation while sharing one cable-free wearable hip interface. The platform modularly adapts its actuation configuration, end-effector sensing path, and low-level control interface. Each cable-driven end-effector (0.405 kg excluding cable and actuation unit) integrates an encoder and a torque sensor. Experiments validated bench-mounted admittance-based motion tracking and backpack-mounted open-loop torque tracking. Human-worn experiments with three healthy participants used myoMOTION to assess wearable-side hip-motion sensing and to verify motion-ready switching across 30 trials.
AI.result: Bench-mounted admittance-based motion tracking and backpack-mounted open-loop torque tracking were validated. Bench-to-backpack and backpack-to-bench motion-ready switching was verified across 30 trials in 30.1±16.3 s. A small-scale multimodal wearable-exoskeleton gait dataset was formed, comprising 8 min of bench-mounted treadmill records and 11 min of backpack-mounted outdoor walking records.
AI.conclusion: By unifying the wearable structure, actuation interface, and sensing path, the proposed platform enables validation of the same hip exoskeleton in both bench-mounted and backpack-mounted configurations, providing reusable hardware for iterative development and applications across scenarios.

title: ArticleMiner: Ontology-Guided Knowledge Graph Construction from Scientific Publications
summary: Scientific papers keep much of their quantitative content in tables and supplementary files, where a number means something only through its header, caption, unit, analytical method, and the conventions of its field. Recovering the rows and columns of a table is therefore not the same as recovering the scientific fact it reports. Most semantic table-interpretation methods assume that a clean table is already available and subsequently map its cells or columns to ontology terms, whereas most publication-level extraction systems are designed for a single domain. We study a middle path: a shared process that reads a paper and its supplementary files, gathers evidence from several parsers and a language model, and reconciles that evidence, while a bounded human-authored task module for each task supplies the domain meaning. The module lists the canonical names the graph may use, the surface forms that map to them, a small set of derivation rules and validity constraints, an identity key, and the bindings used to write RDF. It defines what a task is allowed to emit; it does not try to list every convention of a field. We build four such modules (for drug-discovery chemistry, materials science, machine learning, and mineral geochemistry) in the ArticleMiner framework, and evaluate them on 163 papers, including a new geochemistry benchmark with expert-curated ground truth. In comparisons against a same-LLM few-shot baseline, the point estimates favor ArticleMiner on all four tasks, with uncertainty on the two smaller benchmarks. The geochemistry comparison also includes access to supplementary files, so its improvement cannot be attributed to domain guidance alone.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ArticleMiner, a middle-path framework that combines a shared evidence-gathering and reconciliation pipeline (multiple parsers + a language model) with bounded, human-authored task modules that encode domain meaning, enabling cross-domain extraction of scientific facts from papers and supplementary files (demonstrated on four domains and 163 papers).
AI.motivation: Quantitative scientific content resides in tables and supplementary files, where numbers gain meaning only through headers, captions, units, analytical methods, and field conventions; recovering rows/columns is not equivalent to recovering the reported scientific fact. Existing semantic table-interpretation methods assume a clean table already exists and map cells/columns to ontology terms, while publication-level extraction systems are mostly single-domain. A method that reconciles multi-source evidence while remaining adaptable across domains is therefore needed.
AI.method: A shared process reads a paper and its supplementary files, collects evidence from several parsers and a language model, and reconciles that evidence, while a bounded human-authored task module per task supplies domain meaning. Each module specifies canonical names for the graph, surface forms mapping to them, a small set of derivation rules and validity constraints, an identity key, and RDF write bindings—defining what a task may emit without enumerating every field convention. Four modules (drug-discovery chemistry, materials science, machine learning, mineral geochemistry) are built in the ArticleMiner framework.
AI.result: Evaluation on 163 papers, including a new geochemistry benchmark with expert-curated ground truth, shows that against a same-LLM few-shot baseline, point estimates favor ArticleMiner on all four tasks, with uncertainty on the two smaller benchmarks. The geochemistry comparison also includes access to supplementary files, so its improvement cannot be attributed to domain guidance alone.
AI.conclusion: A middle path—shared evidence-gathering/reconciliation plus bounded, human-authored domain modules—yields consistent (though in some cases statistically uncertain) gains over a same-LLM few-shot baseline across four scientific domains, indicating that combining general extraction infrastructure with lightweight domain guidance is a viable strategy for cross-domain scientific fact extraction.

title: Contact-Stable Deformable Tissue Simulation Using Implicit Integration and Live-Pose Grasp Constraints for Laparoscopic Surgery Robot Policy Evaluation
summary: Closed-loop evaluation of surgical robots requires tissue that deforms, can be grasped and lifted, and reproduces the anatomy in which the robot will operate. We present a simulator in which this tissue is reconstructed from a fixed-view RGB-D recording of the surgical field, composited to remove the instruments, closed into watertight volumes and tetrahedralised; the pipeline was applied unchanged to three specimens of two species (thirteen organs, 146,061 tetrahedra, no inverted elements). For one specimen, the organs are placed in a bimanual cell in which two Franka FR3 arms operate motorised instruments through 6 mm trocars. The core contribution is the numerical and contact design that keeps this cell stable: implicit integration, simulation meshes separate from collision meshes, numerical guards, and a grasp constraint captured at the live tissue pose. In 45 repeated grasp-lifts, a friction grasp held the tissue in 0 of 15 trials and each constraint grasp in 13 of 15; on displaced tissue, a rest-pose constraint produced one-step snaps of up to 17.8 mm, which live-pose capture eliminates. Against the recording, front-surface depth error is 1.33 to 1.41 mm, organ silhouette IoU is 0.80, and in five grasp-lifts reproduced from video the landmark displacement RMSE is 11.8 mm against 14.2 mm for a static prediction. Biofidelity is not claimed; the environment is intended for closed-loop feasibility, safety, contact and policy screening.

AI.tldr: A closed-loop surgical-robot simulator reconstructs deformable, graspable tissue from fixed-view RGB-D recordings (13 organs across 3 specimens, 146k tetrahedra) and keeps a bimanual Franka cell stable via implicit integration, separated sim/collision meshes, numerical guards, and live-pose grasp constraints.
AI.motivation: Closed-loop evaluation of surgical robots needs tissue that deforms, can be grasped and lifted, and reproduces the operative anatomy. Existing phantoms/simulators struggle to provide all three, and contact-rich bimanual cells are numerically unstable, so the paper targets a stable environment for feasibility, safety, contact, and policy screening (biofidelity explicitly not claimed).
AI.method: Fixed-view RGB-D recording of the surgical field is composited to remove instruments, closed into watertight volumes, and tetrahedralised; the unchanged pipeline is applied to 3 specimens (2 species, 13 organs, 146,061 tetrahedra, no inverted elements). One specimen is placed in a bimanual cell with two Franka FR3 arms driving motorised instruments through 6 mm trocars. Stability comes from implicit integration, simulation meshes decoupled from collision meshes, numerical guards, and a grasp constraint captured at the live tissue pose (vs. rest pose).
AI.result: Across 45 repeated grasp-lifts, a friction grasp held tissue in 0/15 trials while each constraint grasp held in 13/15. On displaced tissue, the rest-pose constraint caused one-step snaps up to 17.8 mm, eliminated by live-pose capture. Against the recording: front-surface depth error 1.33-1.41 mm, organ silhouette IoU 0.80; in five video-reproduced grasp-lifts landmark displacement RMSE was 11.8 mm vs. 14.2 mm for a static prediction.
AI.conclusion: The reconstruction plus contact/constraint design yields a stable, realistic-from-recording bimanual surgical simulation cell suited to closed-loop feasibility, safety, contact, and policy screening; biofidelity is not claimed and the organ reconstruction pipeline is reusable across specimens without modification.

title: Reasoning-Preserving Fine-Tuning of Post-RL LLMs with Null-Basis LoRA
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training has become an effective approach for eliciting reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs). However, adapting post-RL models to new knowledge domains or behaviors through subsequent supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can severely overwrite these capabilities. Existing approaches mitigate such forgetting through experience replay, specialized initialization, or constrained optimization using gradient projection, but either provide limited preservation or incur substantial training overhead. Our analysis shows that reasoning activations concentrate in low-dimensional subspaces, leaving substantial null-space capacity for adaptation, and that the corresponding approximate null spaces can be reliably estimated from a modest number of examples. Motivated by these observations, we propose Null-Basis Low-Rank Adaptation (NB-LoRA), a parameter-efficient method for adapting post-RL LLMs while preserving their acquired reasoning ability. We formulate reasoning retention as a layer-wise hidden-state preservation constraint and construct a fixed approximate null basis from reasoning activations. LoRA updates are then reparameterized through this basis, enforcing the preservation constraint throughout fine-tuning. Extensive experiments across multiple RL-trained LLMs and diverse downstream tasks show that NB-LoRA matches standard LoRA in adaptation performance, maintains reasoning accuracy near pre-fine-tuning levels, and generalizes this preservation to held-out reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: NB-LoRA reparameterizes LoRA updates through a fixed approximate null basis derived from reasoning activations, preserving RL-acquired reasoning in LLMs during subsequent SFT while matching standard LoRA adaptation performance.
AI.motivation: RL-based post-training elicits strong reasoning in LLMs, but subsequent supervised fine-tuning for new domains/behaviors severely overwrites these capabilities. Existing mitigations (experience replay, specialized initialization, gradient-projection constrained optimization) either preserve poorly or add substantial training overhead.
AI.method: The authors observe that reasoning activations concentrate in low-dimensional subspaces, leaving large null-space capacity for adaptation, and that these approximate null spaces can be reliably estimated from few examples. They formulate reasoning retention as a layer-wise hidden-state preservation constraint and build a fixed approximate null basis from reasoning activations. LoRA updates are reparameterized through this basis, enforcing the constraint throughout fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across multiple RL-trained LLMs and diverse downstream tasks, NB-LoRA matches standard LoRA on adaptation performance, keeps reasoning accuracy near pre-fine-tuning levels, and generalizes preservation to held-out reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: NB-LoRA provides a parameter-efficient solution to the reasoning-forgetting problem in post-RL LLM adaptation by constraining LoRA updates to an estimated null space, achieving both effective adaptation and robust reasoning retention without significant training overhead.

title: Skill Sequence Planning for Collaborative Multi-Robot Construction
summary: Robots have significant potential to automate construction processes. However, their industry adoption remains limited, partly because of the programming effort required to adapt robots to diverse tasks. This paper presents a skill sequence planning method that enables a heterogeneous team of multi-functional robots to collaboratively perform construction assembly work using reusable, preprogrammed skills such as grasping, drilling, and fastening. A central controller transforms the digital representation of the building into a construction relationship graph that represents construction entities, their states, and their parent-child relationships. Based on this representation, the system selects the next construction target, generates a symbolic sequence of skills for capable members of the robot team, and produces collision-free geometric motion plans for skill execution. The symbolic planning problem is dynamically regenerated as the construction state changes. An interactive digital twin presents the planned skill sequence and robot states to human co-workers for review and approval before execution. The method is evaluated through a construction assembly case study. By reducing the need to program robots separately for each task variation, the proposed approach supports more flexible deployment of collaborative robot teams in construction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a skill sequence planning method enabling a heterogeneous team of multi-functional robots to collaboratively perform construction assembly using reusable preprogrammed skills, coordinated via a construction relationship graph derived from the building's digital representation.
AI.motivation: Robots have significant potential to automate construction, but industry adoption remains limited partly due to the programming effort required to adapt robots to diverse tasks. The work aims to reduce the need to separately program robots for each task variation and support more flexible deployment of collaborative robot teams.
AI.method: A central controller transforms the digital representation of the building into a construction relationship graph encoding construction entities, their states, and parent-child relationships. Based on this, the system selects the next construction target, generates a symbolic skill sequence for capable team members using reusable preprogrammed skills (e.g., grasping, drilling, fastening), and produces collision-free geometric motion plans. The symbolic planning problem is dynamically regenerated as construction state changes, and an interactive digital twin presents the planned skill sequence and robot states to human co-workers for review and approval before execution.
AI.result: The method is evaluated through a construction assembly case study.
AI.conclusion: By reducing the need to program robots separately for each task variation, the proposed approach supports more flexible deployment of collaborative robot teams in construction.

title: ChatT2: An Adaptive Framework for Developing a Large Language Model-Based Agent for Natural Product Domain Research
summary: Scientific investigations into microbial natural products (NPs) present significant challenges for novices, largely due to the complexity of microbial systems, biochemical diversity, technical skill requirements, and the demands of bioinformatics and data analysis processes. To address these issues, we introduce ChatT2, a large language model (LLM)-based agent that is specifically tailored to the unique characteristics of bacterial type II polyketides. These polyketides form a structurally distinct and therapeutically important NP family. ChatT2 was developed within an autonomous multiagent framework composed of a mentor, an executor, and an evaluator, each with defined responsibilities. The mentor acts as an intermediary between ChatT2 and the user, utilizing chain-of-thought prompting to refine the intent of the user. Under the guidance of the mentor, the executor synthesizes multimodal information via retrieval-augmented generation techniques and seamlessly integrates bioinformatics and cheminformatics tools. The evaluator ultimately assesses the output of the executor to ensure the richness and accuracy of the retrieved information. Our research highlights how ChatT2, designed with this multiagent framework, addresses the challenges faced by general LLMs in terms of understanding limited, specialized corpora and complex biological information and provides both experts and novices with a valuable tool for exploring various NPs of interest. The ChatT2 webserver can be accessed at https://chatt2.site/#/chat.

AI.tldr: ChatT2 is an LLM-based multiagent system (mentor, executor, evaluator) specialized for bacterial type II polyketides, enabling both experts and novices to navigate microbial natural product research through refined intent parsing, retrieval-augmented synthesis of multimodal information, and integrated bioinformatics/cheminformatics tools.
AI.motivation: Microbial natural product (NP) investigation is challenging for novices because of microbial system complexity, biochemical diversity, technical skill demands, and burdensome bioinformatics and data analysis. General LLMs struggle with limited, specialized corpora and complex biological information in this domain, creating a need for a tailored agent.
AI.method: ChatT2 is built on an autonomous multiagent framework with three defined roles: a mentor, an executor, and an evaluator. The mentor mediates between the user and ChatT2, using chain-of-thought prompting to refine user intent. The executor, guided by the mentor, synthesizes multimodal information via retrieval-augmented generation and integrates bioinformatics and cheminformatics tools. The evaluator assesses the executor's output to ensure richness and accuracy of retrieved information. The system is specialized for bacterial type II polyketides, a structurally distinct and therapeutically important NP family.
AI.result: ChatT2 addresses the difficulties general LLMs face with limited, specialized corpora and complex biological information, and provides a valuable tool for both experts and novices to explore various NPs of interest. A webserver is available at https://chatt2.site/#/chat.
AI.conclusion: A domain-specialized, multiagent LLM framework with clearly separated mentor, executor, and evaluator roles effectively mitigates the barriers novices face in microbial NP research, offering an accessible platform for exploring bacterial type II polyketides and potentially other NPs.

title: PhyVisGen: Physically and Visually High-Fidelity Robotic Manipulation Data Generation
