summary: Large-scale manipulation demonstrations are essential for learning robust visuomotor policies, yet real-world data collection is expensive and difficult to scale. Simulation offers a promising alternative, but physical and visual discrepancies can limit the transferability of synthetic data, particularly for manipulation with soft grippers. We present PhyVisGen, a physically and visually high-fidelity framework for scalable robotic manipulation data generation. On the physical side, PhyVisGen introduces an arm-gripper coupling method based on the Incremental Potential Contact (IPC), enabling high-fidelity soft contact throughout complete manipulation trajectories. On the visual side, it combines real-scene reconstruction with real-time path tracing to generate visually realistic observations while preserving captured scene appearance. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate the physical and visual fidelity of PhyVisGen. Policies trained exclusively on synthetic manipulation demonstrations achieve 65-95% success across five real-robot tasks, without real-robot demonstration data or policy fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: PhyVisGen is a high-fidelity framework for scalable robotic manipulation data generation, combining IPC-based soft-contact physics with real-scene reconstruction and real-time path tracing; policies trained purely on its synthetic data achieve 65-95% success on five real-robot tasks without real demonstrations or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Large-scale manipulation demonstrations are needed for robust visuomotor policies, but real-world data collection is expensive and hard to scale. Simulation is a promising alternative, yet physical and visual discrepancies limit sim-to-real transferability, especially for soft-gripper manipulation.
AI.method: PhyVisGen addresses both fidelity dimensions. Physically, it introduces an arm-gripper coupling method based on Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) to enable high-fidelity soft contact across complete manipulation trajectories. Visually, it combines real-scene reconstruction with real-time path tracing to generate realistic observations while preserving captured scene appearance.
AI.result: Quantitative evaluations confirm the physical and visual fidelity of PhyVisGen. Policies trained exclusively on its synthetic demonstrations achieve 65-95% success across five real-robot tasks, requiring no real-robot demonstration data and no policy fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: PhyVisGen demonstrates that jointly achieving high physical and visual fidelity in simulation can yield transferable visuomotor policies trained solely on synthetic data, offering a scalable path to soft-gripper manipulation data generation without real-world collection.

title: Ladders of Thought: A Self-Evolving Curriculum of Progressively Simplified Reasoning Traces
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at reasoning when scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but small- and mid-scale models remain brittle reasoners even with knowledge distillation (KD). We present Ladders-of-Thought (LoT), a framework that improves reasoning by combining progressive question rewrites with a self-evolving curriculum. LoT automatically generates semantically faithful but easier variants of reasoning problems, organizes them into difficulty buckets using step-based measures, and employs a self-evolving bandit scheduler to allocate training adaptively. Evaluated on two reasoning domains, math and multi-hop reasoning, across 1-8B models from different families, LoT consistently improves over KD. It delivers large gains on arithmetic tasks (e.g., +32 percentage points on AddSub, +25pp on SVAMP), +2-8pp improvements on in-domain test splits, and strong though dataset-dependent benefits on multi-hop reasoning (e.g., +16pp on QASC, +25pp on StrategyQA). LoT also converges faster than staged curricula, highlighting the value of adaptive progression. These results show that progressive rewrites coupled with adaptive curricula provide a simple yet effective recipe for strengthening reasoning in smaller LLMs.

AI.tldr: LoT improves reasoning in small-to-mid LLMs by generating easier, semantically faithful rewrites of problems and scheduling them via a self-evolving bandit curriculum, beating knowledge distillation across math and multi-hop tasks.
AI.motivation: Small- and mid-scale LLMs remain brittle reasoners even with knowledge distillation, while large models reason well only at huge scale; there is a need for a simple, effective recipe to strengthen reasoning in smaller models.
AI.method: Ladders-of-Thought (LoT) combines progressive question rewrites with a self-evolving curriculum: it auto-generates semantically faithful but easier variants of reasoning problems, buckets them by difficulty using step-based measures, and uses a self-evolving bandit scheduler to allocate training adaptively.
AI.result: Across math and multi-hop reasoning on 1-8B models from different families, LoT consistently beats KD: +32pp on AddSub, +25pp on SVAMP, +2-8pp on in-domain test splits, +16pp on QASC, and +25pp on StrategyQA; it also converges faster than staged curricula.
AI.conclusion: Progressive rewrites coupled with adaptive curricula offer a simple yet effective recipe for strengthening reasoning in smaller LLMs.

title: CODA: Depth-Aligned Scene Completion and Object Decomposition from a Single RGB-D Image
summary: Robots operating safely in cluttered everyday environments often need to infer scene geometry from partial observations. Methods that detect objects in 2D and reconstruct them independently struggle in such scenes: a missed object is never reconstructed, a merged detection can fuse two objects, and separately reconstructed meshes may overlap or fail to touch their supporting surfaces. We introduce CODA (Complete Once, Decompose Afterward), a generative model that instead reconstructs the complete scene geometry from a single unsegmented RGB-D image, then separates the surface into the surrounding environment and movable objects. Still, generated scene geometry can drift from the observed partial point cloud. To reduce this drift, CODA uses two explicit 3D grounding mechanisms to keep reconstructed geometry consistent with observed surfaces while completing unseen regions. Experiments on HomebrewedDB and our custom cluttered-scene dataset show more accurate reconstructions and a higher fraction of objects remaining in place under simulated gravity than both object-first and scene-first baselines.

AI.tldr: CODA reconstructs complete scene geometry from a single unsegmented RGB-D image, then decomposes it into environment and movable objects, using two 3D grounding mechanisms to stay consistent with observed surfaces.
AI.motivation: Robots in cluttered everyday environments must infer scene geometry from partial observations. Existing object-first methods (2D detection + independent reconstruction) fail in such scenes: missed objects are never reconstructed, merged detections fuse objects, and independently reconstructed meshes may overlap or fail to touch supporting surfaces.
AI.method: CODA (Complete Once, Decompose Afterward) is a generative model that reconstructs the complete scene geometry from one unsegmented RGB-D image, then separates the surface into the surrounding environment and movable objects. Two explicit 3D grounding mechanisms are used to reduce drift of generated geometry from the observed partial point cloud, keeping reconstructed geometry consistent with observed surfaces while completing unseen regions.
AI.result: On HomebrewedDB and a custom cluttered-scene dataset, CODA achieves more accurate reconstructions and a higher fraction of objects remaining in place under simulated gravity than both object-first and scene-first baselines.
AI.conclusion: Reconstructing complete scene geometry first and decomposing afterward, with explicit 3D grounding, outperforms object-first and scene-first approaches for safe robot operation in cluttered scenes.

title: Testing-Driven Reliability Audit of Trajectory-Based Early Outcome Prediction for LLM Agents: Target-Specific Calibration Transfer Persists Within a Single Benchmark
summary: Predicting early outcomes based on trajectory can decrease the expenses associated with agent evaluation by terminating a run once the outcome becomes sufficiently predictable, assuming that the predictor's confidence is properly calibrated. Calibration is at risk when a predictor is applied to an agent on which it was never trained, but it is not known whether such transfer failures are broad across agent systems or concentrated in specific target agent/head combinations. Using public SWE-bench Verified trajectories and a frozen dual-head early-outcome prediction pipeline, we ran a leave-one-agent-out calibration audit, a shared-predictor leave-two-agents-out control, oracle prior correction, and a robustness battery over training cohorts, task resampling, task halves, jackknife, and thresholds. Fixed-scaffold TerminalBench analysis served as a pre-registered boundary test. Broad same-predictor pairwise heterogeneity was not supported; the median pairwise corrected-gap differences were 0.0180 (SUCCESS head, 45 pairs) and 0.0385 (FAILURE head, 35 pairs), and the pre-registered heterogeneity criterion was not met on either head. Two specific combinations, gpt-5-mini/SUCCESS and claude-opus-4.6/FAILURE, showed persistent calibration-transfer errors (median corrected gaps 0.1377 and 0.1107) without a sign reversal under any frozen control. TerminalBench did not establish cross-benchmark replication: the success target produced zero decisions (INDETERMINATE), and the failure target did not satisfy the pre-registered persistence criterion. Therefore, a strong target-specific calibration-transfer error can exist within one frozen environment, but the evidence does not establish that the error is intrinsic to the model or general across benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Using SWE-bench Verified trajectories and a frozen dual-head early-outcome predictor, a leave-one-agent-out calibration audit found no broad same-predictor heterogeneity across agents; instead, two specific target agent/head combinations showed persistent calibration-transfer errors, and a pre-registered TerminalBench boundary test failed to replicate the effect across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Early-outcome prediction can cut agent evaluation costs by terminating runs once outcomes are predictable, but this relies on well-calibrated predictor confidence. Calibration may break down when a predictor is applied to an agent it was never trained on. It was unknown whether such transfer failures are broad across agent systems or concentrated in specific target agent/head combinations, motivating a structured audit of calibration transfer.
AI.method: The study used public SWE-bench Verified trajectories with a frozen dual-head (SUCCESS/FAILURE) early-outcome prediction pipeline. It conducted a leave-one-agent-out calibration audit, a shared-predictor leave-two-agents-out control, oracle prior correction, and a robustness battery spanning training cohorts, task resampling, task halves, jackknife, and thresholds. A fixed-scaffold TerminalBench analysis served as a pre-registered boundary test.
AI.result: Broad same-predictor pairwise heterogeneity was not supported: median pairwise corrected-gap differences were 0.0180 (SUCCESS head, 45 pairs) and 0.0385 (FAILURE head, 35 pairs), and the pre-registered heterogeneity criterion was unmet on both heads. Two combinations, gpt-5-mini/SUCCESS and claude-opus-4.6/FAILURE, showed persistent calibration-transfer errors (median corrected gaps 0.1377 and 0.1107) without sign reversal under any frozen control. TerminalBench did not establish cross-benchmark replication: the success target yielded zero decisions (INDETERMINATE) and the failure target missed the pre-registered persistence criterion.
AI.conclusion: A strong target-specific calibration-transfer error can exist within one frozen environment, but the evidence does not establish that this error is intrinsic to the model or general across benchmarks. Transfer failures appear concentrated rather than broad, and cross-benchmark generalization remains unconfirmed.

title: History-Conditioned Flow Matching for Probabilistic Dynamics of Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots
summary: Deterministic dynamics modeling of tendon-driven continuum robots remains challenging owing to uncertainties in material behavior, tendon transmission, friction, and contact. Measured joint configurations and nominal tendon commands do not fully characterize these internal mechanical factors, leaving uncertainty in the subsequent motion. We therefore develop a history-conditioned, physics-informed flow-matching framework for probabilistic dynamics prediction, using motion and actuation histories to predict the distribution of the next complete joint configuration. By recursively sampling next-step configurations under prescribed commands, the model predicts distributions of future whole-body motions. In simulation, scenario-specific models achieve five-second trajectory Energy Scores (lower is better) of 12.05 mm under internal friction variation and 9.29 mm under unobserved actuation disturbances. Relative to the conditional variational autoencoder and diffusion baselines, Flow attains lower Energy Scores and coverage closer to the nominal level in both scenarios. Ablations support history and structural conditioning in both scenarios. On the physical robot, predictions under two tendon-command profiles excluded from training capture the principal motion sequences, with five-second Energy Scores of 11.91 and 11.42 mm, lower than the compared baselines. The predicted-to-measured spread ratios are 1.65 and 1.22 (closer to 1 is better). These results support history-conditioned probabilistic dynamics prediction under incomplete mechanical observations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a history-conditioned, physics-informed flow-matching framework for probabilistic dynamics prediction of tendon-driven continuum robots, predicting distributions of future joint configurations from motion and actuation histories, and outperforming CVAE and diffusion baselines in simulation and on a physical robot.
AI.motivation: Deterministic dynamics modeling of tendon-driven continuum robots is difficult due to uncertainties in material behavior, tendon transmission, friction, and contact. Measured joint configurations and nominal tendon commands do not fully capture these internal mechanical factors, leaving residual uncertainty in subsequent motion that must be modeled probabilistically.
AI.method: A history-conditioned, physics-informed flow-matching framework for probabilistic dynamics prediction. It uses motion and actuation histories to predict the distribution of the next complete joint configuration, and recursively samples next-step configurations under prescribed commands to predict distributions of future whole-body motions. Baselines: conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) and diffusion. Ablations test history and structural conditioning.
AI.result: In simulation, scenario-specific models achieve five-second trajectory Energy Scores of 12.05 mm (internal friction variation) and 9.29 mm (unobserved actuation disturbances), lower than CVAE and diffusion baselines, with coverage closer to nominal. On the physical robot, predictions under two tendon-command profiles excluded from training capture principal motion sequences with five-second Energy Scores of 11.91 and 11.42 mm, lower than baselines; predicted-to-measured spread ratios are 1.65 and 1.22 (closer to 1 is better).
AI.conclusion: The results support history-conditioned probabilistic dynamics prediction under incomplete mechanical observations, with flow matching yielding more accurate and better-calibrated trajectory distributions than CVAE and diffusion baselines in both simulated and physical settings.

title: Seeing Is Not Perceiving: When Synthetic Consumers Can and Cannot Pretest Visual Marketing
comment: 58 pages (30 pages of main text, 23 pages of appendix), 18 figures, 25 tables. All six studies were preregistered on AsPredicted
summary: Marketers now deploy generative AI agents as synthetic consumers to pretest visual assets such as logos, packaging, and advertising at a fraction of human-panel cost. However, this procedure assumes that a model seeing a visual cue can also perceive its consumer meaning, which is largely untested. We stress-test the assumption using six canonical visual marketing experiments, varying the two levers managers control: model generation (GPT-4o-mini vs. GPT-5.4-mini) and input format (plain text vs. JSON). Every resulting configuration passed the manipulation checks; however, none of the configurations reproduced more than two of the six human effects, and the remainder were nonsignificant. The one exception was a significant reversal of the human pattern. Providing conceptual or empirical evidence through in-context learning steers average responses toward the human effect. Yet steering has a limit: even when it succeeds, a configuration reproduces less than half of the natural spread of human responses and so understates consumer heterogeneity. We integrate these results into an AI governance protocol (Calibrate, Intervene, Deploy) that delineates when synthetic consumers can responsibly screen creatives and when human panels remain necessary.

AI.tldr: Across six canonical visual marketing experiments, generative AI "synthetic consumers" passed manipulation checks but reproduced at most two of six human effects, with one significant reversal, and in-context learning steering yielded only partial alignment while understating consumer heterogeneity; the authors propose a Calibrate–Intervene–Deploy governance protocol.
AI.motivation: Marketers increasingly use generative AI agents as synthetic consumers to pretest visual assets (logos, packaging, advertising) at far lower cost than human panels. This practice rests on an untested assumption: that a model which registers a visual cue can also perceive its consumer meaning.
AI.method: The authors stress-test this assumption using six canonical visual marketing experiments, manipulating two managerial levers: model generation (GPT-4o-mini vs. GPT-5.4-mini) and input format (plain text vs. JSON). They then apply in-context learning with conceptual or empirical evidence to attempt to steer responses toward human effects.
AI.result: Every configuration passed the manipulation checks, yet none reproduced more than two of the six human effects; the remaining effects were nonsignificant, with one exception being a significant reversal of the human pattern. In-context learning steering shifted average responses toward human effects, but even successful configurations captured less than half of the natural spread of human responses, understating consumer heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic consumers cannot be assumed to perceive the consumer meaning of visual cues, and steering only partially and incompletely corrects this. The authors integrate these findings into an AI governance protocol (Calibrate, Intervene, Deploy) specifying when synthetic consumers can responsibly screen creatives and when human panels remain necessary.

title: Deploying Foundation Models for Embodied Navigation
summary: We present and tackle two problems associated with deploying Foundation Models (FMs) on Embodied Agents performing navigation: 1) Training bias in FMs leading to poor personalization in unseen environments, and 2) Limited FM context length hindering success, especially on long horizon tasks. Our solution for the former involves priming the FM with human-habit data mined from the scene and our solution for the latter involves active memory management via a novel `memory head' augmentation. We first present a taxonomy of existing literature on FM-based Embodied Navigation, and highlight these limitations. We then present our approaches, Transit-Aware Planning (TAP) and MemCtrl to address the limitations. With TAP, we present real-world results in a lab environment with a Turtlebot for personalized target finding that shows an average improvement of 18% over a non-TAP baseline. On MemCtrl, we report a 6% average improvement across various embodied tasks, with 20% on long instruction subsets, all while using nearly half the context used in the baseline model. Motivated by these result, we present our stance the deployability of FM-based embodied agents in real-world environments, and highlight open research directions.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses two challenges of deploying Foundation Models on embodied navigation agents: training bias causing poor personalization in unseen environments, and limited context length hurting long-horizon tasks. It proposes Transit-Aware Planning (TAP) and MemCtrl, reporting 18% personalization improvement in real-world tests and 6% average (20% on long instructions) gains with nearly half the context.
AI.motivation: Deploying Foundation Models on embodied navigation agents faces two key problems: (1) training bias in FMs leads to poor personalization in unseen environments, and (2) limited FM context length hinders success, especially on long-horizon tasks.
AI.method: The authors first present a taxonomy of existing FM-based embodied navigation literature to highlight these limitations. To address training bias, TAP primes the FM with human-habit data mined from the scene. To address limited context length, MemCtrl performs active memory management via a novel 'memory head' augmentation.
AI.result: TAP achieves real-world results in a lab environment with a Turtlebot for personalized target finding, showing an average 18% improvement over a non-TAP baseline. MemCtrl reports a 6% average improvement across various embodied tasks, including 20% on long instruction subsets, while using nearly half the context of the baseline model.
AI.conclusion: Motivated by these results, the authors present their stance on the deployability of FM-based embodied agents in real-world environments and highlight open research directions.

title: Toolcompass: Guiding Tool Trialing, Not Suppressing It
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents must generalize from tools seen during training to unseen tools at deployment. A key challenge is tool trialing, i.e., excessive trials waste the interaction budget, whereas selective trials enable exploration of unfamiliar tools. Existing outcome-based post-training leaves wasteful trials unguided, while turn-level supervision may suppress necessary exploration. We introduce ToolCompass, a post-training framework that guides tool trialing by organizing tool-call representations according to shared functions. Specifically, ToolCompass models each function class as a von Mises--Fisher distribution and jointly reduces intra-function variation across domains and increases inter-function separation. This structure transfers experience from seen tools to functionally similar unseen tools, directing exploration away from unrelated alternatives. ToolCompass requires no ground-truth call traces or unseen-tool access and incurs no inference overhead. Experiments on AppWorld and FTRL show consistent gains across GRPO, RFT, and DMPO. improves AppWorld OOD task success by up to 10.71 percentage points over vanilla post-training and performs best among competitive baselines on both benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ToolCompass post-trains LLM agents to guide tool trialing by structuring tool-call representations by shared function, using von Mises-Fisher distributions to tighten intra-function and separate inter-function variation, improving generalization to unseen tools without extra data or inference cost.
AI.motivation: LLM agents must generalize from training tools to unseen deployment tools, but tool trialing is inefficient: excessive trials waste the interaction budget while selective trials enable exploration. Outcome-based post-training leaves wasteful trials unguided, and turn-level supervision can suppress necessary exploration.
AI.method: ToolCompass models each function class as a von Mises-Fisher distribution and jointly reduces intra-function variation across domains while increasing inter-function separation, structuring tool-call representations to transfer experience from seen tools to functionally similar unseen ones and steer exploration away from unrelated alternatives. It needs no ground-truth call traces or unseen-tool access and adds no inference overhead.
AI.result: On AppWorld and FTRL, ToolCompass yields consistent gains across GRPO, RFT, and DMPO, improving AppWorld OOD task success by up to 10.71 percentage points over vanilla post-training and achieving the best performance among competitive baselines on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Structuring tool-call representations by shared function provides an effective, low-cost post-training signal for guiding tool trialing and enhancing generalization to unseen tools.

title: CDKF-Track: Cluster-aware Data-Driven Kalman Filtering for Cooperative 3D Multi-Object Tracking
summary: Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) is essential for EdgeAI perception systems, where accurate object localization and reliable identification enable safe decision-making. Singleagent MOT suffers from occlusions, sensor noise, and partial scene understanding in complex real-world scenarios. While multi-agent systems improve robustness by exploiting shared information, they introduce redundant measurements that lead to false data associations, and still struggle to capture nonlinear object dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose CDKFTrack, a Cluster-aware Data-Driven Kalman Filtering framework for Cooperative 3D MOT. The proposed method first fuses multivehicle 3D LiDAR detections through a Graph Laplacian-based formulation. Then, a cluster-aware redundancy reduction scheme groups spatially related detections and selects representative observations to reduce duplicate inputs to the tracker. The resulting detections are processed by a data-driven Kalman filter that learns object motion dynamics from data, reducing dependence on predefined linear motion assumptions. Furthermore, a wavelet-based temporal refinement module leverages the multiresolution decomposition property of wavelets to attenuate shortterm positional fluctuations and improve trajectory continuity. To the best of our knowledge, CDKF-Track is the first framework to jointly address detection-level fusion redundancy and learnable motion modeling in cooperative 3D MOT. Experimental results on the real-world V2V4Real dataset indicate that CDKF-Track achieves up to 27.99% improvements in tracking accuracy over state-of-the-art multi-agent MOT methods.

AI.tldr: CDKF-Track is a cluster-aware, data-driven Kalman filtering framework for cooperative 3D multi-object tracking that jointly tackles redundant detection fusion and nonlinear motion modeling, achieving up to 27.99% accuracy gains on V2V4Real.
AI.motivation: EdgeAI perception requires accurate MOT. Single-agent MOT degrades under occlusions, sensor noise, and partial scene understanding. Multi-agent systems improve robustness but introduce redundant measurements causing false associations, and they still fail to capture nonlinear object dynamics.
AI.method: The framework (1) fuses multi-vehicle 3D LiDAR detections via a Graph Laplacian-based formulation; (2) applies cluster-aware redundancy reduction that groups spatially related detections and selects representative observations; (3) processes them with a data-driven Kalman filter that learns object motion dynamics; (4) adds a wavelet-based temporal refinement module using multiresolution decomposition to attenuate short-term positional fluctuations.
AI.result: On the real-world V2V4Real dataset, CDKF-Track achieves up to 27.99% improvement in tracking accuracy over state-of-the-art multi-agent MOT methods.
AI.conclusion: CDKF-Track is the first framework to jointly address detection-level fusion redundancy and learnable motion modeling in cooperative 3D MOT, delivering substantial accuracy gains.

title: How Strongly Should Task State Influence an LLM Agent?
summary: Long-horizon assigned work requires an LLM agent to track the state of a task: which steps are done, blocked, cancelled, or open to repetition. Agent systems either keep this state as text in the prompt and rely on the model to read that text, or move the state into a module that enforces it, and each system is evaluated as a whole, so no one knows how much reliability comes from the state being shown, told, or enforced. We fix the task rules, the model, and paired episodes and vary how strongly task state reaches the agent: a raw transcript, an exact checklist, per-turn directives from a state machine compiled from the brief and advanced only by execution receipts, or an enforcement gate on that machine that refuses state-violating actions; every episode is scored by exact payload matching against dynamic ground truth. Across three models, two reasoning regimes, and two domains, four findings hold without per-turn reasoning: displaying accurate state is unreliable, an unverified ledger the agent writes itself beats an accurate checklist it is shown, directives help in proportion to the model's obedience, and enforcement needs no obedience but is bounded by the correctness of its state and by the matcher that maps requests to steps; per-turn reasoning at a 235B agent compresses these separations without repairing the text rungs. The same gate, compiled from $τ^2$-bench's airline policy, raises a 235B agent's pass$^1$ from 0.39 to 0.54 and changes nothing for a 35B agent that rarely violates the policy; on PM-Bench, where acting turns on recognizing a cue rather than on state, showing the record is the best rung--matching or beating both gates and reversing the ledger-over-checklist finding--and enforcing the matcher's judgement drops a 35B agent below its raw transcript. Enforcement pays when failures are state-decidable and frequent, and hurts when the gate's judgement is wrong.

AI.tldr: By holding task rules, model, and episodes fixed and varying how strongly task state reaches the agent (raw transcript, exact checklist, per-turn directives from a compiled state machine, or an enforcement gate), the paper isolates how much reliability comes from state being shown, told, or enforced. Findings: accurate displayed state is unreliable; a self-written unverified ledger beats a shown accurate checklist; directives help proportional to model obedience; enforcement is obedience-free but bounded by state correctness and the matcher. Enforcement pays when failures are state-decidable and frequent, and hurts when the gate's judgement is wrong.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon assigned work forces an LLM agent to track task state (done, blocked, cancelled, open to repetition). Existing agent systems either keep state as prompt text the model must read, or move it into a module that enforces it, but each is evaluated as a whole—so no one knows how much reliability derives from state being shown, told, or enforced. The paper aims to disentangle these contributions.
AI.method: The authors fix the task rules, model, and paired episodes, and vary only how strongly task state reaches the agent across four rungs: (1) a raw transcript, (2) an exact checklist, (3) per-turn directives from a state machine compiled from the brief and advanced only by execution receipts, and (4) an enforcement gate on that machine that refuses state-violating actions. Every episode is scored by exact payload matching against dynamic ground truth. The design spans three models, two reasoning regimes, and two domains (including τ²-bench airline policy and PM-Bench).
AI.result: Four findings hold without per-turn reasoning: displaying accurate state is unreliable; an unverified self-written ledger beats an accurate checklist the agent is shown; directives help in proportion to the model's obedience; enforcement needs no obedience but is bounded by the correctness of its state and by the matcher mapping requests to steps. Per-turn reasoning at a 235B agent compresses these separations without repairing the text rungs. The same gate compiled from τ²-bench's airline policy raises a 235B agent's pass^1 from 0.39 to 0.54 yet changes nothing for a 35B agent that rarely violates policy. On PM-Bench, where acting turns on recognizing a cue rather than on state, showing the record is the best rung—matching or beating both gates and reversing the ledger-over-checklist finding—and enforcing the matcher's judgement drops a 35B agent below its raw transcript.
AI.conclusion: Enforcement pays when failures are state-decidable and frequent, and hurts when the gate's judgement is wrong. More broadly, the reliability of long-horizon LLM agents depends on the interaction between the strength of state delivery and domain properties (whether success hinges on state versus cue recognition), so no single rung dominates across settings.

title: Teaching Reinforcement Learning and Humanoid Robotics to High-School Students: An Expert-Validated Curriculum Design on a Low-Cost Open Platform
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for presentation at the IEEE International Conference on Teaching, Assessment, and Learning for Engineering (TALE 2026)
summary: Lower cost open source robots and reinforcement learning (RL) simulation tools create new opportunities for precollege students to engage with contemporary robotics. However, translating a complete research workflow, spanning mechanical assembly, electrical setup, simulation, policy learning, system identification, and physical deployment, into a coherent course for novice learners remains challenging. We present an integrated robotics course framework that organizes these activities around a shared robotic artifact. The framework combines parallel disciplinary tracks, sequencing based on technical dependencies, progressive integration of simulation and hardware, layered performance checkpoints, and structures for balancing collaborative work with individual accountability. We illustrate the framework through a high school curriculum organized around a robot project in which pairs of students assemble an open source humanoid robot, train a walking policy in simulation, and deploy it on the physical platform. The framework was developed through an iterative design process that included formative review by five experts in robotics research, engineering, secondary STEM education, and curriculum design. Expert feedback highlighted three central design tensions: authenticity versus cognitive load, system integration versus timely visible progress, and team construction versus individual accountability. These tensions informed the final framework presented in this paper. This work offers a structured approach for adapting robotics research workflows into interdisciplinary precollege courses; future classroom studies are needed to examine implementation and student learning.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an integrated robotics course framework that adapts a full research workflow (assembly, electronics, simulation, RL policy learning, system identification, deployment) into a precollege curriculum built around a shared open source humanoid robot, validated through expert review that surfaced three key design tensions.
AI.motivation: Lower-cost open source robots and RL simulation tools open new opportunities for precollege students to engage with contemporary robotics, but translating a complete research workflow into a coherent course for novice learners remains challenging. There is a need for a structured pedagogical approach that makes authentic, interdisciplinary robotics research accessible without overwhelming beginners.
AI.method: The authors develop an integrated course framework organized around a shared robotic artifact, combining five elements: parallel disciplinary tracks, sequencing based on technical dependencies, progressive integration of simulation and hardware, layered performance checkpoints, and structures balancing collaborative work with individual accountability. They illustrate it via a high school curriculum in which student pairs assemble an open source humanoid robot, train a walking policy in simulation, and deploy it on the physical platform. Development used an iterative design process with formative review by five experts in robotics research, engineering, secondary STEM education, and curriculum design.
AI.result: Expert feedback identified three central design tensions: authenticity versus cognitive load, system integration versus timely visible progress, and team construction versus individual accountability. These tensions informed the final framework.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a structured approach for adapting robotics research workflows into interdisciplinary precollege courses. Future classroom studies are needed to examine implementation and student learning.

title: TCMaster: Confidence-Aware Querying and Workload-Guided Physical Design for Multi-Source Traditional Chinese Medicine Knowledge Graphs
summary: Multi-source knowledge graphs (KGs) need query mechanisms that expose reliability and exploit domain structure. This paper presents TCMaster, a property-graph query substrate for confidence-aware traversal and workload-guided physical design over Traditional Chinese Medicine KGs. TCMaster integrates pharmacopoeias, prescriptions, molecular databases, and LLM-extracted micro-semantics into a KG with approximately 221K entities and 723K base edges. It annotates edges with provenance-level confidence, rewrites Cypher queries with confidence predicates, ranks multi-hop paths under PRODUCT, MIN, or weighted-average policies, and uses ontology skew through direction selection, herb-attribute bitmaps, and materialized shortcut edges. On Neo4j, direction selection improves attribute lookup by a factor of 1.47, shortcuts accelerate high-fanout target counting by a factor of 4.42, confidence filtering removes 39.3 percent of low-quality heterogeneous paths, and KG retrieval improves TCMbench QA accuracy by 20.0 percentage points.

AI.tldr: TCMaster is a property-graph query substrate for confidence-aware traversal and workload-guided physical design over Traditional Chinese Medicine knowledge graphs, delivering substantial speedups and accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: Multi-source knowledge graphs require query mechanisms that both expose reliability and exploit domain structure, which existing approaches do not adequately address for Traditional Chinese Medicine KGs.
AI.method: TCMaster integrates pharmacopoeias, prescriptions, molecular databases, and LLM-extracted micro-semantics into a property graph (~221K entities, 723K base edges). It annotates edges with provenance-level confidence, rewrites Cypher queries with confidence predicates, ranks multi-hop paths under PRODUCT, MIN, or weighted-average policies, and optimizes physical design via direction selection, herb-attribute bitmaps, and materialized shortcut edges.
AI.result: On Neo4j, direction selection improves attribute lookup by 1.47x, shortcuts accelerate high-fanout target counting by 4.42x, confidence filtering removes 39.3% of low-quality heterogeneous paths, and KG retrieval improves TCMbench QA accuracy by 20.0 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: TCMaster demonstrates that confidence-aware traversal combined with workload-guided physical design yields significant efficiency and quality improvements for querying multi-source Traditional Chinese Medicine knowledge graphs.

title: SG-CPG: Severity-Gated Central Pattern Generators for Adaptive Quadruped Locomotion under Continuous Actuator Degradation
summary: An animal with a weakened limb does not necessarily switch its gait, instead it unloads the affected limb, re-coordinates the remaining limbs, and scales its response with injury severity. This graded adaptation allows locomotion to persist despite partial loss of limb strength, rather than requiring a discrete transition between healthy and failed. Inspired by this behavior, we propose SG-CPG, a central pattern generator (CPG) for quadruped locomotion under continuous actuator degradation. SG-CPG preserves a frozen healthy CPG policy and introduces two severity-driven gates: a residual gate that re-coordinates all four legs and an amplitude gate that progressively shortens the weakened leg's stride as degradation increases. We emulate progressive degradation through two mechanisms: lowering the joint torque ceiling (ceiling mechanism) and scaling its low-level controller gains (gain mechanism), representing distinct forms of actuator weakening. Our simulations on a Unitree Go2 show that SG-CPG maintains a trot gait with 100% survival across an omnidirectional command schedule under 95% joint strength loss while tracking commands within 8%. Under a lowered torque ceiling, removing either severity path, the residual's severity observation or the amplitude gate, raises clipping at the weakened joint from 4.4% to 13.6% and 26.3% of steps at an 80% loss. On a real Go2, SG-CPG survives 28 of 29 forward and turning trials with up to 93% calf torque degradation. These results show that severity-gated adaptation can extend a healthy locomotion policy to progressive actuator degradation without treating the fault as a discrete failure.

AI.tldr: SG-CPG extends a frozen healthy quadruped CPG policy to continuous actuator degradation via two severity-driven gates (residual and amplitude), maintaining locomotion across up to 95% torque loss in simulation and 93% calf degradation on a real Unitree Go2.
AI.motivation: Animals with weakened limbs do not switch gait discretely; they unload the affected limb, re-coordinate remaining limbs, and scale response with injury severity. Existing locomotion policies typically treat actuator faults as discrete healthy/failed transitions, lacking graded adaptation for progressive weakening.
AI.method: SG-CPG preserves a frozen healthy CPG policy and adds two severity-driven gates: a residual gate that re-coordinates all four legs, and an amplitude gate that progressively shortens the weakened leg's stride as degradation increases. Degradation is emulated by lowering the joint torque ceiling (ceiling mechanism) and scaling low-level controller gains (gain mechanism). Evaluated on Unitree Go2 in simulation and hardware.
AI.result: Simulations maintain a trot gait with 100% survival across an omnidirectional command schedule under 95% joint strength loss, tracking commands within 8%. Under a lowered torque ceiling, removing either severity path (residual's severity observation or amplitude gate) raises clipping at the weakened joint from 4.4% to 13.6% and 26.3% of steps at 80% loss. On a real Go2, SG-CPG survives 28 of 29 forward and turning trials with up to 93% calf torque degradation.
AI.conclusion: Severity-gated adaptation can extend a healthy locomotion policy to progressive actuator degradation without treating the fault as a discrete failure. Both severity paths are necessary to limit joint clipping and sustain locomotion under weakening.

title: LingLan: An Advancing Traditional Chinese Medicine Diagnosis LLM with Multimodal Data
summary: Though artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly transforms modern medicine, its integration into Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) has been relatively slow, primarily due to TCM's reliance on holistic, subjective diagnostic methods---namely Inspection, Auscultation and Olfaction, Inquiry, and Palpation(I-AOI-P)---which are difficult to align with quantitative, standardized medical systems. In this work, we introduce a Unification Framework for Multimodal Data (UFMD), which automatically processes tongue and pulse images into structured, clinically standard descriptions, integrating multi-source diagnostic information into a unified digital record of I-AOI-P process. Building on this structured data, we create LingLan-14B, a TCM-specific large language model fine-tuned via supervised learning to emulate the diagnostic logic and workflow of I-AOI-P process. Experimental results show that our method significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy, achieving a relative improvement of 103.5% over the baseline (62.72% vs. 30.82%) and reaching an F1-score of up to 82%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes UFMD, a framework converting tongue and pulse images into structured clinical descriptions to unify multimodal TCM diagnostic data, and LingLan-14B, a TCM-specific LLM fine-tuned to emulate the I-AOI-P diagnostic workflow, achieving up to 82% F1-score and a 103.5% relative accuracy improvement over baseline.
AI.motivation: AI is increasingly transforming modern medicine, but its integration into Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) lags behind. This is largely because TCM relies on holistic, subjective diagnostic methods—Inspection, Auscultation and Olfaction, Inquiry, and Palpation (I-AOI-P)—which are hard to align with quantitative, standardized medical systems.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Unification Framework for Multimodal Data (UFMD), which automatically processes tongue and pulse images into structured, clinically standard descriptions and integrates multi-source diagnostic information into a unified digital record of the I-AOI-P process. On top of this structured data, they build LingLan-14B, a TCM-specific large language model fine-tuned via supervised learning to emulate the diagnostic logic and workflow of the I-AOI-P process.
AI.result: Experimental results show significantly enhanced diagnostic accuracy, with a relative improvement of 103.5% over the baseline (62.72% vs. 30.82%) and an F1-score of up to 82%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed UFMD framework combined with the LingLan-14B model effectively standardizes and structures TCM multimodal diagnostic data, enabling the model to replicate I-AOI-P diagnostic reasoning and substantially outperform the baseline in diagnostic accuracy and F1-score, demonstrating a viable path toward AI integration in TCM.

title: MatcherCompass: A Deployment-Aware Benchmark to Guide Image Matcher Selection in the Wild
summary:
Field robots operating across time of day and sensing modalities require accurate image correspondences within onboard time and resource budgets. However, accuracy and runtime reported for individual methods on a single device provide limited guidance for choosing a matcher and its configuration on a target platform. We present MatcherCompass, a deployment-aware benchmark for choosing local feature matchers in field robotics. Under common input and pose-evaluation procedures, we compare nine classical and learned matching pipelines across four image resolutions and supported numerical precisions. Four visual conditions cover viewpoint variation, day--night matching in visible and thermal imagery, and daytime visible--thermal matching. We evaluate pose accuracy using the area under the error--recall curve (AUC) at $5^\circ$, $10^\circ$, and $20^\circ$, and measure runtime, GPU memory, and energy per image pair on four GPU platforms spanning workstation and onboard computers. The results show that changes in hardware, input resolution, and numerical precision can move a matcher across a runtime budget boundary, altering the feasible choices. We organize the measurements into a selection guide that returns all configurations satisfying user-specified time and resource limits, together with their accuracy under the selected visual condition. MatcherCompass provides measured evidence for choosing matching pipelines that fit a robot's sensing conditions and computing hardware.
  Project page: https://matchercompass.github.io/.

AI.tldr: MatcherCompass is a deployment-aware benchmark for selecting local feature matching pipelines in field robotics, comparing nine classical and learned matchers across resolutions, precisions, visual conditions, and four GPU platforms, organized into a selection guide that returns configurations satisfying user-specified time and resource limits.
AI.motivation: Field robots operating across time of day and sensing modalities require accurate image correspondences within onboard time and resource budgets. However, accuracy and runtime reported for individual methods on a single device provide limited guidance for choosing a matcher and its configuration on a target platform.
AI.method: Under common input and pose-evaluation procedures, the authors compare nine classical and learned matching pipelines across four image resolutions and supported numerical precisions. Four visual conditions cover viewpoint variation, day-night matching in visible and thermal imagery, and daytime visible-thermal matching. Pose accuracy is evaluated using the area under the error-recall curve (AUC) at 5°, 10°, and 20°, with runtime, GPU memory, and energy per image pair measured on four GPU platforms spanning workstation and onboard computers.
AI.result: Changes in hardware, input resolution, and numerical precision can move a matcher across a runtime budget boundary, altering the feasible choices. Measurements are organized into a selection guide that returns all configurations satisfying user-specified time and resource limits, together with their accuracy under the selected visual condition.
AI.conclusion: MatcherCompass provides measured evidence for choosing matching pipelines that fit a robot's sensing conditions and computing hardware.

title: OmniFysics-Nano-V2 Technical Report: Understanding the Physical World Across Modalities
summary: Omni-modal models have expanded multimodal interaction across vision, audio, speech, and language. However, their training is predominantly organized around semantic descriptions and general-purpose objectives, leaving physical attributes, interaction states, and causal mechanisms only partially specified. This gap is not simply a matter of modality coverage: adding more modalities does not by itself provide the supervision needed to connect observations with the physical structure of the world. We present OmniFysics-Nano-V2, a compact omni-modal model for physical-world perception and understanding. The model supports image, video, audio, speech, and text inputs within a shared reasoning framework, together with text and speech generation. To address the lack of explicit physical supervision, we construct a dual-branch physics-aware data pipeline that grounds salient objects in structured physical attributes and aligns visual changes with acoustic events, intermediate responses, and interaction outcomes. To address homogeneous training objectives, we curate reinforcement-learning prompts by reward diversity and adopt a two-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization curriculum that progresses from general task correctness to fine-grained physical perceptual reasoning. Experiments across multimodal, audio-visual, and physical reasoning benchmarks show that the proposed data and training strategy improves physical-world understanding while preserving broad omni-modal competence. The proposed model achieves leading result on 17 of 21 benchmarks against SOTA omni-modal models. By equipping AI systems with both omni-modal and physical-world perception capabilities, OmniFysics-Nano-V2 is poised to become a cornerstone of next-generation Physical AI.

AI.tldr: OmniFysics-Nano-V2 is a compact omni-modal model that adds explicit physical-world supervision via a dual-branch physics-aware data pipeline and a two-stage GRPO curriculum, achieving leading results on 17 of 21 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing omni-modal models are trained mainly around semantic descriptions and general-purpose objectives, leaving physical attributes, interaction states, and causal mechanisms only partially specified. The authors argue this is not merely a modality-coverage issue: adding modalities does not provide the supervision needed to connect observations with the physical structure of the world.
AI.method: The paper introduces OmniFysics-Nano-V2, a compact omni-modal model supporting image, video, audio, speech, and text inputs in a shared reasoning framework, with text and speech generation. To supply explicit physical supervision, the authors build a dual-branch physics-aware data pipeline that grounds salient objects in structured physical attributes and aligns visual changes with acoustic events, intermediate responses, and interaction outcomes. To diversify homogeneous training objectives, they curate RL prompts by reward diversity and adopt a two-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization curriculum moving from general task correctness to fine-grained physical perceptual reasoning.
AI.result: Across multimodal, audio-visual, and physical reasoning benchmarks, the data and training strategy improves physical-world understanding while preserving broad omni-modal competence. The model achieves leading results on 17 of 21 benchmarks against state-of-the-art omni-modal models.
AI.conclusion: By combining omni-modal capability with physical-world perception, OmniFysics-Nano-V2 is positioned as a cornerstone of next-generation Physical AI.

title: MotionForge: A Data Generation Pipeline and Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon Manipulation of Dynamic Objects with Domain Shifts
summary: Recent advances in learning-based robot policies have demonstrated promising progress, yet they are predom- inantly evaluated in static or quasi-static environments. In dynamic manipulation, objects and scenes continuously evolve while the robot perceives, reasons, and acts. However, recent dynamic simulation benchmarks largely focus on short-horizon, reactive interactions with simple motion patterns and offer limited support for both systematic evaluation under domain shifts and model-agnostic real-time execution protocols. To bridge these gaps, we introduce MotionForge, the first large- scale simulation benchmark and data-generation pipeline tailored to jointly evaluate domain shifts and long-horizon interaction in dynamic manipulation. MotionForge comprises 40 dynamic interaction tasks spanning 11 distinct motion patterns, with dedicated support for 17 long-horizon tasks. Our benchmark introduces two key novelties: (1) a systematic evaluation protocol for assessing policy robustness under both single-factor (e.g., only backgrounds shift) and joint domain shifts (e.g., simultaneous shifts of objects, backgrounds, lighting, and speed); and (2) a decoupled, latency-aware execution protocol where the environ- ment continuously evolves independently of policy inference time. Extensive evaluations of representative general-purpose robot policies on our benchmark reveal substantial limitations under joint domain shifts. These findings expose a critical gap between current policy capabilities and the requirements of robust long- horizon manipulation of dynamic objects under domain shifts, establishing MotionForge as a comprehensive testbed for future research in embodied AI.

AI.tldr: MotionForge is a large-scale simulation benchmark and data-generation pipeline for dynamic manipulation that jointly evaluates domain shifts and long-horizon interaction, revealing that general-purpose robot policies degrade substantially under joint domain shifts.
AI.motivation: Learning-based robot policies show progress but are mostly evaluated in static or quasi-static settings. Dynamic manipulation involves continuously evolving objects and scenes during perception, reasoning, and action, yet existing dynamic simulation benchmarks focus on short-horizon reactive interactions, simple motion patterns, and offer limited support for systematic evaluation under domain shifts or model-agnostic real-time execution.
AI.method: MotionForge is introduced as a simulation benchmark and data-generation pipeline comprising 40 dynamic interaction tasks across 11 motion patterns, with dedicated support for 17 long-horizon tasks. It provides (1) a systematic evaluation protocol for policy robustness under single-factor and joint domain shifts (objects, backgrounds, lighting, speed), and (2) a decoupled, latency-aware execution protocol where the environment evolves independently of policy inference time.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations of representative general-purpose robot policies on MotionForge reveal substantial limitations under joint domain shifts.
AI.conclusion: These findings expose a critical gap between current policy capabilities and the requirements of robust long-horizon manipulation of dynamic objects under domain shifts, positioning MotionForge as a comprehensive testbed for future embodied AI research.

title: The Limits of Simulated Societies: How Post-Training and Survey Fine-Tuning Erase Cross-Cultural Variance
summary: Using large language models (LLMs) to simulate diverse human populations has the potential to transform many aspects of computational social science, yet many evaluations score the average response rather than the spread of opinion within real groups. Here, we develop a diagnostic framework that measures point accuracy alongside dispersion retention, the ratio of predicted to human standard deviation ($\dr$), on 10{,}000 respondent--question pairs from the World Values Survey (WVS) spanning twelve countries and six continents. We evaluate eleven zero-shot language models and five variants fine-tuned on WVS data with SFT, DPO, and GRPO. We identify a failure mode we term \textit{consensus collapse}, where alignment training compresses outputs toward one stereotype per group. Along the post-training trajectory from the Llama~3.1 70B base to the Tulu~3 checkpoints, the first stage, supervised instruction tuning, removes half of the spread with minimal accuracy gain ($\dr$ 1.22 to 0.59; accuracy $+0.9$ points), the later stages do not restore it, and a gap opens between WEIRD and non-WEIRD countries that survey fine-tuning then deepens while pursuing higher point accuracy. The most accurate model (Tulu~3 70B-DPO fine-tuned on WVS, 57.9\%) keeps half the human spread overall ($\dr = 0.50$) and 11\% of it for Nigeria, against 0.70--0.87 for WEIRD countries. Raising the sampling temperature to 1.0 leaves the Wasserstein-1 distance ($\wone$) to human distributions unchanged for both fine-tuned DPO models, and GRPO on Qwen~3.5 9B does not restore the spread under either an accuracy reward or a distribution-shaped reward. Mixing the aligned model with an unaligned prior raises $\dr$ from 0.51 to 0.62 on a held-out split but leaves Nigeria at 0.36. Point accuracy alone therefore misjudges these simulators, and current post-training trades diversity for consensus.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a diagnostic framework measuring point accuracy plus "dispersion retention" (ratio of predicted to human standard deviation) and reveals that post-training alignment induces a "consensus collapse" in LLM population simulators, compressing opinion spread far below human levels while giving minimal accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: Most existing evaluations of LLMs as human population simulators score only the average response, ignoring whether models reproduce the spread of opinion within real groups. This misrepresents simulator quality and hides a systematic failure under alignment training.
AI.method: They analyze 10,000 respondent–question pairs from the World Values Survey (WVS) across twelve countries and six continents. A diagnostic framework measures point accuracy and dispersion retention (predicted-to-human SD ratio). They evaluate eleven zero-shot LLMs and five variants fine-tuned on WVS via SFT, DPO, and GRPO, tracing the Llama 3.1 70B base→Tulu 3 post-training trajectory, testing temperature scaling, alternative rewards (GRPO on Qwen 3.5 9B), and mixing with an unaligned prior.
AI.result: Alignment training causes "consensus collapse": SFT halves spread (dispersion retention 1.22→0.59) with minimal accuracy gain (+0.9 points); later stages do not restore it, and a WEIRD vs. non-WEIRD gap opens and deepens. The most accurate model (Tulu 3 70B-DPO on WVS, 57.9%) retains only half the human spread (0.50), and 11% for Nigeria vs. 0.70–0.87 for WEIRD countries. Raising temperature to 1.0 leaves Wasserstein-1 distance unchanged; GRPO with either accuracy or distribution-shaped rewards does not restore spread. Mixing aligned model with unaligned prior raises retention from 0.51 to 0.62 but leaves Nigeria at 0.36.
AI.conclusion: Point accuracy alone misjudges these simulators. Current post-training trades diversity for consensus, systematically collapsing within-group opinion spread, especially for non-WEIRD populations, and standard mitigations (temperature, alternative rewards, prior mixing) do not fix it.

title: Induced Riemannian Metrics for Motion Planning with Constraints
summary: In constrained motion planning problems, task and loop-closure constraints restrict a robot's motion to a curved, lower-dimensional submanifold of its configuration space. Planners measure path length with a metric, which sets the cost of moving in each direction. Under the Euclidean metric, this cost is the same everywhere, whereas under a general Riemannian metric, such as the kinetic-energy metric, the cost can vary with direction and configuration. Existing methods often describe the submanifold either implicitly, as a constraint level set, or explicitly, through a parameterization. The implicit representation is typically combined with the Euclidean metric of the configuration space, and the explicit representation with the parameter domain, so the path length that a planner minimizes depends on the representation. Instead, we measure path length with the induced metric, which the submanifold inherits from a Riemannian metric on the configuration space. The implicit and explicit representations yield the same induced metric, expressed in different coordinates, and hence the same geometry. This result holds for any Riemannian metric on the configuration space, not only the Euclidean one. The choice of metric is therefore independent of the choice of representation. Using this result, we extend planning under a Riemannian metric from unconstrained spaces to constraint submanifolds by applying the induced metric in both a sampling-based planner and a trajectory optimizer. For an explicit representation, the induced metric also accounts for the distortion that the parameterization introduces. In experiments on a bimanual manipulation setup with two Franka arms under end-effector task constraints, we compare the Euclidean and kinetic-energy metrics.

AI.tldr: Constrained planners can use the induced Riemannian metric to measure path length consistently, since implicit (level-set) and explicit (parameterized) representations yield the same induced geometry. The authors apply this induced metric in both a sampling-based planner and a trajectory optimizer, comparing Euclidean and kinetic-energy metrics on a bimanual Franka setup.
AI.motivation: Task and loop-closure constraints confine a robot to a curved, lower-dimensional submanifold of its configuration space. Existing planners typically pair the implicit constraint level-set representation with the Euclidean configuration-space metric, and the explicit parameterization with the parameter-domain metric, so the minimized path length becomes representation-dependent. The paper aims to make path length independent of representation by adopting the submanifold's induced metric.
AI.method: The key insight is that the induced metric, which the submanifold inherits from a Riemannian metric on the configuration space, is identical whether expressed via the implicit or the explicit representation, differing only in coordinates, and this holds for any Riemannian metric, not just the Euclidean one. Building on this, the authors extend Riemannian-metric planning from unconstrained spaces to constraint submanifolds by applying the induced metric in both a sampling-based planner and a trajectory optimizer. For the explicit representation, the induced metric additionally compensates for the distortion introduced by the parameterization.
AI.result: Experiments on a bimanual manipulation setup with two Franka arms under end-effector task constraints compare the Euclidean and kinetic-energy metrics, demonstrating the use of the induced metric within both a sampling-based planner and a trajectory optimizer.
AI.conclusion: Path length under the induced metric is independent of whether the constraint submanifold is represented implicitly or explicitly, so the choice of metric is decoupled from the choice of representation. This enables consistent planning under a Riemannian metric on constraint submanifolds, with the parameterization-induced distortion automatically accounted for.

title: Neurosymbolic Action Model Learning under Partial Observability
summary: AI planning studies how an agent can reach a goal by executing a sequence of actions. To plan correctly, the agent needs an action model describing when each action can be executed and how it changes the world. Constructing such models by hand requires domain expertise, and can be costly and error-prone. Action models can instead be learned from available data using existing neurosymbolic approaches, but they currently assume access to complete traces of fully observable images . These approaches fail to learn action models under partial observability where some of the images might not be present or are not fully informative of the current state of the world. Hence, this paper proposes NeSyAM, a novel neurosymbolic modeling paradigm for action model learning under partial observability. In addition, the paper presents a unified variational framework for theoretically analysing the limitations of existing methods compared to our proposed approach. NeSyAM is then tested extensively on six visual planning domains and three observation regimes to show it consistently recovers relevant parts of the true action model under partial observability.

AI.tldr: NeSyAM is a neurosymbolic paradigm that learns action models for AI planning under partial observability, where existing approaches fail because they assume complete, fully observable traces; a unified variational framework analyzes these limitations, and experiments across six visual planning domains and three observation regimes show NeSyAM consistently recovers relevant parts of the true action model.
AI.motivation: AI planning requires an action model specifying action preconditions and effects. Hand-crafting such models is costly and error-prone, while existing neurosymbolic learning methods assume complete traces of fully observable images. This assumption breaks under partial observability, where some images are missing or uninformative about the true state, so a new learning approach is needed.
AI.method: The paper proposes NeSyAM, a novel neurosymbolic modeling paradigm for action model learning under partial observability. It also introduces a unified variational framework that theoretically analyzes the limitations of existing methods relative to the proposed approach. NeSyAM is evaluated extensively on six visual planning domains under three observation regimes.
AI.result: NeSyAM consistently recovers the relevant parts of the true action model under partial observability, as demonstrated across six visual planning domains and three observation regimes.
AI.conclusion: NeSyAM extends neurosymbolic action model learning beyond the restrictive assumption of complete, fully observable traces, enabling reliable action model recovery under partial observability and providing a theoretical framework for comparing against prior methods.

title: The Cartesian Hand: In-Hand Manipulation with All-Linear Fingers
summary: Robotic manipulation has increasingly pursued human-like dexterous hands with many articulated degrees of freedom, offering rich manipulation capabilities at the cost of mechanical and control complexity. At the other extreme, parallel grippers are simple and robust, but provide little ability to manipulate an object after grasping it. Operating articulated objects such as threaded containers, manufacturing tools, and laboratory instruments often requires a second gripper, an external fixture, or coordinated arm motion. We introduce the Cartesian Hand, a 7-DoF end-effector that rethinks dexterous manipulation by combining independent grasping and relative manipulation within a single end-effector using only linear motion. Two independently actuated parallel grippers hold different parts of an object, while four translating fingertips generate relative motion between the grasped parts. Its configuration-independent fingertip kinematics allow manipulation to be composed from simple linear motion primitives. The Cartesian Hand is particularly suited to objects structured around common mechanisms such as threads, pivots, linear guides, plungers, and triggers. We demonstrate cap opening and closing, pipetting, pumping, two-handle manipulation, screwdriving, trigger actuation, and in-grasp reorientation across 35 objects spanning laboratory, manufacturing, and household settings. The same manipulation procedures transfer from a fixed-base robot arm to a humanoid, where we demonstrate bimanual laboratory manipulation using two Cartesian Hands. These results show that versatile in-hand manipulation capability can emerge from a mechanically simple architecture when independent grasping and relative motion are designed directly into the end-effector. We will open-source all software and hardware design. Our website is https://generalroboticslab.com/cartesian_handv1.

AI.tldr: The Cartesian Hand is a 7-DoF end-effector that integrates two independent parallel grippers with four translating fingertips to enable in-grasp relative manipulation using only linear motion primitives, demonstrated across 35 objects.
AI.motivation: Dexterous multi-fingered hands offer rich manipulation but at high mechanical/control complexity, while parallel grippers are simple and robust yet cannot manipulate an object after grasping. Many everyday tasks (threaded containers, tools, lab instruments) normally require a second gripper, external fixture, or coordinated arm motion, motivating a simpler architecture that still provides in-hand manipulation.
AI.method: The authors introduce a Cartesian Hand: a 7-DoF end-effector combining independent grasping and relative manipulation. Two independently actuated parallel grippers hold different parts of an object, while four translating fingertips generate relative motion between the grasped parts. Fingertip kinematics are configuration-independent, so manipulation is composed from simple linear motion primitives, targeting objects built around threads, pivots, linear guides, plungers, and triggers.
AI.result: Demonstrated cap opening/closing, pipetting, pumping, two-handle manipulation, screwdriving, trigger actuation, and in-grasp reorientation across 35 objects in laboratory, manufacturing, and household settings. The same procedures transfer from a fixed-base arm to a humanoid, where bimanual laboratory manipulation is shown using two Cartesian Hands.
AI.conclusion: Versatile in-hand manipulation capability can emerge from a mechanically simple architecture when independent grasping and relative motion are designed directly into the end-effector. All software and hardware designs will be open-sourced.

title: Towards Omni-dimensional GUI Agent Navigation with Masked Trajectory Prediction
summary: Graphical User Interface (GUI) Agents autonomously interact with software to fulfill user requests, where GUI navigation stands out as the most critical and challenging capability. Mastering this capability demands a complex synergy of step-wise decision-making, state-action alignment, and long-horizon planning. While directly mixing these corresponding navigation tasks seems intuitive to simultaneously acquire these skills, such a direct combination is severely bottlenecked by inconsistent optimization objectives and profound data heterogeneity. To overcome these barriers, we propose the MaP (stands for ``\textbf{M}asked Tr\textbf{a}jectory \textbf{P}rediction''), a unified framework that seamlessly harmonizes divergent GUI navigation tasks. By modeling multi-turn GUI interactions as a trajectory and defining training objectives through component masking and prediction, MaP shifts the optimization from task-specific marginal distributions to a consistent objective. Furthermore, to handle the data heterogeneity across multiple navigation tasks, we design a role-aware adapter learning module that dynamically routes each token to a specialized representation space. Extensive experiments on five representative GUI navigation benchmarks demonstrate that MaP effectively mitigates gradient conflicts and significantly outperforms the direct mixture training, establishing a robust paradigm for multi-task GUI navigation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MaP (Masked Trajectory Prediction), a unified framework that harmonizes divergent GUI navigation tasks by modeling multi-turn interactions as trajectories with component masking/prediction objectives and using a role-aware adapter to handle data heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: GUI navigation requires a complex synergy of step-wise decision-making, state-action alignment, and long-horizon planning. Directly mixing related navigation tasks to acquire these skills is intuitive but is severely bottlenecked by inconsistent optimization objectives and profound data heterogeneity.
AI.method: MaP models multi-turn GUI interactions as a trajectory and defines training objectives through component masking and prediction, shifting optimization from task-specific marginal distributions to a consistent objective. It also introduces a role-aware adapter learning module that dynamically routes each token to a specialized representation space to handle data heterogeneity across navigation tasks.
AI.result: Experiments on five representative GUI navigation benchmarks show that MaP effectively mitigates gradient conflicts and significantly outperforms direct mixture training.
AI.conclusion: MaP establishes a robust paradigm for multi-task GUI navigation by unifying divergent tasks under a consistent objective and addressing data heterogeneity.

title: Zephyron: Integrated Design and Analytical Evaluation of a Solar-Assisted Mobile Manipulator for Multimodal Environmental Reconnaissance and Distributed Visual Inference
summary: Environmental reconnaissance needs mobile platforms that carry sensors, preserve measurement context, and return interpretable evidence under limited energy and communication. We present a literature-informed engineering design for Zephyron, a four-wheel rover with a front manipulator, environmental sensors, distributed computer vision, local recording, and a raised rear solar module. The design keeps the prototype layout but replaces unsupported numerical assumptions with an explicit component and geometry baseline. A reproducible search retrieved 5,000 records (4,858 unique) for screening, followed by targeted review of primary literature and manufacturer documentation. The baseline uses 165 mm wheels, a 12 kg mass budget, a 72 Wh battery-energy basis, and a 20 W photovoltaic module. With rolling-resistance coefficient 0.04, steady ascent of a 10 degree grade needs about 0.517 N m per wheel under equal load sharing. An illustrative 40 W motion load gives 1.44 h from 57.6 Wh usable energy, and a 25 percent driving duty gives 4.19 h without solar input; these are calculated scenarios, not measured performance. Sensor models show how integration time, calibration, temperature, and communication delay constrain interpretation, and a quality-aware stop-and-sample policy links these constraints to mission execution. Lightweight detectors, reference-based sensor learning, and executable data-integrity checks define a reproducible machine-learning evaluation pathway. The contribution is a traceable design and evaluation framework with editable 3D models, subsystem diagrams, and reproducible analytical data. Experimental validation is required before assigning payload, endurance, detection, or field-operating ratings.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a literature-informed engineering design and evaluation framework for Zephyron, a four-wheel environmental reconnaissance rover, establishing an explicit, traceable component and geometry baseline while flagging that experimental validation is still required before any operational ratings are assigned.
AI.motivation: Environmental reconnaissance requires mobile platforms that carry sensors, preserve measurement context, and return interpretable evidence under limited energy and communication budgets. Existing prototype layouts rely on unsupported numerical assumptions, so a traceable baseline is needed to make design and evaluation reproducible.
AI.method: A reproducible literature search retrieved 5,000 records (4,858 unique) for screening, followed by targeted review of primary literature and manufacturer documentation. The baseline specifies 165 mm wheels, a 12 kg mass budget, a 72 Wh battery-energy basis, and a 20 W photovoltaic module; performance is analyzed under a rolling-resistance coefficient of 0.04 and equal-load-sharing assumptions. Sensor models characterize how integration time, calibration, temperature, and communication delay constrain interpretation, and a quality-aware stop-and-sample policy links these constraints to mission execution. Lightweight detectors, reference-based sensor learning, and executable data-integrity checks define a reproducible machine-learning evaluation pathway. Deliverables include editable 3D models, subsystem diagrams, and reproducible analytical data.
AI.result: Steady ascent of a 10 degree grade requires about 0.517 N m per wheel under equal load sharing. An illustrative 40 W motion load yields 1.44 h from 57.6 Wh usable energy, and a 25 percent driving duty yields 4.19 h without solar input. These figures are calculated scenarios rather than measured performance.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a traceable design and evaluation framework that replaces unsupported numerical assumptions with an explicit component and geometry baseline. However, experimental validation is required before assigning payload, endurance, detection, or field-operating ratings.

title: The Tasteful Agent: Measuring and Improving Taste in Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: LLM agents increasingly work on long-horizon tasks, and the decisions they make along the way, such as which hypothesis to test or which implementation to build on, determine the outcome of the whole run. Making these decisions well is becoming a key capability for both engineering and research agents. We refer to the ability to make good long-horizon decisions as the taste of an agent. While existing benchmarks measure the end-to-end success of agents on long-horizon tasks, none of them measures the taste of an agent. To address this problem, we build Taste-Bench, a benchmark of taste questions constructed automatically from trajectories that agents produced in engineering and research tasks. Each question presents a decision fork, a point in a trajectory where multiple directions are available and one of them leads to a better outcome, and the evaluated model chooses among these directions without seeing what happens after the fork. We mine these forks automatically from parallel attempts at the same task and from detours inside a single trajectory, without needing human annotation.
