We evaluate frontier models on Taste-Bench and find that the best model answers only 59.7% of the questions correctly. We further find that forks whose deciding evidence appears later in the trajectory are much harder for every model, and that a larger reasoning budget does not improve the accuracy. Finally, we show that taste can be trained. We distill the judgment of a teacher that has seen the outcome into a student model, and the student makes better decisions on unseen tasks and improves end-to-end success on held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Taste-Bench, an automatically constructed benchmark that measures the "taste" (long-horizon decision-making ability) of LLM agents at decision forks mined from engineering and research trajectories. Frontier models score at most 59.7%, later-resolving forks are harder and more reasoning budget does not help, yet taste can be distilled from a teacher to improve a student's decisions and end-to-end SWE-bench Pro success.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks where intermediate decisions (e.g., which hypothesis to test or which implementation to build on) determine the overall outcome. Although existing benchmarks measure end-to-end task success, none directly measures an agent's ability to make good long-horizon decisions, which the authors call "taste." This gap motivates a dedicated benchmark for evaluating and improving this capability.
AI.method: The authors build Taste-Bench by automatically mining decision forks from agent trajectories on engineering and research tasks. A fork is a point where multiple directions are available and one yields a better outcome; the evaluated model selects among directions without observing post-fork outcomes. Forks are mined automatically from parallel attempts at the same task and from detours within a single trajectory, requiring no human annotation. They evaluate frontier models on this benchmark and additionally distill the judgment of a teacher that has observed the outcome into a student model.
AI.result: The best frontier model answers only 59.7% of Taste-Bench questions correctly. Forks whose deciding evidence appears later in the trajectory are substantially harder for every model, and a larger reasoning budget does not improve accuracy. Distillation transfers taste: the student model makes better decisions on unseen tasks and improves end-to-end success on held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks.
AI.conclusion: Taste is a distinct, measurable, and currently weak capability of LLM agents that existing end-to-end benchmarks fail to capture. It is not improved by more reasoning budget but is trainable via distillation from an outcome-aware teacher, suggesting taste can be acquired and transferred to real long-horizon engineering tasks.

title: Designing an Efficient Excavator Bucket for Lunar ISRU: A Comparative Study with Vision-Based Fill and Displacement Analysis
comment: Accepted and presentaed at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2026)
summary: This paper present a spiral-cavity wheel for lunar regolith excavation and a sensor-light evaluation stack that jointly estimates fill ratio (vision), sinkage (vision), and specific energy from actuator logs. In benchtop tests (four revolutions at 5, 10, and 15~RPM) against two literature baselines, the proposed wheel achieved higher excavated mass and fill ratio, delivering 2.2-3.0 times higher excavation rate while reducing specific energy by 29 % relative to a bucket-drum baseline. Normalized sinkage (mm/kg) was also lower, indicating stable traction without bogging. Effort-time traces show a steady torque envelope with repeatable cut-carry-dump cycles across speeds. We provide a retention index $η$ that correlates with fill ratio and a DEM setup that reproduces experimental trends with low error. Results suggest spiral-cavity wheels can replace heavier multi-actuator diggers when mass, simplicity, and energy efficiency are mission drivers.

AI.tldr: A spiral-cavity lunar regolith excavation wheel with a sensor-light evaluation stack (vision-based fill ratio and sinkage, actuator-log specific energy) outperformed two literature baselines, achieving 2.2-3.0x higher excavation rate and 29% lower specific energy than a bucket-drum baseline.
AI.motivation: Lunar regolith excavation conventionally relies on heavier multi-actuator diggers; when mission drivers are mass, simplicity, and energy efficiency, a lighter and simpler excavation solution is needed.
AI.method: A spiral-cavity wheel for lunar regolith excavation paired with a sensor-light evaluation stack that jointly estimates fill ratio (vision), sinkage (vision), and specific energy from actuator logs. Benchtop tests were run for four revolutions at 5, 10, and 15 RPM against two literature baselines, supplemented by a retention index eta correlating with fill ratio and a DEM setup reproducing experimental trends.
AI.result: The proposed wheel achieved higher excavated mass and fill ratio, delivering 2.2-3.0 times higher excavation rate while reducing specific energy by 29% relative to a bucket-drum baseline. Normalized sinkage (mm/kg) was lower, indicating stable traction without bogging. Effort-time traces showed a steady torque envelope with repeatable cut-carry-dump cycles across speeds, and the DEM setup reproduced experimental trends with low error.
AI.conclusion: Spiral-cavity wheels can replace heavier multi-actuator diggers when mass, simplicity, and energy efficiency are mission drivers.

title: When Are Aggregate Agent Traces Diagnosable? Traffic-Governed Interpretation and Calibrated Abstention
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. The reproducibility artifact is linked in the paper
summary: Runtime traces can appear transparent, but a closed-loop policy determines which states are visited and which failures become visible. We study a simulated hotel-pricing agent mapping time, inventory, and market state to discrete price actions under varying demand regimes. A fault may leave no aggregate trace when the policy rarely visits affected cells. We treat entry into aggregate-only fault interpretation as a diagnosability decision preceding scoring or localization. A reference-map gate requires repeated clean-policy support; a matched runtime gate then requires joint support in clean and current streams. Signal analysis occurs only after both pass. We calibrate false admission on a disjoint clean stream at the physical-component level and model detection by affected clean traffic rather than nominal cell coverage. In a frozen one-shot heldout, 55/72 (76.4%) regime-component units were reference-admitted, representing 20 physical components; 54/55 passed matched runtime admission, while the rejected unit abstained. Stable false admission was 0/20, with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391, meeting the frozen 0.20 criterion. Across 540 repeated unit-arm rows nested in those 20 clusters, affected clean traffic reduced negative log likelihood by 29.3% relative to cell coverage, a gain of 0.1264 nats per row (cluster-bootstrap 95% interval [0.0593, 0.1918]). Adding mask family and its interaction improved log loss by 0.0015 nats per row (one-sided upper bound 0.0066), below the frozen 0.01 practical-sufficiency margin. A development audit found that exact minimum hitting set and greedy selection chose identical supports in 12/12 scenarios because singleton evidence had resolved the conflicts. The result is a bounded rule for interpreting aggregate agent behavior: first establish exposure, then score change, and abstain when the trace cannot support the claim.

AI.tldr: A closed-loop pricing agent's hidden faults may leave no aggregate trace when the policy rarely visits affected states. The paper reframes interpretation of such traces as a diagnosability decision: establish "exposure" via a reference-map gate plus a matched runtime gate before any scoring or localization, and abstain otherwise.
AI.motivation: Runtime traces may look transparent, but a closed-loop policy actively determines which states are visited and which failures become visible. A fault can therefore leave no aggregate trace if the policy rarely visits affected cells, so concluding "no fault" from aggregate-only data risks a false claim. The paper motivates treating entry into aggregate-only fault interpretation as a diagnosability decision that precedes scoring or localization, rather than scoring an unverified trace.
AI.method: Simulated hotel-pricing agent mapping time, inventory, and market state to discrete price actions across demand regimes. Two-stage gating: (1) a reference-map gate requiring repeated clean-policy support, then (2) a matched runtime gate requiring joint support in clean and current streams; signal analysis occurs only if both pass. False admission is calibrated on a disjoint clean stream at the physical-component level, and detection is modeled by affected clean traffic rather than nominal cell coverage. Adjudication includes a frozen one-shot heldout, 540 repeated unit-arm rows nested in clusters, and a development audit comparing exact minimum hitting set versus greedy support selection.
AI.result: In the frozen heldout, 55/72 (76.4%) regime-component units were reference-admitted (20 physical components); 54/55 passed matched runtime admission, with the rejected unit abstaining. Stable false admission was 0/20 (one-sided exact 95% upper bound 0.1391, meeting the frozen 0.20 criterion). Across 540 repeated unit-arm rows nested in 20 clusters, affected clean traffic reduced negative log likelihood by 29.3% versus cell coverage (gain 0.1264 nats per row; cluster-bootstrap 95% interval [0.0593, 0.1918]). Mask family and its interaction improved log loss by 0.0015 nats per row (one-sided upper bound 0.0066), below the 0.01 practical-sufficiency margin. The development audit found exact minimum hitting set and greedy selection chose identical supports in 12/12 scenarios because singleton evidence had resolved the conflicts.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers a bounded rule for interpreting aggregate agent behavior: first establish exposure, then score change, and abstain when the trace cannot support a claim. Empirical calibration supports low stable false admission, and affected clean traffic is a materially better predictor than nominal cell coverage, while more complex mask-based models add no practically sufficient gain.

title: AgriGen: Large-Scale Scene Generation Framework for Photorealistic Agricultural Robotics Simulation
comment: Presented at the ICRA 2026 Workshop on Agricultural Robotics (https://agrifoodroboticsworkshop.wordpress.com/icra2026/)
summary: Agricultural robotics is advancing rapidly, yet progress remains constrained by limited field access, lack of control over field conditions, geographic variability, and seasonal crop cycles. These factors make it difficult and costly to acquire diverse agricultural datasets, resulting in limited evaluation and reduced system robustness. While other robotics domains have scaled learning and evaluation through high-fidelity simulation, agricultural robotics still lacks comparably capable tools. In this paper, we present a ROS-integrated framework, built on Isaac Sim, for large-scale procedural generation of agricultural environments. The framework supports photorealistic rendering, physics simulation, and domain randomization at scales relevant to robotics research, with built-in support for row crops, orchards, and vineyards and straightforward extensibility to additional crop categories. Project Page: https://baj31415.github.io/agrigen/

AI.tldr: The paper presents an Isaac Sim-based, ROS-integrated framework for large-scale procedural generation of agricultural environments, enabling photorealistic rendering, physics simulation, and domain randomization to overcome data scarcity in agricultural robotics.
AI.motivation: Agricultural robotics progress is constrained by limited field access, uncontrolled field conditions, geographic variability, and seasonal crop cycles. These factors make acquiring diverse agricultural datasets difficult and costly, leading to limited evaluation and reduced system robustness. Unlike other robotics domains that scaled learning and evaluation via high-fidelity simulation, agricultural robotics lacks comparably capable tools.
AI.method: The authors develop a ROS-integrated framework built on Isaac Sim for large-scale procedural generation of agricultural environments. It supports photorealistic rendering, physics simulation, and domain randomization at scales relevant to robotics research, with built-in support for row crops, orchards, and vineyards plus straightforward extensibility to additional crop categories.
AI.result: The framework delivers a scalable, high-fidelity simulated agricultural environment capability, addressing the lack of comparably capable simulation tools in agricultural robotics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ROS-integrated, Isaac Sim-based framework enables large-scale procedural generation of agricultural environments, providing a tool to improve dataset acquisition, evaluation, and system robustness in agricultural robotics.

title: Optimizing the Score, Losing Sight of the Task: Reward Hacking Across Weights, Selection, and Prompts
summary: A higher evaluation score does not always mean a better language model system. When optimization exploits an evaluator's mistakes, measured progress can conceal unchanged or deteriorating task performance. This failure can arise through parameter updates, selection among generated outputs, or revisions to persistent prompts. We develop a comparative framework for reward hacking across these three optimization substrates: weights, selection, and text. Building on the Proxy Compression Hypothesis and research on inference-time and in-context reward hacking, we examine how reachable behavior, optimization budgets, and persistent adaptation shape exposure to proxy error. We formalize a distance-dependent upper bound on evaluator disagreement and a capacity ordering for nested policy classes, then show why distance alone cannot establish a universal ranking of vulnerability. An exact finite-output illustration demonstrates how the location of a scoring defect changes the behavior favored by each method. We also map representative defenses across substrates, identifying which mechanisms transfer directly and which offer only functional analogies. Persistent prompts receive particular attention: their contents are inspectable, but the behavior induced by a small textual change may be difficult to anticipate. The formal analysis, numerical illustration, and published evidence together provide a basis for comparing optimization methods and identifying the conditions under which their defenses transfer. The resulting framework connects optimization choices to verification requirements: reliable improvement depends on controlling accessible failure modes and preserving evidence of task quality independent of the score being optimized.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a comparative framework for reward hacking across three optimization substrates—weights, selection, and text—analyzing how reachable behavior, optimization budgets, and persistent adaptation shape exposure to evaluator (proxy) error, and maps which defenses transfer across substrates.
AI.motivation: Higher evaluation scores do not guarantee better language model systems. When optimization exploits an evaluator's mistakes, measured progress can mask unchanged or deteriorating task performance. Such reward hacking arises through parameter updates, selection among generated outputs, or revisions to persistent prompts, yet prior work (Proxy Compression Hypothesis, inference-time and in-context reward hacking) has not systematically compared these substrates.
AI.method: A comparative framework across weights, selection, and text. It formalizes a distance-dependent upper bound on evaluator disagreement and a capacity ordering for nested policy classes, argues why distance alone cannot establish a universal vulnerability ranking, provides an exact finite-output illustration of how the location of a scoring defect changes the behavior each method favors, and maps representative defenses across substrates to identify direct transfers versus functional analogies, with special attention to persistent prompts.
AI.result: Distance alone cannot yield a universal vulnerability ranking across substrates; the distance-dependent upper bound and capacity ordering for nested policy classes hold, and the finite-output illustration shows that a scoring defect's location determines which behavior each optimization method favors. Defenses transfer unevenly—some mechanisms carry over directly, others offer only functional analogies—and persistent prompts are inspectable yet induce behavior from small textual changes that is hard to anticipate.
AI.conclusion: The framework connects optimization choices to verification requirements: reliable improvement depends on controlling accessible failure modes and preserving evidence of task quality independent of the optimized score. This provides a basis for comparing optimization methods and identifying conditions under which their defenses transfer.

title: Dual Covariance Gaussian Splatting SLAM: Decoupling Rendering and Registration for Robust Real-Time Tracking
summary: ICP-based 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) SLAM tracks in real time by registering incoming frames against map Gaussians, using each primitive's covariance for both rendering and registration. These two uses place conflicting demands on one covariance. The mapper shapes it to minimize photometric error, often flattening it against surfaces, while robust registration typically benefits from measurement uncertainty. We propose a dual-covariance parameterization. Each Gaussian keeps a single mean but holds two covariances: a rendering covariance optimized by the mapper, and a tracking covariance derived from an RGB-D sensor noise model. We further use the tracking covariances as Gaussian anchors for image corners, providing constraints in directions where depth geometry is weak. We evaluate on TUM RGB-D, ScanNet, Replica, and two outdoor sequences recorded with a RealSense D435i on wheeled and handheld platforms. We achieve robust tracking performance across multiple scenes and reduced odometry drift, while tracking at $\sim$ 60 FPS.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dual-covariance 3D Gaussian Splatting parameterization for ICP-based SLAM, separating rendering and tracking covariances to resolve their conflicting demands, and additionally uses tracking covariances as anchors for image corners.
AI.motivation: In ICP-based 3DGS SLAM, a single Gaussian covariance serves both rendering and registration, which impose conflicting requirements: the mapper flattens covariances against surfaces to minimize photometric error, whereas robust registration benefits from measurement uncertainty. This conflict degrades tracking performance.
AI.method: Each Gaussian retains a single mean but holds two covariances: a rendering covariance optimized by the mapper and a tracking covariance derived from an RGB-D sensor noise model. The tracking covariances are also used as Gaussian anchors for image corners, adding constraints in directions where depth geometry is weak.
AI.result: Evaluated on TUM RGB-D, ScanNet, Replica, and two outdoor sequences recorded with a RealSense D435i on wheeled and handheld platforms, the method achieves robust tracking across multiple scenes and reduced odometry drift while tracking at approximately 60 FPS.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling rendering and tracking covariances, and leveraging tracking covariances as corner anchors, resolves the covariance conflict in ICP-based 3DGS SLAM, yielding robust and drift-reduced real-time tracking.

title: Prediction Is Not Detection: Evaluating Pre-Recognition Claims in Longitudinal Clinical AI
comment: 27 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables, 1 box; includes Supplementary Note
summary: Clinically useful early detection requires validated pre-recognition lead time. Yet event-based evaluations of longitudinal clinical AI can treat recognition-mediated care-process signals as shortcuts and recognition-dependent endpoints as reference standards, inflating apparent performance and lead time while undermining cross-center transport. Such results may serve prognosis without establishing detection before recognition. We define an interval-censored pre-recognition transition, an independent as-of reference standard, and a prespecified recognition proxy to make the claim testable.

AI.tldr: Event-based evaluations of longitudinal clinical AI can inflate performance and lead time by treating recognition-mediated signals as shortcuts and recognition-dependent endpoints as ground truth. The authors propose an interval-censored pre-recognition transition, an independent as-of reference standard, and a prespecified recognition proxy to make early-detection claims testable.
AI.motivation: Clinically useful early detection demands validated pre-recognition lead time, yet standard event-based evaluation frameworks confound this by using recognition-mediated care-process signals as shortcuts and recognition-dependent endpoints as reference standards. This inflates apparent performance and lead time and harms cross-center transport, yielding prognostic rather than true detection claims.
AI.method: The paper formalizes three components: (1) an interval-censored pre-recognition transition, (2) an independent as-of reference standard, and (3) a prespecified recognition proxy, to render early-detection claims testable under a defined evaluation design.
AI.result: Not reported in the abstract; the abstract is a methodological framing rather than an empirical report.
AI.conclusion: Early-detection claims for clinical AI must be made testable through the proposed formalization; otherwise reported performance and lead time are confounded by recognition and should be interpreted as prognosis, not detection.

title: Fisheye-VLA: Decoupling Coverage and Acuity for Manipulation with a Single Fisheye Camera
summary: Manipulation requires both broad scene awareness and detailed local feedback, yet conventional camera rigs provide them through separate front and wrist cameras. We present Fisheye-VLA, a visual interface that brings these capabilities together using a single passive fisheye. A global view preserves the workspace, while local perspective crops direct detail toward the interaction. The key design question is where this local visual budget should go. We answer it through a controlled re-rendering study, comparing alternative crop directions on the same recorded observations. The study finds that end-effector-centered views capture most of the estimated benefit of a much larger candidate pool, motivating a compact allocation around both hands. Our interface uses calibrated end-effector projection and motion lead to track the crops, while a shared ray encoding preserves their spatial meaning as they move. Integrated with a pretrained VLA, it achieves 84% and 82% success in the two expanded tabletop regions, where some target placements extend beyond the front-camera coverage, and supports shelf and conveyor manipulation. Ablations show that local crops and their viewing directions become more important in the larger workspace regions. The results demonstrate that a single fisheye can support these manipulation tasks without physical wrist cameras.

AI.tldr: Fisheye-VLA replaces the conventional front-plus-wrist camera rig with a single passive fisheye, using a global view plus end-effector-centered local crops to achieve 84%/82% success in expanded tabletop regions without physical wrist cameras.
AI.motivation: Manipulation needs both broad scene awareness and fine local feedback, but conventional camera rigs supply these through separate front and wrist cameras. The paper asks whether a single passive fisheye can unify both capabilities, and specifically where the limited local visual budget should be allocated.
AI.method: Fisheye-VLA is a visual interface built on one passive fisheye: a global view preserves the workspace while local perspective crops provide interaction detail. Crop placement is decided via a controlled re-rendering study comparing alternative crop directions on the same recorded observations. The interface tracks crops using calibrated end-effector projection and motion lead, with a shared ray encoding preserving spatial meaning across motion. It is integrated with a pretrained VLA.
AI.result: The re-rendering study finds end-effector-centered views capture most of the estimated benefit of a much larger candidate pool, motivating a compact allocation around both hands. The integrated system reaches 84% and 82% success in two expanded tabletop regions where some targets lie beyond front-camera coverage, and supports shelf and conveyor manipulation. Ablations show local crops and their viewing directions matter more in larger workspace regions.
AI.conclusion: A single fisheye can support these manipulation tasks without physical wrist cameras, unifying global awareness and local feedback in one passive sensor.

title: AgenticSizing: A Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Framework for Analog Circuit Sizing
summary: Analog circuit sizing remains a challenging and time-consuming task due to the large design space, strong performance trade-offs, and increasing circuit complexity in scaled technologies. Although recent large language model (LLM)-based methods show promise in improving sample efficiency and interpretability, existing approaches often lack explicit circuit-topology understanding and are mainly evaluated on relatively simple analog building blocks. This paper presents a multi-agent LLM-based framework for complex analog circuit sizing. The proposed framework first analyzes the circuit topology and decomposes the netlist into functional blocks and substructures. It also extracts lightweight design knowledge for reuse. Based on the extracted topology and knowledge, a planner coordinates multiple role-specialized sizing agents to update design variables and achieve global performance specifications. This workflow mimics the collaborative process of an expert analog design team and provides a structured, interpretable, and simulation-driven optimization procedure. The framework was validated on eight circuits, with the largest design containing up to 55 transistors and 60 sizing variables. Notably, for the LDO benchmark, the proposed method achieved a 60\% success rate with an average of 83 iterations, where classical optimizers failed to find feasible solutions. Further, ablation studies demonstrate that topology understanding, design-knowledge infusion, and agent specialization provide complementary benefits. The source code is available to support reproducibility.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent LLM framework performs complex analog circuit sizing by analyzing topology, decomposing netlists into functional blocks, extracting reusable design knowledge, and coordinating role-specialized agents; validated on eight circuits (up to 55 transistors, 60 variables), achieving 60% success on an LDO where classical optimizers failed.
AI.motivation: Analog circuit sizing is challenging due to large design space, strong performance trade-offs, and growing circuit complexity in scaled technologies. Existing LLM-based methods lack explicit circuit-topology understanding and are mainly evaluated on relatively simple analog building blocks.
AI.method: A multi-agent LLM-based framework: (1) analyzes circuit topology and decomposes the netlist into functional blocks and substructures; (2) extracts lightweight design knowledge for reuse; (3) a planner coordinates multiple role-specialized sizing agents to update design variables and meet global performance specifications, mimicking an expert analog design team in a structured, interpretable, simulation-driven optimization procedure.
AI.result: Validated on eight circuits, the largest with up to 55 transistors and 60 sizing variables. On the LDO benchmark, it achieved a 60% success rate with an average of 83 iterations, where classical optimizers failed to find feasible solutions. Ablation studies show topology understanding, design-knowledge infusion, and agent specialization provide complementary benefits.
AI.conclusion: Topology-aware, knowledge-infused, role-specialized multi-agent LLM coordination enables effective and interpretable sizing of complex analog circuits, outperforming classical optimizers on hard benchmarks. Source code is released for reproducibility.

title: PLAT: Sparse Timed Keyframe Motion Tracking for Humanoid Control via Privileged Latent Transition Learning
summary: Humanoid motion tracking policies rely on dense frame-by-frame references, limiting their use as high-level motion controllers for planning and interactive motion generation. We study \emph{Sparse Timed Keyframe Motion Tracking}, where a policy receives only sparse future keyframes and their desired arrival times, and must execute stable whole-body motions that reach successive goals. We propose \textbf{PLAT}, a three-stage sparse timed keyframe motion tracking policy learning framework with \textbf{P}rivileged \textbf{LA}tent \textbf{T}ransition learning. PLAT bridges dense motion tracking and sparse goal-conditioned control by exploiting dense goal sequences as privileged supervision during training while requiring only sparse timed keyframe commands at deployment. A pretrained dense tracking expert first provides robust motion priors. A privileged latent prior is then learned through DAgger-style imitation, followed by latent residual reinforcement learning that refines latent transitions instead of directly optimizing actions. Extensive simulation experiments demonstrate that PLAT maintains accurate and stable sparse timed keyframe tracking across varying planning horizons, with particularly strong performance under long-horizon commands. Successful deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot further demonstrates the effectiveness and practicality of PLAT for sparse humanoid motion control.

AI.tldr: PLAT is a three-stage framework that learns a sparse timed keyframe whole-body motion tracking policy for humanoids by exploiting dense motion sequences as privileged supervision during training while deploying with only sparse timed keyframes.
AI.motivation: Humanoid motion tracking policies depend on dense frame-by-frame references, which restricts their use as high-level motion controllers for planning and interactive motion generation. The paper aims to enable tracking from only sparse future keyframes with desired arrival times.
AI.method: PLAT follows a three-stage pipeline: (1) a pretrained dense tracking expert supplies robust motion priors; (2) a privileged latent prior is learned via DAgger-style imitation; (3) latent residual reinforcement learning refines latent transitions rather than directly optimizing actions, with dense goal sequences used as privileged supervision during training.
AI.result: Simulation experiments show PLAT maintains accurate and stable sparse timed keyframe tracking across varying planning horizons, with particularly strong performance under long-horizon commands. It was also successfully deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
AI.conclusion: PLAT effectively bridges dense motion tracking and sparse goal-conditioned control, offering a practical solution for sparse humanoid motion control that supports planning and interactive motion generation.

title: CausalLoss-Fin: Attributing Financial-Agent Loss to Decisions and Infrastructure Faults
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Code and reproducibility materials: https://github.com/abhisheksharma2411/causalloss-fin
summary: When an agent handling a payment exception loses money, the agent-step attribution methods this paper compares against will name one of its actions. They will do so even when a settlement message was dropped and the agent never had a chance: they intervene on agent actions and do not expose infrastructure faults as intervenable variables, so every dollar they explain is charged to a decision. We take a benchmark whose fault process is explicit and replayable, decompose each episode's realised delivery schedule into named, individually repairable messages, and intervene on both the agent's choices and the infrastructure's. A telescoping identity splits any policy's loss exactly three ways: an infrastructure effect, a policy differential against the best implementable policy, and a reference-policy residual. Two of the three can be negative, so none is a share; Shapley then divides the first into signed allocations over individual messages. One result is structural and needs no corpus: an agent-only baseline identifies no infrastructure cause, because its model contains no variable that could name one. What 545 planted episodes across 3 policies measure is the size of that consequence. It misfiles 100% of infrastructure episodes and charges $114,383.40 to the agent. Repairing what it names recovers 0.0% of the available loss; repairing a minimal sufficient set recovers 100.0%. Scoring messages one at a time is not merely imprecise: 27.8% (95% CI: 23.3--32.3%) of episodes do not decompose additively. We evaluate deterministic programmatic policies rather than language-model agents, which is what makes replay exact and which limits external validity to stochastic agents. The prevalence figures are properties of this generator, not field rates.

AI.tldr: Agent-only attribution methods blame an agent's decisions for losses caused by infrastructure faults, because their models contain no variable that could name infrastructure as a cause. The authors build a replayable benchmark with explicit faults, decompose each episode into individually repairable messages, and intervene on both agent and infrastructure. A telescoping identity splits loss into infrastructure, policy-differential, and residual components, and Shapley divides the infrastructure part across messages. An agent-only baseline misfiles 100% of infrastructure episodes and charges $114,383.40 to the agent while recovering 0.0% of loss, versus 100.0% for a minimal sufficient set.
AI.motivation: Attribution methods used for payment-exception agents intervene only on agent actions and do not treat infrastructure faults as intervenable variables. Consequently, when a settlement message is dropped and the agent never had a chance to act, every explained dollar is charged to an agent decision. The paper aims to expose and quantify this structural misattribution.
AI.method: The authors use a benchmark with an explicit, replayable fault process and decompose each episode's realised delivery schedule into named, individually repairable messages. They intervene on both agent choices and infrastructure elements. A telescoping identity decomposes any policy's loss exactly into an infrastructure effect, a policy differential against the best implementable policy, and a reference-policy residual; Shapley values then allocate the infrastructure component into signed allocations over individual messages.
AI.result: Structurally, an agent-only baseline identifies no infrastructure cause because its model lacks a variable capable of naming one. Across 545 planted episodes and 3 policies, it misfiles 100% of infrastructure episodes and charges $114,383.40 to the agent; repairing what it names recovers 0.0% of available loss, while repairing a minimal sufficient set recovers 100.0%. Additionally, 27.8% (95% CI: 23.3–32.3%) of episodes do not decompose additively when messages are scored individually.
AI.conclusion: Agent-only attribution is structurally incapable of naming infrastructure causes and produces severe misattribution in the planted episodes studied. Message-level additive scoring is not merely imprecise, since a substantial fraction of episodes are non-additive. Results apply to deterministic programmatic policies, which permit exact replay but limit external validity to stochastic agents, and prevalence figures are properties of this generator rather than field rates.

title: MedVLA: A Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Framework for Closed-Loop Precision Medical Robot Manipulation
summary: Precision medical robotics demands adaptive decision-making under strict safety, interpretability, and execution constraints. Although recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models show strong multimodal reasoning ability, their continuous action generation paradigm is not well suited for precision medical tasks, where reliable closed-loop operation may also depend on non-action system function calls. To address this gap, we propose MedVLA, a hierarchical framework that couples high-level multimodal reasoning with low-level function-constrained execution. We further introduce a scalable multi-agent pipeline to generate skill-oriented chain-of-thought(CoT) data for structured training. Built on different multimodal large-model backbones, MedVLA consistently improves performance after fine-tuning, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework across model variants. Under identical initial conditions, we perform 100 closed-loop flexible electrode implantation trials. The results show that MedVLA achieves a 95.0\% task success rate, substantially outperforming representative VLA baselines, including OpenVLA (8\%) and $π_0$ (15\%), in accuracy, stability, and safety. These results indicate that structured reasoning with constrained function-level execution is a practical route toward deployable precision medical robotics.

AI.tldr: MedVLA is a hierarchical Vision-Language-Action framework that separates high-level multimodal reasoning from low-level function-constrained execution, achieving a 95.0% success rate in closed-loop flexible electrode implantation trials, far exceeding OpenVLA (8%) and π₀ (15%).
AI.motivation: Precision medical robotics requires adaptive decision-making under strict safety, interpretability, and execution constraints. Although recent VLA models exhibit strong multimodal reasoning, their continuous action generation paradigm is ill-suited for precision medical tasks, where reliable closed-loop operation may also depend on non-action system function calls.
AI.method: MedVLA is a hierarchical framework coupling high-level multimodal reasoning with low-level function-constrained execution. A scalable multi-agent pipeline generates skill-oriented chain-of-thought (CoT) data for structured training. The framework is built on different multimodal large-model backbones and evaluated across model variants.
AI.result: After fine-tuning, MedVLA consistently improves performance across model variants. Under identical initial conditions, 100 closed-loop flexible electrode implantation trials yielded a 95.0% task success rate, substantially outperforming representative VLA baselines OpenVLA (8%) and π₀ (15%) in accuracy, stability, and safety.
AI.conclusion: Structured reasoning combined with constrained function-level execution is a practical route toward deployable precision medical robotics.

title: VideoX-Qwen: Data-Centric Instruction-Based Video Editing
summary: Progress in general-purpose video editing depends on constructing large-scale paired supervision and effectively adapting video-generation backbones to instruction-driven editing. Unlike video generation, video editing must execute a requested transformation while preserving unrelated subjects, scene structure, motion, and temporal continuity. We present VideoX-Qwen, an integrated data-construction and model-training framework for general instruction-based video editing. Our scalable production pipeline organizes specialized generation and understanding models into complementary routes for addition, removal, replacement, and attribute editing, followed by quality screening and instruction enrichment. It produces more than 1.2 million directional video-editing records, including over 400,000 records in each major task group, with an automatic acceptance rate of 89%. The resulting corpus provides broad and structured coverage of common editing operations through a unified source-instruction-target interface. We further develop a unified Qwen-Wan editor that combines multimodal semantic conditioning with dense source-video latent guidance. A progressive image-video training strategy aligns the multimodal instruction interface, adapts the video generator to source-conditioned editing, and refines output quality with selected high-resolution data. In a 100-example comparison with UniVideo and Kling O1, VideoX-Qwen achieves the best mean result on nine of eleven reported metrics, including instruction following, editing quality, content preservation, structural and perceptual similarity, and video-distribution quality. Together, the large-scale data-production system and unified training framework provide a practical foundation for more capable instruction-driven video editing.

AI.tldr: VideoX-Qwen is an integrated data-construction and model-training framework for general instruction-based video editing, producing 1.2M+ paired editing records and a unified Qwen-Wan editor that outperforms baselines on most metrics.
AI.motivation: Progress in general-purpose video editing is limited by the lack of large-scale paired supervision and by the difficulty of adapting video-generation backbones to instruction-driven editing. Unlike video generation, video editing must perform a requested transformation while preserving unrelated subjects, scene structure, motion, and temporal continuity.
AI.method: A scalable production pipeline organizes specialized generation and understanding models into complementary routes for addition, removal, replacement, and attribute editing, followed by quality screening and instruction enrichment, yielding 1.2M+ directional video-editing records with a unified source-instruction-target interface. A unified Qwen-Wan editor combines multimodal semantic conditioning with dense source-video latent guidance, trained via a progressive image-video strategy that aligns the instruction interface, adapts the generator to source-conditioned editing, and refines quality with selected high-resolution data.
AI.result: The corpus contains over 1.2 million records, including 400,000+ in each major task group, with an 89% automatic acceptance rate. In a 100-example comparison against UniVideo and Kling O1, VideoX-Qwen achieves the best mean result on nine of eleven reported metrics, covering instruction following, editing quality, content preservation, structural and perceptual similarity, and video-distribution quality.
AI.conclusion: The large-scale data-production system and unified training framework together provide a practical foundation for more capable instruction-driven video editing.

title: VisForce: Visual Grounding of Current and Desired Forces for Goal-Conditioned Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as general-purpose robotic manipulation policies. However, in dexterous hand manipulation, contact forces are typically provided as separate states or force-specific representations, making it difficult to explicitly represent the spatial correspondence between force and their corresponding visual locations. In this work, we propose VisForce, which visually grounds the current and desired forces at their corresponding fingertip locations. VisForce renders current and desired visual force cues on the current wrist image and a task-specific goal image, and combines the two representations through goal-conditioned cross-attention to generate force-aware actions. We evaluate VisForce using a real UR10 robot equipped with an RH56F1 dexterous hand through force-conditioned grasping and three multi-stage manipulation tasks. In force-conditioned grasping experiments, VisForce exhibited a consistent grip-force response as the desired force increased, and achieved grasp-and-lift success rates of 70% and 80% for an egg and a toothpaste tube, respectively. It further achieved final success rates of 70%, 55%, and 40% on cup insertion/bottle pouring, tong-assisted bread transfer, and slip-modulated peg-in-hole, respectively. These results show that fingertip-aligned visual force representations can be effectively used for force-aware conditioning in VLA-based dexterous hand manipulation.

AI.tldr: VisForce is a VLA framework that visually grounds current and desired contact forces at their corresponding fingertip locations on images, enabling force-aware conditioning for dexterous hand manipulation.
AI.motivation: In dexterous hand manipulation, VLA models typically treat contact forces as separate states or force-specific representations, which fails to explicitly capture the spatial correspondence between a force and its visual location. This limits force-aware conditioning.
AI.method: VisForce renders current and desired visual force cues directly at the corresponding fingertip locations on the current wrist image and a task-specific goal image. The two representations are then fused via goal-conditioned cross-attention to generate force-aware actions.
AI.result: Evaluated on a real UR10 robot with an RH56F1 dexterous hand. In force-conditioned grasping, VisForce showed consistent grip-force response as desired force increased, with grasp-and-lift success rates of 70% (egg) and 80% (toothpaste tube). Final success rates were 70% (cup insertion/bottle pouring), 55% (tong-assisted bread transfer), and 40% (slip-modulated peg-in-hole).
AI.conclusion: Fingertip-aligned visual force representations can be effectively used for force-aware conditioning in VLA-based dexterous hand manipulation.

title: CQ4OE: A benchmark for assessing LLM-assisted ontology generation from competency questions
summary: Ontology generation from Competency Questions (CQs) is a central yet labor-intensive phase of Ontology Engineering. While large language models (LLMs) offer promising automation capabilities, current evaluations remain fragmented. Task formulations are heterogeneous, gold standards often lack fine-grained CQ provenance, metrics conflate lexical overlap with structural and logical adequacy, and reference ontologies are not always explicitly designed around the evaluation CQs. Here, we address these limitations with CQ4OE, a benchmark for the systematic and reproducible evaluation of LLM-based ontology generation from CQs. For each ontology in the benchmark, we build a CQ-driven gold OWL ontology with explicit provenance linking each CQ to the classes, properties, and axioms required to answer it. From this resource, we define two complementary evaluation tasks. CQ2Term supports term-level evaluation of CQ-specific class and property prediction over 99 CQs, and CQ2Onto supports ontology-level evaluation over 118 CQs, including hierarchy, property modeling, and axiom-level structure. We demonstrate CQ4OE with experiments using nine LLMs under zero-shot, iterative, and multi-agent generation strategies, showing that LLMs recover explicit vocabulary terms more reliably than creating ontologies, particularly in property modeling, hierarchy construction, and axiom generation.

AI.tldr: CQ4OE is a benchmark for systematic, reproducible evaluation of LLM-based ontology generation from Competency Questions, with CQ-driven gold OWL ontologies, explicit CQ provenance, and two tasks (CQ2Term, CQ2Onto).
AI.motivation: Ontology generation from Competency Questions is a central but labor-intensive phase of Ontology Engineering. LLM automation is promising, but current evaluations are fragmented: heterogeneous task formulations, gold standards lacking fine-grained CQ provenance, metrics conflating lexical overlap with structural/logical adequacy, and reference ontologies not explicitly designed around the evaluation CQs.
AI.method: The authors build CQ4OE, in which each ontology is paired with a CQ-driven gold OWL ontology with explicit provenance linking each CQ to the classes, properties, and axioms required to answer it. Two complementary tasks are defined: CQ2Term for term-level evaluation of CQ-specific class and property prediction over 99 CQs, and CQ2Onto for ontology-level evaluation over 118 CQs covering hierarchy, property modeling, and axiom-level structure. Experiments use nine LLMs under zero-shot, iterative, and multi-agent generation strategies.
AI.result: LLMs recover explicit vocabulary terms more reliably than they create full ontologies, with particular weaknesses in property modeling, hierarchy construction, and axiom generation.
AI.conclusion: CQ4OE provides a systematic and reproducible benchmark for evaluating LLM-based ontology generation from CQs, enabling fine-grained, provenance-aware assessment across term-level and ontology-level tasks.

title: MOLA LiDAR-Inertial Odometry (MOLA-LIO) on the COMFORT Localization Benchmark
summary: This short report documents our entry to the COMFORT Localization Benchmark (IROS 2026), evaluated on the GrandTour dataset recorded with the Boxi payload. It extends MOLA-LO into a LiDAR-inertial system that also ingests IMU and, optionally, legged kinematic odometry. We describe the architecture, the streams consumed, the local protocol that selected the submitted configuration, and the measurements backing our real-time claim.

AI.tldr: This short report describes an entry to the COMFORT Localization Benchmark (IROS 2026) evaluated on the GrandTour dataset with the Boxi payload, extending MOLA-LO into a LiDAR-inertial system that optionally fuses IMU and legged kinematic odometry.
AI.motivation: The work targets the COMFORT Localization Benchmark at IROS 2026, aiming to provide a robust localization solution for the GrandTour dataset collected with the Boxi payload, where LiDAR-only odometry is likely insufficient and additional sensing modalities can improve performance.
AI.method: MOLA-LO is extended into a LiDAR-inertial system that ingests IMU data and, optionally, legged kinematic odometry. The paper details the architecture, the sensor streams consumed, the local protocol used to select the submitted configuration, and the measurements supporting the real-time claim.
AI.result: Measurements are reported that substantiate the real-time performance claim; the system consumes LiDAR, IMU, and optionally legged kinematic odometry streams and was configured via a local selection protocol for submission.
AI.conclusion: The extended MOLA-LO LiDAR-inertial system, with optional IMU and legged kinematic odometry fusion, constitutes the authors' submission to the COMFORT Localization Benchmark, with reported evidence of real-time operation.

title: Canonical locks that encode part-whole hierarchies
summary:
One of the challenges in representational learning is how to encode part-whole hierarchies in a neural net. Prior works rely on flattening tree-like structures into string-like sequences and training a sequence-to-sequence model via autoregression. While such a representation works for parse-trees in NLP, it is not entirely clear how to make it work for images. Thus, we propose a geometric primitive called canonical locks. The key idea is that parts/wholes can be modelled as higher-dimensional vectors ($d \geq 4$), and information can be encoded in their relative phase differences.
  Inductively, the net consists of positionally-bound bottom-up and top-down neural fields, which drive each other to achieve a state of thermal equilibrium. Additionally, we show the existence of a few symmetrical configurations in the net. The computational iterations taken to break these symmetries depend on the angle between parts/wholes arranged on a disk (or more precisely a ring) in higher dimensions. It also appears to have connections to the psychological phenomenon of mental rotation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "canonical locks," a geometric primitive that encodes part-whole hierarchies as higher-dimensional vectors (d ≥ 4) using relative phase differences, replacing sequence-based autoregressive approaches for images. The net uses positionally-bound bottom-up and top-down neural fields driving each other to thermal equilibrium, with symmetry-breaking dynamics tied to angular arrangement on a higher-dimensional ring.
AI.motivation: Encoding part-whole hierarchies in neural nets is a core challenge in representational learning. Prior methods flatten tree-like structures into string-like sequences and train seq2seq models via autoregression; this works for parse-trees in NLP but does not clearly transfer to images.
AI.method: Introduces a geometric primitive called canonical locks: parts/wholes are modelled as higher-dimensional vectors (d ≥ 4), with information encoded in their relative phase differences. Inductively, the net consists of positionally-bound bottom-up and top-down neural fields that drive each other toward a state of thermal equilibrium.
AI.result: The paper shows the existence of a few symmetrical configurations in the net. The computational iterations needed to break these symmetries depend on the angle between parts/wholes arranged on a disk (more precisely a ring) in higher dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Canonical locks offer an alternative to sequence-based autoregression for encoding part-whole hierarchies, notably suited to images. The symmetry-breaking iteration count relates to angular geometry in higher dimensions and appears connected to the psychological phenomenon of mental rotation.

title: Beyond Reconstruction Error: Analytical and Data-Driven Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Discrete action tokenization is central to autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models, yet action representations are often evaluated primarily through reconstruction fidelity. We ask which representation properties actually matter for closed-loop control by comparing fixed analytical, data-driven linear, and nonlinear neural representations under a unified tokenization interface. Across rate-distortion analysis, sequence-modeling diagnostics, and 3,500 LIBERO rollouts, representation rankings change with the evaluation criterion. PCA achieves lower nominal reconstruction error than Temporal-DCT, but produces less predictable token sequences and 3.0 percentage points lower mean seen-task success across three policy-training seeds, with the policy ordering reversing in one seed. In a matched seed-42 ablation, an autoencoder further reduces reconstruction error yet does not yield the strongest policy and exhibits greater sensitivity to discrete token perturbations. These findings show that reconstruction fidelity alone cannot reliably select action representations for autoregressive control, motivating joint evaluation of geometric fidelity, sequence predictability, decoder stability, and closed-loop performance.

AI.tldr: Reconstruction fidelity alone is an unreliable criterion for selecting action representations in autoregressive VLA models; a joint evaluation across geometric fidelity, sequence predictability, decoder stability, and closed-loop control is needed.
AI.motivation: Discrete action tokenization is central to autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models, yet action representations are typically evaluated mainly through reconstruction fidelity. The paper asks which representation properties actually matter for closed-loop control.
AI.method: The authors compare fixed analytical, data-driven linear, and nonlinear neural action representations under a unified tokenization interface. Evaluation spans rate-distortion analysis, sequence-modeling diagnostics, and 3,500 LIBERO rollouts.
AI.result: Representation rankings change with the evaluation criterion. PCA attains lower nominal reconstruction error than Temporal-DCT but produces less predictable token sequences and 3.0 percentage points lower mean seen-task success across three policy-training seeds, with policy ordering reversing in one seed. In a matched seed-42 ablation, an autoencoder further reduces reconstruction error but does not yield the strongest policy and shows greater sensitivity to discrete token perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Reconstruction fidelity alone cannot reliably select action representations for autoregressive control, motivating joint evaluation of geometric fidelity, sequence predictability, decoder stability, and closed-loop performance.

title: FIRE: Failure-Informed Runtime Engineering for Reliable Language-Model Agents
summary: Language-model agents often reach a working solution and then fail to consistently deliver it. We study runtime policies: targeted natural-language instructions and action denials applied by the agent harness at states that preceded observed failures, without changing model weights or the user prompt. With this, keeping capability constant, we observe a meaningful unlock in delivered reliability. Across the complete 87-task Terminal-Bench 2.1 suite, with two attempts per task, policies increase repeated success (pass^2) in all three GPT-5.6 tiers: 50.6% to 54.0% for Luna, 55.2% to 60.9% for Terra, and 64.4% to 73.6% for Sol. Sol's best-of-two success changes by 1.2 points while repeated success rises by 9.2, showing that policies chiefly convert reachable solutions into dependable delivery. We further cover 14 tasks under Terra's frozen portfolio. Policy-guided Terra reaches 71.4%, compared with 64.3% for unassisted Sol, at about half the cost, demonstrating how engineering around models could unlock dependability for a use case. To isolate the mechanism we run a randomized five-arm experiment: real policies reach 61% on eligible tasks, versus 39% without a policy, 36% with a timing-matched sham, and 39 to 43% with generic verification or reconsideration. The intended corrective behavior appears in 22 of 24 coded policy attempts, against at most 14 in any other arm. Runtime policies are therefore a practical reliability layer: they make capabilities an agent already possesses substantially more repeatable.

AI.tldr: Runtime policies—targeted natural-language instructions and action denials applied by the agent harness at states preceding observed failures, without changing weights or prompts—substantially raise repeated success (pass^2) across all GPT-5.6 tiers on Terminal-Bench 2.1, mainly by converting already-reachable solutions into dependable delivery.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents often reach a working solution yet fail to deliver it consistently. The authors seek to improve delivered reliability while holding model capability constant, i.e., without retraining or prompt engineering.
AI.method: Runtime policies are injected by the agent harness as natural-language instructions and action denials at states that preceded observed failures. Evaluation uses the full 87-task Terminal-Bench 2.1 suite with two attempts per task across three GPT-5.6 tiers (Luna, Terra, Sol), plus 14 tasks under Terra's frozen portfolio. Mechanism isolation uses a randomized five-arm experiment comparing real policies against no policy, a timing-matched sham, and generic verification/reconsideration interventions, with coded policy attempts measuring intended corrective behavior.
AI.result: Repeated success (pass^2) rises in all tiers: 50.6%→54.0% (Luna), 55.2%→60.9% (Terra), 64.4%→73.6% (Sol). Sol's best-of-two success moves only 1.2 points while repeated success gains 9.2. Policy-guided Terra reaches 71.4% versus 64.3% for unassisted Sol at roughly half the cost. In the five-arm experiment, real policies reach 61% on eligible tasks versus 39% (no policy), 36% (timing-matched sham), and 39–43% (generic verification/reconsideration); intended corrective behavior appears in 22 of 24 coded policy attempts versus at most 14 in any other arm.
AI.conclusion: Runtime policies act as a practical reliability layer: they make capabilities an agent already possesses substantially more repeatable, converting reachable solutions into dependable delivery and enabling cheaper tiered models to outperform stronger unassisted ones.

title: Sometimes You Gotta Run Before You Can Walk: Run-then-Walk Scheduling Strategy for VLM Autonomous Driving
summary: Recent VLM-based autonomous driving planners adopt GRPO-style reinforcement learning to optimize driving performance. However, existing GRPO recipes either optimize driving efficiency, risking progress-seeking but unsafe behavior, or enforce early safety constraints, leading to overly conservative behavior; both require lengthy training. To solve these problems, we first reveal two distinct RL regimes: a progress regime (Run-GRPO) that aggressively explores high progress, and a safety regime (Walk-GRPO) that restores safety under stable progress. Based on this finding, we propose $\textit{Run-then-Walk}$, a simple yet effective two-stage reward scheduling strategy for GRPO, achieving both better performance and faster convergence. Unlike one-stage RL, which may focus on progress, safety, or a mixture of both within a single training phase, this schedule explicitly separates progress discovery from safety repair. In the $\textit{Run}$ phase, we focus on progress, allowing the policy to escape the conservative bias and discover high-progress modes. In the subsequent $\textit{Walk}$ phase, we introduce endpoint and safety strategy to repair unsafe behaviors from the Run phase. This reversed schedule overcomes the conservatism of Walk-first methods and the unsafe progress-seeking of joint optimization. We validate it with various VLM-based planners on multiple benchmarks: NAVSIMv1, NAVSIMv2, Navhard, and nuScenes. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved driving performance while requiring 40--50\% fewer RL training epochs than the baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "Run-then-Walk," a two-stage reward scheduling strategy for GRPO-based VLM autonomous driving planners that separates progress discovery (Run) from safety repair (Walk), achieving better performance with 40-50% fewer training epochs.
AI.motivation: Existing GRPO recipes for VLM-based driving planners face a trade-off: optimizing driving efficiency risks unsafe behavior, while enforcing early safety constraints yields overly conservative behavior. Both approaches require lengthy training, and single-phase RL struggles to balance progress and safety.
AI.method: The authors identify two distinct RL regimes: a progress regime (Run-GRPO) exploring high progress aggressively, and a safety regime (Walk-GRPO) restoring safety under stable progress. Based on this, they propose Run-then-Walk, a two-stage reward scheduling for GRPO. The Run phase allows the policy to escape conservative bias and discover high-progress modes, followed by a Walk phase introducing endpoint and safety strategies to repair unsafe behaviors.
AI.result: Validated across VLM-based planners on NAVSIMv1, NAVSIMv2, Navhard, and nuScenes benchmarks, showing improved driving performance while requiring 40-50% fewer RL training epochs than baselines.
AI.conclusion: The reversed Run-then-Walk schedule overcomes both the conservatism of Walk-first methods and the unsafe progress-seeking of joint optimization, offering improved performance and faster convergence.

title: Adversarial Course-of-Action Generation: Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Algorithms for COA matching & COA generation
comment: 5 pages. DAI 2026 Industry Track submission. Includes public reproducibility artifact link. Uses synthetic offline scenarios only; no classified data, proprietary data, human-subject data, or operational planning systems
summary: Course-of-action (COA) generation is a distributed planning problem: a system must propose structured candidate actions, evaluate them against an adversarial response, and surface options that remain tactically coherent under changing conditions. We present COA-Bench, a small offline benchmark and reproducibility artifact for comparing COA generation policies through self-play. Following the BattleCOA terminology, we reserve COA matching for asset-effect matching and COA generation for course-of-action generation; the present artifact does not implement either DecisionFunction directly. Instead, it represents COAs as typed action chains with conditional branches, assigns a synthetic COA quality score, compares opposing COAs with a BLUE-vs-RED advantage score and Nash-gap distance, and scores doctrinal coherence with an FM 3-0-inspired heuristic rubric. Across 50 synthetic scenarios spanning five operational templates, a sampled best-response policy that draws eight RED candidates reduces BLUE advantage from .516 to .485 and BLUE wargame win rate from .920 to .820; a two-stage multi-agent council with five BLUE proposer agents, RED-team adjudication, and critique-driven revision obtains .509 BLUE advantage and .820 BLUE win rate. We also identify and fix a benchmark-design issue in which scenario framing was stored as metadata but had no effect on generated COA content. COA-Bench is not an operational battle-management system and uses no real, classified, proprietary, or human-subject data. The contribution is an inspectable evaluation harness, preliminary benchmark evidence, and lessons for building auditable agentic planning artifacts.

AI.tldr: COA-Bench is a small offline, reproducible benchmark for comparing course-of-action (COA) generation policies via self-play, using typed action chains, synthetic quality/advantage/Nash-gap scores, and a doctrinal coherence rubric, evaluated over 50 synthetic scenarios.
AI.motivation: COA generation is framed as a distributed planning problem requiring structured candidate proposals, adversarial evaluation, and tactical coherence under changing conditions. There is a need for an inspectable, reproducible evaluation harness to compare COA generation policies, along with auditable lessons for building agentic planning artifacts.
AI.method: COAs are represented as typed action chains with conditional branches. Synthetic COA quality scores are assigned; opposing COAs are compared via a BLUE-vs-RED advantage score and Nash-gap distance; doctrinal coherence is scored with an FM 3-0-inspired heuristic rubric. Following BattleCOA terminology, COA matching and COA generation are distinguished, and neither DecisionFunction is implemented directly. Policies compared include a sampled best-response policy (eight RED candidates) and a two-stage multi-agent council (five BLUE proposers, RED-team adjudication, critique-driven revision).
AI.result: Across 50 synthetic scenarios spanning five operational templates, the sampled best-response policy reduced BLUE advantage from .516 to .485 and BLUE wargame win rate from .920 to .820. The two-stage multi-agent council achieved .509 BLUE advantage and .820 BLUE win rate. A benchmark-design issue was also identified and fixed: scenario framing was stored as metadata but had no effect on generated COA content.
AI.conclusion: COA-Bench is an inspectable evaluation harness with preliminary benchmark evidence and transferable lessons for building auditable agentic planning artifacts. It is not an operational battle-management system and uses no real, classified, proprietary, or human-subject data.

title: What is the Better Curriculum: Controller-Shaped Grasping Behavior for Contact Force-Sensitive Manipulation
summary: How should a robot learn to manipulate objects so fragile that sub-Newton contact forces can cause irreversible damage? Existing visuo-tactile policy learning typically treats tactile sensing as an additional policy input. In direct-contact force-sensitive manipulation, however, the bottleneck can arise earlier, during data collection: manual gripper control is too delayed and coarse-grained to reliably maintain the narrow force range required for stable grasping. We therefore use a deterministic 25 Hz tactile reflex controller as a collection-time teacher, producing demonstrations with controller-shaped grasping behavior for tactile-free policy learning. On Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), policies trained from reflex-shaped demonstrations recover the teacher's grasping profile and achieve 95% stable grasps on the nominal plastic-cup task, substantially outperforming visually screened manual demonstrations. The same intervention improves in-distribution stability on $π_{0.5}$ and shows a favorable exploratory trend on an unseen paper-cup variant. Under randomized external disturbance, however, the reflex-data $π_{0.5}$ policy still fails in 45% of policy-only trials, whereas a deployment-time reflex arbiter retains all grasps. These results reveal a new role for tactile feedback in force-sensitive manipulation: rather than integrating tactile into the policy, we use it as a collection-time teacher that shapes grasping behavior in demonstrations for policy learning, while disturbance rejection remains controller-dependent, revealing the boundary of tactile-free policy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using a deterministic 25 Hz tactile reflex controller as a collection-time teacher to generate demonstrations for tactile-free policy learning in force-sensitive manipulation. Reflex-shaped demonstrations boost ACT performance and stability, but under external disturbance the learned policy still fails while the reflex controller preserves all grasps, defining the boundary of tactile-free policies.
AI.motivation: Manipulating fragile objects requires maintaining a narrow contact force range; since sub-Newton forces can cause irreversible damage. The bottleneck in direct-contact force-sensitive manipulation arises earlier than policy learning—during data collection—where manual gripper control is too delayed and coarse-grained to reliably sustain stable grasping forces. Standard visuo-tactile policy learning treats tactile sensing only as an extra policy input, missing this collection-time limitation.
AI.method: A deterministic 25 Hz tactile reflex controller is used as a collection-time teacher to produce demonstrations with controller-shaped grasping behavior for tactile-free policy learning. Policies are trained on these reflex-shaped demonstrations using Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) and π_{0.5}. A deployment-time reflex arbiter is also tested for disturbance rejection.
AI.result: ACT policies trained from reflex-shaped demonstrations recover the teacher's grasping profile and achieve 95% stable grasps on the nominal plastic-cup task, substantially outperforming visually screened manual demonstrations. The same intervention improves in-distribution stability on π_{0.5} and shows a favorable exploratory trend on an unseen paper-cup variant. Under randomized external disturbance, the reflex-data π_{0.5} policy still fails in 45% of policy-only trials, whereas the deployment-time reflex arbiter retains all grasps.
AI.conclusion: Tactile feedback plays a new role in force-sensitive manipulation: rather than integrating tactile into the policy, it serves as a collection-time teacher that shapes grasping behavior in demonstrations for policy learning. Disturbance rejection nonetheless remains controller-dependent, revealing the boundary of tactile-free policy learning.

title: ChainUQ: Reasoning Consistency-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models
summary: While large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive reasoning capabilities, response-level confidence may remain unreliable when intermediate claims conflict with the final conclusion. Therefore, effective uncertainty quantification (UQ) is required to capture logical inconsistencies within the reasoning chain, not just the correctness of the final output. Current approaches have two major limitations: (1) their reliance on token-level probabilities fails to capture reasoning consistency, and (2) they lack mechanisms to dynamically calibrate confidence using the structural logic of the generated chain. To advance existing research, we introduce ChainUQ, a reasoning consistency-aware uncertainty quantification framework for LLMs. ChainUQ consists of two key technical components: an alignment-aware lightweight UQ module that estimates a raw intrinsic model confidence score from frozen features aligned to the final conclusion, and a reasoning consistency-aware calibrator that refines this score using reasoning-chain consistency evidence. Evaluations across diverse in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks show that ChainUQ consistently improves response-level uncertainty estimation, achieving an average 3.1% relative gain in AUROC and up to 45.0% relative reduction in ECE, and can be directly transferred to new settings without additional fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: ChainUQ is a reasoning consistency-aware uncertainty quantification framework for LLMs that estimates intrinsic confidence from conclusion-aligned frozen features and refines it via reasoning-chain consistency evidence, improving AUROC and ECE across ID/OOD benchmarks and transferring without extra fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Response-level confidence in LLMs can be unreliable when intermediate claims conflict with the final conclusion, so uncertainty quantification must capture logical inconsistencies within the reasoning chain rather than only final-output correctness. Existing methods are limited by (1) reliance on token-level probabilities that miss reasoning consistency and (2) lack of mechanisms to dynamically calibrate confidence using the structural logic of the generated chain.
AI.method: ChainUQ comprises two components: (1) an alignment-aware lightweight UQ module that estimates a raw intrinsic model confidence score from frozen features aligned to the final conclusion, and (2) a reasoning consistency-aware calibrator that refines this score using reasoning-chain consistency evidence.
AI.result: Across diverse in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks, ChainUQ consistently improves response-level uncertainty estimation, with an average 3.1% relative gain in AUROC and up to 45.0% relative reduction in ECE; it can be directly transferred to new settings without additional fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: ChainUQ advances UQ for LLM reasoning by explicitly modeling reasoning-chain consistency, yielding more reliable response-level uncertainty and strong transferability without retraining.

title: Robust Active-Perception Control for Global-State-Free Aerial-Ground Cooperation
summary: Aerial-ground cooperation requires real-time UAV--UGV relative-state information. Instead of maintaining global estimates for both robots, direct control in a UGV-attached non-inertial frame avoids reliance on global localization. Vision-based relative pose estimation with a passive marker offers a low-cost and effective solution. However, a fixed camera may lose sight of the moving UGV when the required UAV attitude conflicts with the field-of-view (FOV) constraint. To address this, we propose COPA, a robust active-perception framework for global-state-free aerial-ground cooperation. We use a single-axis gimbal to decouple the camera optical axis from the UAV pitch attitude. We derive an active-perception model that relates UAV motion, gimbal angle, and UGV motion to the target image-plane state.A Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) predicts short-horizon UGV acceleration and angular velocity from recent motion history without global-state measurements. The model predictive control (MPC) uses these predictions to jointly optimize UAV and gimbal control. Simulations show that COPA maintains continuous target visibility, while ablation studies confirm that the TCN reduces peak errors during UGV motion transitions. Real-world experiments with UGV accelerations up to 3m/s^2 and yaw rates up to 1.0rad/s demonstrate robust tracking.

AI.tldr: COPA is a global-state-free active-perception framework for aerial-ground cooperation that uses a single-axis gimbal to decouple the camera optical axis from UAV pitch and a TCN-MPC pipeline to keep a moving UGV continuously in view, validated in simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Aerial-ground cooperation requires real-time UAV--UGV relative-state information. Direct control in a UGV-attached non-inertial frame avoids reliance on global localization, and vision-based relative pose estimation with a passive marker is low-cost. However, a fixed camera may lose sight of the moving UGV when the required UAV attitude conflicts with the field-of-view (FOV) constraint.
AI.method: COPA uses a single-axis gimbal to decouple the camera optical axis from UAV pitch attitude. It derives an active-perception model relating UAV motion, gimbal angle, and UGV motion to the target image-plane state. A Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) predicts short-horizon UGV acceleration and angular velocity from recent motion history without global-state measurements, and MPC jointly optimizes UAV and gimbal control using these predictions.
AI.result: Simulations show COPA maintains continuous target visibility, and ablation studies confirm that the TCN reduces peak errors during UGV motion transitions. Real-world experiments with UGV accelerations up to 3 m/s^2 and yaw rates up to 1.0 rad/s demonstrate robust tracking.
AI.conclusion: COPA enables robust, global-state-free aerial-ground cooperation by combining gimbal-based active perception with learned UGV motion prediction and joint MPC, achieving continuous target visibility and robust tracking under aggressive UGV maneuvers.

title: RankCert: When Can Simulated Learners Safely Select an AI Tutor? Robust Decision Certification Under Structural Uncertainty
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology (TIST)
summary: Simulation-based tutor selection can be unstable when predictively adequate learner models imply different policy rankings. RankCert certifies one of eight equal-budget tutoring policies only when model-averaged utility, probability-best, posterior regret, cross-domain rank, family coverage, and leave-one-domain-out and leave-one-visible-family-out averages support the same candidate; otherwise it abstains. We evaluated RankCert in 1,280 frozen held-out settings spanning five rotating held-out oracle families, 64 scenarios per family, and four cohort sizes. Calibration used a licensed, de-identified EdNet-KT1 derivative with 5,000 learners and 590,056 retained responses; all five family representatives passed the frozen adequacy gate. Minimum-domain mean pairwise top-1 agreement was 0.272917 (95% CI [0.253646, 0.293229]), showing substantial structural disagreement. Cohort-noise variance decreased from n = 30 to n = 300, while the structural family share remained nonzero. RankCert reduced total held-out decision loss relative to full-coverage point selection by 0.006605 normalized-outcome units (95% CI [0.004859, 0.008407]). At comparable coverage, however, it did not reduce selective risk relative to a confidence-gated point certificate (difference -0.000213; 95% CI [-0.003238, 0.002384]; Holm p = 0.929654). Certification occurred in 3.75% of settings and only in stable scenarios; RankCert abstained in every ambiguous, misspecified, and structural-conflict setting. "Safe" denotes only benchmark-scoped decision certification under the declared utility and uncertainty set; no human-learning, causal, deployment-effectiveness, or general-safety claim is made.
