AI.tldr: RankCert is a model-averaged certification procedure that endorses one of eight equal-budget tutoring policies only when seven distinct evidence criteria agree, otherwise it abstains; certification occurred in just 3.75% of 1,280 frozen held-out settings and reduced total decision loss versus full-coverage point selection, but did not beat a confidence-gated point certificate on selective risk at comparable coverage.
AI.motivation: Simulation-based tutor selection is unstable because multiple predictively adequate learner models can imply different rankings of candidate tutoring policies. The paper aims to provide a decision certificate that licenses a single policy only when the ranking is robust across models, domains, and families, abstaining under ambiguity, misspecification, or structural conflict.
AI.method: RankCert certifies one of eight equal-budget tutoring policies only when seven criteria agree: model-averaged utility, probability-best, posterior regret, cross-domain rank, family coverage, and leave-one-domain-out and leave-one-visible-family-out averages. Evaluation covered 1,280 frozen held-out settings: five rotating held-out oracle families, 64 scenarios per family, and four cohort sizes. Calibration used a licensed, de-identified EdNet-KT1 derivative with 5,000 learners and 590,056 retained responses; all five family representatives passed the frozen adequacy gate.
AI.result: Minimum-domain mean pairwise top-1 agreement was 0.272917 (95% CI [0.253646, 0.293229]), indicating substantial structural disagreement. Cohort-noise variance decreased from n = 30 to n = 300 while the structural family share remained nonzero. RankCert reduced total held-out decision loss versus full-coverage point selection by 0.006605 normalized-outcome units (95% CI [0.004859, 0.008407]). At comparable coverage, it did not reduce selective risk versus a confidence-gated point certificate (difference -0.000213; 95% CI [-0.003238, 0.002384]; Holm p = 0.929654). Certification occurred in 3.75% of settings and only in stable scenarios; RankCert abstained in every ambiguous, misspecified, and structural-conflict setting.
AI.conclusion: RankCert provides benchmark-scoped decision certification under the declared utility and uncertainty set, reliably abstaining in ambiguous, misspecified, and structurally conflicting settings. It improves total decision loss over full-coverage point selection but offers no selective-risk advantage over a confidence-gated point certificate at comparable coverage. The authors explicitly make no human-learning, causal, deployment-effectiveness, or general-safety claim.

title: You Should Be Properly Scoring Your Odometry
summary: When we evaluate the performance of our odometry, it is common practice to score the estimated track against a ground truth. Unfortunately, scoring uses point metrics, such as the root mean square error, that ignore the covariance matrix which estimators like filters and smoothers already report. Using the covariance matters for two reasons. First, the covariance encodes the estimator's uncertainty, so it tells us whether the estimator trusts its own output. An overconfident estimator will not report itself lost. Second, the covariance weights the error in each direction of the estimate. Without the covariance, an estimator is unduly penalized for a high error in an uncertain direction. Instead of point metrics, we should use strictly proper scoring rules. These rules score the estimate together with its reported uncertainty. Strictly proper scoring rules recover the point metrics when no covariance is reported, and they diagnose covariance inconsistency when covariance is reported. Using a one-sided pairwise test, we show that two estimators can expose overconfidence in at least one of them without a ground truth. Strictly proper scoring rules and our pairwise test are available in our open-source framework smfeval. As a case study, we use smfeval to assess the uncertainty quality of the translational component of ground-based LiDAR-inertial odometry. Across four filters we find overconfidence - the worst case reports centimeter certainty with kilometer error. Knowing the filters are overconfident, we investigate the mechanism. The investigation traces overconfidence to filters crediting LiDAR measurements with more new information than they carry.

AI.tldr: Odometry should be scored with strictly proper scoring rules that use the estimator's covariance, not point metrics like RMSE; this diagnoses overconfidence, and a pairwise test can even expose it without ground truth.
AI.motivation: Standard odometry evaluation uses point metrics (e.g., RMSE) that ignore the covariance already reported by filters and smoothers. This matters because the covariance encodes the estimator's uncertainty (whether it trusts its output, e.g., an overconfident estimator won't report itself lost) and weights error per direction, so ignoring it unduly penalizes large errors in uncertain directions.
AI.method: The authors replace point metrics with strictly proper scoring rules, which score the estimate together with reported uncertainty, recover point metrics when no covariance is reported, and diagnose covariance inconsistency when covariance is present. They also develop a one-sided pairwise test to expose overconfidence in at least one of two estimators without ground truth, and implement both in the open-source framework smfeval.
AI.result: As a case study, smfeval assessed the uncertainty quality of the translational component of ground-based LiDAR-inertial odometry. Across four filters, overconfidence was found—the worst case reported centimeter certainty while exhibiting kilometer error. Investigation traced the overconfidence to filters crediting LiDAR measurements with more new information than they actually carry.
AI.conclusion: Covariance-aware, strictly proper scoring rules are preferable to point metrics for odometry evaluation. They enable diagnosis of overconfidence and covariance inconsistency, and the pairwise test can reveal overconfidence without a ground truth. The open-source smfeval framework supports this evaluation, and the LiDAR-inertial case study demonstrates real overconfidence rooted in overestimated measurement information.

title: Selection-Invariant Communication Compilers for Privacy-Aware Multi-Agent LLM Workflows
summary: Structured multi-agent workflows exchange intermediate messages whose content and form can reveal private state even when the final output is safe. We identify selection-channel leakage: after authorization fixes what may be released, a private-state-aware choice among semantically valid realizations creates an additional inference channel. We introduce the selection-invariant communication compiler(SICC), which constrains this post-authorization representation kernel rather than prescribing templates. Any deterministic or independently public-randomized generator satisfying the invariant is valid; requirement-indexed canonical forms are one auditable implementation. We prove a compositional communication-layer guarantee: authorization, public-only form generation, and a dependency-safe utility gate make the emitted transcript reveal no information beyond the complete authorized view. Private-state-aware selection remains vulnerable after surface-disjoint and length-matched controls. Across 132 AgentLeak communication replays and 100 executable LangGraph tasks, deterministic SICC retains complete protocol utility without a positive excess-gain signal; independent public randomization preserves the same result in AgentLeak and 480 controlled cases.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "selection-channel leakage" in structured multi-agent workflows—where private-state-aware choices among semantically equivalent messages leak information even after authorization—and proposes SICC, a selection-invariant communication compiler that provably removes this post-authorization inference channel while preserving protocol utility.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent workflows, intermediate messages are exchanged whose content and form can reveal private state even when the final output is safe. Even after authorization determines what may be released, a private-state-aware choice among semantically valid realizations creates an additional inference channel—termed selection-channel leakage—that existing surface-level defenses do not address.
AI.method: The authors formalize selection-channel leakage and introduce the Selection-Invariant Communication Compiler (SICC), which constrains the post-authorization representation kernel rather than prescribing fixed templates. Any deterministic or independently public-randomized generator satisfying the selection-invariance invariant is admissible, with requirement-indexed canonical forms offered as one auditable implementation. The approach combines authorization, public-only form generation, and a dependency-safe utility gate into a compositional communication-layer guarantee.
AI.result: The authors prove a compositional guarantee that the emitted transcript reveals no information beyond the complete authorized view. Empirically, private-state-aware selection remains vulnerable after surface-disjoint and length-matched controls. Across 132 AgentLeak communication replays and 100 executable LangGraph tasks, deterministic SICC retains complete protocol utility without a positive excess-gain signal, while independent public randomization preserves the same result in AgentLeak and 480 controlled cases.
AI.conclusion: Selection-channel leakage is a genuine, previously under-addressed threat that survives standard surface-disjoint and length-matched defenses. SICC eliminates this channel through selection invariance, providing a formal communication-layer guarantee alongside full protocol utility across real and controlled evaluations.

title: Control Barrier Functions for Safe Free-Flying Robotic Spacecraft Operations in Tumbling Target Capture
comment: Accepted to the international Conference on Space Robotics (iSpaRo) 2026
summary: This paper presents a modular control barrier function (CBF) framework for safe free-flying robotic spacecraft operations during tumbling target capture. Motivated by latest ESA guidelines for safe close proximity operations, safety zones and requirements are translated into dedicated CBFs. The 13-DoF system is decomposed into translational, attitude, and robotic subsystems, each equipped with a safety filter that minimally modifies nominal control inputs in a lightweight quadratic program. The filters enforce a conical approach corridor, collision avoidance zone, attitude line-of-sight pointing, angular velocity limits, robotic joint limits, link-base collision avoidance, and actuator constraints. Dynamic coupling between subsystems is handled by treating upstream safe control commands as known interconnection inputs in the downstream safety filters, preserving modularity while supporting system-level safety. The framework is validated in an on-orbit servicing scenario, including final approach, angular rate synchronization, and tumbling target grasping, using the high-fidelity astrodynamics simulator Basilisk. Monte Carlo simulation results demonstrate runtime efficiency and operational safety for various tumbling rates.

AI.tldr: A modular control barrier function framework decomposes a 13-DoF free-flying spacecraft-manipulator system into translational, attitude, and robotic subsystems, each with a lightweight quadratic-program safety filter, and validates safe tumbling-target capture in Basilisk simulations.
AI.motivation: Motivated by recent ESA guidelines for safe close-proximity operations, this work aims to translate safety zones and operational requirements into verifiable constraints for free-flying robotic spacecraft capturing a tumbling target.
AI.method: The 13-DoF system is decomposed into translational, attitude, and robotic subsystems. Each subsystem has a safety filter formulated as a lightweight quadratic program that minimally modifies nominal control inputs. Dedicated CBFs enforce a conical approach corridor, collision avoidance zone, attitude line-of-sight pointing, angular velocity limits, joint limits, link-base collision avoidance, and actuator constraints. Inter-subsystem dynamic coupling is handled by treating upstream safe commands as known interconnection inputs in downstream filters, preserving modularity and system-level safety.
AI.result: Validated in an on-orbit servicing scenario covering final approach, angular rate synchronization, and tumbling target grasping using the high-fidelity astrodynamics simulator Basilisk. Monte Carlo simulations show runtime efficiency and operational safety across various tumbling rates.
AI.conclusion: The modular CBF framework provides a scalable, computationally efficient approach to enforcing system-level safety in free-flying robotic spacecraft operations, with demonstrated effectiveness in tumbling target capture under ESA-inspired safety requirements.

title: The Architect, the Adversary, and the Judge: Closed-Loop Generation of Standards-Aligned Assessment Items at Scale
comment: 31 pages, 8 figures, 16 tables. Companion paper: arXiv:2608.01000
summary: We present CLAIM, a production pipeline for K-12 assessment-item generation coupling a two-stage generate-then-attack protocol (the model drafts as a "curriculum architect", then re-enters the same conversation as a hostile adversarial reviewer), bi-directional few-shot conditioning on accepted and rejected items, the latter carrying the evaluator's diagnosis, and a knowledge dictionary of 44,844 error-correction rules mined from that feedback and retrieved per standard and item type. Across 43,227 scored items over 755 Common Core ELA standards, three item types, and ten LLMs, the pipeline reaches a 97.8% expert-evaluator pass rate on a 9,074-item production run. We then ask what that rate certifies. Re-scoring a stratified sample with three judges from other vendors, blind to the deployed verdict, reproduces the format ordering under every judge and recovers a larger open-set deficit than the deployed evaluator does; but agreement on the accept/reject binary is weak at production prevalence (kappa about 0.13), and the judges agree with each other no better. The level is therefore judge-relative, and with no student-response data our quality evidence is evaluator-judged throughout. The corpus also exposes a robust asymmetry. Multiple-choice and multiple-select generation saturate at 98% or above for both frontier models under a dozen static rules, whereas fill-in-the-blank generation is capability-tiered (82.8-96.7% across five models under a matched rule set, standards, and judge) and plateaus under prompt-only optimization, with error mass shifting between answer-key over-inclusion and omission as rules accumulate. We analyze this as open-set boundary determination, a task autoregressive decoders are structurally ill-equipped to solve, and show the asymmetry recurring when the evaluator itself is distilled: fail-recall rises from 8% to 63% while F1 saturates at 0.25.

AI.tldr: CLAIM is a production pipeline for K-12 assessment-item generation whose 97.8% pass rate is judge-relative (weak cross-vendor agreement, kappa ~0.13); generation is easy for multiple-choice/multiple-select (>=98%) but capability-tiered and plateauing for fill-in-the-blank, which is framed as open-set boundary determination that autoregressive decoders handle poorly.
AI.motivation: The paper questions what a high automated pass rate actually certifies for generated assessment items, and investigates whether difficulty is uniform across item types or reflects a structural limitation of autoregressive decoders.
AI.method: Two-stage generate-then-attack protocol (curriculum architect then hostile adversarial reviewer in the same conversation); bi-directional few-shot conditioning on accepted and rejected items with evaluator diagnoses; a knowledge dictionary of 44,844 error-correction rules mined from feedback and retrieved per standard and item type. Evaluation spans 43,227 scored items, 755 Common Core ELA standards, three item types, and ten LLMs, plus re-scoring of a stratified sample by three vendor-external blinded judges and a distilled-evaluator study.
AI.result: 97.8% expert-evaluator pass rate on a 9,074-item production run; blind external judges reproduce the format ordering and recover a larger open-set deficit, but accept/reject agreement is weak at production prevalence (kappa ~0.13) and inter-judge agreement is no better. Multiple-choice and multiple-select saturate at >=98% for frontier models under a dozen static rules, whereas fill-in-the-blank is capability-tiered (82.8-96.7% across five models under matched rules, standards, and judge) and plateaus under prompt-only optimization, with error mass shifting between answer-key over-inclusion and omission. When the evaluator is distilled, fail-recall rises from 8% to 63% while F1 saturates at 0.25.
AI.conclusion: High pass rates are judge-relative rather than absolute, and the pipeline's quality evidence is evaluator-judged throughout since no student-response data exists. The item-type asymmetry is explained as open-set boundary determination, a task autoregressive decoders are structurally ill-equipped to solve, and the asymmetry recurs when the evaluator itself is distilled.

title: Vision-based Underwater Formation Control With Input Saturations via Barrier Lyapunov Functions
summary: In this work, we propose a communication-free framework for vision-based formation control of fully actuated underwater robots subject to sensing constraints, collision-avoidance requirements, and input saturations. Recentered barrier Lyapunov functions encode sensing and collision-avoidance constraints, while command-filtered backstepping extends the design to the second-order vehicle dynamics. The resulting control objective is enforced through a quadratic program that explicitly accounts for actuator limits. Conservative sensing domains provide margins from the physical limits and are adaptively relaxed when necessary, allowing temporary violation of the conservative bounds. The proposed approach is validated through realistic Software-in-the-Loop (SITL) simulations in Gazebo.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a communication-free, vision-based formation control framework for fully actuated underwater robots that handles sensing constraints, collision avoidance, and input saturations simultaneously.
AI.motivation: Underwater robots operating in formation face sensing constraints, collision-avoidance requirements, and actuator saturation, while communication-free operation is desirable to avoid unreliable acoustic links. These coupled constraints motivate a unified control design.
AI.method: Recentered barrier Lyapunov functions (RBLFs) encode sensing and collision-avoidance constraints. Command-filtered backstepping extends the design to second-order vehicle dynamics. A quadratic program enforces the control objective while explicitly accounting for actuator limits. Conservative sensing domains provide margins from physical limits and are adaptively relaxed, permitting temporary violation of the conservative bounds.
AI.result: The approach is validated through realistic Software-in-the-Loop (SITL) simulations in Gazebo, demonstrating effective vision-based formation control under the stated constraints.
AI.conclusion: A communication-free vision-based formation control scheme for fully actuated underwater robots is achieved, integrating RBLFs, command-filtered backstepping, and a QP-based constraint handling with adaptive relaxation of conservative sensing bounds.

title: FusionMMT: A Unified Multimodal and Multitask Learning Framework for Nuclear Fusion
summary: With the growing global demand for energy, nuclear fusion has emerged as a promising direction for future clean energy. Tokamaks represent one of the leading approaches to magnetic-confinement fusion. Achieving high-performance, long-pulse, and steady-state operation requires effective diagnosis of plasma states. However, existing intelligent diagnostic methods are largely limited to either multimodal single-task or unimodal multitask learning, while a unified multimodal multitask learning framework remains underexplored. To address this gap, we construct EAST-VTD640, a multimodal multitask dataset that integrates vision and time-series diagnostics from 640 EAST shots for disruption prediction, edge-localized mode (ELM) recognition, and H98 regression. On this basis, we present FusionMMT, the first unified multimodal multitask framework for intelligent tokamak plasma diagnostics. FusionMMT employs multi-scale, time-aware, and variable-aware modeling to handle heterogeneous sampling rates and the high computational cost of high-frequency sequences. It further combines task-adaptive multimodal fusion with progressive multitask optimization to learn shared and task-specific representations while mitigating cross-task conflicts and optimization imbalance. Extensive experiments on EAST-VTD640 show that FusionMMT outperforms representative multimodal multitask methods across disruption prediction, ELM recognition, and H98 regression. The source code will be released on https://github.com/Event-AHU/OpenFusion

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EAST-VTD640, a multimodal multitask dataset from 640 EAST shots, and FusionMMT, the first unified multimodal multitask framework for tokamak plasma diagnostics, outperforming representative methods on disruption prediction, ELM recognition, and H98 regression.
AI.motivation: Tokamaks are a leading magnetic-confinement fusion approach, but high-performance, long-pulse, steady-state operation demands effective plasma-state diagnosis. Existing intelligent diagnostic methods are restricted to either multimodal single-task or unimodal multitask learning, leaving a unified multimodal multitask framework underexplored.
AI.method: The authors build EAST-VTD640, a multimodal multitask dataset combining vision and time-series diagnostics from 640 EAST shots for three tasks: disruption prediction, ELM recognition, and H98 regression. They propose FusionMMT, which uses multi-scale, time-aware, and variable-aware modeling to handle heterogeneous sampling rates and the high computational cost of high-frequency sequences, and combines task-adaptive multimodal fusion with progressive multitask optimization to learn shared and task-specific representations while mitigating cross-task conflicts and optimization imbalance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on EAST-VTD640 show that FusionMMT outperforms representative multimodal multitask methods across disruption prediction, ELM recognition, and H98 regression.
AI.conclusion: FusionMMT is presented as the first unified multimodal multitask framework for intelligent tokamak plasma diagnostics, with source code to be released at https://github.com/Event-AHU/OpenFusion.

title: Unsigned Distance Maps on 2D Point Cloud Registration
comment: 8 pages, 0 figures, 4 tables. Accepted to the 9th Iberian Robotics Conference (ROBOT2026), November 18-20, 2026, Barcelona, Spain. Source code: https://github.com/INESCTEC/ricoslam
summary: 2D point cloud registration arises in laser odometry and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) for mobile robots. Iterative Closest Point (ICP) is one of the most widely used approaches. Still, its iterative procedure recomputes correspondences via nearest-neighbor search at every iteration, whereas correspondence-free alternatives focus on scan-to-map alignment. This paper proposes a 2D point cloud registration approach based on unsigned distance maps, precomputing the Euclidean distance to the nearest reference point, along with its spatial derivatives, over a discrete grid, replacing the per-iteration search with O(1) lookups. Moreover, point-to-point and point-to-plane error formulations are derived on the SE(2) manifold and solved via Gauss-Newton optimization. On a synthetic benchmark and the real-world IILABS 3D dataset, the precomputed point-to-point variant outperforms its analytical counterparts, achieving competitive laser-odometry drift compared to point-to-plane formulations, as the precomputed gradient regularizes correspondences in the presence of sensor noise.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a 2D point cloud registration method using precomputed unsigned distance maps with spatial derivatives on a discrete grid, replacing per-iteration nearest-neighbor search with O(1) lookups, and solves point-to-point/point-to-plane error on SE(2) via Gauss-Newton.
AI.motivation: ICP is widely used for 2D point cloud registration in laser odometry and SLAM, but its iterative procedure recomputes correspondences through nearest-neighbor search at every iteration, which is costly. Existing correspondence-free alternatives mainly target scan-to-map alignment.
AI.method: The approach precomputes unsigned distance maps: the Euclidean distance to the nearest reference point and its spatial derivatives over a discrete grid, turning the per-iteration correspondence search into O(1) lookups. Point-to-point and point-to-plane error formulations are derived on the SE(2) manifold and optimized with Gauss-Newton.
AI.result: On a synthetic benchmark and the real-world IILABS 3D dataset, the precomputed point-to-point variant outperforms its analytical counterparts and achieves competitive laser-odometry drift compared to point-to-plane formulations.
AI.conclusion: The precomputed gradient regularizes correspondences in the presence of sensor noise, making the proposed distance-map-based formulation effective and competitive for 2D registration.

title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy response prediction using pretreatment diffusion and contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging with clinical variables
summary: Prediction of pathological complete response before neoadjuvant chemotherapy may facilitate more tailored therapeutic planning for breast cancer patients. This work proposes a deep-learning model for pretreatment data only, combining apparent diffusion coefficient maps, dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, and clinical variables. The study uses the public ACRIN 6698/I-SPY2 multicenter dataset. The architecture employs EfficientNet-B0 pretrained encoders for image feature extraction and late fusion with clinical information. Multiple clinical variables were evaluated, including age, race, histological type, HR/HER2 subtype, SBR grade, and maximum diameter. Only HR/HER2 subtype improved the average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and was retained in the final model. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation, standalone apparent diffusion coefficient maps achieved a mean AUC of 0.79, whereas dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging achieved 0.74. Adding HR/HER2 subtype improved performance to 0.83 and 0.81, respectively. The final configuration, using both imaging modalities and HR/HER2 subtype, achieved an AUC of 0.86. These results support pretreatment multimodal learning for response prediction, although external validation is required before clinical use.

AI.tldr: A deep-learning model using pretreatment ADC maps, DCE-MRI, and clinical variables (only HR/HER2 subtype retained) predicts pathological complete response in breast cancer, achieving AUC 0.86 on ACRIN 6698/I-SPY2.
AI.motivation: Predicting pathological complete response before neoadjuvant chemotherapy would enable more tailored therapeutic planning for breast cancer patients.
AI.method: Deep-learning model for pretreatment data only, combining apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI, and clinical variables. Uses the public ACRIN 6698/I-SPY2 multicenter dataset. Architecture: EfficientNet-B0 pretrained encoders for image feature extraction plus late fusion with clinical information. Clinical variables evaluated: age, race, histological type, HR/HER2 subtype, SBR grade, maximum diameter; only HR/HER2 subtype improved average AUC and was retained. Stratified five-fold cross-validation.
AI.result: Standalone ADC maps: mean AUC 0.79; DCE-MRI: 0.74. Adding HR/HER2 subtype improved to 0.83 (ADC) and 0.81 (DCE-MRI). Final configuration (both modalities + HR/HER2 subtype): AUC 0.86.
AI.conclusion: Results support pretreatment multimodal learning for response prediction, though external validation is required before clinical use.

title: Destination Support Restoration for Finite-Set Multimodal Trajectory Prediction
comment: Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2027)
summary: Robots operating around pedestrians often reason over a finite set of predicted human futures. Repeated online updates can concentrate this limited prediction budget on dominant destinations and leave plausible alternatives underrepresented or absent, removing those alternatives from the finite representation available to downstream decision making. We introduce Destination Support Restoration (DSR), a causal post-selection operator that repairs destination support without retraining the host predictor or increasing the maintained set size. At a repair step, DSR evaluates a temporary destination-stratified candidate bank from the observed prefix, converts candidate evidence into integer target counts, protects representatives of active modes, and reallocates redundant surplus hypotheses to deficient modes. The maintained and returned sets retain exactly $N$ hypotheses, and DSR replaces at most $\lceilρN\rceil$ entries. Protected representatives preserve current categorical support; lineage-aware particle filters also preserve surviving resampling ancestors. Each replacement reduces the allocation mismatch to the evidence-driven target by one. On the complete 3,719-trajectory Edinburgh protocol over three seeds, DSR reduces MIF weighted ADE and FDE by 13.36% and 13.30% at $N=64$. Paired integrations with CLiFF, PPT, causal GDTS, Social Informer, and PECNet improve both metrics in every evaluated pair. These results show that finite-set support allocation is a useful prediction-side control point when a fixed hypothesis set serves as the interface to downstream systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Destination Support Restoration (DSR), a post-selection operator that repairs underrepresented destination modes in finite human-trajectory prediction sets without retraining or enlarging the set, reducing MIF weighted ADE/FDE by ~13% and improving five host predictors.
AI.motivation: Robots reasoning about pedestrians rely on a finite set of predicted futures. Repeated online updates concentrate the limited prediction budget on dominant destinations, leaving plausible alternatives underrepresented or absent, which removes those options from downstream decision making.
AI.method: DSR is a causal post-selection operator that repairs destination support without retraining the host predictor or increasing the maintained set size. At a repair step it builds a temporary destination-stratified candidate bank from the observed prefix, converts candidate evidence into integer target counts, protects representatives of active modes, and reallocates redundant surplus hypotheses to deficient modes. It keeps exactly N hypotheses, replaces at most ceil(rho*N) entries, preserves current categorical support via protected representatives, and in lineage-aware particle filters preserves surviving resampling ancestors.
AI.result: On the complete 3,719-trajectory Edinburgh protocol over three seeds, DSR reduces MIF weighted ADE and FDE by 13.36% and 13.30% at N=64. Paired integrations with CLiFF, PPT, causal GDTS, Social Informer, and PECNet improve both metrics in every evaluated pair. Each replacement reduces the allocation mismatch to the evidence-driven target by one.
AI.conclusion: Finite-set support allocation is a useful prediction-side control point when a fixed hypothesis set serves as the interface to downstream systems, and DSR effectively restores destination support without retraining or enlarging the maintained set.

title: Early Prediction of Pathological Complete Response to Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy Using Temporal Deep Learning on DWI
summary: Early identification of non-responders to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) is crucial for timely treatment adaptation in breast cancer. However, many existing predictive models rely on multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), late treatment time points, or extensive clinical data, which limits their applicability. This study proposes a deep learning framework for early prediction of pathological complete response (pCR) using only diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) acquired at baseline and after the first NACT cycle. This framework feeds cropped tumor-centered patches to an EfficientNet-based temporal model that directly learns tumor shape and local tissue characteristics without explicit radiomic feature engineering. The model, trained with 10-fold cross-validation, achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.90 for pCR prediction after one cycle, providing actionable information after a single treatment cycle while avoiding gadolinium administration and reducing dependence on heterogeneous clinical data. By focusing on the baseline-to-first-cycle window instead of later stages, the approach supports earlier escalation or de-escalation of NACT, and its exclusive reliance on DW-MRI facilitates protocol standardization, multi-centre deployment and privacy-preserving data sharing. These results demonstrate that DW-MRI-based deep learning on tumor-centered patches constitutes a minimally invasive, clinically deployable strategy for early pCR prediction, with direct implications for personalized treatment adaptation in neoadjuvant breast cancer therapy.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework predicts pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in breast cancer using only diffusion-weighted MRI at baseline and after the first cycle, achieving 0.90 AUC.
AI.motivation: Early identification of non-responders to neoadjuvant chemotherapy is critical for timely treatment adaptation in breast cancer, but existing predictive models depend on multiparametric MRI, late treatment time points, or extensive clinical data, limiting their applicability.
AI.method: Cropped tumor-centered patches from DW-MRI acquired at baseline and after the first NACT cycle are fed to an EfficientNet-based temporal model that directly learns tumor shape and local tissue characteristics without explicit radiomic feature engineering; the model is trained with 10-fold cross-validation.
AI.result: The model achieved an AUC of 0.90 for pCR prediction after one treatment cycle, providing actionable information after a single cycle while avoiding gadolinium administration and reducing dependence on heterogeneous clinical data.
AI.conclusion: DW-MRI-based deep learning on tumor-centered patches is a minimally invasive, clinically deployable strategy for early pCR prediction, supporting earlier escalation or de-escalation of NACT, protocol standardization, multi-centre deployment, and privacy-preserving data sharing, with direct implications for personalized treatment adaptation.

title: An Action Is Worth One Patch: Unified World-Action Modeling with PatchWAM
summary: Generative visual models offer a foundation for learning representations of physical dynamics, yet their extension to continuous control raises a fundamental question: do visual prediction and action generation require separate computational pathways? Existing approaches usually introduce trainable action heads or separate action experts to bridge low-dimensional states and high-dimensional visual representations. In this work, we explore whether the visual backbone's existing capacity can also support control when actions are expressed in a compatible representation. Thus, we introduce PatchWAM (Patch World-Action Model), which treats continuous actions as another type of patch through a fixed mapping called Action-as-Patch. This allows a single model to predict both how the robot should move and what the scene may look like afterward. Visual prediction and action generation become parts of the same generative process, without a dedicated action head or separate action expert. Experiments with subsampled training windows show gains over a matched dual-expert control, while benchmark evaluations reach 91.8% success rate on LIBERO-Plus and 96.12% on RoboTwin 2.0 in a full-data setting with additional augmented demonstrations. More broadly, the result suggests that capability need not be added where it can be inherited: the constraint on extending a generative backbone is the interface a new signal is written in, not the capacity to model it.

AI.tldr: PatchWAM treats continuous actions as patches via a fixed Action-as-Patch mapping, letting a single generative visual backbone perform both visual prediction and action generation without a dedicated action head or expert, achieving strong control benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches typically add trainable action heads or separate action experts to bridge low-dimensional states and high-dimensional visual representations, raising the question of whether visual prediction and action generation truly require separate computational pathways.
AI.method: The paper introduces PatchWAM (Patch World-Action Model), which represents continuous actions as another type of patch through a fixed mapping called Action-as-Patch, unifying visual prediction and action generation within a single generative process.
AI.result: Experiments with subsampled training windows show gains over a matched dual-expert control; benchmark evaluations reach 91.8% success on LIBERO-Plus and 96.12% on RoboTwin 2.0 in a full-data setting with additional augmented demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: Capability need not be added where it can be inherited: the constraint on extending a generative backbone is the interface a new signal is written in, not the capacity to model it.

title: DTOC: Dynamic Tool Output Compression for Adaptive Context Management in AI Agents
comment: Accepted for 29th International Conference on Discovery Science, October 5-9, 2026, Mainz, Germany
summary: As agent capabilities have grown, practical limitations increasingly stem from constrained context windows rather than model capacity. Common strategies, such as truncation, heuristic aging, and lossy summarization, may discard useful information or introduce hallucination risk. To address these challenges, we propose Dynamic Tool Output Compression (DTOC), a framework for scalable context management in LLM-based agents that models context updates as explicit and reversible operations within the agent reasoning loop. DTOC retains full tool outputs in external memory while inserting compact placeholders into the active context, enabling selective reconstruction when needed. We formalize the DTOC mechanism, integrate it into a ReAct-style agent architecture, and provide a production-oriented implementation supporting on-demand restoration of compressed outputs. Experiments on DeepSWE reveal model-dependent effects: for responsive models (Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4), DTOC reduces input tokens (10.3 and 12.7%) and agent steps (2.4 and 32.3%), while increasing solve rates (2.5 and 1.5 times higher) and lowering cost per solved task (3 and 3.5 times lower cost per solved task). For the other models results are more mixed, with GPT-5.5 doubling solve rate and halving cost, but no impact on solve rate and negative impact on cost for the other models. Ablation results show reversibility is critical: disable-only compression variants degraded performance, while full DTOC recovered baseline accuracy at substantially lower context cost. These findings indicate that explicit, reversible context management can improve the efficiency of long-horizon agent reasoning without degrading task performance.

AI.tldr: DTOC is a context-management framework for LLM agents that stores full tool outputs in external memory and inserts compact placeholders into the active context, enabling reversible, on-demand reconstruction. Experiments on DeepSWE show model-dependent gains in token use, steps, solve rate, and cost, with reversibility identified as the critical design element.
AI.motivation: As agent capabilities grow, practical limitations stem from constrained context windows rather than model capacity. Existing strategies such as truncation, heuristic aging, and lossy summarization risk discarding useful information or introducing hallucination, motivating a more principled and reversible approach to context management.
AI.method: The paper proposes Dynamic Tool Output Compression (DTOC), which models context updates as explicit, reversible operations within the agent reasoning loop. Full tool outputs are retained in external memory while compact placeholders are inserted into the active context for selective reconstruction when needed. The mechanism is formalized, integrated into a ReAct-style agent architecture, and implemented in a production-oriented system supporting on-demand restoration of compressed outputs.
AI.result: On DeepSWE, effects are model-dependent. For responsive models (Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4), DTOC reduces input tokens (10.3% and 12.7%) and agent steps (2.4% and 32.3%), increases solve rates (2.5x and 1.5x), and lowers cost per solved task (3x and 3.5x lower). Other models show mixed results: GPT-5.5 doubles solve rate and halves cost, while others show no solve-rate impact and negative cost impact. Ablations show reversibility is critical: disable-only compression variants degraded performance, whereas full DTOC recovered baseline accuracy at substantially lower context cost.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, reversible context management can improve the efficiency of long-horizon agent reasoning without degrading task performance, though benefits vary across models and reversibility is essential to preserving accuracy.

title: Predict Before You Step: Auditable Occupancy Forecasting for Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance under Sparse Guidance
summary: Legged robots under sparse waypoint guidance must avoid moving obstacles using partial, rapidly changing LiDAR observations. We present LOOP (Latent-recurrent Occupancy rollOut Policy), a local avoidance policy that connects sparse waypoint guidance to a frozen locomotion controller at 50 Hz. From occupancy and ego-velocity histories, a recurrent predictor forecasts future occupancy over a 1 s horizon by warping the current map with learned flow and visibility gates. These maps guide velocity selection through map-derived features and geometric risk estimates, providing an explicit interface for inspecting and replacing predictions. In encounter-synchronised Isaac Lab evaluations, LOOP achieves 57.1% head-on success at obstacle speeds of 2.5-3.2 m/s, exceeding a retrained reactive baseline by 8.2 percentage points. Comparisons with a rollout-free BEV policy show smaller, scenario-dependent gains from the prediction branch, including improved crossing success and reduced variability across training seeds at the highest head-on speeds. The adapter runs onboard a Unitree Go2 in 14.5 ms per step and completes all 16 real-world crossing trials without collision, demonstrating deployment feasibility.

AI.tldr: LOOP is a 50 Hz latent-recurrent local avoidance policy that forecasts future occupancy via learned flow and visibility gates to steer a frozen locomotion controller under sparse waypoint guidance, improving head-on success and demonstrating real-world feasibility on a Unitree Go2.
AI.motivation: Legged robots relying on sparse waypoint guidance need to avoid moving obstacles but only receive partial, rapidly changing LiDAR observations, making reactive avoidance insufficient and motivating an explicit, inspectable prediction interface.
AI.method: From occupancy and ego-velocity histories, a recurrent predictor forecasts future occupancy over a 1 s horizon by warping the current map with learned flow and visibility gates. These predicted maps are converted into map-derived features and geometric risk estimates that guide velocity selection, forming an explicit interface between the frozen locomotion controller and sparse waypoint guidance; the policy is evaluated in encounter-synchronised Isaac Lab and compared against a retrained reactive baseline and a rollout-free BEV policy.
AI.result: LOOP achieves 57.1% head-on success at obstacle speeds of 2.5-3.2 m/s, exceeding the retrained reactive baseline by 8.2 percentage points. Gains from the prediction branch over the rollout-free BEV policy are smaller and scenario-dependent, including improved crossing success and reduced variability across training seeds at the highest head-on speeds. Onboard a Unitree Go2, the adapter runs at 14.5 ms per step and completes all 16 real-world crossing trials without collision.
AI.conclusion: Prediction-based latent-recurrent occupancy rollout provides measurable yet scenario-dependent benefits for moving-obstacle avoidance, and its efficiency and collision-free real-world trials confirm deployment feasibility on legged hardware.

title: FairMon: A Tool for Monitoring and Visualizing Algorithmic Fairness
summary: Runtime monitoring has recently been proposed as a rigorous method for analyzing algorithmic fairness of autonomous decision systems used in critical scenarios such as credit lending, job application, and the criminal justice system. Prior work has shown that runtime monitoring, in principle, can be an effective technique for establishing the kind of human oversight required by legislation such as the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. In practice, the available monitoring tools have not been developed with this application in mind and display several critical shortcomings in these scenarios. In this paper, we present FairMon, a runtime monitoring tool tailored to fairness analysis of high-stakes decision systems. FairMon uses RTLola as a flexible specification language for monitors, which we have extended with conditional probability operators that allow for concise descriptions of algorithmic fairness properties. The tool also features a real-time visualization of intermediary values, enabling human insight into the dynamics of the monitored system.

AI.tldr: FairMon is a runtime monitoring tool tailored to fairness analysis of high-stakes autonomous decision systems, using an extended RTLola specification language with conditional probability operators and real-time visualization.
AI.motivation: Runtime monitoring has been proposed as a rigorous method for analyzing algorithmic fairness in critical scenarios (credit lending, job application, criminal justice) and for establishing the human oversight required by legislation such as the EU AI Act. However, existing monitoring tools were not designed for this application and exhibit critical shortcomings in these scenarios.
AI.method: The authors present FairMon, a runtime monitoring tool tailored to fairness analysis of high-stakes decision systems. It employs RTLola as a flexible specification language for monitors, extended with conditional probability operators enabling concise descriptions of algorithmic fairness properties. The tool also provides real-time visualization of intermediary values to give humans insight into the monitored system's dynamics.
AI.result: The abstract reports the tool design and its capabilities (extended specification language with conditional probability operators, real-time visualization) rather than empirical evaluation results. No quantitative performance or accuracy figures are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: FairMon addresses the shortcomings of prior monitoring tools for fairness analysis in high-stakes decision systems, offering a tailored specification language and visualization to support human oversight and regulatory compliance.

title: Safety-Constrained Model Predictive Control for an Omnidirectional Walking Assistive Robot Using Control Barrier Function
summary: Providing safe and effective mobility assistance plays a crucial role in restoring independence and enhancing the quality of life for individuals with motor impairments. In this context, robotic walking assistive devices have recently emerged as promising solutions to provide physically compliant interaction while ensuring user safety and support. This paper presents a novel control framework for an omnidirectional Walking Assistive Robot (I-WANDER) that integrates a Control Barrier Function (CBF) formulation into a Model Predictive Control (MPC) scheme to explicitly enforce collision-avoidance safety constraints while optimizing for energy efficiency and smooth human-robot collaboration. The method was experimentally evaluated with 12 healthy participants performing two different walking tasks using both the proposed CBF-based MPC controller (CB-MPC) and a variable admittance controller (AC). The first task involved structured navigation through a U-shaped corridor, whereas the second consisted of a single-obstacle avoidance task performed blindfolded to ensure the obstacle was unexpected. Comparative results show that the CB-MPC architecture significantly reduces energy consumption and mechanical work (p < 0.01) without compromising motion smoothness, while also decreasing the number of obstacle collisions. Overall, the findings highlight the potential of the proposed control architecture to enhance both safety and efficiency in robotic walking assistance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based Model Predictive Control (CB-MPC) framework for an omnidirectional Walking Assistive Robot (I-WANDER), enforcing collision-avoidance safety while optimizing energy efficiency and smooth human-robot collaboration. In experiments with 12 healthy participants across a U-shaped corridor navigation task and a blindfolded single-obstacle avoidance task, CB-MPC significantly reduced energy consumption and mechanical work (p < 0.01) and decreased obstacle collisions compared to a variable admittance controller, without compromising motion smoothness.
AI.motivation: Safe and effective mobility assistance is essential for restoring independence and improving quality of life for individuals with motor impairments. Robotic walking assistive devices are promising for providing physically compliant interaction while ensuring user safety and support, motivating a control approach that explicitly guarantees safety while remaining efficient and collaborative.
AI.method: The authors propose a novel control framework for an omnidirectional Walking Assistive Robot (I-WANDER) that integrates a Control Barrier Function (CBF) formulation into a Model Predictive Control (MPC) scheme. This CB-MPC architecture explicitly enforces collision-avoidance safety constraints while optimizing for energy efficiency and smooth human-robot collaboration. It was experimentally evaluated with 12 healthy participants performing two walking tasks: structured navigation through a U-shaped corridor, and a blindfolded single-obstacle avoidance task to ensure the obstacle was unexpected. Performance was compared against a variable admittance controller (AC).
AI.result: Comparative results show that the CB-MPC architecture significantly reduces energy consumption and mechanical work (p < 0.01) without compromising motion smoothness, while also decreasing the number of obstacle collisions.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the potential of the proposed control architecture to enhance both safety and efficiency in robotic walking assistance.

title: MAC-RRG: Iterative Multi-Agent Collaboration for X-ray Radiology Report Generation
summary: Despite the remarkable progress of LLM-based and knowledge graph-augmented Radiology Report Generation (RRG) methods, existing techniques still suffer from inherent defects. Conventional LLM-only models lack structured medical prior knowledge, resulting in frequent medical hallucinations and low diagnostic interpretability. Current knowledge graph-enhanced schemes adopt static one-round knowledge fusion with single-source knowledge, incapable of dynamic knowledge updating according to generation feedback. This paper proposes a novel Multi-Agent Collaborative iterative framework for X-ray Radiology Report Generation, termed MAC-RRG. Inspired by multi-agent technology, our framework constructs a closed-loop optimization paradigm based on task decoupling and collaborative reasoning. Specifically, the framework first generates a preliminary radiology report from input X-ray images via a vision encoder and a basic LLM. Subsequently, a multimodal knowledge graph (MM-KG) agent mines structured disease correlation and anatomical knowledge from medical knowledge graphs, while an auxiliary knowledge agent extracts unstructured domain knowledge from public medical databases. The multi-source knowledge acquired by dual agents is fused and embedded to guide the LLM in iteratively refining the initial report. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments on mainstream X-ray RRG datasets, including IU X-ray, MIMIC, and CheXpert Plus, fully verify the superiority of our proposed method. The source code and pre-trained models have been released on https://github.com/Event-AHU/Medical_Image_Analysis

AI.tldr: MAC-RRG is a multi-agent collaborative iterative framework for X-ray radiology report generation that combines a multimodal knowledge graph agent and an auxiliary knowledge agent to iteratively refine LLM-generated reports using multi-source knowledge fusion.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-only RRG models lack structured medical prior knowledge, leading to frequent medical hallucinations and low diagnostic interpretability. Current knowledge-graph-enhanced methods rely on static, one-round knowledge fusion from a single source, which prevents dynamic knowledge updating based on generation feedback.
AI.method: The framework first generates a preliminary report from input X-ray images using a vision encoder and a basic LLM. Then a multimodal knowledge graph (MM-KG) agent mines structured disease correlation and anatomical knowledge from medical knowledge graphs, while an auxiliary knowledge agent extracts unstructured domain knowledge from public medical databases. The multi-source knowledge from both agents is fused and embedded to guide the LLM in iteratively refining the initial report, forming a closed-loop optimization paradigm based on task decoupling and collaborative reasoning.
AI.result: Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments on mainstream X-ray RRG datasets (IU X-ray, MIMIC, and CheXpert Plus) fully verify the superiority of the proposed method. Source code and pre-trained models are released at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: MAC-RRG demonstrates that a multi-agent, iterative, multi-source knowledge fusion approach effectively addresses the limitations of LLM-only and static knowledge-graph-enhanced RRG methods, improving radiology report generation quality.

title: Manipulation with Stability Guarantees: Linear Deformable Objects with Non-negligible Physical Response Grasped at Multiple Location
summary: Most research on the manipulation of deformable objects focuses on lightweight systems with negligible mechanical response, effectively restricting attention to quasi-static regimes. This assumption excludes a broad class of practically relevant objects, such as hoses, pipes, and wiring harnesses, whose dynamics cannot be ignored during manipulation. In this work, we address this limitation by introducing a closed-loop control architecture that explicitly accounts for object dynamics and recasts manipulation as a shape-regulation problem. Control is achieved by modulating forces and torques applied at multiple fixed points along the object. This approach builds on three methodological contributions: a fully dynamic model of linear deformable objects based on discrete strain parameterizations; an extension of the notion of actuation coordinates to SE(3), yielding a structured and inherently underactuated control architecture; and nonlinear feedback strategies providing explicit conditions for steady-state convergence to desired configurations. Extensive simulations on representative manipulation tasks demonstrate the performance gains enabled by the proposed modelbased formulation. We finally validate the approach experimentally through a real-time closed-loop implementation with online shape estimation, confirming its practical feasibility and effectiveness

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a closed-loop control architecture for manipulating deformable objects whose dynamics cannot be neglected (e.g., hoses, pipes, wiring harnesses), recasting manipulation as a shape-regulation problem with a fully dynamic model, an SE(3)-based underactuated control formulation, and nonlinear feedback strategies guaranteeing steady-state convergence.
AI.motivation: Most prior work on deformable object manipulation assumes quasi-static regimes with negligible mechanical response, which excludes practically relevant objects such as hoses, pipes, and wiring harnesses whose dynamics matter during manipulation. The paper aims to remove this quasi-static limitation.
AI.method: The approach uses a closed-loop control architecture that explicitly accounts for object dynamics and formulates manipulation as shape regulation. Control is achieved by modulating forces and torques at multiple fixed points along the object. Three methodological contributions support this: (1) a fully dynamic model of linear deformable objects based on discrete strain parameterizations; (2) an extension of actuation coordinates to SE(3), yielding a structured and inherently underactuated control architecture; and (3) nonlinear feedback strategies with explicit conditions for steady-state convergence to desired configurations.
AI.result: Extensive simulations on representative manipulation tasks show performance gains from the proposed model-based formulation. Experimental validation via a real-time closed-loop implementation with online shape estimation confirms practical feasibility and effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Accounting explicitly for object dynamics and casting manipulation as shape regulation enables effective control of dynamically significant deformable objects, and the approach is both practically feasible and effective as validated in real-time experiments.

title: When Big Data Becomes a Curse: Spatial Heterogeneity and the Limits of Learning from Passive Acoustic Monitoring Data
summary: Passive Acoustic Monitoring produces large archives whose recordings are clustered by deployment, season, station identifier, and acquisition configuration. We analyze 908,072 AIS-labeled 679-second recordings from 38 deployments, 20 Atlantic Canadian station identifiers, and 21 receiver positions. The AIS-contact prior varies by more than 200-fold, and per-deployment screening distributions require local interpretation. Bidirectional cross-season transfer over the 18 station identifiers observed in both seasons predicts station identity above the 5.56% uniform-chance level, with balanced accuracy of 15.9% for AIS-contact and 16.4% for no-AIS-contact recordings. The same descriptors predict the two hydrophone models at 74.1% and 85.6% balanced accuracy, respectively, but hydrophone model is strongly confounded with season and other deployment-level acquisition differences. On a retrospectively screened and capped benchmark of 54m507 recordings, repeated station-grouped holdout yields an ROC-AUC of 0.612 with a station-bootstrap 95% interval of 0.582 to 0.648, compared with 0.661 under a random-window diagnostic. Their paired difference is 0.049 (0.040 to 0.056). Removing raw energy changes unseen-station ROC-AUC from 0.612 to 0.603, while an exploratory training-station scale analysis is non-monotonic. These results show that random-window validation overstates transfer to unseen station identifiers in this corpus. They support dependence-aware validation and broader independent spatial sampling, while spatial-expert models remain a hypothesis rather than an established remedy.

AI.tldr: Station-grouped validation reveals that random-window accuracy overstates transfer to unseen hydrophone stations, and hydrophone model is confounded with season.
AI.motivation: Passive Acoustic Monitoring archives are clustered by deployment, season, station identifier, and acquisition configuration, so random splits may leak station-specific and acquisition-specific structure and overstate generalization to new recording sites.
AI.method: Analyzed 908,072 AIS-labeled 679-second recordings from 38 deployments, 20 Atlantic Canadian station identifiers, and 21 receiver positions covering two seasons. Performed bidirectional cross-season transfer tests on 18 shared station identifiers, predicted hydrophone model from acoustic descriptors, and evaluated a retrospectively screened and capped benchmark of 54,507 recordings using repeated station-grouped holdout versus random-window validation, including ablations of raw energy.
AI.result: AIS-contact prior varies over 200-fold and per-deployment screening distributions demand local interpretation. Cross-season station-identity prediction reaches balanced accuracy of 15.9% (AIS-contact) and 16.4% (no-AIS-contact) versus 5.56% chance. Hydrophone models are predicted at 74.1% and 85.6% balanced accuracy but confounded with season and deployment-level acquisition differences. On the benchmark, station-grouped holdout yields ROC-AUC 0.612 (95% station-bootstrap interval 0.582-0.648) versus 0.661 for random-window, with paired difference 0.049 (0.040-0.056). Removing raw energy changes unseen-station ROC-AUC from 0.612 to 0.603; an exploratory training-station scale analysis is non-monotonic.
AI.conclusion: Random-window validation overstates transfer to unseen station identifiers in this corpus, supporting dependence-aware validation and broader independent spatial sampling. Spatial-expert models remain an unproven hypothesis rather than an established remedy.

title: Skytopia: Monocular Drone Navigation with Action-Conditioned Latent World Models
summary: Monocular drone navigation requires reaching a goal in an unseen environment from a single forward-facing camera, which offers few cues for depth and scale. World models address this by modelling how observations evolve under actions, but they are built to be executed: the prediction is produced at deployment and fed back into action generation at every control step. We argue that what a policy needs from a world model is not the prediction but the representation required to produce it: in flight the executed action explains almost all of the change between observations, so prediction reduces to reprojecting a static scene under a known displacement. We therefore introduce skytopia, a policy built on an action-conditioned latent world model, and the 3D Gaussian Splatting platform on which it is trained. A forward objective predicts the representation of the next observation from the intended motion, and an inverse objective recovers that motion from the predicted transition. Because the prediction never reaches action generation, the predictor is discarded and one policy serves point-goal, image-goal, and goal-free navigation. Simulation experiments show that skytopia outperforms every baseline under all three specifications, attaining 57.8%, 66.0%, and 49.0% success rate, while discarding the predictor removes 59.4% of the inference cost. The same policy is subsequently deployed on a physical drone without fine-tuning and reaches goals in indoor, open outdoor, and woodland environments.

AI.tldr: skytopia is a policy for monocular drone navigation built on an action-conditioned latent world model; it learns the representation needed to predict, then discards the predictor, achieving SOTA results across three navigation specifications and transferring to a real drone without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Monocular drone navigation must reach a goal in an unseen environment using only a single forward-facing camera, which provides scarce depth and scale cues. Existing world-model approaches predict future observations and feed those predictions back into action generation at every control step, incurring high inference cost, yet this prediction may be unnecessary because in flight the executed action explains nearly all inter-observation change, reducing prediction to reprojecting a static scene under known displacement.
AI.method: The authors introduce skytopia, a policy built on an action-conditioned latent world model, together with the 3D Gaussian Splatting platform used for training. A forward objective predicts the representation of the next observation from intended motion, and an inverse objective recovers that motion from the predicted transition. Since prediction never enters action generation, the predictor is discarded at inference, allowing a single policy to serve point-goal, image-goal, and goal-free navigation.
AI.result: In simulation, skytopia outperforms all baselines under all three specifications, reaching success rates of 57.8% (point-goal), 66.0% (image-goal), and 49.0% (goal-free). Discarding the predictor cuts inference cost by 59.4%. The same policy is deployed on a physical drone without fine-tuning and successfully reaches goals in indoor, open outdoor, and woodland environments.
AI.conclusion: The key insight is that a policy needs the representation underlying a world model's prediction rather than the prediction itself. This enables a single, deployment-efficient monocular navigation policy that generalizes across goal specifications in simulation and transfers zero-shot to real-world drone flight.

title: The Cost of Conservation: Coordination-Memory Laws for Exact-Support Generation
summary: Many AI systems make decisions locally, even when every realized output must obey an additive conservation law, such as selecting exactly a fixed number of items. This constraint can be statistically invisible: small subsets of a balanced fixed-budget output look increasingly independent, yet communication-free coordinate-parallel generation needs exponentially many pre-shared plans, while a sequential exact sampler needs only logarithmic memory. We study product measures conditioned on additive conservation laws in the intermediate regime where one plan is selected before a fixed-order pass, every plan is a bounded-state stochastic executor whose support is entirely legal, and the mixture of plan laws approximates the target distribution in total variation. Our main result identifies the optimal asymptotic selector rate, up to constant factors, with the killed spectral profile of the conservation-difference walk. The resulting coordination cost decreases as an inverse power of live-state width, with an exponent determined by intrinsic conservation rank rather than alphabet size; the law extends to noncentral budgets and heterogeneous local scores. The converse is driven by a state-versus-resource-sum obstruction, while a rate-matching construction compiles discrepancy control into exact-support finite-state plans. Complementary results characterize block-parallel plan complexity and the benefit of programmable output order. Together, these results show precisely how online memory substitutes for front-loaded coordination in exact-support generation.

It identifies the optimal asymptotic selector rate, up to constants, via the killed spectral profile of the conservation-difference walk, showing that coordination cost decays as an inverse power of live-state width with an exponent governed by intrinsic conservation rank rather than alphabet size.

Plans are bounded-state stochastic executors with entirely legal support, and the mixture of plan laws approximates the target distribution in total variation. The optimal asymptotic selector rate is characterized, up to constant factors, using the killed spectral profile of the conservation-difference walk. A converse is established via a state-versus-resource-sum obstruction, and a rate-matching construction compiles discrepancy control into exact-support finite-state plans. Additional results characterize block-parallel plan complexity and the benefit of programmable output order. The law is extended to noncentral budgets and heterogeneous local scores.

Coordination cost decreases as an inverse power of live-state width, with an exponent determined by intrinsic conservation rank rather than alphabet size. The law extends to noncentral budgets and heterogeneous local scores. Complementary results characterize block-parallel plan complexity and the benefit of programmable output order.

title: Towards Intent-Aware Human-Robot Teaming: A Platform for Search-and-Rescue Operations
comment: Accepted to the 23rd European Conference on Multi-Agent Systems (EUMAS 2026)
summary: We investigate the challenges of enabling effective collaboration between human operators and heterogeneous autonomous agents in complex, dynamic environments by developing an interaction platform that allows study of operator behavior and supports intent inference and decision-making using state-of-the-art frameworks. We demonstrate the extent to which the operator's perception, decisions, and actions could be supported by autonomous systems during search-and-rescue operations with our platform.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an interaction platform to study human-operator collaboration with heterogeneous autonomous agents, supporting intent inference and decision-making, demonstrated in search-and-rescue scenarios.
AI.motivation: Enabling effective collaboration between human operators and heterogeneous autonomous agents is challenging in complex, dynamic environments. There is a need to understand operator behavior and provide decision support.
AI.method: An interaction platform allowing study of operator behavior and supporting intent inference and decision-making, built using state-of-the-art frameworks.
AI.result: Demonstrates the extent to which an operator's perception, decisions, and actions can be supported by autonomous systems during search-and-rescue operations.
AI.conclusion: The platform shows promise for supporting human–autonomous agent collaboration, evidenced through search-and-rescue operations.

title: VACS: Value-Aligned Compositional Shielding for Multi-Agent Reasoning
summary: Multi-agent reasoning systems in high-stakes domains must be both accurate and safe, yet agents often follow heterogeneous value priorities (e.g., rigor, conciseness, safety), causing conflicting recommendations. Existing methods do not jointly provide: (i) principled inference of each agent's implicit values from behavior, (ii) compositional formal safety guarantees without full online communication, and (iii) value-aware conflict resolution with faithful explanations. We present VACS (Value-Aligned Compositional Shielding), a four-layer framework addressing all three. Layer 1 learns value-dimension rewards from pairwise preferences using Bradley-Terry modeling and infers per-agent value weights via deep MaxEnt IRL. Layer 2 encodes value constraints in a Lean-inspired DSL and synthesizes compositional assume-guarantee shields for runtime safety. Layer 3 resolves disagreement through nucleolus-based credit allocation and Hamiltonian consensus optimization under long-term value constraints. Layer 4 extracts a critical reasoning path from co-state sensitivities and generates formally grounded natural-language explanations. Our contribution is primarily a unified systems design with formalized interfaces and operational guarantees at the verifier-constrained decision level, rather than a complete end-to-end formal proof of all language-model internals. In controlled proof-of-concept evaluations with role-conditioned agent panels on NEJM-AI QA, MathInstruct-Subset, and a cybersecurity incident-response benchmark (CyberSec-Eval), VACS outperforms strong baselines in accuracy (85.4%, 95.0%, and 90.0%) while reducing logical inconsistency rates to near zero.

AI.tldr: VACS is a four-layer framework that jointly infers agents' implicit values, provides compositional formal safety guarantees, and resolves value-aware conflicts with faithful explanations, evaluated on three high-stakes benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent reasoning systems in high-stakes domains must be accurate and safe, but agents with heterogeneous value priorities (rigor, conciseness, safety) produce conflicting recommendations. Existing methods fail to jointly offer principled inference of implicit values, compositional formal safety guarantees without full online communication, and value-aware conflict resolution with faithful explanations.
AI.method: Four-layer design. Layer 1 learns value-dimension rewards from pairwise preferences via Bradley-Terry modeling and infers per-agent value weights via deep MaxEnt IRL. Layer 2 encodes value constraints in a Lean-inspired DSL and synthesizes compositional assume-guarantee shields for runtime safety. Layer 3 resolves disagreement via nucleolus-based credit allocation and Hamiltonian consensus optimization under long-term value constraints. Layer 4 extracts a critical reasoning path from co-state sensitivities and generates formally grounded natural-language explanations.
AI.result: In controlled proof-of-concept evaluations with role-conditioned agent panels on NEJM-AI QA, MathInstruct-Subset, and CyberSec-Eval, VACS outperforms strong baselines in accuracy (85.4%, 95.0%, 90.0%) and reduces logical inconsistency rates to near zero.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a unified systems design with formalized interfaces and operational guarantees at the verifier-constrained decision level, rather than a complete end-to-end formal proof of all language-model internals.

title: StrataVLA: Hierarchical and Efficient 3D Geometric Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models inherit strong semantic priors from large-scale vision-language pretraining, yet remain limited in robotic manipulation by insufficient 3D spatial awareness. Existing approaches either require explicit depth or point-cloud inputs, compress geometry into training-time supervision, or inject it only at the model input or action expert, leaving the vision-language backbone without persistent access to task-relevant spatial information. We introduce StrataVLA, a plug-and-play framework for hierarchical geometric grounding. A frozen geometry foundation model extracts shared geometric features from RGB observations, while sparse, layer-specific Geometry Adapters allow visual representations at selected backbone depths to retrieve relevant geometric evidence through cross-attention. To make inference-time geometry practical, StrataVLA further combines task-aware routing with an LRU feature cache that exploits temporal redundancy during task manipulation. Experiments on LIBERO, SimplerEnv, and real-world manipulation demonstrate consistent gains over strong VLA baselines. StrataVLA achieves 98.53% average success on LIBERO suites while reducing geometry-model invocations by up to 88%, establishing hierarchical geometry injection as an effective and efficient way to achieve spatially grounded robotic control.

AI.tldr: StrataVLA is a plug-and-play framework that injects hierarchical geometric grounding into VLA models via a frozen geometry foundation model and sparse layer-specific Geometry Adapters, achieving 98.53% average success on LIBERO while cutting geometry-model invocations by up to 88%.
AI.motivation: VLA models inherit strong semantic priors from large-scale vision-language pretraining but lack 3D spatial awareness for robotic manipulation. Existing solutions are limited: they require explicit depth/point-cloud inputs, compress geometry into training-time supervision, or inject geometry only at the model input or action expert—leaving the vision-language backbone without persistent access to task-relevant spatial information.
AI.method: StrataVLA performs hierarchical geometric grounding. A frozen geometry foundation model extracts shared geometric features from RGB observations. Sparse, layer-specific Geometry Adapters enable visual representations at selected backbone depths to retrieve relevant geometric evidence via cross-attention. For practical inference-time geometry, it combines task-aware routing with an LRU feature cache that exploits temporal redundancy during manipulation.
AI.result: On LIBERO, SimplerEnv, and real-world manipulation, StrataVLA consistently outperforms strong VLA baselines. It reaches 98.53% average success across LIBERO suites while reducing geometry-model invocations by up to 88%.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical geometry injection is an effective and efficient approach for achieving spatially grounded robotic control, providing persistent spatial access to the vision-language backbone without explicit depth or point-cloud inputs.

title: When Verifiers Vote Backwards under Verdict Substitution: Signed Pivotal Value in Correlated Self-Consistency
summary: Replacing one ballot can change a majority decision only on queries decided by a single vote; this structural fact requires no independence assumption. We study the sign of that change using a labeled, verdict-style intervention: one correctness signal replaces one correctness-indicator ballot in $k{=}7$ self-consistency panels. This diagnostic intervention is not identical to deployed answer-identity plurality. A primary MATH-500 experiment ($n{=}570$) gives a different-model verifier a $+24.2$pp pivotal gain, whereas a role-reversed configuration gives $-11.2$pp; an exploratory code stress test (14 pivotal rows across 9 tasks) gives $-24.5$pp. An exact signed-gain decomposition accounts for all observed signs through the verifier's state-specific accuracy and the composition of the two one-vote tally states, rather than global accuracy or model provenance. Same-source signals lose accuracy on the pivotal stratum (65$\to$44\% in the primary configuration), while error correlations provide a descriptive error-association diagnostic. Controlled degradation and a $k\in\{3,5,7\}$ subset sensitivity analysis probe the stability of the observed pattern around this accounting. Under the evaluated ties-incorrect answer-identity plurality analysis, the structural zero and strong-verifier benefit persist, but the role-reversed harm attenuates to $-0.9$pp and is not significant. The results therefore establish harmful verdict substitution, not universally harmful deployed plurality, and motivate a testable but unverified hypothesis for negative process-reward-model weights.

AI.tldr: A verdict-style intervention in k=7 self-consistency panels shows that replacing one ballot with a correctness signal can produce signed pivotal gains (e.g., +24.2pp for a different-model verifier) or harm (-11.2pp role-reversed), explained by verifier state-specific accuracy rather than global accuracy.
AI.motivation: Majority decisions can only change when a ballot shift occurs on queries decided by a single vote, a structural fact requiring no independence assumption. The paper aims to characterize the sign of such pivotal changes and clarify when substituting a verdict-style correctness signal for a ballot helps or harms.
