AI.method: Labeled verdict-style intervention replacing one correctness-indicator ballot in k=7 self-consistency panels; primary MATH-500 experiment (n=570) with different-model and role-reversed verifier configurations; exploratory code stress test (14 pivotal rows across 9 tasks); exact signed-gain decomposition; controlled degradation and k∈{3,5,7} sensitivity analysis; descriptive error-correlation diagnostic.
AI.result: Different-model verifier yields +24.2pp pivotal gain; role-reversed configuration yields -11.2pp; code stress test yields -24.5pp. Same-source signals drop accuracy on the pivotal stratum (65→44%). Under ties-incorrect answer-identity plurality, the structural zero and strong-verifier benefit persist, but role-reversed harm attenuates to -0.9pp (not significant).
AI.conclusion: The decomposition accounts for all observed signs via verifier state-specific accuracy and the composition of two one-vote tally states. Results establish harmful verdict substitution, not universally harmful deployed plurality, and motivate a testable but unverified hypothesis regarding negative process-reward-model weights.

title: Situation Aware Locomotion for Dual Mobile Cobots in Shared Environments
summary: This paper presents a situation aware locomotion framework for two mobile collaborative robots operating in shared industrial environments. The proposed method models situation awareness through perception, comprehension, and projection to support locomotion decisions. Robot pose, load state, manipulator state, shared zone occupancy, obstacle state, and predicted inter robot conflict were used to select safe locomotion actions. The framework was implemented in simulation and evaluated in simulated industrial scenarios designed to match a feasible 4 m by 4 m physical test area. The proposed method was compared with two other baselines over multiple trials and randomized seeds. The results show that the situation aware method achieved 100% task success across all scenarios, while the independent and fixed priority baselines each achieved 33.3% overall success. The proposed method eliminated shared zone conflicts and safety stops, maintained the largest average minimum inter robot distance, and completed the tasks with the lowest average completion time. These results indicate that situational awareness can improve the locomotion of dual robots by combining load state, manipulator state, reasoning about the shared zone, and prediction of short-horizon conflicts.

AI.tldr: A situation-aware locomotion framework for two collaborative mobile robots in shared industrial spaces achieves 100% task success and eliminates conflicts, outperforming independent and fixed-priority baselines (33.3% success).
AI.motivation: Dual mobile collaborative robots operating in shared industrial environments face safety and coordination challenges, such as shared-zone conflicts and inter-robot collisions, that conventional independent or fixed-priority locomotion approaches fail to handle reliably.
AI.method: The framework models situation awareness via perception, comprehension, and projection to drive locomotion decisions. It uses robot pose, load state, manipulator state, shared zone occupancy, obstacle state, and predicted inter-robot conflict to select safe locomotion actions. It was implemented in simulation and evaluated in industrial scenarios matching a feasible 4 m x 4 m physical test area, compared against two baselines across multiple trials with randomized seeds.
AI.result: The situation-aware method achieved 100% task success across all scenarios, whereas the independent and fixed-priority baselines each reached only 33.3% overall success. It eliminated shared zone conflicts and safety stops, maintained the largest average minimum inter-robot distance, and completed tasks with the lowest average completion time.
AI.conclusion: Situational awareness improves dual-robot locomotion by integrating load state, manipulator state, reasoning about the shared zone, and prediction of short-horizon conflicts.

title: Unanimity Without Persuasion: A Single Round of Debate Erases the Disagreement That Verification Needs
summary: A debate panel can become unanimous without becoming more correct. This is dangerous for downstream safeguards: a substituted verification ballot can change only narrow-margin votes, while richer arbiters lose disagreement as a natural targeting signal. We show that one debate round can erase that resource without requiring persuasion. Tracking a heterogeneous 7-judge panel through a blind round and three debate rounds on 600 code-correctness candidates, unanimity on a fixed cohort jumps from 39.5\% to 95.2\% in round 1 (93.1\% of the total collapse), while accuracy moves by less than one point and 96.3\% of verdict flips follow the displayed peer majority. An execution-based verification ballot corrects 8 of 2,037 pre-debate candidate-substitution instances but changes zero in every later round; by round 3 every wrong decision is unanimous, erasing dissent that had flagged two-thirds of the panel's errors. Identical-cohort controls explain why: no-peer reconsideration reproduces 79.6\% of the collapse, real labels without reasoning reproduce 91.5\%, and random labels steer flips toward whatever they display; the full-debate condition adds 4.3 percentage points over labels only (clustered 95\% CI 0.7--8.1). The one-round collapse reproduces in two additional real runs and two fake-label seeds, remains under panel sizes 3--7, and appears in MATH-500. Parse failures concentrate on contested candidates ($p<0.001$), making attrition non-ignorable. The design implication is operational: verify before any second-pass evaluation or peer exposure, and never treat post-debate unanimity as independent evidence of reliability.

AI.tldr: A single debate round sharply inflates panel unanimity (39.5%→95.2%) without improving accuracy, because judges follow the displayed peer majority; dissenting votes—a useful target for verification—vanish. Verify before peer exposure and never equate post-debate unanimity with reliability.
AI.motivation: Unanimity is often read as evidence of correctness, but panels can converge without becoming more accurate. This is dangerous for downstream safeguards: substituted verification ballots can only flip narrow-margin votes, and richer arbiters lose disagreement as a natural targeting signal. The paper asks whether a debate round destroys that disagreement resource without persuasion.
AI.method: Track a heterogeneous 7-judge panel through one blind round plus three debate rounds over 600 code-correctness candidates. Measure unanimity, accuracy, and verdict flips; add an execution-based verification ballot; run identical-cohort controls (no-peer reconsideration, real labels without reasoning, random labels) and full-debate conditions; probe robustness across additional runs, fake-label seeds, panel sizes 3–7, and MATH-500; analyze parse-failure attrition.
AI.result: Unanimity on a fixed cohort jumps from 39.5% to 95.2% in round 1 (93.1% of the total collapse) while accuracy moves under one point; 96.3% of flips follow the displayed peer majority. The execution-based ballot corrects 8 of 2,037 pre-debate substitution instances but zero in later rounds; by round 3 every wrong decision is unanimous, erasing dissent that had flagged two-thirds of panel errors. Controls: no-peer reconsideration reproduces 79.6% of the collapse, real labels without reasoning 91.5%, random labels steer flips toward what they display; full debate adds 4.3pp over labels only (95% CI 0.7–8.1). The collapse reproduces in two more real runs, two fake-label seeds, panel sizes 3–7, and MATH-500. Parse failures concentrate on contested candidates (p<0.001), making attrition non-ignorable.
AI.conclusion: Post-debate unanimity is not independent evidence of reliability; the accuracy gain is largely label-driven conformity rather than reasoning. Operationally, verification must occur before any second-pass evaluation or peer exposure, and unanimity should not be treated as a correctness signal.

title: Vision-Language Models as copilots for Autonomous UAV Navigation: Analysis of Latency and Reliability in Degraded Environments
summary: The integration of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in autonomous Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) offers unprecedented semantic reasoning capabilities. However, real-time closed-loop navigation requires not only low inference latency but also obedience to structured flight commands. This paper proposes a hybrid FSM-VLM control architecture for UAVs in GPS-free environments. The system combines a deterministic Finite State Machine (FSM) for low-level physical control with an asynchronous VLM copilot for high-level semantic pathfinding. We evaluate three models with different parameter scales in a Software-In-The-Loop (SITL) simulation. The framework isolates and measures syntax errors at the format level versus semantic hallucinations at the logic level in a normal and degraded scenario. This study demonstrates that parameter scaling, and not pure latency, remains the primary bottleneck for the safe and compatible integration of VLM into autonomous flights.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid FSM-VLM control architecture for GPS-free UAV navigation, combining a deterministic Finite State Machine for low-level control with an asynchronous VLM copilot for high-level semantic pathfinding, and evaluates three model scales in SITL simulation to show that parameter scaling—not latency—is the primary bottleneck for safe VLM integration.
AI.motivation: VLMs offer strong semantic reasoning for autonomous UAVs, but real-time closed-loop navigation demands both low inference latency and obedience to structured flight commands. There is a need to understand what actually limits safe integration of VLMs into autonomous flight.
AI.method: A hybrid FSM-VLM control architecture is introduced: a deterministic Finite State Machine handles low-level physical control, while an asynchronous VLM copilot performs high-level semantic pathfinding in GPS-free environments. Three models of different parameter scales are evaluated in Software-In-The-Loop (SITL) simulation, with the framework separately isolating and measuring format-level syntax errors versus logic-level semantic hallucinations across normal and degraded scenarios.
AI.result: The framework distinguishes format-level syntax errors from logic-level semantic hallucinations under both normal and degraded conditions, enabling assessment of how model scale and latency affect safe, compatible integration across the three evaluated models.
AI.conclusion: Parameter scaling, rather than pure latency, remains the primary bottleneck for the safe and compatible integration of VLMs into autonomous UAV flight.

title: Toward User-Mediated Self-Repair in Ubiquitous Robots Through Goal-Oriented Agentic AI
summary: Ubiquitous robotic systems often lack traditional visual interfaces, necessitating resilient natural language interaction for maintenance and repair tasks. This paper presents a goal oriented agentic AI architecture designed to enable non-expert users to perform technical repairs through situated dialogue. The framework utilizes a multi-layered approach that decouples high-level strategic planning from reactive conversational execution to transform unconstrained human instructions into a structured hierarchy of goals. We conducted a study involving twenty participants to evaluate the system's efficacy using a physical hardware testbed. The architecture achieved a 95\% task completion rate, and participants reported positive self-efficacy following real-time guidance that adapted to conversational diversions and linguistic variations. A comparative analysis with an online baseline revealed that the transition to a physical environment significantly decreased perceived social presence (p=.0005), and trust and competence, (p=.037), while the agentic framework remained robust throughout the interaction. These findings indicate that goal oriented agentic AI can support the sustainability of body-worn technologies by empowering users to perform critical maintenance in ubiquitous contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a goal-oriented agentic AI architecture that enables non-expert users to perform technical repairs on ubiquitous robotic systems through situated natural-language dialogue, achieving a 95% task completion rate in a 20-participant physical testbed study.
AI.motivation: Ubiquitous robotic systems frequently lack conventional visual interfaces, which makes maintenance and repair difficult for non-expert users. Resilient natural language interaction is therefore needed to support situated technical repair tasks in such contexts.
AI.method: The framework uses a multi-layered architecture that decouples high-level strategic planning from reactive conversational execution, transforming unconstrained human instructions into a structured hierarchy of goals. A study with twenty participants was conducted on a physical hardware testbed, including a comparative analysis against an online baseline.
AI.result: The architecture achieved a 95% task completion rate, and participants reported positive self-efficacy after real-time guidance that adapted to conversational diversions and linguistic variations. Compared with the online baseline, the physical environment significantly decreased perceived social presence (p=.0005) and trust and competence (p=.037), while the agentic framework remained robust throughout.
AI.conclusion: Goal-oriented agentic AI can support the sustainability of body-worn technologies by empowering users to perform critical maintenance in ubiquitous contexts.

title: Acoustic Ellipses: Bio-Inspired Omnidirectional Echolocation in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems using Frequency Sweeps
summary:
Inspired by the flight and song of birds, we propose an approach that enables cooperating agents to effectively identify obstacles in their environment by having a stationary source agent emit a frequency-modulated chirp while one or more listener agents observe the direct and reflected signals while in motion. We present a novel mapping approach that exploits the ``frequency gap'' between direct and reflected chirp signals to define candidate reflection ellipses, which are then fed into a 2D accumulation filter to identify locations with the highest density of potential reflections.
  We demonstrate this work first with simulation results derived from an efficient, bespoke audio simulator, examining the effect of obstacle count, sampling rate, and path curvature on the ability to accurately identify environmental obstacles for a one-listener scenario. We then examine different cooperative motion strategies for two-listener configurations. Finally, we validate the real-world viability of this approach through field experiments in an outdoor park setting to demonstrate the ability to identify frequency gaps using off-the-shelf hardware. Our results provide a foundation for a low-cost approach to environmental mapping in swarm robotic systems.

AI.tldr: A stationary source emits frequency-modulated chirps while moving listener agents observe direct and reflected signals; the frequency gap between them defines candidate reflection ellipses that are accumulated in 2D to localize obstacles, validated in simulation and field experiments.
AI.motivation: Inspired by bird flight and song, the authors aim to enable cooperating agents to identify environmental obstacles cheaply, providing a foundation for low-cost environmental mapping in swarm robotic systems.
AI.method: A stationary source agent emits a frequency-modulated chirp; one or more moving listener agents observe direct and reflected signals. A novel mapping approach exploits the "frequency gap" between direct and reflected chirp signals to define candidate reflection ellipses, which are fed into a 2D accumulation filter to identify locations with the highest density of potential reflections.
AI.result: A bespoke efficient audio simulator examined the effect of obstacle count, sampling rate, and path curvature on obstacle identification accuracy for a one-listener scenario; different cooperative motion strategies were examined for two-listener configurations; and field experiments in an outdoor park validated real-world viability, identifying frequency gaps using off-the-shelf hardware.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a foundation for a low-cost approach to environmental mapping in swarm robotic systems.

title: The Free-Recipe Limit: Every Recipe Effect Measures Which Premise of an Idealised Learner Broke
comment: 42 pages, 9 figures, 17 tables (incl. appendices); code, pre-registration files, and result base to be released with the paper
summary: Fix a corpus and send recipe search to infinity: try every order of the skills, every arrangement from blocked to interleaved, every composition, and keep the best. Two quantities decide what that search was worth: the diameter of the reachable set it explores, and the resolution at which anyone can tell two endpoints apart. Where the diameter falls below the resolution, no amount of search converts into a decision, and the signature is not an absence of winners but winners that do not survive re-running. We measure this recipe-search wall with 761 fine-tuning runs on 12 base models (0.5B-14B, three pretraining families) over competition-mathematics skills: base checkpoints, supervised fine-tuning under AdamW, exact-match scoring at k=4. Within one coherent domain at fixed volume the three classical freedoms average 0.010-0.021 against a 0.019 floor, and the largest contrast, 0.0619, clears a three-seed resolution and then reads +0.010 and -0.015 on two reruns. The departure with a systematic answer is coherence: halving one pooled corpus and letting the halves write answers under incompatible but equally correct conventions moves arrangement from capability to allocation between conventions, by two orders of magnitude over a same-convention control, and writing the convention into the input switches the phenomenon off. The switch replicates on a second pretraining family and survives an independent re-execution of its own protocol, with a re-execution spread (0.087) smaller than the resolution a search-selected order cell carries (0.144). Order itself is a transient whose sign crosses zero three times inside a single run. Volume, the one lever nobody calls a recipe, is the one that reliably pays. A public scorecard grades all 26 pre-registered claims: 18 supported, 5 failed, 2 untested, 1 mixed.

AI.tldr: This paper audits "recipe search" in fine-tuning by asking whether the explored space is large enough to yield decisions. Across 761 runs on 12 base models, arrangement/composition/order effects are near the resolution floor, while data volume and corpus coherence are the factors that reliably matter.
AI.motivation: Recipe search over skill order, arrangement, and composition is treated as an unlimited lever, but if the reachable set's diameter is smaller than the resolution distinguishing endpoints, search cannot produce decisions. The paper formalizes and measures this "recipe-search wall."
AI.method: 761 fine-tuning runs on 12 base models (0.5B-14B, three pretraining families) over competition-mathematics skills, using base checkpoints, supervised fine-tuning under AdamW, and exact-match scoring at k=4. It compares the three classical freedoms (order, arrangement, composition) at fixed volume, and manipulates corpus coherence by splitting one pooled corpus into halves that answer under incompatible but equally correct conventions, with controls and an input-convention switch, replicated on a second pretraining family.
AI.result: Within one coherent domain at fixed volume, the three classical freedoms average 0.010-0.021 against a 0.019 floor; the largest contrast, 0.0619, clears a three-seed resolution but reads +0.010 and -0.015 on reruns. Coherence moves arrangement from capability to allocation between conventions by two orders of magnitude over a same-convention control; writing the convention into the input switches the phenomenon off. The switch replicates on a second pretraining family and survives re-execution, with re-execution spread (0.087) below the resolution of a search-selected order cell (0.144). Order's sign crosses zero three times within a run. Volume reliably pays.
AI.conclusion: Where the reachable diameter falls below resolution, search yields winners that do not survive re-running. The systematic departure is coherence, which converts arrangement from a capability question into allocation between conventions; order is a transient. Among non-recipe levers, data volume is the one that reliably pays. A public scorecard grades all 26 pre-registered claims: 18 supported, 5 failed, 2 untested, 1 mixed.

title: GDLAM: Group-Disentangled Latent Action Model for Highly Disentangled Embodied Pretraining
summary: Latent action models (LAMs) learn action-related representations from action-free videos via self-supervised future prediction, offering a scalable paradigm for embodied intelligence pretraining. However, existing LAMs collapse heterogeneous sources of visual change, including camera motion, object dynamics, and interaction events, into a single latent vector, resulting in entangled representations with limited semantic structure and consequently restricting world model controllability and VLA policy generalization. We introduce the Group-Disentangled Latent Action Model (GDLAM), a latent action model whose code is factorized by construction into N groups, each with an independent variational bottleneck and a spatially gated routing pathway, and trained with a set of information-geometric objectives: mutual exclusivity, group and gate sparsity, and static-dynamic orthogonality, that make the groups mutually causally distinct rather than merely decorrelated. Quantitatively, intervening on any single group changes only that group and leaves the others intact, and GDLAM improves label-free disentanglement metrics, including Modularity, MIG, and DCI, by wide margins over a strong unstructured LAM. Notably, this factorization is not at the expense of action information: across three mutual-information estimators and a linear probe, the grouped code is more informative than monolithic baselines both in- and out-of-distribution. As supporting evidence that the disentangled code is a reusable pretraining currency, we further transfer it to two downstream regimes: (1) World Modeling: World models pretrained with GDLAM achieve superior rollout fidelity and action-following capability compared with SOTA baselines. (2) VLA Policies: Pretraining with GDLAM substantially improves task success rates over previous methods across multiple simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GDLAM, a group-disentangled latent action model that factorizes action-related representations from action-free video into N causal groups via independent variational bottlenecks, spatial gating, and information-geometric objectives, improving disentanglement, action informativeness, world modeling, and VLA policy generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing latent action models (LAMs) collapse heterogeneous sources of visual change—camera motion, object dynamics, and interaction events—into a single latent vector. This produces entangled representations with limited semantic structure, restricting world model controllability and VLA policy generalization.
AI.method: GDLAM factorizes its code by construction into N groups, each with an independent variational bottleneck and a spatially gated routing pathway. It is trained with information-geometric objectives: mutual exclusivity, group and gate sparsity, and static-dynamic orthogonality, enforcing mutual causal distinctness rather than mere decorrelation.
AI.result: Intervening on any single group changes only that group while leaving others intact. GDLAM improves label-free disentanglement metrics (Modularity, MIG, DCI) by wide margins over a strong unstructured LAM. Across three mutual-information estimators and a linear probe, the grouped code is more informative than monolithic baselines both in- and out-of-distribution. Transferring GDLAM yields superior rollout fidelity and action-following in world modeling, and substantially higher task success rates in VLA policies across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Group-disentangled latent action modeling provides a reusable, semantically structured pretraining representation that enhances disentanglement and action informativeness, serving as an effective pretraining currency for both world models and VLA policies.

title: EADC: Evaluation of Advanced and Deep-level Compliance in Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been used in various industries. However, ensuring their compliance with complex laws and regulatory frameworks remains a great challenge. Existing evaluation paradigms mainly rely on static benchmarks that suffer from three severe limitations: First, the compliance rules being used do not comply with the requirements of Artificial Intelligence (AI) laws and regulations; Second, they only handle apparent, explicit compliance risks, leaving implicit and covert compliance risks undetected; Third, they fail to track the systematic propagation of risks along logical dependency chains or evaluate compliance within nuanced, context-based real-world scenarios. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce EADC, a novel advanced evaluation benchmark of LLMs based on an AI compliance knowledge graph and AI compliance legal experts. By mapping abstract legal rules into structured logical multi-relational graphs, our framework enables automated, evolving agents to distill and synthesize highly sophisticated adversarial scenarios. This compliance benchmark is reviewed and corrected by human AI legal experts throughout the whole process. The resulting dataset (4,435+ QA pairs) provides an extensive, multi-dimensional taxonomy covering critical regulatory frontiers, including bias and discrimination, fairness, personal privacy protection, and values. Crucially, our compliance dataset moves beyond shallow string-matching by incorporating contextual long-horizon interactions and logic-driven hazard chains, capturing deeply embedded compliance anomalies that bypass traditional filters. Experiment evaluations demonstrate that our framework exposes critical regulatory blind spots in state-of-the-art LLMs, offering a rigorous, AI laws and regulations-aligned benchmark to safeguard high-level and deep compliance in the application of LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EADC, a knowledge-graph-based evaluation benchmark for assessing LLM compliance with AI laws and regulations, using AI legal experts to synthesize adversarial, context-rich compliance scenarios that expose regulatory blind spots missed by traditional static benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed across industries, but ensuring they comply with complex legal and regulatory frameworks remains difficult. Existing evaluation paradigms rely on static benchmarks with three major flaws: (1) their compliance rules do not align with AI laws and regulations; (2) they only detect explicit compliance risks, missing implicit/covert ones; and (3) they fail to track risk propagation along logical dependency chains or evaluate compliance in nuanced, context-based real-world scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose EADC, a compliance evaluation benchmark grounded in an AI compliance knowledge graph and validated by AI legal experts. Abstract legal rules are mapped into structured logical multi-relational graphs. Automated, evolving agents use this graph to distill and synthesize sophisticated adversarial scenarios, with human AI legal experts reviewing and correcting the process end-to-end.
AI.result: The resulting dataset contains 4,435+ QA pairs with an extensive multi-dimensional taxonomy spanning bias and discrimination, fairness, personal privacy protection, and values. By incorporating contextual long-horizon interactions and logic-driven hazard chains, it captures deeply embedded compliance anomalies that bypass traditional string-matching filters. Experiments show the framework exposes critical regulatory blind spots in state-of-the-art LLMs.
AI.conclusion: EADC offers a rigorous, AI laws-and-regulations-aligned benchmark to safeguard high-level and deep compliance in LLM applications, advancing beyond the shallow, explicit-risk focus of prior static benchmarks.

title: Design and Implementation of an Ultra-Low-Cost Wall-Climbing Robot for Infrastructure Crack Detection
summary: Crack detection is a crucial process to ensure the safety and longevity of buildings and other infrastructure. In this paper, we developed a low-cost, automated crack detection robot that leverages CNN, EfficientNet-B0, and YOLOv8 for efficient identification of cracks in concrete surfaces with a curated crack image dataset introduced to support training and evaluation. YOLOv8's real-time object detection enhances crack localization, while CNN and EfficientNet-B0 provide binary classification, ensuring high precision and recall. The system consists of two stages. In the first stage, YOLOv8 detects and localizes wall regions from the video frame, and the bounding boxes are cropped. The second stage performs crack detection using one of three models by analyzing the cropped regions. Cost-effective approaches are also taken for robot design. The robot features a fan-based negative pressure adhesion system, a 4-wheeled skid-steering drive, and an ESP32-CAM for real-time image capture. Its lightweight 3D-printed chassis ensures stability, allowing it to navigate both walls and ceilings while capturing images for crack analysis. Unlike conventional wall-climbing robot designs, this robot incorporates a funnel-shaped body that enhances negative pressure generation and achieves a 44% reduction in duty cycle, significantly lowering power consumption. By combining low-cost hardware with a deep learning pipeline, our system provides a scalable, efficient, and accessible solution for real-time infrastructure inspection at an approximate total cost of $25, with a lightweight web application enabling smartphone-based control. This affordability makes the system more suitable for the developing world, where infrastructure inspection is often limited by budget constraints, labor intensity, and safety risks.

AI.tldr: A low-cost (~$25) wall/ceiling-climbing robot with a two-stage deep learning pipeline (YOLOv8 for wall localization, CNN/EfficientNet-B0 for crack classification) enables affordable, real-time concrete crack inspection, targeting budget-constrained regions.
AI.motivation: Ensuring the safety and longevity of buildings and infrastructure requires regular crack detection, but conventional inspection is limited by budget constraints, labor intensity, and safety risks—especially in the developing world. Existing wall-climbing robots are typically expensive and power-hungry, motivating a scalable, accessible, low-cost alternative.
AI.method: The system uses a two-stage pipeline: (1) YOLOv8 detects and localizes wall regions from video frames and crops the bounding boxes; (2) crack detection is performed on the cropped regions using one of three models (CNN, EfficientNet-B0, or YOLOv8) for binary classification, supported by a curated crack image dataset. The hardware features a fan-based negative-pressure adhesion system, 4-wheeled skid-steering drive, ESP32-CAM for real-time capture, a lightweight 3D-printed chassis, and a funnel-shaped body that boosts negative pressure generation and cuts duty cycle by 44%. A lightweight web application enables smartphone-based control.
AI.result: The robot navigates both walls and ceilings while capturing images for crack analysis, achieving high precision and recall in crack identification. The funnel-shaped design yields a 44% reduction in duty cycle, significantly lowering power consumption. The total system cost is approximately $25.
AI.conclusion: Combining low-cost hardware with a deep learning pipeline yields a scalable, efficient, and accessible solution for real-time infrastructure inspection. Its affordability makes it especially suitable for the developing world, where inspection is constrained by budget, labor intensity, and safety risks.

title: TREND-10K: A Comprehensive Dataset for Next-Generation Video Quality Assessment Based on Preference-Driven Media
summary: The increasing prominence of short-video platforms, coupled with the advanced commercialization of AI-generated content (AIGC) videos, has led to a shift in the types of video media trend consumed by users in their daily lives. Traditional user-generated content (UGC) is gradually being replaced by professional short dramas and AIGC entertainment. Consequently, VQA for contemporary media content has become increasingly important. This requires a unified evaluation framework that can handle diverse video content and evolving media trends. In this context, we introduce TREND-10K, a next-generation comprehensive VQA dataset consisting of the trend-driven part and the static part, containing $10,000$ videos across a wide spectrum of content types. The trend-driven part is based on the TREND-Search framework, which captures user preference profiles from trending lists on online platforms and formulates sampling strategies based on these profiles. The static part, on the other hand, is composed of supplementary samples selected from publicly available datasets. To support unified evaluation for various video types, we incorporate three evaluation dimensions: technical, aesthetic, and AIGC-trace. Experiments show that our dataset ensures high annotation quality and exhibits remarkable generalization across multiple content categories. In conclusion, our work presents a robust framework for advancing VQA, addressing challenges caused by the temporal evolution of user perceptual habits and preferences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TREND-10K, a comprehensive next-generation VQA dataset of 10,000 videos spanning trend-driven and static parts, with three evaluation dimensions (technical, aesthetic, AIGC-trace), designed to handle evolving short-video and AIGC media trends.
AI.motivation: Short-video platforms and commercialized AIGC videos are shifting user media consumption away from traditional UGC toward professional short dramas and AIGC entertainment. This evolution demands a unified VQA evaluation framework capable of handling diverse content types and adapting to changing media trends, which existing approaches lack.
AI.method: The authors construct TREND-10K, consisting of a trend-driven part and a static part, totaling 10,000 videos across a wide spectrum of content types. The trend-driven part uses the TREND-Search framework, which extracts user preference profiles from trending lists on online platforms and derives sampling strategies from them; the static part comprises supplementary samples drawn from publicly available datasets. Three evaluation dimensions are incorporated: technical, aesthetic, and AIGC-trace.
AI.result: Experiments show that TREND-10K ensures high annotation quality and demonstrates remarkable generalization across multiple content categories.
AI.conclusion: TREND-10K provides a robust framework for advancing VQA, addressing the challenges posed by the temporal evolution of user perceptual habits and preferences.

title: StepTrigger: Contact-State-Triggered Backdoor Attacks on VLM-Powered Legged Robots
summary:
Large language models and vision-language models are increasingly used as high-level planners in robotic systems, using task goals and sensor summaries to select navigation or manipulation actions. This creates a new backdoor surface: a compromised planner can behave normally in most runs, yet change its target selection when a hidden trigger is present. Prior attacks on LLM-powered or embodied agents mainly rely on triggers that appear in language, camera-visible objects, scene semantics, or specific sequences of past actions. This paper presents StepTrigger, a contact-state-triggered backdoor attack for VLM-powered legged robots. The trigger is not a prompt token or a visible marker. It is produced by pressure and foot-ground contact patterns that arise when a Unitree Go1 quadruped walks across a dense terrain patch.
  Unlike conventional visual or textual triggers, contact signals are inherently noisy and may also arise during benign locomotion. To avoid treating every pressure anomaly as a trigger, StepTrigger learns a selective backdoor policy from multimodal robot state, using incidental pressure events as benign examples and dense-patch contacts as poisoned examples. In a stratified offline evaluation, the trained planner achieved 98.75% clean behavior preservation, 92.50% false-trigger rejection, 76.25% true-trigger activation, and 89.17% overall parsed behavior accuracy. These results reveal a backdoor surface in proprioceptive and contact channels that is not captured by defenses focused only on language, vision, or action history.

AI.tldr: StepTrigger introduces a contact-state-triggered backdoor attack against VLM-powered legged robots, where the trigger is a pressure/foot-ground contact pattern generated by walking over a dense terrain patch rather than any text or visual cue.
AI.motivation: LLMs and VLMs are increasingly deployed as high-level planners in robotic systems, creating a new backdoor surface: a compromised planner behaves normally most of the time but alters target selection when a hidden trigger appears. Prior attacks rely on triggers in language, camera-visible objects, scene semantics, or action sequences, leaving contact/proprioceptive channels unexplored.
AI.method: StepTrigger uses a contact-state trigger produced by pressure and foot-ground contact patterns when a Unitree Go1 quadruped walks across a dense terrain patch. Because contact signals are noisy and can also occur during benign locomotion, the attack learns a selective backdoor policy from multimodal robot state, treating incidental pressure events as benign examples and dense-patch contacts as poisoned examples.
AI.result: In a stratified offline evaluation, the trained planner achieved 98.75% clean behavior preservation, 92.50% false-trigger rejection, 76.25% true-trigger activation, and 89.17% overall parsed behavior accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal a backdoor surface in proprioceptive and contact channels that is not captured by defenses focused only on language, vision, or action history.

title: Identifying Intelligent Processes via Online Sequential Testing
summary: Active sequential hypothesis testing studies how to identify an unknown hypothesis with a given set of sensing actions. We study this in the setting of identifying large language models (LLMs), \textit{i.e.}, if a user is conversing with an LLM drawn from a known set of models, how can they identify which one is in use? Here, the available sensing actions (evaluations) are themselves a design choice: an evaluator must first decide which environments and prompt families to construct, and only then decide how to use them sequentially. We formalize these two levels as an outer probe-design problem and an inner identification problem. Simply put, the outer stage selects a set of probes to be sent to the entire set of models, creating a kind of fingerprint dataset. This is followed by the inner stage, which sequentially sends a budget-minimizing set of those probes to identify the model in use. For the outer problem, we show that selecting which evaluations to construct at minimum cost, so that every pair of candidates is distinguished, is exactly a weighted set cover problem. Since the response distributions of the candidate models are not known exactly but only through calibration samples, we give a one-shot procedure that estimates the cover instance from these samples. For the inner problem, we bound the number of evaluations needed to identify the unknown model in terms of how well the available evaluations distinguish each pair of candidates.

AI.tldr: This paper studies active sequential hypothesis testing for identifying which LLM a user is conversing with, splitting the problem into an outer probe-design stage and an inner sequential identification stage, and derives set-cover and pairwise-distinguishability guarantees.
AI.motivation: A user conversing with an LLM drawn from a known set of models may want to identify which model is in use, but the sensing actions themselves are a design choice: one must first decide which environments and prompt families (probes) to construct and only then use them sequentially under a budget. The paper formalizes and analyzes this two-level problem.
AI.method: The authors cast the problem in the active sequential hypothesis testing framework with two levels. The outer probe-design problem selects a set of probes sent to the entire model set, forming a fingerprint dataset; they show that selecting evaluations at minimum cost so that every pair of candidates is distinguished is exactly a weighted set cover problem. Since response distributions are known only through calibration samples, they give a one-shot procedure estimating the cover instance from these samples. The inner identification problem sequentially sends a budget-minimizing subset of probes to identify the model in use, with the required number of evaluations bounded in terms of how well the available evaluations distinguish each pair of candidates.
AI.result: The outer probe-design problem is exactly equivalent to a weighted set cover problem, and a one-shot estimator recovers the cover instance from calibration samples. For the inner problem, the number of evaluations needed to identify the unknown model is bounded as a function of pairwise distinguishability of candidates by the available evaluations.
AI.conclusion: LLM identification via sequential probing can be decomposed into a weighted set cover probe-design stage and a budget-minimizing sequential identification stage, yielding a principled characterization and performance bounds for the number of evaluations required.

title: Toward Self-Repairing Ubiquitous Robots Using Goal-Oriented Agentic AI in Human-Robot Interactions
summary: Ubiquitous robotic systems often lack traditional visual interfaces, making natural language interaction important for maintenance and repair. This paper presents a goal-oriented agentic AI architecture that enables non-expert users to complete technical repair tasks through situated dialogue. The architecture separates pre-interaction goal decomposition, persistent state tracking, strategic goal management, and real-time conversational execution. We evaluated the system in a physical hardware repair task with twenty participants. Nineteen participants completed the task, corresponding to a 95% completion rate. Participants rated the system as helpful and competent, and the agent remained robust to conversational diversions such as meta-queries and code-switching. A comparison with a prior online baseline showed that physical interaction significantly reduced perceived social presence, (p=.0005), and trust and competence, (p=.037), while perceived helpfulness remained high.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a goal-oriented agentic AI architecture enabling non-expert users to complete physical robotic repair tasks via situated natural-language dialogue, achieving a 95% task completion rate, though physical interaction reduced perceived social presence and trust relative to an online baseline.
AI.motivation: Ubiquitous robotic systems frequently lack conventional visual interfaces, which makes natural language interaction essential for maintenance and repair scenarios. Non-expert users need to perform technical repair tasks, motivating an agentic, dialogue-based architecture rather than one relying on graphical interfaces.
AI.method: A goal-oriented agentic AI architecture is proposed that separates four components: pre-interaction goal decomposition, persistent state tracking, strategic goal management, and real-time conversational execution. The system was evaluated in a physical hardware repair task with twenty participants, and compared against a prior online baseline.
AI.result: Nineteen of twenty participants completed the repair task (95% completion). Participants rated the system as helpful and competent, and the agent proved robust to conversational diversions such as meta-queries and code-switching. Compared with the online baseline, physical interaction significantly reduced perceived social presence (p=.0005) and trust and competence (p=.037), while perceived helpfulness remained high.
AI.conclusion: The agentic architecture effectively supports non-expert users in completing physical robotic repair tasks through situated dialogue, demonstrating high completion and robustness. However, the embodied, physical setting diminished perceived social presence and trust compared to online interaction, even as helpfulness perceptions stayed high—highlighting a trade-off between task success and user-perceived social qualities.

title: RCShift: Certifying When Partial Linkage Suffices for Finite-Sample Decisions
summary: Systems with costly gold outcomes and cheaper auxiliary observations must decide how much record linkage to retain. Complete pairing retains every joint counter, while separate margins retain none. Neither endpoint is calibrated to a declared finite-sample decision. Universal reconstruction can retain cycle directions invisible to the likelihood-ratio family. Family-exact storage can exceed what the decision requires because certified residual loss may fit within finite-sample slack. We introduce RCShift, which certifies two routes to sufficiency under a declared observation contract. Its exact mode characterizes minimum-cost family-exact storage through LR-visible cycle directions. Its approximate mode bounds reverse Le Cam deficiency. Its integer mode certifies whether a chosen set preserves the full experiment's minimum integer record count at specified size and power. In a rank-two witness, one aligned counter preserves a four-record minimum. An equal-cost misaligned counter and the margins require eleven records, while universal reconstruction requires two counters. A local perturbation has positive reverse deficiency yet retains the four-record minimum. Proof-checked scheduling bounds instantiate the contract before gold computation and yield exact reconstruction on the admitted tree support. RCShift turns partial-linkage storage into decision-calibrated measurement design for the declared family, costs, target, and common strictly positive support.

AI.tldr: RCShift is a framework for decision-calibrated partial record linkage: its exact, approximate, and integer modes certify when reduced linkage storage remains sufficient for a declared finite-sample decision, using LR-visible cycle directions, reverse Le Cam deficiency, and integer record-count certificates.
AI.motivation: Systems face a trade-off between costly gold outcomes and cheaper auxiliary observations, so they must decide how much record linkage to retain. Complete pairing keeps all joint counters but is expensive, while separate margins discard all linkage. Neither endpoint is calibrated to a declared finite-sample decision. The paper seeks a principled way to retain only the linkage needed for the specified decision.
AI.method: The paper introduces RCShift, which certifies two routes to sufficiency under a declared observation contract. Its exact mode characterizes minimum-cost family-exact storage via LR-visible cycle directions. Its approximate mode bounds reverse Le Cam deficiency. Its integer mode certifies whether a chosen set preserves the full experiment's minimum integer record count at specified size and power. Proof-checked scheduling bounds instantiate the contract before gold computation.
AI.result: In a rank-two witness, one aligned counter preserves a four-record minimum. An equal-cost misaligned counter and the margins require eleven records, while universal reconstruction requires two counters. A local perturbation has positive reverse deficiency yet still retains the four-record minimum. RCShift yields exact reconstruction on the admitted tree support.
AI.conclusion: RCShift turns partial-linkage storage into decision-calibrated measurement design for the declared family, costs, target, and common strictly positive support.

title: Silent Sabotage: Internal State Triggered Backdoor Attacks on LLM-Powered Robotic Systems
summary: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into robotic control systems is enabling a new generation of autonomous agents capable of complex reasoning and planning. While this paradigm shift accelerates progress, it also introduces novel security risks that remain largely unexplored. Current research into LLM backdoors has focused on attacks triggered by external stimuli, such as specific words, visual objects, or environmental states. These attacks, while potent, overlook a more insidious class of vulnerability where the trigger is internal to the agent's own operational logic. This paper presents the first comprehensive study of history-based backdoor attacks on LLM-powered robotic systems. We demonstrate that an attacker can embed a stealthy backdoor into an LLM-based robot controller by manipulating its instructions. This backdoor is triggered not by an external cue, but by a specific, rare sequence of the robot's own past actions. It remains dormant during normal operation, preserving the robot's utility, but can be activated to induce a malicious behavior, such as a complete stop or a collision. Our experiments, conducted in a simulated environment with a variety of robots and LLMs, show that this history-based attack is highly effective, achieving a near-perfect attack success rate while remaining exceptionally difficult to detect. These findings reveal a critical and previously unaddressed vulnerability in autonomous systems and underscore the urgent need for security measures that account for an agent's internal state.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first study of history-based backdoor attacks on LLM-powered robotic systems, where the trigger is a rare sequence of the robot's own past actions rather than an external cue, achieving near-perfect attack success while evading detection.
AI.motivation: LLMs are being integrated into robotic control, enabling advanced reasoning but introducing novel security risks. Existing LLM backdoor research focuses only on external triggers (words, visual objects, environmental states), overlooking a more insidious vulnerability class where the trigger is internal to the agent's own operational logic.
AI.method: An attacker embeds a stealthy backdoor into an LLM-based robot controller by manipulating its instructions. The backdoor is triggered by a specific, rare sequence of the robot's own past actions. It stays dormant during normal operation (preserving utility) and activates to induce malicious behavior such as a complete stop or a collision. Experiments were conducted in a simulated environment with various robots and LLMs.
AI.result: The history-based attack is highly effective, achieving a near-perfect attack success rate while being exceptionally difficult to detect, all while remaining dormant during normal operation.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals a critical, previously unaddressed vulnerability in autonomous systems, underscoring the urgent need for security measures that account for an agent's internal state.

title: Improved Multiplayer Bandit Algorithm for Bernoulli Rewards
summary: We study the multiplayer multi-armed bandit problem with information asymmetry under Bernoulli rewards, for three information structures: asymmetry in actions, in rewards, and in both. Replacing the Hoeffding-style confidence intervals of prior work with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-based bounds gives strictly tighter regret guarantees in each case. We propose \texttt{mKL-UCB}, \texttt{mKL-UCB-Intervals} and \texttt{mKL-DSEE}, and show that the improvement factor is at least two by Pinsker's inequality and far larger when reward means are near zero or one. For asymmetry in rewards we prove that two arms' KL intervals separate after a deterministic number of samples, and that $M$ independent players accelerate elimination further.

AI.tldr: This paper studies multiplayer multi-armed bandits with information asymmetry under Bernoulli rewards, replacing Hoeffding-style confidence intervals with KL-divergence-based bounds to achieve strictly tighter regret guarantees.
AI.motivation: Prior work on multiplayer multi-armed bandits with information asymmetry relies on Hoeffding-style confidence intervals, which yield loose regret guarantees. Tighter concentration bounds could substantially improve performance, especially under Bernoulli rewards where distribution-specific divergence measures are more informative.
AI.method: The authors consider three information structures: asymmetry in actions, in rewards, and in both. They substitute KL divergence-based confidence bounds for Hoeffding-style intervals and propose three algorithms: mKL-UCB, mKL-UCB-Intervals, and mKL-DSEE.
AI.result: The KL-based bounds yield strictly tighter regret guarantees in each setting, with an improvement factor of at least two by Pinsker's inequality, and far larger when reward means are near zero or one. For reward asymmetry, two arms' KL intervals separate after a deterministic number of samples, and M independent players accelerate elimination further.
AI.conclusion: KL divergence-based confidence bounds strictly improve regret over Hoeffding-style approaches in multiplayer multi-armed bandits with information asymmetry, with gains amplified near extreme reward means and further accelerated by multiple independent players.

title: Manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects Using Model Predictive Path Integral Control with Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory Learning
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables, 22nd International Conference on Informatics in Control, Automation and Robotics (ICINCO 2025)
summary: The manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) such as cables poses a significant challenge for automation due to their infinite degrees of freedom and non-linear dynamics. In this paper we present a machine learning based optimal control approach for the manipulation of DLOs. This approach is divided into two main components: modeling and control. For modeling the dynamics of the DLO, we propose a learning based approach using a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (biLSTM) network. The biLSTM network is trained on synthetic data generated by the MuJoCo physics engine. For manipulating the DLO, a model predictive control strategy that employs Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is selected. The proposed approach is evaluated through simulation and experiments. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving accurate and efficient manipulation of DLOs.

AI.tldr: A machine learning based optimal control approach is proposed for manipulating Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs), combining a biLSTM dynamics model trained on MuJoCo synthetic data with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, validated in simulation and experiments.
AI.motivation: DLOs such as cables have infinite degrees of freedom and non-linear dynamics, making their manipulation a significant challenge for automation.
AI.method: The approach has two components: (1) Modeling—a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (biLSTM) network learns DLO dynamics from synthetic data generated by the MuJoCo physics engine; (2) Control—a model predictive control strategy employing Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control.
AI.result: Evaluation through simulation and experiments demonstrates that the proposed method achieves accurate and efficient manipulation of DLOs.
AI.conclusion: The integration of a learned biLSTM dynamics model with MPPI-based predictive control is effective for DLO manipulation.

title: A Hybrid AI Framework for Academic Advising: Integrating Ensemble-Based Grade Prediction and a Rule-Based Expert System
summary: The rapidly increasing student population has posed serious challenges to the traditional academic advising process. This study designs and implements a multi-purpose intelligent system to support students' academic progress, based on a two-part hybrid framework: (1) an advanced model for grade prediction and (2) a rule-based recommendation engine. Using a dataset containing 416,558 educational records from the University of Birjand, students were first divided into homogeneous clusters using the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). Subsequently, a Stacking Ensemble model combining Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and MLP was trained specifically for each cluster. Evaluation results demonstrated that the Stacking model outperformed base models across all clusters, achieving a final aggregated RMSE of 2.35. The second component is an expert system that provides intelligent recommendations by synergizing educational regulations with the grades predicted by the first component. This system has been implemented as a practical tool on the University of Birjand portal, offering students real-time feedback such as semester GPA prediction, probation risk warnings, and course suggestions for GPA improvement.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a two-part intelligent academic advising system: a cluster-wise Stacking ensemble for grade prediction (aggregated RMSE 2.35) and a rule-based expert system that combines predicted grades with university regulations to deliver real-time student feedback.
AI.motivation: The rapidly growing student population places serious strain on traditional academic advising, which cannot scale to provide timely, personalized guidance. There is a need for an automated, intelligent system that supports students' academic progress at scale.
AI.method: The system uses a two-part hybrid framework. (1) Grade prediction: 416,558 educational records from the University of Birjand were used to partition students into homogeneous clusters via the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM); a Stacking Ensemble combining Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and MLP was then trained separately per cluster. (2) Recommendation: a rule-based expert system synergizes educational regulations with the predicted grades to generate recommendations.
AI.result: The Stacking model outperformed all base models across every cluster, yielding a final aggregated RMSE of 2.35. The system was deployed as a practical tool on the University of Birjand portal, delivering real-time feedback including semester GPA prediction, probation risk warnings, and course suggestions for GPA improvement.
AI.conclusion: Clustering students and training cluster-specific Stacking ensembles improves grade prediction accuracy over base models, and coupling these predictions with a rule-based expert system yields a deployable, real-world academic advising tool that provides students with actionable, real-time guidance.

title: High-Bandwidth Biomimetic Finger for Tactile-Transparent Remote Texture Sensing
summary: High-fidelity tactile feedback is essential for robotic teleoperation, enabling precise manipulation and critical decision-making. While biomimetic fingertip sensors can capture surface-texture features, how their design shapes the tactile transparency of rendered feedback remains poorly understood. This paper presents a biomimetic fingertip replicating the human finger's multilayer mechanical gradient and fingerprint morphology, with an embedded high-sensitivity inertial measurement unit capturing texture-induced vibrations for remote vibrotactile rendering. Three variants are compared with the human fingertip through temporal and spectral analyses and a user study spanning three perceptual dimensions, establishing a transmission chain from fingertip design through signal characteristics to tactile transparency. The multilayer mechanical gradient yields the clearest improvements in signal intensity and texture-feature representation, whereas a stiffer skin layer amplifies vibration intensity at the expense of feature representation. The perceptual dimensions draw on distinct signal attributes: roughness on energy scaling, granularity on spectral shape, and repetitivity on characteristic-peak representation. These findings offer design principles for application-specific fingertips in robotic teleoperation.

AI.tldr: This paper designs a biomimetic fingertip with a multilayer mechanical gradient and fingerprint morphology plus an embedded IMU, and shows through temporal/spectral analyses and a user study that fingertip design parameters propagate through signal characteristics to determine tactile transparency in vibrotactile rendering.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity tactile feedback is essential for robotic teleoperation and critical decision-making, but how biomimetic fingertip design shapes the tactile transparency of rendered feedback is poorly understood.
AI.method: A biomimetic fingertip replicating the human finger's multilayer mechanical gradient and fingerprint morphology, with an embedded high-sensitivity IMU capturing texture-induced vibrations for remote vibrotactile rendering. Three design variants are compared with the human fingertip via temporal and spectral analyses and a user study across three perceptual dimensions, establishing a transmission chain from fingertip design through signal characteristics to tactile transparency.
AI.result: The multilayer mechanical gradient yields the clearest improvements in signal intensity and texture-feature representation, whereas a stiffer skin layer amplifies vibration intensity at the expense of feature representation. Perceptual dimensions rely on distinct signal attributes: roughness on energy scaling, granularity on spectral shape, and repetitivity on characteristic-peak representation.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide design principles for application-specific fingertips in robotic teleoperation.

title: A Multi-Timestep LSTM Ensemble regressor for Enhanced Short-Term Runoff Prediction
summary: Accurately forecasting river runoff is key to managing water resources, controlling floods, and planning agriculture. This study examines the Ajichay River in northwest Iran, a major tributary of Lake Urmia that has experienced increasing water-related stress in recent years. We introduce a daily runoff prediction model based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. The model combines five LSTM units, each trained on different time intervals ranging from 2 to 6 days, to better capture variations in river flow patterns. To improve performance, each model was fine-tuned using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), a population-based optimization algorithm. The proposed approach was evaluated on unseen data from 2017-2018 using $R^2$, RMSE, and MSE as performance metrics. The results showed strong predictive accuracy, with $R^2$ values ranging from 74.95% to 91.42%. In addition, multiple feature-importance methods were applied to identify the most influential variables, providing further insight into the factors that drive runoff variations.

AI.tldr: A daily river runoff prediction model using five PSO-tuned LSTM units trained on 2-6 day intervals is proposed and evaluated on the Ajichay River, achieving R² of 74.95%-91.42%.
AI.motivation: Accurate river runoff forecasting is essential for water resource management, flood control, and agricultural planning. The Ajichay River, a major tributary of Lake Urmia in northwest Iran, faces increasing water-related stress, motivating a reliable daily prediction model.
AI.method: The study introduces a daily runoff prediction model based on LSTM networks, combining five LSTM units each trained on different time intervals ranging from 2 to 6 days to capture flow variations. Each model is fine-tuned using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), a population-based optimization algorithm. Evaluation uses unseen 2017-2018 data with R², RMSE, and MSE metrics, plus multiple feature-importance methods to identify influential variables.
AI.result: The approach demonstrated strong predictive accuracy with R² values ranging from 74.95% to 91.42% on the unseen test data.
AI.conclusion: The PSO-tuned multi-interval LSTM ensemble effectively predicts daily runoff on the Ajichay River, and feature-importance analysis provides insight into the factors driving runoff variations.

title: Multi-Axis Selective Decoupling Framework for Free-Floating Space Manipulators
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures, 2026 AAS/AIAA Astrodynamics Specialist Conference
summary: Free-floating space manipulator systems face operational challenges due to dynamic coupling. While traditional reactionless manipulation eliminates base disturbances, enforcing the null-space projections across all rotational axes imposes excessive constraints on the system and drastically reduces the available workspace. To address this limitation, this work proposes a multi-axis selective decoupling framework that nullifies momentum transfer exclusively along mission-critical directions. By leveraging a directionally constrained sub-coupling matrix, the framework relaxes the null-space constraints. Numerical simulations confirm that this approach mathematically eliminates constrained directional disturbances along the targeted axes while preserving the remaining degrees of freedom, enabling the manipulator to execute task-space operations successfully.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-axis selective decoupling framework for free-floating space manipulators that cancels momentum transfer only along mission-critical directions, relaxing the excessive null-space constraints of traditional reactionless manipulation while preserving workspace.
AI.motivation: Free-floating space manipulator systems face operational challenges due to dynamic coupling. Traditional reactionless manipulation eliminates base disturbances but enforcing null-space projections across all rotational axes imposes excessive constraints and drastically reduces the available workspace.
AI.method: The work proposes a multi-axis selective decoupling framework that nullifies momentum transfer exclusively along mission-critical directions. It leverages a directionally constrained sub-coupling matrix to relax the null-space constraints.
AI.result: Numerical simulations confirm that this approach mathematically eliminates constrained directional disturbances along the targeted axes while preserving the remaining degrees of freedom.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables the manipulator to execute task-space operations successfully, overcoming the workspace reduction of traditional reactionless manipulation.

title: Coding Agents are Strong Prompt Optimizers
summary: Search-based prompt optimizers improve prompts through iterative search: they propose edits, execute fresh rollouts, score the resulting trajectories, and retain only edits that improve a validation metric. We show that this optimization loop is unnecessary. Given only a static corpus of agent trajectories, an off-the-shelf coding agent can directly synthesize an optimized prompt, requiring neither environment access nor validation data. We call this approach \textit{Coding-Agent Skill Distillation} (CASD). The key insight is reflection scope. Rather than reasoning over a small batch of trajectories at each optimization step, the coding agent writes and executes analysis code to compute corpus-wide statistics, identifies systematic failure modes, inspects representative episodes, and distills the resulting insights into behavioral rules. Across four agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, $τ^2$-bench retail and telecom, and SpreadsheetBench-Verified), under matched data access, a single CASD pass outperforms GEPA, a state-of-the-art reflective prompt optimizer, on three of four benchmarks and outperforms validation-gated reflective search (SkillOpt) on all four, improving the unoptimized baseline by 16.6 percentage points on average versus 10.9 for GEPA and 5.3 for SkillOpt. Because CASD performs a single offline analysis pass rather than iterative search, producing an optimized prompt costs approximately \$1.60---over $22\times$ cheaper than validation-gated search. Even when competing methods are granted additional validation data and unrestricted environment access, CASD remains ahead on two of four benchmarks. These results suggest that corpus-scale statistical reflection is a viable alternative to iterative search for prompt optimization.

AI.tldr: CASD replaces iterative search-based prompt optimization with a single offline pass: a coding agent writes and executes analysis code over a static corpus of agent trajectories to compute corpus-wide statistics, identify systematic failure modes, and distill behavioral rules—outperforming GEPA, SkillOpt, and the unoptimized baseline at ~$1.60 per prompt (>22× cheaper than validation-gated search).
AI.motivation: Search-based prompt optimizers rely on an expensive iterative loop: propose edits, run fresh rollouts, score trajectories, and retain only metric-improving edits, which requires environment access and validation data. The authors question whether this iterative optimization loop is actually necessary.
AI.method: Coding-Agent Skill Distillation (CASD). Given only a static corpus of agent trajectories, an off-the-shelf coding agent synthesizes an optimized prompt directly, with no environment access and no validation data. The key insight is reflection scope: instead of reasoning over a small batch of trajectories per step, the coding agent writes and executes analysis code to compute corpus-wide statistics, identifies systematic failure modes, inspects representative episodes, and distills insights into behavioral rules. It is a single offline analysis pass rather than iterative search.
AI.result: Across four agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, τ²-bench retail and telecom, SpreadsheetBench-Verified) under matched data access, one CASD pass beats GEPA on 3 of 4 benchmarks and beats validation-gated reflective search (SkillOpt) on all 4, improving the unoptimized baseline by 16.6 percentage points on average (vs. 10.9 for GEPA, 5.3 for SkillOpt). Cost is approximately $1.60 per optimized prompt, over 22× cheaper than validation-gated search. Even with competitors granted extra validation data and unrestricted environment access, CASD stays ahead on 2 of 4 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Iterative search is not required for prompt optimization; corpus-scale statistical reflection offers a cheaper, simpler, and often stronger alternative. The findings position corpus-scale statistical reflection as a viable alternative to iterative search for prompt optimization.

title: RoboTwin-Phys: Do WAMs and VLAs Understand the Physical World?
summary: Physical-condition diversity is largely missing from current benchmarks for robot manipulation. While large-scale simulation benchmarks increasingly incorporate variations in object appearance, scene layout, and visual observations, they typically keep the underlying physical parameters fixed. As a result, important sources of real-world variability, such as changes in mass, friction, and joint dynamics, remain largely untested. We introduce RoboTwin-Phys, a physics-diverse benchmark that treats physical-condition diversity as an explicit dimension of robot manipulation evaluation. The benchmark continuously varies 13 physical attributes within physically plausible ranges, providing a unified setting for evaluating policies across diverse physical operating conditions. We further release more than 5,000 expert demonstrations with ground-truth physical parameters, enabling physical-attribute estimation, condition-aware modeling, and physics-conditioned policy training. Evaluations of representative WAMs and VLAs reveal a substantial robustness gap: models that remain effective under existing visual and layout randomization can degrade markedly under changes in physical conditions. RoboTwin-Phys provides the benchmark, data, and evaluation protocol needed to systematically measure and improve robustness to physical-condition diversity in robot manipulation.

AI.tldr: RoboTwin-Phys is a new benchmark for robot manipulation that explicitly varies physical conditions (13 physical attributes) alongside visual and layout randomization, and it reveals a substantial robustness gap in current WAMs and VLAs.
AI.motivation: Existing robot manipulation benchmarks increasingly vary object appearance, scene layout, and visual observations in simulation, but they keep physical parameters fixed. Important real-world variability sources—mass, friction, joint dynamics—remain largely untested, leaving physical-condition diversity missing from evaluation.
AI.method: The authors introduce RoboTwin-Phys, a physics-diverse benchmark that treats physical-condition diversity as an explicit evaluation dimension. It continuously varies 13 physical attributes within physically plausible ranges, providing a unified setting to evaluate policies across diverse physical operating conditions. They also release over 5,000 expert demonstrations with ground-truth physical parameters to support physical-attribute estimation, condition-aware modeling, and physics-conditioned policy training.
AI.result: Evaluations of representative World Action Models (WAMs) and Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) show a substantial robustness gap: models that remain effective under existing visual and layout randomization can degrade markedly when physical conditions change.
AI.conclusion: RoboTwin-Phys supplies the benchmark, data, and evaluation protocol needed to systematically measure and improve robustness to physical-condition diversity in robot manipulation.

title: Decoupling Is Not Identification: Supervised Evidential Learning in Next-Token Prediction
summary: A next-token probability says what a model predicts, not how much training support lies behind it. A Dirichlet head can represent this distinction by separating mean $m$ from concentration $S$, but decoupling does not identify what $S$ means. Here we propose an Evidential Next-Token Prediction (ENTOP) framework to audit this gap on character-level Moby-Dick, using exact 8-gram count as a reproducible lexical-support label and withholding count regression from 20% of context types. Standard implicit evidential training carries essentially no count signal beyond confidence on held-out-label types (partial Spearman $ρ= 0.001 \pm 0.014$), whereas explicit supervision generalizes ($ρ= 0.201 \pm 0.010$; matched-pair win $= 0.822 \pm 0.021$). CE predictive entropy is at chance for unseen 8-grams (AUROC $= 0.490 \pm 0.004$), while supervised vacuity reaches $0.772 \pm 0.003$, comparable with an indexed CE-representation baseline ($0.769$) but below the tautological corpus oracle ($1.000$). Neither longest-suffix nor representation-distance strata explain where amortization succeeds. Increasing count weight under the digamma objective improves support fit only by sacrificing prediction. A constant predictor wins natural log-RMSE, and vacuity does not improve error deferral. These results motivate a minimum evidence protocol---confidence control, matched pairs, held-out labels, a constant baseline, and a decision test---and show that concentration can pass identification while failing calibration and utility.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Evidential Next-Token Prediction (ENTOP), a framework that audits whether a Dirichlet head's concentration parameter S actually encodes training support (lexical evidence) or merely confidence, using exact 8-gram counts on character-level Moby-Dick as a reproducible support label.
AI.motivation: A next-token probability expresses only what a model predicts, not how much training evidence underlies that prediction. Although Dirichlet heads formally separate mean m from concentration S, this decoupling does not by itself establish what S semantically represents. The work aims to test whether a learned concentration signal can be identified as genuine evidential support and whether it remains useful for calibration and downstream decisions.
AI.method: The authors introduce ENTOP to probe the mean/concentration gap on a character-level Moby-Dick corpus, adopting exact 8-gram counts as ground-truth lexical-support labels and withholding count regression on 20% of context types. They compare implicit evidential training against explicit supervision, using a digamma objective with varying count weight. Evaluation includes partial Spearman correlations, matched-pair win rates, AUROC for unseen 8-grams, an indexed cross-entropy representation baseline, a corpus oracle, and stratification by longest-suffix and representation distance.
AI.result: Standard implicit evidential training yields essentially no count signal beyond confidence on held-out-label types (partial Spearman ρ = 0.001 ± 0.014), while explicit supervision generalizes (ρ = 0.201 ± 0.010; matched-pair win = 0.822 ± 0.021). Cross-entropy predictive entropy is at chance for unseen 8-grams (AUROC = 0.490 ± 0.004), whereas supervised vacuity reaches 0.772 ± 0.003, comparable to an indexed CE representation baseline (0.769) but below the corpus oracle (1.000). Neither longest-suffix nor representation-distance strata explain where amortization succeeds. Increasing count weight under the digamma objective improves support fit only at the cost of prediction, a constant predictor attains the best natural log-RMSE, and vacuity does not improve error deferral.
AI.conclusion: Concentration can satisfy identifiability criteria while failing calibration and utility, so a Dirichlet head's S should not be assumed to mean evidential support. The authors advocate a minimum evidence protocol comprising confidence control, matched pairs, held-out labels, a constant baseline, and a decision test.

title: Shaft-Configuration-Adaptive Catheter Tip Position Estimation via Motor-History Conditioned Residual Learning
summary: Tendon-driven continuum manipulators are widely used in medical applications, where accurate tip-position estimation is essential for precise navigation and instrument positioning. However, patient anatomy and procedural setup impose task-dependent unknown shaft configurations, while friction, slack, and compliance introduce hysteresis, making tip estimation challenging. This paper presents a motor-history-conditioned gated recurrent unit (GRU) residual estimator for three-dimensional catheter tip estimation without direct shaft-configuration sensing. First, an initial multidirectional sweep strategy is applied to calibrate a geometric catheter model backbone, and encode the motor-angle and drive-torque response into a shaft-configuration context vector. During subsequent motion, the context conditions a GRU that predicts a task-space residual correcting this backbone, relying on motor measurements alone. The context remains fixed for the current shaft configuration, while the recurrent state captures the evolving actuation history. Across four disposable intra-cardiac echocardiography catheters and 16 bent shaft configurations, the method achieves 3.3mm open-loop tip RMSE, a 59% reduction relative to the constant-curvature baseline.
