AI.tldr: A motor-history-conditioned GRU residual estimator achieves 3.3 mm open-loop 3D tip estimation for tendon-driven catheters without shaft-configuration sensing, a 59% improvement over constant-curvature.
AI.motivation: Accurate tip-position estimation is essential for navigation and instrument positioning of tendon-driven continuum manipulators in medical use, but task-dependent unknown shaft configurations plus friction, slack, and compliance-induced hysteresis make tip estimation difficult, especially without direct shaft-configuration sensing.
AI.method: An initial multidirectional sweep calibrates a geometric catheter model backbone and encodes motor-angle and drive-torque responses into a shaft-configuration context vector. This context conditions a GRU that predicts a task-space residual correcting the backbone using only motor measurements; the context stays fixed per shaft configuration while the recurrent state captures evolving actuation history.
AI.result: Across four disposable intra-cardiac echocardiography catheters and 16 bent shaft configurations, the method reaches 3.3 mm open-loop tip RMSE, a 59% reduction versus the constant-curvature baseline.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning a GRU residual estimator on a motor-history-derived shaft-configuration context enables accurate 3D tip estimation under unknown, hysteresis-affected configurations without direct shaft sensing, substantially outperforming the constant-curvature baseline.

title: FISSION: Label Augmentation for Bot Detection
summary: Bot accounts and coordinated influence operations are often discovered via heuristic methods, leaving a dearth of reliable ground-truth labels for training detection systems. To address this challenge, we study a natural question: can we generate labels to assist in learning embeddings in which bots and accounts from the same coordinated operation are close? We present FISSION, a method to generate labels by splitting each account's activity into positively labeled sub-accounts. Given this label source, we train detection models which preserve behavioral regularities recurring across positive sub-accounts. We evaluate FISSION and show it outperforms prior methods in detecting Wikipedia sockpuppets and Twitter/X bots.

AI.tldr: FISSION generates synthetic labels by splitting each account's activity into sub-accounts, then trains embedding models that cluster bots and coordinated accounts, outperforming prior methods on Wikipedia sockpuppet and Twitter/X bot detection.
AI.motivation: Bot and coordinated influence operation detection relies on heuristic methods, which results in a scarcity of reliable ground-truth labels needed to train supervised detection systems.
AI.method: FISSION addresses the label scarcity by splitting each account's activity into positively labeled sub-accounts, creating a label source. Detection models are then trained on these sub-account labels to preserve behavioral regularities that recur across the positive sub-accounts, learning embeddings in which bots and accounts from the same coordinated operation are close.
AI.result: FISSION outperforms prior methods in detecting Wikipedia sockpuppets and Twitter/X bots.
AI.conclusion: Generating labels by splitting account activity into positively labeled sub-accounts is an effective strategy for learning embeddings that cluster bots and coordinated accounts, yielding improved detection performance.

title: SafeLoop: Risk-Aware Rollback for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models are promising for general-purpose manipulation, but long-horizon execution remains fragile. Small state-estimation or control errors can lead to irreversible failures (e.g., collisions and object drops). Avoiding these risks requires a proactive safety mechanism capable of anticipating hazards. In this paper, we introduce SafeLoop, a non-invasive external wrapper that adds hazard prediction and rollback-based recovery to a VLA model without changing its parameters. SafeLoop trains a risk predictor from vision and proprioception to output four values: the probability and time-to-hazard for body collisions and for object failures. A lightweight controller then chooses one of three actions based on the predicted risk: continue execution (noop), save a safety checkpoint (record), or retreat in joint space (rollback). Rollback moves the robot back to a recent safe waypoint and queries the base policy again, which may yield an alternative continuation. Across 24 LIBERO tasks (16 random seeds each) and three real-robot tasks (25 rollouts each), SafeLoop achieves a stronger overall safety-success trade-off than alternative methods, reducing hazard cases by roughly 70% while preserving task success and the base-policy control rate. Project code is available at https://github.com/Loule0-0/SafeLoop/tree/release/safeloop.

AI.tldr: SafeLoop is a non-invasive external wrapper that adds hazard prediction and rollback-based recovery to vision-language-action (VLA) models without changing their parameters, trained from vision and proprioception.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon execution in VLA models remains fragile; small state-estimation or control errors can cause irreversible failures such as collisions and object drops, requiring proactive hazard anticipation.
AI.method: SafeLoop trains a risk predictor from vision and proprioception to output four values: probability and time-to-hazard for body collisions and object failures. A lightweight controller selects among three actions based on predicted risk: noop (continue), record (save a safety checkpoint), or rollback (retreat in joint space to a recent safe waypoint and re-query the base policy).
AI.result: Across 24 LIBERO tasks (16 random seeds each) and three real-robot tasks (25 rollouts each), SafeLoop achieves a stronger safety-success trade-off than alternatives, reducing hazard cases by roughly 70% while preserving task success and base-policy control rate.
AI.conclusion: SafeLoop provides an effective, non-invasive safety mechanism for VLA-based manipulation, substantially cutting hazards without retraining or modifying the base policy.

title: Dual-Frontier: When Can an Agent Trust Its World Model?
summary: Learned world models are becoming essential to general-purpose agents: by predicting action consequences, they support planning and decision-making while reducing reliance on costly trial and error. This reliance creates a fundamental ambiguity: when a world-model-guided decision fails, the trajectory alone may not reveal whether the agent's decision rule or the world model caused the loss. We formalize this failure-attribution problem as a counterfactual decomposition of return loss and prove that its components are not identifiable from passive interaction, even for finite-horizon planners. This obstruction motivates Dual-Frontier, a learning principle that admits a world-model-guided decision only when its predicted advantage exceeds a certified bound on decision-relevant world-model error; otherwise, evidence is allocated to world-model verification. Action-conditioned value bounds and a closed-loop extension guarantee non-decreasing return for admitted decisions. Calibrated gates and simultaneous confidence sequences support adaptive evidence reuse, with sufficient and necessary verification bounds. Controlled learned-model experiments validate the predicted failure modes and certification behavior, while cross-backbone tool-use benchmarks instantiate the same verify-then-promote rule in realistic agent world-model pipelines, consistently improving decision quality and reliability.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes the "failure-attribution problem" in world-model-guided agents as a counterfactual decomposition of return loss, proves its non-identifiability from passive interaction, and proposes Dual-Frontier: a verify-then-promote principle that admits a decision only if predicted advantage exceeds a certified bound on decision-relevant world-model error.
AI.motivation: Learned world models increasingly drive planning and decision-making by predicting action consequences, reducing reliance on costly trial and error. However, this reliance creates a fundamental ambiguity: when a world-model-guided decision fails, the observed trajectory alone cannot reveal whether the decision rule or the world model is responsible. The motivation is to resolve whether the loss stems from the agent's policy or the model, and to prevent unreliable model predictions from degrading decisions.
AI.method: The authors formalize the failure-attribution problem as a counterfactual decomposition of return loss and prove that its components are not identifiable from passive interaction, even for finite-horizon planners. To address this obstruction, they introduce Dual-Frontier, a learning principle that admits a world-model-guided decision only when its predicted advantage exceeds a certified bound on decision-relevant world-model error; otherwise, evidence is allocated to world-model verification. The method employs action-conditioned value bounds and a closed-loop extension that guarantees non-decreasing return for admitted decisions, along with calibrated gates and simultaneous confidence sequences for adaptive evidence reuse, with sufficient and necessary verification bounds.
AI.result: Controlled learned-model experiments validate the predicted failure modes and certification behavior. Cross-backbone tool-use benchmarks instantiate the same verify-then-promote rule in realistic agent world-model pipelines, consistently improving decision quality and reliability.
AI.conclusion: The non-identifiability of failure attribution from passive interaction justifies a shift from passive learning to active verification. Dual-Frontier operationalizes this by admitting decisions only under certified error bounds and reallocating effort to verification otherwise, yielding non-decreasing returns and empirically improved decision quality and reliability across controlled experiments and realistic tool-use benchmarks.

title: TriWorldBench: A Tri-View Consistency Perspective on Embodied World Models
summary: Embodied world models predict the outcomes of robot actions to support learning and planning. For robots equipped with head and wrist cameras, this requires complementary views: the head view captures the overall task, while wrist views reveal local gripper-object interactions. However, evaluating these views independently cannot determine whether they describe the same action and object state. We introduce TRIWORLDBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating embodied world models through synchronized head, left-wrist, and right-wrist videos. It contains 500 episodes across 50 bimanual manipulation tasks and uses 19 metrics to assess tri-view consistency, task alignment, physical and 3D coherence, motion quality, temporal consistency, and visual quality. By combining cross-view checks with measurements tailored to each camera, the benchmark evaluates whether plausible individual videos also form a consistent prediction of the intended task. We summarize overall performance with TWB-Score and retain per-view results to identify where predictions fail. This extends world-model evaluation beyond single-view visual quality. Code, data, and metric definitions are available at https://github.com/TriWorldBench/TriWorldBench.

AI.tldr: TriWorldBench is a benchmark evaluating embodied world models using synchronized tri-view (head, left-wrist, right-wrist) videos from 500 bimanual manipulation episodes across 50 tasks, scored with 19 metrics covering cross-view consistency, task alignment, physical/3D coherence, motion quality, temporal consistency, and visual quality, summarized by a TWB-Score.
AI.motivation: Existing world-model evaluation for robots with head and wrist cameras evaluates views independently, which cannot verify whether those views describe the same action and object state. Plausible individual videos do not guarantee a consistent, task-correct prediction.
AI.method: Introduce TriWorldBench, a benchmark with synchronized head, left-wrist, and right-wrist videos across 500 episodes and 50 bimanual manipulation tasks. It defines 19 metrics assessing tri-view consistency, task alignment, physical and 3D coherence, motion quality, temporal consistency, and visual quality, combining cross-view checks with per-camera measurements, and summarizes results via the TWB-Score while retaining per-view results.
AI.result: The benchmark provides a standardized setting and metrics to evaluate whether individually plausible per-view predictions jointly form a consistent prediction of the intended task, reporting overall TWB-Score plus per-view results to localize failures. Data, code, and metric definitions are released at the project repository.
AI.conclusion: TriWorldBench extends embodied world-model evaluation beyond single-view visual quality toward multi-view, task-level consistency, enabling diagnosis of where predictions fail.

title: Reliability Theory for AI Control
summary: Reliability theory gives a mature language for layered systems, but its formal tools are not yet standard in frontier AI control. We apply them to Google DeepMind's defenses against rogue deployment. The same control stack can have cubic, quadratic, or linear rare-failure suppression depending on its failure domains. Birnbaum importance identifies which component improvements buy the most nominal reliability, while prevention changes the population on which recovery is demanded. These results give concrete guidance about what to separate, improve, measure, and test.

AI.tldr: This paper applies reliability theory to formalize and evaluate Google DeepMind's defenses against rogue AI deployment, showing that a control stack's failure suppression scales cubically, quadratically, or linearly depending on how failure domains are structured, and using Birnbaum importance to prioritize component improvements.
AI.motivation: Reliability theory offers a mature formal language for layered systems, but these tools are not yet standard in frontier AI control research. The authors aim to bring this rigor to bear on real AI control stacks.
AI.method: The authors apply reliability-theoretic formalisms—including failure-domain analysis and Birnbaum importance—to Google DeepMind's defenses against rogue deployment, analyzing how the reliability of the control stack varies with its failure-domain structure.
AI.result: The same control stack can exhibit cubic, quadratic, or linear suppression of rare failures depending on its failure domains. Birnbaum importance identifies which components yield the greatest gains in nominal reliability, and prevention shifts the population on which recovery is required.
AI.conclusion: Reliability theory provides concrete guidance on what to separate, improve, measure, and test in frontier AI control stacks, offering a principled framework for prioritizing defenses against rogue deployment.

title: ArborSplat: Online Semantic Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Orchards
summary: Orchard robots need maps that preserve small but semantically important structures such as trunks, trellises, and fruit. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) SLAM achieves high photometric fidelity. However, its optimization remains appearance-driven, and transferring image semantics to 3D points is unreliable for thin structures, whose pixels may receive depth from background surfaces. We present ArborSplat, an online semantic 3DGS SLAM system that tracks with LiDAR odometry and optimizes semantics directly on the Gaussian map, constrained by class-specific height bands above a ground plane fitted to each keyframe's stereo point cloud, and fuses multi-view evidence into a semantic point cloud online while rejecting labels inconsistent with the local ground surface or with monocular depth. Class-constrained refinement reserves Gaussian capacity for underrepresented structures and, under reduced budgets, increases training-view accuracy on tree classes. We evaluate the approach on apple and pear orchards during dormancy, flowering, and harvesting. On full routes, it keeps ATE below 0.5 m on all 12 traversals. On shared 301-frame segments, it exceeds SGS-SLAM and GS3LAM by 0.23 to 0.50 training-view and 0.15 to 0.36 held-out mIoU while running 1.7 to 7.5 times faster, whereas SemGauss-SLAM runs out of GPU memory on all six.

AI.tldr: ArborSplat is an online semantic 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM system for orchards that uses LiDAR odometry for tracking and optimizes semantics directly on the Gaussian map, achieving accurate, fast semantic mapping of thin structures like trunks and trellises.
AI.motivation: Orchard robots require maps that preserve small but semantically important structures such as trunks, trellises, and fruit. While 3DGS SLAM achieves high photometric fidelity, its optimization is appearance-driven, and transferring image semantics to 3D points is unreliable for thin structures whose pixels may receive depth from background surfaces.
AI.method: ArborSplat tracks with LiDAR odometry and optimizes semantics directly on the Gaussian map, constrained by class-specific height bands above a ground plane fitted to each keyframe's stereo point cloud. It fuses multi-view evidence into a semantic point cloud online while rejecting labels inconsistent with the local ground surface or with monocular depth. Class-constrained refinement reserves Gaussian capacity for underrepresented structures.
AI.result: Evaluated on apple and pear orchards during dormancy, flowering, and harvesting: ATE stays below 0.5 m on all 12 full-route traversals. On shared 301-frame segments, it exceeds SGS-SLAM and GS3LAM by 0.23–0.50 training-view and 0.15–0.36 held-out mIoU while running 1.7–7.5× faster; SemGauss-SLAM runs out of GPU memory on all six.
AI.conclusion: ArborSplat delivers accurate, efficient online semantic 3DGS SLAM for orchards, improving semantic accuracy on thin structures and tree classes under reduced budgets while maintaining low tracking error and faster runtime than competing methods.

title: The Source of Disturbance Matters: External, Internal, and Control-Generated Noise in Adaptive Regulation
summary: Adaptive regulation can itself perturb the state it is intended to stabilize. In replicated simulations of an adaptive agent, we compare external disturbance, persistent internally generated disturbance, and control-generated disturbance under regulation-first and disturbance-first ordering. Persistent internal disturbance produces the largest exposure and regulatory burden within the tested parameter grid. When positive controller updates generate an immediate disturbance cost, increasing that cost produces a nonmonotonic response: effective disturbance initially rises, variability across stochastic runs increases over an intermediate range, and corrective activity becomes strongly suppressed at higher costs. The results show how disturbance source and timing shape exposure and controller burden in this model. They motivate testing adaptive agents with distinct disturbance sources and assessing regulatory activity alongside exposure.

AI.tldr: Using replicated simulations of an adaptive agent, the study compares how external, persistent internal, and control-generated disturbances affect exposure and regulatory burden, revealing that control-generated disturbance cost yields nonmonotonic dynamics.
AI.motivation: Adaptive regulation can perturb the very state it aims to stabilize, so the paper argues that disturbance source and timing must be disentangled to understand exposure and controller burden.
AI.method: Replicated simulations of an adaptive agent compare external disturbance, persistent internally generated disturbance, and control-generated disturbance under regulation-first versus disturbance-first ordering, within a tested parameter grid.
AI.result: External, persistent internal, and control-generated disturbances are compared in terms of exposure and regulatory burden. Persistent internal disturbance produces the largest exposure and regulatory burden. When positive controller updates incur an immediate disturbance cost, increasing that cost produces a nonmonotonic response: effective disturbance first rises, run-to-run variability peaks over an intermediate range, and corrective activity is strongly suppressed at higher costs.
AI.conclusion: Disturbance source and timing jointly shape exposure and controller burden. The authors recommend testing adaptive agents with distinct disturbance sources and evaluating regulatory activity alongside exposure.

title: Hierarchical Floorplan-Guided Vision-Language Exploration for Embodied Question Answering
summary: Embodied Question Answering (EQA) requires an agent to explore a previously unseen environment, gather relevant information, and answer questions about the scene. Recent approaches leverage Vision-Language Models (VLMs) together with semantic maps or scene graphs to guide exploration. However, exploration is typically driven only by local observations, while structural priors about the environment remain largely unused. We propose HFLEX-EQA, a hierarchical EQA framework that combines online scene graph construction, VLM- based planning, semantic frontier exploration, and floorplan priors. The system incrementally builds a hierarchical scene graph and an open-vocabulary occupancy map from RGB-D observations, enabling a VLM to jointly reason over the scene graph, task-relevant visual observations, exploration history, and an estimated topological floorplan. Furthermore, we introduce a room-discovery strategy that leverages the floorplan and open-vocabulary frontier semantics to guide exploration toward semantically relevant yet currently unobserved room types. We evaluate HFLEX-EQA on the OpenEQA and ExploreEQA benchmarks and demonstrate deployment on a quadruped robot in real indoor environments. Our results demonstrate the benefit of combining VLM-based hierarchical planning with structural floorplan priors for the EQA task.

AI.tldr: HFLEX-EQA is a hierarchical Embodied Question Answering framework that fuses online hierarchical scene graphs, VLM-based planning, semantic frontier exploration, and floorplan priors, improving exploration and answering on OpenEQA/ExploreEQA and a real quadruped robot.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM-based EQA approaches rely mostly on local observations and typically leave structural priors of the environment unused, limiting exploration efficiency and question answering.
AI.method: The framework incrementally builds a hierarchical scene graph and an open-vocabulary occupancy map from RGB-D observations. A VLM jointly reasons over the scene graph, task-relevant visual observations, exploration history, and an estimated topological floorplan. A room-discovery strategy uses the floorplan and open-vocabulary frontier semantics to steer exploration toward semantically relevant but unobserved room types.
AI.result: Evaluated on OpenEQA and ExploreEQA benchmarks and deployed on a quadruped robot in real indoor environments; results show benefit of combining VLM-based hierarchical planning with structural floorplan priors for EQA.
AI.conclusion: Combining VLM-based hierarchical planning with structural floorplan priors improves exploration and answering in Embodied Question Answering.

title: Recursive self-improvement of AI research agents
summary: AI agents are beginning to automate research and development across the AI stack, from improving training efficiency to optimizing inference. A natural next step is to improve the research efficiency of the agents themselves. When an AI research agent's own code is the object of optimization, each accepted rewrite becomes the agent that the next round edits. We refer to this loop as recursive self-improvement. Its significance lies in a long-standing trend, in which increased cumulative spending on R&D yields diminishing returns. Sustained self-improvement offers a way to counter this trend. We present AIDE^2, a system that implements this loop for a frontier AI research agent. It proposes changes to its own code, benchmarks modified versions of itself on a suite of AI R&D tasks, and keeps the changes that perform best on hidden evaluations. In an autonomous 8-day run, AIDE^2 discovered seven successive improvements, ranging from a new search policy to memory mechanisms that compress and manage the agent's growing context. These gains generalize to four held-out benchmarks spanning machine learning engineering, heuristic algorithm engineering, and physics-based weather forecasting, the last of which is out of distribution from the selection tasks. On all four, the strongest discovered agent matches or exceeds a human-engineered production research agent that ranks among the strongest on FML-Bench. On a separate held-out task family, the discovered agents also exhibit reduced reward hacking, a property the loop never explicitly optimized for: the rate falls from 55% to 32% during the run, 7 percentage points below the human-engineered agent. Together, these results show that an AI research agent can improve its own research efficiency through recursive self-improvement, and that these gains transfer to tasks and domains the loop never encountered.

AI.tldr: AIDE^2 implements recursive self-improvement for an AI research agent: it rewrites its own code, benchmarks the modified versions on AI R&D tasks, and retains the best-performing variants. Over an 8-day autonomous run it found seven successive improvements that transfer to four held-out benchmarks and reduce reward hacking.
AI.motivation: AI agents increasingly automate R&D across the AI stack, so improving the research efficiency of the agents themselves is a natural next step. When an agent's own code is the object of optimization, each accepted rewrite becomes the agent that performs the next round of edits (recursive self-improvement). This matters because cumulative R&D spending shows diminishing returns, and sustained self-improvement offers a way to counter that trend.
AI.method: AIDE^2 operationalizes the recursive self-improvement loop for a frontier AI research agent. It proposes changes to its own code, benchmarks modified versions of itself on a suite of AI R&D tasks, and keeps only changes that perform best on hidden evaluations. The loop was run autonomously for 8 days.
AI.result: In the 8-day autonomous run, AIDE^2 discovered seven successive improvements, ranging from a new search policy to memory mechanisms that compress and manage the agent's growing context. Gains generalized to four held-out benchmarks spanning machine learning engineering, heuristic algorithm engineering, and physics-based weather forecasting (the last out of distribution from selection tasks). On all four, the strongest discovered agent matches or exceeds a human-engineered production research agent ranking among the strongest on FML-Bench. On a separate held-out task family, reward hacking fell from 55% to 32% during the run, 7 percentage points below the human-engineered agent, despite never being explicitly optimized for.
AI.conclusion: An AI research agent can improve its own research efficiency through recursive self-improvement, and these gains transfer to tasks and domains the loop never encountered.

title: MAVP: Map-Aware Visuomotor Policies for Mobile Manipulation
summary: Successful mobile manipulation requires coordinated base and arm motion while maintaining accurate spatial positioning. However, demonstration-trained policies can struggle to realise the intended base motion reliably, leading to spatial misalignment and subsequent manipulation failures. We present MAVP (Map-Aware Visuomotor Policies), a framework that improves execution reliability by predicting explicit base-pose targets and tracking them using localisation feedback. MAVP reconstructs a static map from teleoperated demonstrations and expresses demonstrated base trajectories in a shared map frame, providing consistent spatial supervision across demonstrations. At execution time, the policy receives RGB observations, joint states, and the robot's current map-frame base pose, and jointly predicts target base poses, arm actions, and gripper actions. A low-level controller tracks the predicted base targets using feedforward motion and pose error feedback, enabling correction of execution deviations. We additionally use pose-noise augmentation during training to improve robustness to errors in the policy's pose input. Across six real-world manipulation tasks and three policy families, MAVP achieves higher task success rates than unanchored velocity control in all tasks. Videos and additional results are available at https://123qwedsa123.github.io/mavp/.

AI.tldr: MAVP is a map-aware visuomotor policy framework for mobile manipulation that predicts explicit base-pose targets and tracks them with localisation feedback, improving execution reliability across six real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Demonstration-trained mobile manipulation policies often fail to realise intended base motion reliably, causing spatial misalignment and subsequent manipulation failures. Existing unanchored velocity control lacks consistent spatial supervision and cannot correct execution deviations.
AI.method: MAVP reconstructs a static map from teleoperated demonstrations and expresses demonstrated base trajectories in a shared map frame, yielding consistent spatial supervision. At execution, the policy takes RGB observations, joint states, and current map-frame base pose as input, and jointly predicts target base poses, arm actions, and gripper actions. A low-level controller tracks the predicted base targets via feedforward motion and pose-error feedback. Pose-noise augmentation during training improves robustness to pose-input errors.
AI.result: Across six real-world manipulation tasks and three policy families, MAVP achieves higher task success rates than unanchored velocity control in all tasks.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring base-pose prediction and tracking to a shared map frame, combined with localisation feedback, substantially improves the reliability of demonstration-trained mobile manipulation policies.

title: Reproducible AI Requires Reproducible Randomness
summary: Pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs) constitute indispensable computational tools across multiple scientific domains, including Monte Carlo simulations, stochastic computing, and artificial intelligence (AI). The reproducibility of such applications critically depends on the ability of PRNG implementations to generate identical sequences across software environments when initialized from the same internal state. These algorithms enable the simulation of stochastic processes while providing deterministic and repeatable behaviour, thereby facilitating reproducible experiments. Modern PRNG implementations may be initialized through either a seed or, more accurately, an initial state that exceeds the capacity of a conventional integer seed. However, reliance on a simple seed alone frequently proves insufficient to ensure consistent program execution traces across different implementations. A natural assumption is that transferring the complete internal state of a generator should guarantee identical outputs regardless of the software library used. This study examines the validity of this assumption by investigating whether complete initial states can ensure cross-library fidelity and portability of PRNG streams. We focus on two widely deployed generators, Mersenne Twister and Philox, and evaluate their implementations across four major Python ecosystems-Random, NumPy, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. We compare the sequences produced by these implementations against those generated by the original reference algorithms under identical initialization conditions. Our results demonstrate that reproducibility cannot be assumed from PRNG state transfer alone, even when implementations claim to follow the same underlying algorithm. While fidelity was successfully achieved for several implementations, significant discrepancies were observed in others. Most notably, the Philox implementation in PyTorch exhibits fundamental incompatibilities with the reference algorithm, preventing exact reproduction of generator outputs across environments. These findings challenge the common expectation that access to a full internal state of a PRNG is sufficient to ensure reproducibility across software stacks. They further highlight that implementation-specific design choices can introduce hidden barriers to experimental replication, particularly in AI workflows that rely on multiple frameworks. This work shows that implementation fidelity of a PRNG is a necessary condition for scientific reproducibility and makes two primary contributions. First, it identifies practical guidelines for achieving reliable PRNG usage and reproducibility within the Python scientific and AI ecosystem. Second, it evaluates the extent to which cross-library portability and fidelity can be recovered through user-level techniques, without requiring modifications to library source code.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether transferring the complete internal state of a PRNG guarantees identical output sequences across different software libraries, testing Mersenne Twister and Philox in Random, NumPy, PyTorch, and TensorFlow.
AI.motivation: Reproducibility in Monte Carlo simulations, stochastic computing, and AI depends on PRNGs producing identical sequences across software environments from the same internal state. A common assumption is that transferring the full internal state (not just a seed) ensures identical outputs regardless of library, but this assumption is untested.
AI.method: The study focuses on two widely deployed generators, Mersenne Twister and Philox, and evaluates their implementations across four major Python ecosystems: Random, NumPy, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. The sequences produced by these implementations are compared against the original reference algorithms under identical initialization conditions.
AI.result: Reproducibility cannot be assumed from PRNG state transfer alone, even when implementations claim to follow the same algorithm. Fidelity was achieved for several implementations, but significant discrepancies were observed in others. Most notably, the Philox implementation in PyTorch exhibits fundamental incompatibilities with the reference algorithm, preventing exact reproduction across environments.
AI.conclusion: Full internal state access is insufficient to guarantee cross-library reproducibility; implementation-specific design choices introduce hidden barriers to replication, especially in multi-framework AI workflows. The paper makes two contributions: identifying practical guidelines for reliable PRNG usage and reproducibility in the Python scientific/AI ecosystem, and evaluating how far cross-library portability and fidelity can be recovered through user-level techniques without modifying library source code.

title: SparseNav: Instruction-conditioned Sparse Semantic Perception for Training-Free Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Map-based vision-language navigation (VLN) relies on persistent spatial representations to connect language understanding with geometric planning. However, acquiring semantics beyond the needs of the current instruction can introduce unnecessary perception cost and irrelevant annotations. Continuously accumulating unrelated objects may not only waste computation, but also clutter the visual-spatial representation consumed by the vision-language model (VLM) planner. To address this problem, we present SparseNav, a training-free framework that follows a less-is-more principle for semantic navigation. SparseNav persistently maintains a lightweight geometric bird's-eye-view (BEV) map and sparse landmark memory, acquiring new semantics on demand using the active sub-instruction to decide what is worth grounding. An instruction manager first tracks navigation progress and identifies the active landmark query. An instruction-conditioned perception mechanism then invokes open-vocabulary segmentation when the queried landmark is visible and its metric location can inform the next decision. The resulting landmark memory supports VLM selection among hybrid frontier and local directional waypoint candidates. Without any additional training, SparseNav achieves success rates of 42.8% on R2R-CE and 40.7% on RxR-CE, both on the Val-Unseen splits. Controlled ablations examine semantic perception strategies and the contributions of individual framework components. Furthermore, we successfully deployed SparseNav on a Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with an Intel RealSense D455 RGB-D camera for geometric mapping and landmark grounding and a Livox MID-360 LiDAR for localization, without a prebuilt map. We validated its effectiveness across multiple indoor environments using instruction-conditioned waypoint navigation.

AI.tldr: SparseNav is a training-free, map-based VLN framework that maintains a lightweight geometric BEV map plus sparse landmark memory, grounding semantics on demand from the active sub-instruction, achieving 42.8% SR on R2R-CE and 40.7% on RxR-CE (Val-Unseen) and deploying on a Unitree Go2 quadruped without a prebuilt map.
AI.motivation: Map-based VLN relies on persistent spatial representations, but acquiring semantics beyond the current instruction incurs unnecessary perception cost and irrelevant annotations. Continuously accumulating unrelated objects wastes computation and clutters the visual-spatial representation consumed by the VLM planner, motivating a less-is-more, on-demand semantic perception approach.
AI.method: SparseNav is training-free and follows a less-is-more principle. It persistently maintains a lightweight geometric BEV map and sparse landmark memory, acquiring new semantics on demand. An instruction manager tracks navigation progress and identifies the active landmark query; an instruction-conditioned perception mechanism invokes open-vocabulary segmentation only when the queried landmark is visible and its metric location can inform the next decision. The resulting landmark memory supports VLM selection among hybrid frontier and local directional waypoint candidates.
AI.result: Without additional training, SparseNav achieves 42.8% success rate on R2R-CE and 40.7% on RxR-CE (Val-Unseen). Controlled ablations examine semantic perception strategies and individual framework components. It was deployed on a Unitree Go2 quadruped with an Intel RealSense D455 RGB-D camera (geometric mapping and landmark grounding) and a Livox MID-360 LiDAR (localization), without a prebuilt map, validated across multiple indoor environments via instruction-conditioned waypoint navigation.
AI.conclusion: SparseNav demonstrates that training-free, on-demand sparse semantic grounding combined with a lightweight geometric BEV map enables effective map-based VLN, achieving competitive success rates and transferring to real-world legged robot deployment without a prebuilt map.

title: REFLEX with Jev for Efficient Selective Control in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents often use generative models for bounded decisions, raising the question of when these decisions can be handled more efficiently without reducing task success. We study REFLEX, an agent architecture that uses Jev as a fast, typed decision layer and calls a strong LLM when confidence is low, or generation is required. On a frozen 100-task benchmark, REFLEX achieves 95% success with 72.7% fewer strong-model calls than a strong-only agent, with reductions persisting across three fallback families. Controlled interventions show that reliability depends on action-set size and near-valid alternatives near authorization boundaries. External BFCL and $τ$-style evaluations reveal limited advantages over a cheap generative cascade when ordinary routing is already highly accurate. These findings identify when selective control with Jev can reduce computation and where its benefits are limited.

AI.tldr: REFLEX is an LLM agent architecture that uses a fast, typed decision layer (Jev) for bounded decisions and escalates to a strong LLM only when confidence is low or generation is needed. It attains 95% success on a frozen 100-task benchmark with 72.7% fewer strong-model calls than a strong-only agent, but its advantage shrinks when ordinary routing is already highly accurate.
AI.motivation: LLM agents often invoke generative models for bounded decisions; the paper asks when such decisions can be handled more efficiently—without lowering task success—by replacing unnecessary strong-model calls with lightweight, typed decision-making.
AI.method: The authors design REFLEX, an agent architecture with Jev as a fast, typed decision layer that handles bounded decisions, and a strong LLM that is called only when confidence is low or generation is required. They evaluate on a frozen 100-task benchmark, compare three fallback families, run controlled interventions on action-set size and near-valid alternatives near authorization boundaries, and conduct external BFCL and τ-style evaluations against a cheap generative cascade.
AI.result: REFLEX reaches 95% success with 72.7% fewer strong-model calls than a strong-only agent, and the reductions persist across three fallback families. Reliability is shown to depend on action-set size and near-valid alternatives near authorization boundaries. External BFCL and τ-style evaluations show limited advantages over a cheap generative cascade when ordinary routing is already highly accurate.
AI.conclusion: Selective control with Jev can meaningfully reduce computation for bounded agent decisions while preserving task success, but the benefit is conditional—it is strongest where decisions are constrained and routing is imperfect, and limited where existing routing is already highly accurate. The work delineates when selective control helps and where its benefits are bounded.

title: Sample, Simulate, Select: Physics-in-the-Loop Text-to-Motion for Humanoids Without Training
summary: Text-to-motion models generate plausible human motion but do not model a robot's dynamics; whole-body tracking controllers execute robot references reliably but cannot replan an infeasible one. Recent language-to-humanoid systems bridge this gap by training. We measure how much of the gap closes with no training at all, by putting the deployment controller itself in the loop. Sample-simulate-select (S$^3$) draws $N$ motions per prompt from a frozen text-to-motion model, retargets each to a Unitree G1 by direction-matching inverse kinematics, rolls all of them out under full rigid-body dynamics with the pretrained SONIC tracking policy, and keeps the candidate the policy executed best. Because the verifier is the deterministic simulator itself, S$^3$ attains the any-of-$N$ ceiling by construction; what we measure is where that ceiling lies and what falls short of it. On 200 stratified HumanML3D test prompts with $N=8$, upright execution rises from 83.5% to 89.5% and hardware-gate passes from 33 to 85; on the complete test split (4,184 prompts) it rises from 80.5% to 89.5%. A kinematic verifier that predicts falls well (AUROC 0.90) recovers only a quarter of this gain: ranking a prompt's own candidates is harder than classifying the population. What selection cannot fix is one class, prompts that lower the pelvis, which a generator trained on retargeted robot data does execute. We further score the semantic fidelity of the executed motion with the standard text-motion evaluator, with a real-mocap control that attributes the loss to the robot projection, ablate the retargeter against GMR (complementary failures: the any-of-8 ceiling rises to 95.0% over both), and execute all 177 gate-selected clips on the real G1: every one completes standing, with hardware tracking error matching simulation ($r=0.94$).

AI.tldr: S$^3$ (sample-simulate-select) closes much of the text-to-humanoid gap with no training by verifying text-to-motion candidates through the deployment controller in simulation, raising upright execution and hardware-gate pass rates at cost only of pelvis-lowering prompts.
AI.motivation: Text-to-motion models produce plausible motion but are dynamics-agnostic, while whole-body tracking controllers execute feasible references reliably but cannot replan infeasible ones. Existing language-to-humanoid systems bridge this gap through training; this work asks how much of the gap can be closed with no training at all by placing the deployment controller itself in the loop.
AI.method: Sample-simulate-select: for each prompt, draw N=8 motions from a frozen text-to-motion model, retarget each to a Unitree G1 via direction-matching inverse kinematics, roll out all candidates under full rigid-body dynamics with the pretrained SONIC tracking policy, and select the candidate the policy executes best. The deterministic simulator serves as the verifier, so S$^3$ attains the any-of-N ceiling by construction; ablations include a kinematic fall predictor, GMR retargeter comparison, and a generator trained on retargeted robot data.
AI.result: On 200 stratified HumanML3D test prompts (N=8), upright execution rises 83.5%→89.5% and hardware-gate passes 33→85; over the full test split (4,184 prompts) 80.5%→89.5%. A kinematic verifier with AUROC 0.90 for fall prediction recovers only a quarter of the gain, showing within-prompt ranking is harder than population classification. Pelvis-lowering prompts remain unfixable by selection but are executed by a generator trained on retargeted robot data. Ablating the retargeter against GMR yields complementary failures, raising the any-of-8 ceiling to 95.0% over both. All 177 gate-selected clips execute standing on the real G1, with hardware tracking error matching simulation (r=0.94).
AI.conclusion: Training-free in-the-loop verification via sampling, simulation, and selection substantially closes the text-to-humanoid execution gap, bounded by the any-of-N ceiling. What selection cannot fix is one identifiable failure class (pelvis-lowering prompts), which motivates retargeted-robot-data training, while retargeter and verifier choices present complementary trade-offs worth combining.

title: JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure
summary: LLM-as-a-judge enables evaluation across diverse tasks, but inference cost and confidence reliability become critical at scale. We study whether a decision-only judge can provide an economical first pass and identify when stronger evaluation is needed. Comparing jev-as-a-judge with sixteen generative and reward-model judges, with blinded human adjudication, we find it within three percentage points of a state-of-the-art LLM judge, our strongest comparator, on ordinary preference and evidence-grounded factuality at 0.36% of the comparator's fee. Larger gaps arise when judgments require checking a derivation or resisting an elaborately written wrong answer. On several benchmarks, JEV's gap to this comparator is concentrated in low-confidence decisions. A frozen cascade that accepts confident verdicts and escalates uncertain ones retains 99% of the comparator's accuracy at lower cost.

AI.tldr: A decision-only judge (JEV) can serve as an economical first pass for LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, matching a state-of-the-art LLM judge within three percentage points on ordinary preference and factuality tasks at 0.36% of the cost; a confidence-based cascade retains 99% of the comparator's accuracy more cheaply.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-judge is widely applicable but suffers from high inference cost and unreliable confidence at scale. The authors investigate whether a lightweight decision-only judge can act as a cheap first-pass evaluator and signal when more expensive evaluation is warranted.
AI.method: The authors compare a decision-only judge (JEV) against sixteen generative and reward-model judges, using blinded human adjudication as ground truth. They analyze accuracy and cost gaps across task types (preference, evidence-grounded factuality, derivation-checking, resisting elaborate wrong answers) and examine confidence calibration. They then build a frozen cascade that accepts confident verdicts and escalates uncertain ones to a stronger judge.
AI.result: JEV comes within three percentage points of the strongest comparator (a state-of-the-art LLM judge) on ordinary preference and evidence-grounded factuality, at 0.36% of the comparator's cost. Larger gaps emerge on tasks requiring derivation checking or resistance to elaborately written wrong answers. On several benchmarks, the gap concentrates in low-confidence decisions. The frozen cascade retains 99% of the comparator's accuracy at lower cost.
AI.conclusion: A decision-only judge offers an economical first-pass evaluation, and confidence-based escalation enables a cost-effective cascade that preserves nearly all of a state-of-the-art judge's accuracy.

title: Dr-LiSA: Direct Radar-Lidar Scan Alignment for $SE(3)$ Localization
summary: This paper introduces Dr-LiSA, a first-of-its-kind direct method for localizing 2D spinning radar intensity measurements in $SE(3)$ against 3D lidar maps. Radar-lidar localization combines the complementary strengths of the two sensing modalities: radar is robust to adverse weather and precipitation, while lidar provides high-fidelity 3D maps in favourable conditions. However, existing radar-lidar localization methods are restricted to planar $SE(2)$ localization and have generally fallen short of the accuracy achieved by lidar-lidar and even radar-radar systems. A key challenge is the substantial sensing-modality gap between radar and lidar, which observe and represent scene structure in fundamentally different ways. Dr-LiSA bridges this gap using a learned forward model that predicts radar measurements from a lidar submap at a candidate pose, enabling direct photometric alignment of predicted and observed radar scans in $SE(3)$. Dr-LiSA outperforms prior radar-lidar approaches in $SE(2)$ while achieving planar accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art radar-radar localization across more than 90 km of on-road data.

AI.tldr: Dr-LiSA is a direct method for localizing 2D spinning radar intensity measurements in SE(3) against 3D lidar maps, bridging the radar-lidar modality gap via a learned forward model for direct photometric alignment.
AI.motivation: Radar-lidar localization leverages complementary sensing strengths: radar is robust to adverse weather while lidar provides high-fidelity 3D maps. However, existing radar-lidar methods are limited to planar SE(2) localization and underperform compared to lidar-lidar and even radar-radar systems. The core challenge is the substantial sensing-modality gap, as radar and lidar observe and represent scene structure fundamentally differently.
AI.method: Dr-LiSA employs a learned forward model that predicts radar measurements from a lidar submap at a candidate pose, enabling direct photometric alignment of predicted and observed radar scans in SE(3).
AI.result: Dr-LiSA outperforms prior radar-lidar approaches in SE(2) and achieves planar accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art radar-radar localization across more than 90 km of on-road data.
AI.conclusion: Dr-LiSA is the first-of-its-kind direct method for SE(3) radar-lidar localization, bridging the modality gap through learned radar prediction from lidar submaps and demonstrating strong planar accuracy over extensive real-world driving data.

title: Neutral-Atom-based Quantum Optimization for Resource Allocation in NOMA Networks
summary: In wireless communication networks, many resource optimization problems are nondeterministic polynomial-time hard (NP-hard) due to their combinatorial nature and high computational complexity. Recently, neutral-atom-based quantum computing has emerged as a promising platform for efficiently solving such problems by leveraging quantum superposition and entanglement. However, its application to wireless communication optimization problems remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the use of neutral-atom quantum platforms to solve the maximum access problem (MAP), formulated as a mixed-integer programming task that jointly considers admission control, user clustering, channel assignment, and power allocation in a non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-enabled uplink network. To reduce the computational burden, the MAP is equivalently reformulated as a maximum independent set (MIS) problem in graph theory. This reformulation enables the use of the neutral atom platform based on Rydberg atom arrays, where the MIS problem is naturally encoded into the physical geometry and blockade constraints of the quantum system. Numerical results demonstrate the feasibility and potential of this approach for addressing large-scale wireless resource optimization problems.

AI.tldr: This paper applies neutral-atom-based quantum computing to solve the maximum access problem in NOMA-enabled uplink networks, reformulating it as a maximum independent set problem for encoding on Rydberg atom arrays.
AI.motivation: Many resource optimization problems in wireless communication networks are NP-hard due to their combinatorial nature and high computational complexity. Neutral-atom-based quantum computing has recently emerged as a promising platform for efficiently solving such problems by leveraging quantum superposition and entanglement. However, its application to wireless communication optimization problems remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The maximum access problem (MAP) is formulated as a mixed-integer programming task that jointly considers admission control, user clustering, channel assignment, and power allocation in a NOMA-enabled uplink network. To reduce computational burden, the MAP is equivalently reformulated as a maximum independent set (MIS) problem in graph theory, enabling its use on a neutral-atom platform based on Rydberg atom arrays, where the MIS problem is naturally encoded into the physical geometry and blockade constraints of the quantum system.
AI.result: Numerical results demonstrate the feasibility and potential of this approach for addressing large-scale wireless resource optimization problems.
AI.conclusion: Neutral-atom quantum platforms, via the MIS reformulation, offer a feasible and promising approach to solving large-scale wireless resource optimization problems such as the MAP.

title: RouteRLT: Learning When and Which RL Specialist Should Control a Vision-Language-Action Policy
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at the IROS 2026 International Workshop on Industrial Applications of Robot Learning (IARL)
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide broad manipulation competence, but often struggle during the precision-critical stages that dominate contact-rich industrial tasks such as connector insertion and cable management. A common remedy is to refine a pretrained VLA with reinforcement learning (RL), enabling task-specific improvement beyond behavior cloning. However, how to preserve its generalist behavior while deciding when RL refinement is needed and which specialized policy should act remains an open question. In this work, we present RouteRLT, a routing framework that learns when and which RL specialist, an RL policy trained for a single precision-critical phase, should take control from a generalist VLA. A phase selector identifies the active controller, a stabilizer suppresses transient switches, and an action-boundary manager handles transitions between chunked policy outputs. We evaluate RouteRLT on multi-object pick-and-place tasks in LIBERO, as well as on a real-world cable pickup and port-insertion task with multiple precision-critical stages. In simulation, the learned routing improves over the base VLA and matches routing with privileged phase boundaries, without accessing those boundaries at deployment. The real-robot evaluation validates automatic routing to both the pickup and insertion specialists under an operator-aligned handoff protocol. Altogether, these results show that learned routing applies RL specialist control where precise adaptation is most valuable while preserving generalist VLA behavior, including recovery from failed execution attempts.

AI.tldr: RouteRLT is a routing framework that learns when and which RL specialist policy should take control from a generalist VLA, preserving generalist behavior while applying task-specific RL refinement only in precision-critical phases.
AI.motivation: VLA models offer broad manipulation competence but struggle in precision-critical stages of contact-rich industrial tasks (e.g., connector insertion, cable management). RL refinement of a pretrained VLA can improve such tasks, but it is unclear how to preserve generalist behavior, decide when RL refinement is needed, and select which specialized policy should act.
AI.method: RouteRLT comprises three components: (1) a phase selector that identifies the active controller, (2) a stabilizer that suppresses transient switches, and (3) an action-boundary manager that handles transitions between chunked policy outputs. RL specialists are each trained for a single precision-critical phase and routed alongside a generalist VLA.
AI.result: Evaluated on multi-object pick-and-place tasks in LIBERO and a real-world cable pickup and port-insertion task with multiple precision-critical stages. In simulation, learned routing improves over the base VLA and matches routing with privileged phase boundaries without accessing those boundaries at deployment. Real-robot evaluation validates automatic routing to pickup and insertion specialists under an operator-aligned handoff protocol.
AI.conclusion: Learned routing applies RL specialist control where precise adaptation is most valuable while preserving generalist VLA behavior, including recovery from failed execution attempts.

title: Quantum-Aided Active Device Detection in Energy-Harvesting Symbiotic Radio Networks
summary: Massive connectivity in next-generation networks demands energy- and spectrum-efficient solutions for large-scale Internet of Things (IoT) deployments. Symbiotic radio (SR) enables passive IoT devices to communicate by backscattering existing cellular transmissions. A key challenge in uplink SR is active device detection (ADD), which directly affects decoding reliability, interference management, and system throughput. We propose an energy-harvesting code-domain non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-SR system in which IoT devices harvest energy from ambient uplink signals and backscatter information using low-density spreading (LDS) codes. To reduce the complexity of ADD, Grover's quantum search algorithm is employed, providing a quadratic reduction in oracle-query complexity over exhaustive maximum-likelihood (ML) search. Numerical results show that the proposed approach closely approaches ML performance while substantially reducing the number of search iterations, demonstrating its potential for scalable ambient IoT systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an energy-harvesting code-domain NOMA-SR uplink system for passive IoT, applying Grover's quantum search to active device detection with quadratic oracle-query complexity reduction versus exhaustive ML search.
AI.motivation: Massive connectivity in next-generation networks requires energy- and spectrum-efficient solutions for large-scale IoT. Symbiotic radio (SR) lets passive devices communicate by backscattering cellular transmissions, but uplink SR faces a key challenge: active device detection (ADD), which affects decoding reliability, interference management, and throughput. Exhaustive maximum-likelihood (ML) search for ADD is prohibitively complex.
AI.method: The authors design an energy-harvesting code-domain NOMA-SR system in which IoT devices harvest energy from ambient uplink signals and backscatter information using low-density spreading (LDS) codes. To reduce ADD complexity, Grover's quantum search algorithm is employed, yielding a quadratic reduction in oracle-query complexity relative to exhaustive ML search.
AI.result: Numerical results show that the proposed approach closely approaches ML performance while substantially reducing the number of search iterations.
AI.conclusion: The quantum-search-based ADD scheme demonstrates potential for scalable ambient IoT systems, offering near-ML accuracy with substantially lower detection complexity.

title: Benchmarking Robots for Everyday Environments: From Lab Experiments to Real-World Operations
comment: 46 pages, 14 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in Frontiers in Robotics and AI (Field Robotics)
summary: This study introduces an interdisciplinary framework for benchmarking robots deployed in public environments, addressing the gap between traditional laboratory metrics and real-world benchmarking requirements. We evaluate three distinct robots across diverse use cases - outdoor park cleaning, pedestrian underpass cleaning, and interactive library assistance - each representing unique challenges in public daily life. Over a three-year benchmarking process (2023-2025) comprising seven benchmarking events, a consensus workshop and six on-site evaluations (two per use case), we utilized realistic indoor and outdoor test environments to assess not only technical performance but also the broader implications of deploying robots in unstructured, human-centric settings. An expert panel, spanning robotics, human-robot interaction, safety, and economics, systematically developed and refined an evaluation concept to analyze the transition from laboratory prototypes to operational systems. Our findings highlight critical factors for successful deployment, including task fulfillment, interaction quality, safety, and economic feasibility. This work provides actionable insights for researchers and practitioners aiming to bridge the gap between robotic innovation and real-world applicability.

AI.tldr: Introduces an interdisciplinary benchmarking framework for robots in public environments, validated over three years (2023–2025) using three robots across park cleaning, underpass cleaning, and library assistance, evaluated through six on-site events and a consensus workshop by an expert panel.
AI.motivation: Traditional laboratory robotics metrics fail to capture real-world benchmarking requirements for robots deployed in unstructured, human-centric public spaces.
AI.method: A three-year benchmarking process (2023–2025) including seven events: a consensus workshop and six on-site evaluations (two per use case). Three robots were tested in realistic indoor and outdoor environments across outdoor park cleaning, pedestrian underpass cleaning, and interactive library assistance. An expert panel spanning robotics, human-robot interaction, safety, and economics developed and refined the evaluation concept.
AI.result: The evaluation concept revealed key deployment factors, including task fulfillment, interaction quality, safety, and economic feasibility, distinguishing laboratory prototype performance from operational system viability.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers actionable insights for researchers and practitioners seeking to bridge robotic innovation and real-world applicability in public environments.

title: The Delegation Blind Spot: Auditing Product Decisions from Agent Choices
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Computational technical report with proofs and synthetic-task experiments; no human participants. Code: https://github.com/shi1720/delegation-blind-spot
summary: Successful agent execution need not identify which future product improvement its user would value. We present a decision-specific audit that maps a declared observation channel and product-value contrast to compatible intervals and witness populations. Its foundations are established identification and decision theory; the contribution is an executable measurement workflow and a controlled study of its limits. A frozen experiment makes 4,800 requests to two pinned model snapshots on shared synthetic tasks. All 36 conservative primary intervals remain unresolved despite different execution accuracy. An exploratory 2,400-call follow-up records supplied preferences and resolves three of nine comparisons per model. A deterministic extractor resolves seven of nine without model calls or calibration observations, exposing unnecessary uncertainty introduced by model-generated reports. A further 14,400 controlled multinomial simulations distinguish structural ambiguity from weak identification and finite calibration precision. We propose a source-labeled decision receipt and provide an offline viewer for inspecting the audit. These results motivate preserving decision-relevant structured input and diagnosing why a decision is unresolved before collecting more telemetry. The study contains no human participants or real customer outcomes. Full proofs, raw model provenance, controlled experiments, and reproducible analyses accompany the report.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a decision-specific audit that maps a declared observation channel and product-value contrast to compatible intervals and witness populations, grounded in identification and decision theory, and validates it through a frozen 4,800-request experiment, an exploratory 2,400-call follow-up, a deterministic extractor, and 14,400 multinomial simulations, all supported by an offline viewer and source-labeled decision receipts.
AI.motivation: Successful agent execution does not require identifying which future product improvement its user would value, yet decisions about agent performance still hinge on this unobservable quantity. The work is motivated by the need to diagnose why a decision remains unresolved rather than collecting more telemetry blindly, and by the observation that model-generated reports can introduce unnecessary uncertainty relative to structured inputs.
AI.method: The authors develop a decision-specific audit that maps a declared observation channel and product-value contrast to compatible intervals and witness populations, building on established identification and decision theory. They conduct a frozen experiment with 4,800 requests to two pinned model snapshots on shared synthetic tasks; an exploratory 2,400-call follow-up recording supplied preferences; a deterministic extractor requiring no model calls or calibration observations; and 14,400 controlled multinomial simulations separating structural ambiguity from weak identification and finite calibration precision. They also propose a source-labeled decision receipt and an offline viewer for inspecting the audit.
AI.result: All 36 conservative primary intervals remain unresolved despite differing execution accuracy. The follow-up resolves three of nine comparisons per model. The deterministic extractor resolves seven of nine comparisons without model calls or calibration observations, exposing unnecessary uncertainty introduced by model-generated reports. The multinomial simulations distinguish structural ambiguity from weak identification and finite calibration precision.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate preserving decision-relevant structured input and diagnosing why a decision is unresolved before collecting more telemetry. The study involves no human participants or real customer outcomes, and full proofs, raw model provenance, controlled experiments, and reproducible analyses accompany the report.

title: Generalizing Manipulation Skills with a Local Coding Agent
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Raman Talwar and Elias Nijs contributed equally
summary: Today, progress in open-weight language models enables systems capable of writing, executing and debugging code while still running on a single workstation. Most language-driven robots give the model a fixed action interface or a trained policy. Generalizing to a new task therefore means more engineering effort or more data collection, both time-consuming. We investigate whether a local open-weight vision-language model can control a robot and one-shot generalize to new variations of a task without new human programming or training. We let a local open-weight VLM, Qwen3.8-27B, drive a UR3e robotic arm from a coding-agent harness. It writes and runs its own code above a service that implements kinematics, safety limits and classic computer vision techniques. We investigate if this system is capable of generalizing to unseen tasks. Specifically, we test it on nine tasks built from children's toys designed to probe generalization capability across various object characteristics: color, size, shape, and task variation of those. With five trials for each task, we observe generalization in 30 out of 45 trials with durations ranging from 3.4 to 67.5 minutes depending on task complexity. We further test if there is a speedup when an agent is asked to redo the task after successful completion. This resulted in a 50% reduction in duration, indicating that there is self-improvement over time. Finally, we expose the limitations of a local coding agent. We believe that solving those limitations combined with further investigation of self-improvement over time points at a direct path toward real-world deployment of a local coding agent.

AI.tldr: A local open-weight VLM (Qwen3.8-27B) drives a UR3e arm via a coding-agent harness that writes/runs its own code over a service with kinematics, safety limits, and classic CV; it generalizes zero-shot to unseen toy-manipulation tasks in 30/45 trials and nearly halves repeat-task duration.
AI.motivation: Open-weight models can now write, execute and debug code on a single workstation, yet most language-driven robots rely on fixed action interfaces or trained policies, so generalizing to a new task requires extra engineering or data collection. The authors ask whether a local open-weight VLM can control a robot and one-shot generalize to new task variations without new human programming or training.
AI.method: A local open-weight vision-language model, Qwen3.8-27B, drives a UR3e robotic arm from a coding-agent harness. The agent writes and executes its own code on top of a service exposing kinematics, safety limits, and classic computer vision. Generalization is probed on nine tasks built from children's toys varying in color, size, shape, and task variation, with five trials per task. A repeat-task experiment measures whether re-doing a successfully completed task yields a speedup.
AI.result: Generalization is observed in 30 of 45 trials, with durations from 3.4 to 67.5 minutes depending on task complexity. Repeating a task after successful completion reduces duration by 50%, indicating self-improvement over time. The authors also report the limitations of a local coding agent.
AI.conclusion: A local open-weight coding agent can control a robot and one-shot generalize to unseen task variations without new programming or training, and it self-improves on repeated tasks. Addressing the identified limitations, combined with further study of self-improvement, points to a direct path toward real-world deployment of local coding agents.

title: Type-Safe Is Not Error-Free: A Constrained Decision Head Follows the Option Name, Not the Rubric Bound to It
summary: Typed decision models are built for settings where model outputs are consumed directly by software. Instead of generating free-form text, they return a decision over a predefined set of options. By construction, every output conforms to the required schema. Yet this guarantee does not tell us whether the model interprets the options as intended. We study Jev and two Jev-like models with open weights by changing how option names are assigned to rubrics. Each option consists of an option name and a textual rubric that defines what the option means. We change only which option name is assigned to each rubric; the question, state, rubric wording, and set of option names remain exactly the same. On 1200 workflow decisions with task-specific rubrics, renaming the two options from 0/1 to no/yes changes 70.4 more answers per hundred (95% CI: [67.6, 73.1]) and shifts AUC from .94 to .23, revealing a systematic reversal in the decision ranking rather than simple uncertainty. The same operation has little effect with neutral option names. This pattern holds across all 4 predicates, where the effect is at least 7.4x larger than under the neutral control, and becomes stronger as the number of options increases. The effect also depends on the read-out geometry: a second model family that mean-pools over the full option span flips 4.1x less often. The hosted model exhibits the same behavior: the swap changes AUC from .8146 to .5806 and produces 24x as many answer flips as its test-retest floor. In contrast, replacing the option names with random character strings returns all model families to the neutral-control regime without reducing accuracy. The failure therefore depends on the semantic polarity of the option names rather than on the renaming operation itself. Across all conditions, the type-error rate remains 0%, even when decision accuracy degrades substantially.

AI.tldr: Typed decision models guarantee schema-valid outputs but not correct interpretation of option labels. Swapping semantically polarized option names (0/1 to no/yes) while keeping rubrics fixed systematically reverses decisions and collapses AUC, even though type-error rate stays 0%.
AI.motivation: Typed decision models return a choice over a predefined set of options, so every output is schema-conformant by construction. However, conformance does not ensure the model interprets option names as intended. The paper investigates whether output correctness guarantees are decoupled from semantic interpretation of option names, and whether this failure mode is systematic.
AI.method: Controlled renaming experiment on Jev and two Jev-like open-weight models. Each option has a name and a rubric defining its meaning; only the assignment of option names to rubrics is changed, holding question, state, rubric wording, and the option-name set constant. Evaluated on 1200 workflow decisions with task-specific rubrics, across 4 predicates, varying the number of options. Compared polarized names (0/1 vs no/yes), neutral names, and random character strings.  Also tested a second model family using mean-pooling over the full option span, and a hosted model with a test-retest floor.
AI.result: Renaming options from 0/1 to no/yes changes 70.4 more answers per hundred (95% CI: [67.6, 73.1]) and shifts AUC from .94 to .23, a systematic reversal in decision ranking rather than mere uncertainty. Effect is small under neutral names, holds across all 4 predicates (at least 7.4x larger than the neutral control), and strengthens with more options. A mean-pooling model family flips 4.1x less often. Hosted model: AUC .8146 to .5806, with 24x the answer flips of its test-retest floor. Random character strings restore the neutral-control regime without reducing accuracy. Type-error rate remains 0% throughout.
AI.conclusion: The failure depends on the semantic polarity of option names, not on renaming per se. Type-conformance and semantic interpretability are decoupled: a model can maintain 0% type-error rate while decision accuracy degrades substantially. Read-out geometry (option-span pooling) modulates susceptibility. This exposes a blind spot in typed decision-model evaluation.

title: MATE: Multi-Agent Virtual Teleoperation Platform for Humanoid Collaboration Data Collection
summary: Humanoid robots require diverse embodied experiences to acquire complex loco-manipulation and collaborative skills. However, existing humanoid data pipelines primarily focus on individual agents, while physical multi-robot collaboration remains difficult to scale due to costly hardware, dedicated spaces, and repeated resets. In this work, we introduce MATE, a Multi-Agent virtual TEleoperation platform for humanoid collaboration data collection that enables multiple geographically distributed operators to simultaneously control whole-body humanoids in a shared physics-based environment. MATE removes the need for multiple physical robots and co-located operation while preserving physically coupled interactions among humanoids, objects, and environments. Using MATE, we construct a multi-humanoid collaboration dataset comprising 24.1 hours of coordinated behavior across 2,500 joint episodes and five long-horizon tasks, including object handover, relay delivery, environment interaction, and cooperative transport. To improve learning from these interaction-rich demonstrations, we introduce EAIS, an Execution-Aligned Interaction Sampling strategy that computes sampling signals within an execution-aligned prefix and prioritizes task-progressing and interaction-critical behaviors. We evaluate MATE with representative imitation learning and vision-language-action policies across diverse collaboration tasks. Experiments demonstrate efficient data collection, effective policy learning, and zero-shot transfer from virtual demonstrations to a physical humanoid without real-world fine-tuning. Project page: https://yerik-yu.github.io/MATE/

AI.tldr: MATE is a multi-agent virtual teleoperation platform that lets geographically distributed operators control whole-body humanoids in a shared physics-based environment to collect multi-robot collaboration data, and EAIS is an execution-aligned interaction sampling strategy for learning from these demonstrations. It yields a 24.1-hour, 2,500-episode, five-task multi-humanoid collaboration dataset and enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots need diverse embodied experience to acquire complex loco-manipulation and collaborative skills, but existing humanoid data pipelines target individual agents. Physical multi-robot collaboration is hard to scale owing to costly hardware, dedicated spaces, and repeated resets.
AI.method: MATE: a multi-agent virtual teleoperation platform enabling multiple geographically distributed operators to simultaneously control whole-body humanoids in a shared physics-based environment, preserving physically coupled interactions among humanoids, objects, and environments while eliminating the need for multiple physical robots and co-located operation. EAIS: an Execution-Aligned Interaction Sampling strategy that computes sampling signals within an execution-aligned prefix and prioritizes task-progressing and interaction-critical behaviors.
AI.result: A multi-humanoid collaboration dataset of 24.1 hours of coordinated behavior across 2,500 joint episodes and five long-horizon tasks (object handover, relay delivery, environment interaction, cooperative transport). Evaluation with representative imitation learning and vision-language-action (VLA) policies shows efficient data collection, effective policy learning, and zero-shot transfer from virtual demonstrations to a physical humanoid without real-world fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: MATE provides a scalable virtual route to collecting physically coupled multi-humanoid collaboration data, and combined with EAIS it supports effective policy learning and direct sim-to-real deployment, offering a practical pipeline for humanoid collaborative skill acquisition.

title: Grow the Harness, Not the Context: From Strategy-Free Scaffolds to Reusable Specialist Agents
