summary: Large language model (LLM) agents often handle streams of related tasks, yet standard harnesses repeatedly ask the model to reconstruct the same control decisions inside each task's context. We study whether task feedback can instead turn recurring control into reusable executable code, while reserving LLM calls for task-specific semantic reasoning. We introduce Growing Harness, a failure-guided training paradigm that learns the agent harness itself from a strategy-free scaffold that exposes fixed model and tool interfaces but encodes no task-solving controller. Function-level execution traces localize each failure to a bounded code surface, an optimizer repairs a window of failures jointly, and a success-first held-out gate rolls back repair sequences that harm prior capability. Accepted edits accumulate in one shared harness, allowing its control structure to emerge from task feedback. Across BrowseComp-Plus and WebArena-Verified with three deployment models from 4B to 120B parameters, Growing Harness achieves the highest mean success in five of six benchmark-model settings and trails the best mean by 0.7 pp. in the sixth. Relative to a Tool-Calling agent, it reduces LLM calls by 76.0-91.8% and deployed-agent inference cost by 74.4-98.6%. On WebArena-Verified, its success remains 44.7-45.3% across model scales, whereas Tool-Calling falls to 6.7% with the 4B model. Ablations show that trace-local edits, joint repair, and gate-based rollback each improve final success. These results show that persistent program growth can move recurring control out of model context and into low-cost code, yielding reusable specialist agents that remain effective with smaller deployment models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Growing Harness, a failure-guided paradigm that learns an agent's control logic as reusable executable code from a strategy-free scaffold, cutting LLM calls and cost while maintaining success across model scales.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM agent harnesses repeatedly ask the model to reconstruct identical control decisions within each task context, which bloats context and wastes expensive LLM calls on recurring control logic rather than task-specific reasoning.
AI.method: Starting from a strategy-free scaffold exposing fixed model/tool interfaces but no controller, the method uses function-level execution traces to localize failures to bounded code regions. An optimizer jointly repairs a window of failures, and a success-first held-out gate rolls back repairs that degrade prior capability. Accepted edits accumulate in one shared harness so control structure emerges from task feedback.
AI.result: On BrowseComp-Plus and WebArena-Verified across three models (4B-120B), Growing Harness attains the highest mean success in five of six settings and trails the best by 0.7 pp in the sixth. It reduces LLM calls by 76.0-91.8% and inference cost by 74.4-98.6% vs. Tool-Calling. On WebArena-Verified it holds 44.7-45.3% success across scales, while Tool-Calling drops to 6.7% at 4B. Ablations confirm benefits of trace-local edits, joint repair, and gate-based rollback.
AI.conclusion: Persistent program growth can migrate recurring control from model context into low-cost code, producing reusable specialist agents that remain effective even with smaller deployment models.

title: Learning Air-Ground Motion Control with Temporal Mode Switching and Cross-Terrain Tracking
summary: Passive-wheeled terrestrial-aerial bimodal vehicles (TABVs) combine aerial mobility with energy-efficient ground locomotion. However, reliable air-ground mode switching under limited onboard perception and robust ground trajectory tracking across diverse terrains remain challenging when targeting real-world applications. In this work, we propose a learning-based air-ground motion control framework for passive-wheeled TABVs: 1) a learned mode selector for autonomous air-ground motion mode switching. The selector uses historical single-point time-of-flight (ToF) measurements and robot states together with future reference information to determine the active locomotion mode. 2) a reinforcement learning control policy for trajectory tracking. The policy combines proprioceptive observations with future reference information to anticipate trajectory changes. For ground locomotion, multi-terrain training and dynamics randomization enable robust tracking across different terrains. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate reliable air-ground switching under limited perception and accurate ground tracking across diverse terrain conditions. The learned selector outperforms a rule-based mode selector in challenging transitions, while the ground controller achieves lower position RMSE than PID across all tested conditions and maintains decent tracking where NMPC fails. With these capabilities integrated, the system tracks a 101m air-ground trajectory through multiple autonomous mode transitions with a position RMSE of 0.08m.

AI.tldr: A learning-based control framework for passive-wheeled terrestrial-aerial bimodal vehicles enables autonomous air-ground switching via a learned mode selector and RL trajectory tracking, achieving 0.08m RMSE over a 101m trajectory with multiple transitions.
AI.motivation: Passive-wheeled TABVs combine aerial mobility with energy-efficient ground locomotion, but reliable air-ground mode switching under limited onboard perception and robust ground tracking across diverse terrains remain challenging for real-world deployment.
AI.method: The framework has two components: (1) a learned mode selector that uses historical single-point ToF measurements, robot states, and future reference information to autonomously decide the active locomotion mode; and (2) a reinforcement learning control policy for trajectory tracking that fuses proprioceptive observations with future reference information to anticipate trajectory changes. Ground locomotion robustness is achieved through multi-terrain training and dynamics randomization.
AI.result: Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate reliable air-ground switching under limited perception and accurate ground tracking across diverse terrains. The learned selector outperforms a rule-based selector in challenging transitions. The ground controller attains lower position RMSE than PID in all tested conditions and maintains decent tracking where NMPC fails. The integrated system tracks a 101m air-ground trajectory with multiple autonomous mode transitions at 0.08m position RMSE.
AI.conclusion: The proposed learning-based framework delivers reliable mode switching and precise ground tracking for passive-wheeled TABVs, outperforming rule-based switching, PID, and NMPC baselines, validating its potential for real-world air-ground applications.

title: SWE-Serve: Benchmarking Agentic Engineering For Production Inference Serving
summary: We introduce SWE-Serve, a benchmark for evaluating agents on production inference engineering tasks. Implementing an inference feature can require coordinating multiple changes across the serving stack, including model support, runtime execution, and public APIs. Existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of production inference engineering: repository-level software engineering benchmarks do not target inference, while general terminal-agent benchmarks include only a few inference tasks. Dedicated inference benchmarks, meanwhile, focus primarily on isolated kernel generation or performance optimization rather than repository-scale production feature implementation. SWE-Serve provides 53 repository-grounded tasks derived from recent production changes to SGLang, spanning six inference engineering families. Each task executes on either CPU or a single GPU (H100) and is evaluated with hidden functional and regression tests, including, where applicable, end-to-end (E2E) serving tests and calibrated performance gates. Executable no-op and oracle controls, adversarial verifier review, and closed-book execution support task validity and evaluation integrity. Across 11 models and 31 model-effort configurations, the best-performing configuration achieves 75% mean pass@1. SWE-Serve exposes a substantial gap between completing tasks locally and achieving production correctness. On 19 tasks with end-to-end coverage, model-serving E2E tests reject roughly one-third of patches that pass every other test (45.9% under the verifier versus 69.4% with E2E tests excluded from scoring), with pass rate increasing for each model's best-performing configuration. By making the production correctness gap directly measurable, SWE-Serve enables the field to track whether future agents move beyond completing tasks locally to achieving production correctness.

AI.tldr: SWE-Serve is a benchmark of 53 repository-grounded production inference engineering tasks derived from recent SGLang changes, evaluated with hidden functional, regression, E2E serving tests and calibrated performance gates, revealing a substantial gap between local task completion and production correctness.
AI.motivation: Implementing an inference feature requires coordinating changes across the serving stack (model support, runtime execution, public APIs). Existing benchmarks cover this poorly: repository-level SWE benchmarks do not target inference, terminal-agent benchmarks include few inference tasks, and dedicated inference benchmarks focus on isolated kernel generation or performance optimization rather than repository-scale production feature implementation.
AI.method: The benchmark provides 53 repository-grounded tasks derived from recent production changes to SGLang, spanning six inference engineering families. Each task runs on either CPU or a single H100 GPU and is scored with hidden functional and regression tests, including E2E serving tests and calibrated performance gates where applicable. Validity and evaluation integrity are supported by executable no-op and oracle controls, adversarial verifier review, and closed-book execution. Evaluation spans 11 models and 31 model-effort configurations.
AI.result: The best configuration reaches 75% mean pass@1. On the 19 tasks with E2E coverage, model-serving E2E tests reject roughly one-third of patches that pass all other tests (45.9% under the verifier versus 69.4% with E2E tests excluded from scoring), with pass rates increasing for each model's best-performing configuration.
AI.conclusion: SWE-Serve exposes a substantial gap between completing tasks locally and achieving production correctness. By making this gap directly measurable, it enables the field to track whether future agents move beyond local task completion toward production correctness.

title: Beyond End-Task Success: How to Audit Visual Experience Retrieval in Robotics
comment: Accepted to the IROS 2026 Workshop on Embodied Neuro-Symbolic AI for Reliable and Safe Robotics (ReS AI)
summary: Robots that store past experiences must select which one to reuse in a new scene. Most systems select by visual similarity, and most evaluations report only the success of the selected experience. That number does not show whether the selection was good: a rule can score well by repeatedly using one broadly transferable experience, or poorly because its preferred experience is weak. Since robots increasingly adapt by reuse rather than retraining, a score that describes the library rather than the rule misleads what the field builds next. We contribute an audit methodology: execute every stored experience in every query scene, over two manipulation tasks, three reuse mechanisms, and libraries of $K=3$, $10$, and $50$. Because every alternative's outcome is known, a score can be traced to per-scene selection or to library quality. The audited rules select by nearest-neighbor distance in five visual embeddings, from raw pixels to CLIP. (1) One fixed experience, chosen with hindsight, captures 30-58% of the gap between random selection and an oracle; per-scene selection competes for the remaining 0.07-0.15 in success rate. (2) At $K\ge10$, visual rules concentrate on one experience 1.5-3 times more than the oracle does, and their scores then follow that experience's quality. (3) Wherever a rule differs significantly from a shuffle that keeps its selection rates but pairs them with scenes at random, the rule is worse, for every learned image policy. (4) Visual distance predicts well whether a given pair will succeed (AUROC up to 0.96), yet ranks the candidates within one scene no better than chance for four of five embeddings at $K=50$ (AUROC 0.45-0.52). Exhaustive execution is usually infeasible, so the audit reduces to two cheap reports any study can give: the distribution of selected experiences, and the success of the best single experience in hindsight.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an audit methodology that exhaustively executes every stored experience in every query scene to disentangle whether a reuse rule's success stems from good per-scene selection or merely from a broadly transferable experience in the library.
AI.motivation: Robot reuse systems typically select past experiences by visual similarity, and evaluations report only the success of the selected experience. Such a single number cannot distinguish a good selection rule from a rule that scores well by repeatedly reusing one broadly transferable experience, or poorly because its preferred experience is weak. As robots increasingly adapt by reuse rather than retraining, a score describing the library rather than the rule misleads the field.
AI.method: The audit executes every stored experience in every query scene across two manipulation tasks, three reuse mechanisms, and libraries of K=3, 10, and 50. Because every alternative's outcome is known, scores can be traced to per-scene selection or to library quality. Audited rules select by nearest-neighbor distance in five visual embeddings, from raw pixels to CLIP. The design also includes comparisons against a shuffle that preserves selection rates but randomizes scene pairing.
AI.result: (1) One fixed experience, chosen with hindsight, captures 30-58% of the gap between random selection and an oracle, with per-scene selection competing for the remaining 0.07-0.15 in success rate. (2) At K>=10, visual rules concentrate on one experience 1.5-3 times more than the oracle, and scores then follow that experience's quality. (3) Wherever a rule differs significantly from the rate-preserving shuffle, the rule is worse, for every learned image policy. (4) Visual distance predicts pairwise success well (AUROC up to 0.96), yet ranks candidates within a scene no better than chance for four of five embeddings at K=50 (AUROC 0.45-0.52).
AI.conclusion: Exhaustive execution is usually infeasible, so the audit reduces to two cheap reports any study can give: the distribution of selected experiences and the success of the best single experience in hindsight. These two reports suffice to expose whether reported success reflects the selection rule or the library.

title: CliffCompaction: Cost-Efficient Compaction for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
summary: Agents often work on complex problems that require millions of tokens of context, which necessitates compacting across sessions due to limited context windows. We develop CliffCompaction, an autocompaction technique that reduces cost by up to 50% under a bounded context while maintaining or improving performance on Terminal-Bench and achieving new levels of efficiency for test-time scaling and state-of-the-art results on KernelBench. The per-rollout savings of CliffCompaction make the performance--cost trade-off of test-time scaling more efficient, adding over 10 percentage points on Terminal-Bench for less than the cost of two full-context runs. Under parallel test-time scaling, CliffCompaction lets Kimi K2.6 match Opus 4.7, and exceed Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.3 Codex at lower cost. The key to CliffCompaction's effectiveness is that it keeps compacted information faithful by only truncating or dropping content, never rephrasing or rewriting it. We never compact a compaction---each pass operates only on original content, and prior compacted output is discarded, preventing context drift from accumulating. These properties sustain continual learning over sessions exceeding a million tokens: on KernelBench, CliffCompaction reaches CUDA kernel speedups of $2.23\times$ after 200 steps and $3.58\times$ after 400 steps, surpassing specialized search algorithms and trained agents despite being a general-purpose compaction technique. We open-source a scaffold-agnostic API-proxy implementation of CliffCompaction usable with Claude Code, Codex and other harnesses.

AI.tldr: CliffCompaction is an autocompaction technique for long-horizon agents that reduces cost by up to 50% under a bounded context while maintaining or improving performance, achieved by lossless (truncate/drop-only) compaction of original content without recompacting prior summaries.
AI.motivation: Agents solving complex problems require millions of tokens of context, but limited context windows force compaction across sessions. Existing compaction risks context drift and cost inefficiency during test-time scaling, so a faithful, cheap compaction method is needed.
AI.method: CliffCompaction keeps compacted information faithful by only truncating or dropping content, never rephrasing or rewriting. It never compacts a compaction: each pass operates only on original content, and prior compacted output is discarded, preventing accumulation of context drift. It is implemented as a scaffold-agnostic API-proxy usable with Claude Code, Codex, and other harnesses.
AI.result: Up to 50% cost reduction under bounded context while maintaining or improving Terminal-Bench performance; adds over 10 percentage points on Terminal-Bench for less than the cost of two full-context runs; under parallel test-time scaling Kimi K2.6 matches Opus 4.7 and exceeds Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.3 Codex at lower cost; on KernelBench reaches CUDA kernel speedups of 2.23x after 200 steps and 3.58x after 400 steps, surpassing specialized search algorithms and trained agents.
AI.conclusion: Faithful, non-recursive compaction sustains continual learning over sessions exceeding a million tokens, making test-time scaling more cost-efficient and delivering state-of-the-art efficiency, with an open-source API-proxy implementation released.

title: Wheel-loader V-Cycle Automation with Deep Koopman MPC
summary: The repeated forward-reverse maneuvers performed by wheel loaders during earthmoving operations make them well suited for automation. However, the nonlinear dynamics of articulated vehicles and complex vehicle-terrain interactions limit the effectiveness of conventional model-based approaches. This paper presents a hierarchical framework that combines long-horizon geometric planning with data-driven predictive control for autonomous wheel-loader operation. A reduced-order articulated kinematic model is used to generate the maneuver geometry, where the forward and reverse trajectories are jointly optimized through a shared intermediate state. To capture the vehicle dynamics, two data-driven deep bilinear Koopman models are learned for the forward and reverse motions using data generated from high-fidelity simulations in Algoryx Dynamics. The learned Koopman representations are subsequently incorporated into a computationally efficient model predictive control (MPC) formulation for trajectory tracking. The resulting controller operates in real time within a 50-ms execution loop. High-fidelity simulation results demonstrate that the proposed end-to-end framework enables accurate and computationally efficient execution of wheel-loader V-cycle maneuvers, providing a promising approach toward autonomous operation of articulated heavy-duty machinery.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hierarchical framework combining long-horizon geometric planning with data-driven predictive control for autonomous wheel-loader operation. Two deep bilinear Koopman models learned from high-fidelity simulation data capture forward and reverse vehicle dynamics and are integrated into a real-time MPC for trajectory tracking, enabling accurate V-cycle maneuvers.
AI.motivation: Wheel loaders perform repeated forward-reverse maneuvers during earthmoving, making them suitable for automation, but nonlinear articulated-vehicle dynamics and complex vehicle-terrain interactions degrade conventional model-based methods.
AI.method: A hierarchical framework: (1) a reduced-order articulated kinematic model generates maneuver geometry, jointly optimizing forward and reverse trajectories through a shared intermediate state; (2) two data-driven deep bilinear Koopman models are learned from high-fidelity Algoryx Dynamics simulations for forward and reverse motions; (3) the Koopman representations feed a computationally efficient MPC formulation for trajectory tracking, running in a 50-ms real-time loop.
AI.result: High-fidelity simulations show the end-to-end framework achieves accurate and computationally efficient execution of wheel-loader V-cycle maneuvers in real time.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical planning-plus-Koopman-MPC approach offers a promising path toward autonomous operation of articulated heavy-duty machinery.

title: NavSafe-$\infty$: Benchmarking Closed-Loop Driving Safety in Photorealistic Environments
summary: End-to-end (E2E) driving policies have progressed rapidly on open-loop (OL) benchmarks, yet OL evaluation cannot reveal whether a policy withstands compounding errors, recovers from failures, or interacts safely with surrounding actors. We introduce NavSafe-$\infty$, a photorealistic closed-loop (CL) benchmark of 280 scenarios spanning 28 event types, each with success and failure criteria defined within a structured traffic-safety taxonomy, which yields category-level capability scores for Traffic Crashes, Vulnerable Road User Crashes, Traffic Violations, and Traffic Incidents. Evaluating 20 E2E policies, we find that OL gains do not reliably transfer to CL safety. Analyzing two common remedies further shows that passive demonstration perturbation helps mainly when CL rollouts stay near its perturbed training states, and that OL reinforcement-learning fine-tuning exhibits reward hacking by trading safety margin for ego progress, which CL feedback amplifies into compounding safety-critical errors. Together, these results demonstrate the blind spot of OL benchmarks indicating CL safety success. The benchmark and an extensible toolbox for customizable event curation and policy diagnosis will be open-sourced and maintained to facilitate future research.

AI.tldr: NavSafe-∞, a photorealistic closed-loop benchmark of 280 scenarios across 28 event types, reveals that open-loop gains of 20 E2E driving policies do not reliably transfer to closed-loop safety, and that common remedies (demonstration perturbation, OL RL fine-tuning) fail or induce reward hacking.
AI.motivation: Open-loop (OL) benchmarks for end-to-end driving policies cannot reveal whether a policy withstands compounding errors, recovers from failures, or interacts safely with surrounding actors, leaving a blind spot regarding real closed-loop safety.
AI.method: Introduce NavSafe-∞, a photorealistic closed-loop (CL) benchmark of 280 scenarios spanning 28 event types, each with success and failure criteria defined within a structured traffic-safety taxonomy, yielding category-level capability scores across Traffic Crashes, Vulnerable Road User Crashes, Traffic Violations, and Traffic Incidents. Evaluate 20 E2E policies and analyze two common remedies.
AI.result: OL gains do not reliably transfer to CL safety. Passive demonstration perturbation helps mainly when CL rollouts stay near its perturbed training states; OL reinforcement-learning fine-tuning exhibits reward hacking by trading safety margin for ego progress, which CL feedback amplifies into compounding safety-critical errors.
AI.conclusion: These results demonstrate the blind spot of OL benchmarks in indicating CL safety success. The benchmark and an extensible toolbox for customizable event curation and policy diagnosis will be open-sourced to facilitate future research.

title: Imperfection for Precision: Upcycling Imperfect Data for High-Precision Robotic Manipulation
summary: Training vision-language-action (VLA) models for high-precision manipulation typically requires task-specific, high-quality data (e.g., teleoperation), which is slow and expensive to collect. To reduce this burden without compromising manipulation precision, we propose $\varepsilon$4P (Imperfection for Precision), a simple yet effective method that "upcycles" two otherwise discarded data sources: (1) low-precision data from the target task and (2) high-precision data from mismatched tasks. Rather than naively mixing these imperfect data sources throughout co-training, $\varepsilon$4P controls where each source contributes along the flow-matching trajectory. Specifically, low-precision, target-task data is used at high noise to preserve high-level task context and high-precision, task-mismatched data is used at low noise to transfer low-level action precision. Through real-robot experiments on both sub-millimeter, high-precision tasks and coarse-grained tasks, we demonstrate that the proposed method (1) effectively leverages additional imperfect data to improve policy performance by up to 31.7 percentage points, and (2) can replace an equal amount of task-specific, high-quality data with an average performance drop of only 4.2 percentage points. Overall, $\varepsilon$4P points toward a scalable paradigm for high-precision manipulation, in which heterogeneous, imperfect data can be systematically repurposed to reduce reliance on costly task-specific, high-quality data. More details are available at https://varepsilon4p.github.io/.

AI.tldr: ε4P is a method that "upcycles" discarded imperfect data sources (low-precision target-task data and high-precision mismatched-task data) by controlling where each contributes along the flow-matching trajectory, improving high-precision manipulation VLA policies while reducing reliance on costly task-specific high-quality data.

The goal is to reduce this data-collection burden without sacrificing manipulation precision by repurposing two otherwise discarded data sources.
AI.method: ε4P (Imperfection for Precision) upcycles two imperfect data sources: (1) low-precision data from the target task and (2) high-precision data from mismatched tasks. Instead of naively mixing these sources throughout co-training, it controls where each source contributes along the flow-matching trajectory: low-precision target-task data is used at high noise to preserve high-level task context, while high-precision task-mismatched data is used at low noise to transfer low-level action precision.
AI.result: Real-robot experiments on sub-millimeter, high-precision tasks and coarse-grained tasks show that ε4P (1) effectively leverages additional imperfect data to improve policy performance by up to 31.7 percentage points, and (2) can replace an equal amount of task-specific high-quality data with an average performance drop of only 4.2 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: ε4P points toward a scalable paradigm for high-precision manipulation in which heterogeneous, imperfect data can be systematically repurposed to reduce reliance on costly task-specific, high-quality data.

title: Underwater Navigation in Unsteady Flows Using Measurement Histories from a Single Sensing Unit
comment: This paper is under review at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
summary: Spatial flow measurements support underwater navigation, but distributed sensing is constrained by robot size and sensor layout. We use a causal observer to estimate current lateral velocities from a finite history of measurements collected by a single sensing unit, supplying the inputs of a fixed navigation controller. In two-dimensional wake simulations with access to body-frame ambient velocity, this virtual sensing interface reduces simultaneous flow sampling from three points to the robot center. Trained only in a circular-cylinder wake at Re = 100, the flow-history observer achieves 84.4% and 80.6% success at held-out Re = 205 and 240 without retraining. These rates are 7.4 and 4.6 percentage points below direct spatial sensing and more than 30 points above a matched current-only observer. Past flow remains beneficial when past goal and yaw information is available. Across obstacle geometries, performance remains close to direct sensing in square-prism wakes but declines in triangular-prism wakes. Component replacement identifies the lateral velocity difference as control-relevant, while controlled perturbations reveal sensitivity to error persistence. The results demonstrate the closed-loop utility of single-point flow histories under the assumed observation model.

AI.tldr: A causal flow-history observer enables a single-point sensing unit to estimate lateral current velocities and drive a fixed navigation controller, reducing three-point spatial sampling to the robot center and retaining most of the direct-sensing success across held-out Reynolds numbers and geometries.
AI.motivation: Spatial flow measurements support underwater navigation, but distributed sensing is constrained by robot size and sensor layout. The goal is to replace spatially distributed flow sampling with a single sensing unit by exploiting temporal flow history.
AI.method: A causal observer estimates current lateral velocities from a finite history of measurements taken by a single sensing unit, supplying inputs to a fixed navigation controller. Evaluated in two-dimensional wake simulations with body-frame ambient velocity access, trained only in a circular-cylinder wake at Re = 100 and tested without retraining at Re = 205 and 240, plus square- and triangular-prism wakes. Component replacement and controlled perturbation analyses probe control-relevant inputs and error persistence.
AI.result: The observer reduces simultaneous flow sampling from three points to the robot center, achieving 84.4% and 80.6% success at held-out Re = 205 and 240, 7.4 and 4.6 percentage points below direct spatial sensing and over 30 points above a matched current-only observer. Past flow remains beneficial with past goal and yaw information. Performance is near direct sensing in square-prism wakes but declines in triangular-prism wakes. Lateral velocity difference is identified as control-relevant, and sensitivity to error persistence is revealed.
AI.conclusion: Single-point flow histories provide closed-loop navigational utility under the assumed observation model, generalizing across Reynolds numbers and some geometries without retraining, though performance degrades for triangular-prism wakes and is sensitive to error persistence.

title: TM-APR: Thermal Temporal-Memory Localization via Analytic Online Adaptation
summary: Thermal Visual Place Recognition (Thermal VPR) maps camera observations to metric poses within a mapped environment, serving as a prerequisite for autonomous navigation. However, thermal VPR suffers from severe environmental dependence, heavy online retraining overheads, and an inability to model dynamic non-linear shifts, causing existing frameworks to fail during online deployment. To achieve robust domain-invariant place recognition, we bridge Analytic Class-Incremental Learning (ACIL) with domain-invariant VPR for the first time, revealing that its gradient-free matrix updates construct a surprisingly strong baseline that outperforms conventional fine-tuning. Nevertheless, standard ACIL exhibits a critical vulnerability to extreme non-linear thermal fluctuations due to its structural linear assumptions. To overcome this limitation, we exploit a novel algebraic equivalence between ACIL and modern control theory, proposing a framework which embeds Unscented propagation (U-ACIL), Gaussian Mixture partitioning (GMM-ACIL), and minimax $H_\infty$ optimization ($H_\infty$-ACIL) directly into the update loop. Our formulation guarantees exact closed-form matrix updates within $\mathcal{O}(1)$ computational complexity, bypassing backpropagation to ensure that the online update latency ($Δt_{\mathrm{learn}}$) remains strictly bounded below the sensor acquisition interval ($Δt_{\mathrm{acquire}}$), thereby eliminating trajectory jumps in real-time SLAM pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper connects Analytic Class-Incremental Learning (ACIL) with domain-invariant Thermal Visual Place Recognition, showing ACIL's gradient-free matrix updates outperform fine-tuning but fail under extreme non-linear thermal shifts; the proposed control-theory-based framework (U-ACIL, GMM-ACIL, H∞-ACIL) achieves closed-form O(1) updates with bounded latency for real-time SLAM.
AI.motivation: Thermal VPR is essential for autonomous navigation but suffers from severe environmental dependence, heavy online retraining overheads, and an inability to model dynamic non-linear shifts, causing existing frameworks to fail during online deployment. Robust domain-invariant place recognition is therefore needed.
AI.method: The authors bridge Analytic Class-Incremental Learning (ACIL) with domain-invariant VPR for the first time, leveraging its gradient-free matrix updates as a strong baseline. To address ACIL's vulnerability to extreme non-linear thermal fluctuations due to linear structural assumptions, they exploit a novel algebraic equivalence between ACIL and modern control theory, embedding Unscented propagation (U-ACIL), Gaussian Mixture partitioning (GMM-ACIL), and minimax H∞ optimization (H∞-ACIL) directly into the update loop. The formulation guarantees exact closed-form matrix updates within O(1) computational complexity, bypassing backpropagation.
AI.result: ACIL's gradient-free matrix updates construct a surprisingly strong baseline that outperforms conventional fine-tuning. The proposed framework ensures online update latency (Δt_learn) remains strictly bounded below the sensor acquisition interval (Δt_acquire), eliminating trajectory jumps in real-time SLAM pipelines.
AI.conclusion: By unifying ACIL with control-theoretic techniques (Unscented propagation, Gaussian Mixture partitioning, H∞ optimization), the paper achieves robust domain-invariant Thermal VPR with O(1) closed-form updates and bounded latency, enabling reliable real-time online deployment in SLAM pipelines.

title: DreamStream: Towards Policy-Oriented Generative Simulation for End-to-End Driving
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026. Project page: https://vail-ucla.github.io/DreamStream/
summary: Faithfully evaluating end-to-end driving policies in simulation requires observations that are not merely photo-realistic, but preserve the scene features a policy relies on to make decisions. Existing platforms, however, exhibit a sim-to-real visual gap that corrupts policy perception, undermining their ability to assess a policy's closed-loop decision-making. To this end, we propose DreamStream, a generative, closed-loop simulator that achieves policy-oriented fidelity using a simulator-grounded autoregressive video model. Our video model is distilled from a large pretrained video model via traffic layout guidance, varying visual appearance while preserving policy-relevant features such as scenario layout and the temporal consistency of dynamic objects. We further observe that perceptual metrics like FID misrank how well these features are preserved. To tackle this, we introduce FD$π$, a new multi-representation metric that measures the sim-to-real gap as the Fréchet distance over scene-context features from public E2E policies. Under FD$π$, DreamStream improves over the strongest prior closed-loop simulator by $1.6\times$ on nuScenes and $4.7\times$ on NAVSIM, and induces the least perturbation to policy's perceptual observability. Based on DreamStream, we construct Navhard-CL benchmark, which turns non-reactive real-world benchmark NAVSIM into interactive testing environments with adversarial driving behaviors and weather variations. This benchmark exposes many failure modes of driving policies, such as scorer bias and lack of recovery behaviors, that prior closed-loop benchmarks overlook. Code and data are available at https://github.com/VAIL-UCLA/DreamStream.

AI.tldr: DreamStream is a generative, closed-loop driving simulator built on a simulator-grounded autoregressive video model that preserves policy-relevant scene features, and introduces FD$\pi$, a new multi-representation sim-to-real gap metric; it improves over prior closed-loop simulators by 1.6$\times$ (nuScenes) and 4.7$\times$ (NAVSIM) under FD$\pi$, and underpins the Navhard-CL benchmark.
AI.motivation: Faithful evaluation of end-to-end (E2E) driving policies in simulation requires observations that preserve the scene features policies rely on for decisions, not just photorealism. Existing platforms suffer a sim-to-real visual gap that corrupts policy perception and undermines assessment of closed-loop decision-making. Additionally, common perceptual metrics like FID misrank how well policy-relevant features are preserved.
AI.method: DreamStream: a generative, closed-loop simulator using a simulator-grounded autoregressive video model distilled from a large pretrained video model via traffic layout guidance, varying visual appearance while preserving policy-relevant features (scenario layout, temporal consistency of dynamic objects). FD$\pi$: a multi-representation metric measuring the sim-to-real gap as the Fréchet distance over scene-context features from public E2E policies. Navhard-CL: a benchmark converting non-reactive real-world NAVSIM into interactive testing environments with adversarial driving behaviors and weather variations.
AI.result: Under FD$\pi$, DreamStream improves over the strongest prior closed-loop simulator by 1.6$\times$ on nuScenes and 4.7$\times$ on NAVSIM, and induces the least perturbation to policy perceptual observability. Navhard-CL exposes failure modes of driving policies—such as scorer bias and lack of recovery behaviors—that prior closed-loop benchmarks overlook.
AI.conclusion: DreamStream achieves policy-oriented fidelity in closed-loop simulation via a distilled autoregressive video model, validated by the new FD$\pi$ metric, and enables the Navhard-CL benchmark that reveals overlooked policy failure modes. Code and data are available at https://github.com/VAIL-UCLA/DreamStream.

title: φ-RIE: From Photorealistic Reconstruction to Interactive Environments
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can reconstruct a captured scene photorealistically, but the resulting representation does not by itself support physical interaction. Robot simulation instead requires object-level change, \textit{i.e.}, objects must move independently, make contact, and reveal previously occluded surroundings. This gap arises because object appearance may remain entangled with the background, while hidden object geometry and occluded background content may be unobserved. To address this challenge, we present φ-RIE, a Gaussian-native pipeline that converts selected objects into movable simulator assets while preserving the remaining reconstruction. Our key observation is that asset construction and source removal should be coupled, \textit{i.e.}, one object identity should define the movable asset and the scene content to remove and complete. Accordingly, Scene Observation supplies shared evidence to Coupled Scene Construction, which creates registered assets and completed background Gaussians for simulator-driven rendering in an Interactive Environment. This coupling preserves unedited Gaussians while aligning visual and physical state. On 50 ScanNet++ scenes, evidence-based selection and registration retry increase matched F1 at 20\,mm from 0.336 to 0.383 at fixed retention. Further tests demonstrate asset executability, manipulation gains over a single-generator baseline, and the visual cost of conversion. Together, these results demonstrate that \name\ enables interactive scene conversion.

AI.tldr: The paper presents φ-RIE, a Gaussian-native pipeline that converts selected objects in a 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction into movable simulator assets while preserving and completing the remaining scene, enabling interactive physical simulation.
AI.motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting can reconstruct a scene photorealistically, but the resulting representation does not support physical interaction. Robot simulation requires object-level change: objects must move independently, make contact, and reveal previously occluded surroundings. This gap exists because object appearance may remain entangled with the background, and hidden object geometry plus occluded background content may be unobserved.
AI.method: φ-RIE is a Gaussian-native pipeline that couples asset construction and source removal under a single object identity. Scene Observation supplies shared evidence to Coupled Scene Construction, which produces registered assets and completed background Gaussians. These are then used for simulator-driven rendering in an Interactive Environment, preserving unedited Gaussians while aligning visual and physical state.
AI.result: On 50 ScanNet++ scenes, evidence-based selection and registration retry raise matched F1 at 20 mm from 0.336 to 0.383 at fixed retention. Further tests show asset executability, manipulation gains over a single-generator baseline, and the visual cost of conversion.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that φ-RIE enables interactive scene conversion, turning photorealistic 3DGS reconstructions into physically interactive simulator-ready environments.
